Fourth, a bar graph plots transpiration rates for different conditions — bright sun, shade, windy, still — so the highest and lowest values jump out at a glance.
Fifth, charts record experiments: the coloured‑flower activity with Petunia or balsam is captured in a table of time versus distance the dye travels, turning a hands‑on activity into analysable data.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to draw pictures of plants”) reveals confusion between decorative diagrams and process flow charts, indicating the student thinks charts are only for illustration, not for logical sequencing.
remember: What is the primary purpose of a flow chart in the chapter on transport in plants.
Why is a bar graph more suitable than a line graph for comparing transpiration rates at different humidity levels.
A student uses a pie chart to represent the proportion of macro‑nutrients (N, P, K) in a plant. Evaluate this choice.

cards.title: In science education, a model is a simplified representation of a system or…
cards.subject: Biology
cards.definition: In science education, a model is a simplified representation of a system or process that highlights essential features while omitting unnecessary details. For the transport of food and minerals in plants, models serve as conceptual tools to visualise pathways and mechanisms that cannot be directly observed. Three main types are used: physical models (e.g., straws or tubing to mimic xylem vessels and phloem sieve tubes), diagrammatic models (labelled drawings showing cohesion‑tension in xylem and pressure‑flow in phloem), and conceptual models (the pressure‑flow hypothesis and root‑pressure explanation). Physical models demonstrate continuous water columns and the effect of suction (transpiration pull) on water ascent. Diagrammatic models illustrate how solutes are loaded at sources (leaves) and unloaded at sinks (roots, fruits), creating pressure gradients that drive bulk flow. Conceptual models link root pressure to guttation and explain how active transport of ions into xylem generates positive pressure. All models are iterative: they are tested against experiments (such as coloured‑water uptake in balsam stems) and refined. They connect to prior knowledge of diffusion, osmosis, and transpiration, and they prepare students for more advanced representations like charts and digital presentations.
steps: Models are simplified representations that make the invisible transport of water and food in plants visible and understandable.
Here is why: first, models let us see processes that happen inside stems and roots where we cannot look directly.
Second, a physical model like a straw shows how a continuous water column moves upward when suction is applied at the top, mirroring the cohesion‑tension theory.
Third, a tubing model with sugar solution and a gentle pump demonstrates how pressure differences drive bulk flow in phloem, illustrating the pressure‑flow hypothesis.
Fourth, diagrammatic models on paper or board map the pathway from root hair to leaf, labelling cohesion, adhesion, and transpiration pull.
Fifth, conceptual models connect root pressure to guttation, explaining why droplets appear on leaf margins early in the morning.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “A model is an exact replica of the plant”) reveals the misconception that models must be perfect copies rather than purposeful simplifications.
remember: What is a scientific model in the context of plant transport.
Why is a drinking straw a good physical model for xylem vessels.

cards.title: A PowerPoint Presentation (PPT) in the context of Class 7 Biology Chapter 5 is…
cards.subject: Biology
cards.definition: A PowerPoint Presentation (PPT) in the context of Class 7 Biology Chapter 5 is a structured digital slideshow used to convey the concepts of transport of food and minerals in plants. It consists of a sequence of slides that combine text, labelled diagrams, photographs of plant specimens (e.g., Petunia, Balsam, Vinca, mustard, mango, neem), animations of diffusion and osmosis, and embedded video clips of laboratory experiments such as the coloured flower stem experiment. The PPT aligns with the CISCE curriculum by presenting the definitions of diffusion, osmosis, semipermeable membrane, root pressure, active transport, transpiration, and the structure and function of xylem and phloem. It also highlights the importance of macro‑ and micro‑nutrients, the presence or absence of conducting tissues in simple versus higher plants, and the experimental evidence from charts, models, and laboratory work. The PPT serves as a visual scaffold that links prior knowledge of cell structure (Class 6) to the current chapter and prepares students for later topics on plant physiology. It is not a substitute for hands‑on experiments but a complementary tool to reinforce conceptual understanding through visual representation.
steps: A well‑designed PPT turns the invisible movement of water, food, and minerals inside plants into a clear visual story that Class 7 students can follow step by step.
First, a PPT breaks each complex process into a discrete slide so students focus on one idea at a time.
Second, animations show dynamic events like water crossing a semipermeable membrane during osmosis, which static diagrams cannot.
Third, real photographs of Indian plants — Petunia, Balsam, Vinca, mustard, mango, neem — connect the lesson to the flora students see around them.
Fourth, embedded videos of the coloured flower stem experiment let the class watch the procedure without needing every group to set it up simultaneously.
Fifth, consistent colour coding (blue for xylem, orange for phloem) reinforces the structure‑function link across slides.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "to replace laboratory experiments entirely") reveals the misconception that digital tools can substitute for direct observation, ignoring the CISCE emphasis on practical work.
remember: What is the primary purpose of using a PPT when teaching Chapter 5: Transport of Food and Minerals in Plants.
Why is it important to include photographs of local plants such as Petunia, Balsam, and mango in the PPT.
Evaluate the statement: "Animations in a PPT are unnecessary because static diagrams can show osmosis equally well.".

cards.title: A physical change alters the form, appearance…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A physical change alters the form, appearance, or state of a substance without producing any new substance. The chemical composition remains identical; only physical properties such as shape, size, state (solid, liquid, gas), colour, or texture may change. These changes are usually reversible — for example, ice melting to water and freezing back to ice. A chemical change, in contrast, results in the formation of one or more new substances with different chemical compositions and properties. Indicators of a chemical change include a permanent colour change, evolution of heat or light, production of a gas (often seen as bubbles), formation of a precipitate, and a change in taste or odour. Chemical changes are generally irreversible under normal conditions. The key distinction lies in whether the identity of the substance changes: physical changes preserve the substance’s identity, while chemical changes create new substances. Understanding this difference helps classify everyday processes — tearing paper (physical) versus burning paper (chemical), dissolving salt in water (physical) versus rusting of iron (chemical). The chapter further explores specific indicators (state, colour, size, shape, heat, light, gas, taste) through experiments and apparatus assembly, using materials like paper, common salt, chalk, iron, sulphur, and copper to illustrate each type of change.
steps: Physical changes alter only the form or appearance of a substance without creating new substances, while chemical changes produce one or more new substances with different properties.
Here is why: first, in a physical change the particles of the substance remain the same; they may move farther apart (melting) or rearrange (breaking), but no new particles form.

Second, chemical changes involve breaking and forming of chemical bonds, resulting in new substances — for instance, when iron reacts with oxygen and moisture, rust (iron oxide) forms, which has properties unlike iron.
Third, observable signs such as colour change, gas evolution, heat or light emission, and taste change are reliable clues that a chemical reaction has taken place.
Consider a piece of chalk: crushing it into powder changes its size and shape — a physical change.
Heating it strongly drives off carbon dioxide, leaving calcium oxide — a chemical change because a new substance appears.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing (a) Burning of magnesium ribbon) reveals the misconception that any visible change like bright light indicates a physical change, confusing energy release with substance identity.
remember: Which of the following is a physical change? (a) Burning of magnesium ribbon (b) Dissolving sugar in water (c) Rusting of iron (d) Digestion of food.

cards.title: A physical change alters the form, state, size…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A physical change alters the form, state, size, shape or appearance of a substance without changing its chemical composition; no new substance is formed and the change is usually reversible (e.g., melting ice, tearing paper, dissolving common salt in water). A chemical change involves a chemical reaction that produces one or more new substances with different properties; it is often accompanied by observable indicators such as a permanent colour change, evolution of heat or light, formation of a gas, change in taste, or formation of a precipitate, and is generally irreversible (e.g., burning paper, rusting iron, cooking food). The key relationship is that physical changes affect only physical properties (state, shape, size) while chemical changes affect chemical identity. Indicators like evolution of gas, heat, light, colour change, or taste change help differentiate the two, but a single indicator alone is not conclusive; a combination of evidence confirms a chemical change. Reversibility is a useful guide but not absolute — some physical changes (e.g., breaking chalk) are not easily reversed, while some chemical changes can be reversed under specific conditions.
steps: The key to telling a physical change from a chemical change is to ask whether a new substance with different properties is formed.
First, physical changes only modify physical properties such as state, shape, size or appearance; the substance’s chemical identity stays the same.
Second, chemical changes create new substances with new chemical properties, often shown by permanent colour change, gas bubbles, heat or light release, or a change in taste.
Third, reversibility is a helpful clue: most physical changes can be undone (ice ↔ water), while chemical changes usually cannot (ash cannot become paper).
Fourth, some changes display both types — dissolving salt is physical, but if the solution is electrolysed, a chemical change occurs.
Fifth, relying on a single indicator can mislead; a colour change alone might be physical (mixing paints) or chemical (rusting).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any visible transformation like burning is physical because it looks dramatic, confusing energy release with chemical identity change.
remember: Which of the following is a physical change? A) Burning of paper B) Rusting of iron C) Melting of ice D) Cooking of an egg.
A student observes that when copper sulphate crystals are heated, they turn white and water vapour is released. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain your reasoning.
Evaluate the statement: “If a change produces heat, it must be a chemical change.” Provide two examples to support your evaluation.

cards.title: A change of state is a physical transformation in which a substance alters its…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A change of state is a physical transformation in which a substance alters its phase — solid, liquid, or gas — without forming new chemical substances. The key experimental evidence includes: (1) mass conservation — the mass before and after the change remains identical when measured in a closed system; (2) temperature constancy — during melting, freezing, boiling, or condensation at constant pressure, the temperature stays fixed at the melting or boiling point until the phase transition completes; (3) reversibility — the process can be reversed by adding or removing heat, returning the material to its original state. Experiments typically use ice, water, steam, iodine (sublimation), or wax to demonstrate these principles. The observations link directly to the particle model: particles gain or lose kinetic energy, changing arrangement and motion but not identity. Understanding these experiments builds the foundation for later study of latent heat and thermodynamic phase diagrams.
steps: Changes of state are physical changes that can be proved by experiments showing mass stays the same and temperature stays constant during the transition.
Here is why: first, mass conservation is observed when ice melts in a sealed bag — the bag’s mass before and after melting is identical, proving no matter is lost.
Second, a thermometer placed in melting ice reads 0 °C until all ice becomes water, showing temperature constancy while particles rearrange.
Third, boiling water in a flask with a delivery tube into a cooled condenser collects steam that condenses back to liquid; the collected water equals the original mass, confirming reversibility.
Fourth, sublimation of iodine crystals in a covered dish produces violet vapour that deposits as crystals on the cooler lid, again with no mass change.

Consider a Class 7 student heating a measured 50 g ice cube in a beaker on a tripod: they record the mass, watch the temperature hold at 0 °C, then weigh the resulting water — it is still 50 g. Repeating with 100 g…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “colour change proves it is physical”) reveals the misconception that any visible alteration signals a physical change, confusing physical appearance with chemical identity.
remember: What is the main observation that confirms a change of state is a physical change and not a chemical change.
Why does the temperature of melting ice stay at 0 °C until all ice has melted.
A student places 80 g of ice at 0 °C in a sealed insulated container and supplies heat until all ice….

cards.title: A colour change is an observable alteration in the hue, intensity…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A colour change is an observable alteration in the hue, intensity, or transparency of a substance. In the context of physical and chemical changes, it serves as a key indicator: a new colour typically signals the formation of one or more new substances, which is the hallmark of a chemical change. For example, when blue copper(II) sulphate crystals are heated, they lose water and turn white; the colour shift from blue to white accompanies the breakdown of the hydrated crystal into anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, a chemical transformation. Conversely, a physical change such as dissolving potassium permanganate in water produces a purple solution, but the purple colour originates from the same permanganate ions – no new substance forms, so the change is physical. Colour changes can also arise from physical processes like mixing two coloured solutions (e.g., blue ink + yellow ink = green) where the resulting colour is a simple additive effect without chemical reaction. In the ICSE Class 7 curriculum, colour change is studied alongside changes in state, size, shape, evolution of heat, light, gases, and taste to build a comprehensive toolkit for distinguishing physical from chemical changes. Experiments such as heating iron filings with sulphur (forming black iron sulphide), burning magnesium ribbon (bright white flame), and adding dilute hydrochloric acid to sodium carbonate (colourless gas evolution with no colour change) illustrate how colour either appears, disappears, or remains constant. Students learn to record the initial and final colours, note whether the change is reversible, and correlate the observation with other evidence (heat, gas, precipitate) to classify the change correctly.
steps: A colour change that produces a new hue usually means a chemical reaction has created a new substance, while a colour that stays the same after melting, dissolving, or mixing typically indicates a physical change.
Here is why: Colour is a direct visual clue about the particles present.

In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to form different compounds with distinct light‑absorption properties, so the colour shifts – for instance, blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate becomes white anhydrous copper(II)…

In a physical change, the same particles remain; only their arrangement or state alters, so the colour either persists (melting blue ice) or combines additively (mixing blue and yellow inks to give green) without any…
Consider the classic classroom experiment: heat a few crystals of copper(II) sulphate in a dry test tube.
The blue crystals gradually turn white, and water droplets condense near the mouth.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "mixing blue and yellow paint to get green is a chemical change") reveals the misconception that any colour mixing is a chemical reaction, confusing additive colour mixing with substance formation.
remember: State one example of a colour change that indicates a chemical change and one that indicates a physical change.

In an experiment, a colourless solution turns pink after adding a few drops of….

cards.title: Size change refers to any measurable alteration in the linear dimensions…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Size change refers to any measurable alteration in the linear dimensions, volume, or mass distribution of a sample without implying a change in its chemical identity. In a physical change, particles are rearranged or separated but retain their original composition; examples include thermal expansion of a metal rod, crushing of chalk, or dissolving common salt where crystal size disappears but the substance remains NaCl. In a chemical change, size alteration accompanies the formation of new substances with different composition; for instance, burning magnesium reduces the ribbon’s length and mass as it converts to magnesium oxide, and heating iron filings with sulphur produces iron sulphide, changing both size and identity. Size alone cannot classify a change; it must be correlated with other indicators such as colour, gas evolution, heat, or taste (covered in sibling nodes). Experiments demonstrating size as an indicator: (1) heating a copper rod and measuring its length increase; (2) grinding chalk and observing particle size reduction; (3) igniting magnesium ribbon and noting length and mass loss; (4) dissolving salt and noting disappearance of visible crystals. These activities show that size change is observable, measurable, and useful when combined with other evidence to differentiate physical from chemical changes.
steps: Size change is a visible, measurable clue that a substance has undergone a transformation, but it does not by itself tell you whether the transformation is physical or chemical.
Here is why: first, many physical processes such as heating a metal rod cause the particles to vibrate more and push apart, increasing length without altering composition.
Second, mechanical actions like crushing chalk or grinding salt break particles into smaller pieces, again a physical change because the substance remains chemically identical.

Third, in a chemical reaction the reactants are converted into new products; the size of the original sample may shrink (magnesium ribbon burning) or grow (iron + sulphur forming a larger lump of iron sulphide), and…
Fourth, size change can be quantified — for example, measuring a copper rod before and after heating gives a percentage expansion that is reproducible and characteristic of the material.

Fifth, because both physical and chemical events can produce size alterations, students must always check for accompanying signs such as colour change, gas evolution, heat, light, or taste (covered in later nodes)…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “burning magnesium ribbon”) reveals the misconception that any visible size reduction must be chemical, confusing combustion with simple mechanical breakdown.
remember: State one example of a physical change that involves a change in size.
A copper rod 50 cm long is heated and its length becomes 50.08 cm. Calculate the percentage increase in length.
When magnesium ribbon burns, its length decreases and a white ash forms. Evaluate whether the size change alone proves a chemical change.

cards.title: A change in shape is an alteration of the external form or geometry of a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A change in shape is an alteration of the external form or geometry of a substance without any change in its chemical composition. In the context of physical and chemical changes, a shape change is classified as a physical change because the particles of the material remain the same; only their arrangement relative to each other is modified. Such changes are usually reversible (e.g., bending a metal strip, folding paper) and do not involve the formation of new substances, evolution of gas, heat, light, or a permanent colour change. Shape change is one of several observable indicators — alongside changes in state, colour, size, temperature, and gas evolution — used to distinguish physical from chemical changes. While a change in shape alone signals a physical change, it can accompany a chemical change (e.g., burning paper curls and turns to ash), but the decisive factor is whether new substances are produced. Understanding shape change helps students recognise that not every visible alteration implies a chemical reaction, reinforcing the particle model of matter where physical changes involve rearrangement of particles without breaking or forming chemical bonds.
steps: Shape change is a physical change because only the arrangement of particles is altered, not their identity.
Here is why: first, no new substance forms when you bend a copper wire — the copper atoms remain copper atoms.
Second, the change is often reversible; you can straighten the wire back, showing the particles can return to their original arrangement.
Third, mass is conserved — the wire weighs the same before and after bending.
Fourth, shape change does not involve heat, light, or gas evolution unless a chemical reaction also occurs.
Consider a lump of clay: you can roll it into a sphere, flatten it into a plate, or shape it into a pot. Each time the clay’s shape changes, but it remains clay.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing melting ice) reveals the misconception that any visible alteration — including state change — is a shape change, confusing different physical change indicators.
remember: Which of the following is an example of a shape change that is a physical change? a) Burning paper b) Melting ice c) Bending a copper wire d) Rusting iron.
A student says that when a piece of chalk is broken into smaller pieces, a chemical change occurs because the shape changes. Explain why this is incorrect.
Evaluate the statement: “Any change in shape of a material always indicates a physical change.” Provide a counterexample.

cards.title: Evolution of heat is the observable release of thermal energy during a process…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Evolution of heat is the observable release of thermal energy during a process, detected as a rise in temperature of the surroundings. In chemistry, it serves as a primary indicator of a chemical change because bond breaking and forming in reactants often releases (exothermic) or absorbs (endothermic) energy. Unlike physical changes — such as melting, boiling, or reshaping — where heat may be absorbed or released only to change state without altering composition, a chemical change involves rearrangement of atoms into new substances, and the associated enthalpy change (ΔH) is typically non‑zero. In Class 7 ICSE, students learn to recognise heat evolution through simple experiments: neutralisation of an acid with a base, combustion of magnesium ribbon, or the reaction of iron with sulphur. The temperature rise is measured with a laboratory thermometer, and the qualitative observation “the test tube becomes hot” is recorded as evidence of a chemical reaction. The concept links to earlier nodes on state, colour, size, and shape changes, reinforcing that heat evolution distinguishes chemical from physical transformations.
steps: Heat evolution is a clear sign that a chemical reaction has taken place because new bonds form and release energy.

Here is why: when reactants transform into products, the total bond energy of the products is often lower than that of the reactants; the excess energy leaves the system as heat, raising the temperature of the…
Consider the classic classroom experiment: dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide solution in a test tube.
The thermometer shows a rise from 25 °C to 32 °C, and the tube feels warm.
This temperature jump cannot be explained by mere mixing — it signals the formation of water and sodium chloride, a new substance.
A second example is burning a magnesium ribbon; the intense white flame and the hot ash demonstrate a vigorous exothermic reaction producing magnesium oxide.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the solution changes colour”) reveals the misconception that colour change alone signals heat evolution, confusing a different chemical indicator with thermal evidence.
remember: What is the primary observation that indicates heat evolution during a chemical reaction in a school laboratory.
Explain why melting ice does not count as heat evolution indicating a chemical change, even though heat is absorbed.
A student mixes equal volumes of 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH in a polystyrene cup and records a temperature rise of 6….

cards.title: Light evolution is the emission of visible radiation during a process.
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Light evolution is the emission of visible radiation during a process. In physical changes, light may appear only due to temperature rise (incandescence) without new substances forming, e.g., a heated iron rod glowing red. In chemical changes, light emission accompanies bond breaking and forming, releasing energy as photons; classic examples include magnesium burning with intense white light, or the blue flame of a gas stove indicating complete combustion. The key relationship: light signals energy release; if the energy originates from rearrangement of atoms, the change is chemical. If light merely reflects heating of the same material, the change is physical. Observing colour, intensity, and duration of light helps differentiate the two. Light is thus an observable indicator linking macroscopic observation to microscopic energy transformations.
steps: Light emission tells us that energy is being released, and the nature of that release reveals whether a change is physical or chemical.
Here is why: light appears when particles gain enough energy to emit photons; in a chemical reaction, bond breaking and forming liberates stored chemical energy, often as bright, coloured light.
In a physical change, only the kinetic energy of particles increases, causing dull incandescence without new substances.
Consider a magnesium ribbon burning in air: it produces an intense white light, and the product magnesium oxide is a new compound — a chemical change.
Now heat an iron nail until it glows red; the nail remains iron, only its temperature rose — a physical change.
In the kitchen, caramelising sugar turns brown and emits a faint glow as sugar molecules decompose into new compounds — chemical.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “light means temperature only”) reveals the misconception that light is solely a thermal effect, ignoring chemical energy release.
remember: What does the emission of light during a process primarily indicate about energy.
Why is the bright white light from burning magnesium considered evidence of a chemical change, whereas the red glow of a heated iron rod is not.
A reaction in a test tube produces a steady blue flame with a power output of 0.8 W for 15 s. Calculate the total light energy emitted.

cards.title: Physical changes alter only the form or state of a substance without creating…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Physical changes alter only the form or state of a substance without creating new chemical species; examples include melting ice, tearing paper, or dissolving common salt in water. Chemical changes produce one or more new substances with different properties, such as burning iron to form iron oxide or reacting sulphur with copper to form copper sulphide. The evolution of a gas can occur in both types: boiling water (physical) releases water vapour, whereas adding dilute hydrochloric acid to marble chips (chemical) releases carbon dioxide. A change in taste is a reliable indicator of a chemical change because new substances interact differently with taste receptors; for instance, the sour taste of vinegar becomes less acidic after reacting with baking soda. In contrast, physical changes like dissolving sugar in water do not alter the sweet taste of the solution. These two indicators — gas evolution and taste change — complement other observable signs (state, colour, size, shape, heat, light) covered in sibling nodes to help students classify changes accurately. Understanding that gas bubbles alone do not guarantee a chemical change, and that taste alteration is exclusive to chemical transformations, builds a robust conceptual framework for later study of reaction types and equations.
steps: The release of a gas or a change in taste during a process tells you that a chemical change has occurred, because new substances with different properties are formed.

First, gas evolution can happen in both physical and chemical changes, but only a chemical change produces a gas that is a new substance; for example, boiling water gives steam (same H₂O), while vinegar reacting with…

Second, a change in taste is exclusive to chemical changes because taste depends on molecular structure; when iron rusts, the metallic taste disappears as iron oxide forms, whereas melting ice leaves the taste of water…
Third, safe classroom tests let students see these signs: bubbling in a test tube with acid and carbonate, and a sip of the product (under supervision) to notice flavour shift.
Fourth, linking these observations to earlier indicators — colour change, heat, light — builds a complete toolkit for classifying any change.
Consider a typical Indian kitchen: when you add a pinch of baking soda to a bowl of curd, tiny bubbles rise and the sourness softens — a chemical change.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any gas evolution signals a chemical change, confusing state change with substance formation.

cards.title: Assembly of apparatus means arranging laboratory equipment in a correct…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Assembly of apparatus means arranging laboratory equipment in a correct, safe and purposeful way so that an intended observation can be made clearly. In the study of physical and chemical changes, two classic assemblies are used. The first is the heating assembly: a hard-glass test tube (or a boiling tube) containing a small amount of water, held obliquely with a test-tube holder over a Bunsen burner or spirit lamp, so that steam released during boiling can be seen escaping from the mouth of the tube. The second is the gas-evolution assembly: a flat-bottom flask or wide test tube containing a reactant (for example, marble chips or baking soda), fitted with a tight cork carrying a delivery tube, whose free end dips into an empty gas jar or a second test tube, so that the gas produced in the reaction (for example, carbon dioxide when dilute acid meets a carbonate) is carried over and can be collected or tested. Each piece of apparatus has a fixed duty: the flask is the reaction vessel, the cork seals it and directs the gas, the delivery tube transports the gas, and the receiver collects it. Correct assembly also means correct placement of heat (small flame, tube held at an angle, mouth pointing away from people) and correct sequence of joining parts (clamp first, then cork, then delivery tube, then receiver). A well-assembled setup protects the student, prevents gas leaks, and makes the difference between physical and chemical change visible: steam from boiling is the same substance, while carbon dioxide from a carbonate is a new substance.
steps: A correct apparatus assembly turns an invisible idea into a visible observation: the same bench setup that boils water shows a physical change, and the cork-and-delivery-tube setup shows a chemical change by carrying a…
First argument: apparatus is chosen for its duty.

A boiling tube holds liquid safely over a flame; a test-tube holder grips it so fingers stay cool; a wide flask gives space for fizzing; a tight cork with a delivery tube gives the gas only one path to travel.
Second argument: the heating assembly for a physical change is minimal — water in the tube, holder in hand, flame below, mouth of the tube pointing away.
Misty droplets appear near the cooler mouth; that mist is condensed steam, still water.
No new substance is made, so the assembly itself hints at the physical nature of the change.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that sealing and transporting are the same job, i.e., the student has memorised "cork goes on top" without assigning a function to each part of the assembly.
remember: Which single part of the gas-evolution assembly actually transports the new gas from the reaction flask to the….
Why must the mouth of a test tube being heated never point towards any person.

cards.title: A physical change in paper involves alteration of its physical properties…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A physical change in paper involves alteration of its physical properties — size, shape, state (e.g., wet paper drying), or texture — without changing its chemical composition. Examples include tearing, cutting, folding, crumpling, or dissolving paper in water (though dissolution may involve some chemical interaction, at this level it is treated as physical because the paper fibres remain cellulose). A chemical change in paper occurs when the cellulose fibres react with oxygen (combustion), acids, or other reagents to form new substances such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, ash (mostly carbon), and other combustion products. Indicators of a chemical change include evolution of heat and light (flame), production of gases (smell of burning), irreversible colour change (white to black), and change in taste (though tasting is not recommended). The key distinction is reversibility: physical changes are generally reversible (e.g., unfolding folded paper), while chemical changes are irreversible under normal classroom conditions. This node focuses on paper as a representative material to illustrate these concepts, linking to the broader chapter themes of state change, colour change, gas evolution, heat and light emission, and taste change. It builds on the apparatus assembly skills from the previous node and prepares students for similar investigations with common salt, chalk, iron, sulphur, and copper in subsequent nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: paper shows both physical changes (like tearing) and chemical changes (like burning), and we can tell them apart by checking if new substances appear.
Here is why: first, physical changes only rearrange the paper’s fibres — you can still recognise it as paper.
Second, chemical changes transform the cellulose into ash, gases, and heat — the original paper cannot be recovered.
Third, indicators such as flame, smoke, colour change from white to black, and heat evolution confirm a chemical change.
Fourth, simple classroom activities — tearing a sheet, folding it, then burning a corner — let students observe these differences directly.
Consider a typical Indian classroom: you have a notebook page.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing (a) burning) reveals the misconception that any visible alteration like fire or colour change is physical, confusing dramatic appearance with chemical transformation.
remember: Which of the following is a physical change involving….
A student observes that when paper burns it produces a yellow flame, heat, and black ash. Which two indicators from this observation confirm a chemical change.
Evaluate the statement: "Wetting a piece of paper and then drying it is a chemical change because the paper feels different when wet." Provide a reason.

cards.title: Common salt, chemically sodium chloride (NaCl)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Common salt, chemically sodium chloride (NaCl), is an ionic compound composed of sodium cations (Na⁺) and chloride anions (Cl⁻) held together by strong electrostatic forces in a crystal lattice. In the context of physical and chemical changes, common salt serves as a classic example of a substance that undergoes physical changes such as dissolution, crystallisation, and change of state (solid ↔ aqueous) without altering its chemical identity. When solid NaCl is added to water, the polar water molecules surround and separate the ions, producing a homogeneous mixture called a solution; the process is reversible by evaporation, which removes water and allows the ions to re‑assemble into the original crystal lattice. No new chemical bonds are formed or broken, so the composition remains NaCl throughout. In contrast, a chemical change involving common salt would require a reaction that transforms NaCl into different substances (e.g., electrolysis producing sodium metal and chlorine gas), which is not observed in simple classroom experiments at this level. The key relationships are: (1) dissolution ⇄ crystallisation are opposite physical processes; (2) the mass of salt is conserved during these physical changes; (3) observable indicators such as disappearance of solid, formation of a clear solution, and re‑appearance of crystals on evaporation signal a physical change, whereas colour change, gas evolution, or heat release would signal a chemical change.
steps: Takeaway: Common salt dissolves in water and recrystallises on evaporation without becoming a new substance, demonstrating a reversible physical change that conserves mass.
Here is why: 1.
Ionic lattice breaks, ions disperse – In solid NaCl, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in a regular three‑dimensional lattice.
Water molecules, being polar, surround each ion and pull it away, forming a homogeneous aqueous solution. 2.
No new chemical bonds form – The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions remain unchanged; they are simply solvated.
Because the chemical identity stays NaCl, the process is physical. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “NaCl becomes NaOH and HCl”) reveals the misconception that dissolving is a chemical reaction that splits the compound into new products, confusing physical dissociation with chemical decomposition.
remember: What happens to the chemical composition of common salt when it dissolves in water.
If 8 g of common salt is dissolved in 200 mL of water and the solution is completely evaporated, what mass of solid salt will be recovered.
A student observes that the temperature of the water drops slightly when common salt dissolves. Does this temperature change indicate a chemical change.

cards.title: Chalk (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) is a white, soft…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Chalk (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) is a white, soft, porous solid used in school laboratories to demonstrate both physical and chemical changes. A physical change in chalk involves alterations in size, shape, or state without forming new substances — e.g., breaking a stick into powder, grinding it, or dissolving a tiny amount in water (slight solubility). These changes are reversible in principle (the powder can be pressed back) and do not alter the chemical identity. A chemical change occurs when chalk reacts with acids (like dilute HCl or vinegar) to produce calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide gas — observed as effervescence, evolution of gas, and disappearance of the solid. Another chemical change is thermal decomposition: on strong heating (≈900 °C), chalk decomposes into calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide, accompanied by absorption of heat (endothermic) and a permanent loss of mass. Indicators linking to the chapter subtopics include: change in state (solid → gas), evolution of a gas (CO₂), evolution/absorption of heat, change in mass, and irreversibility. No colour change or light emission occurs. Chalk does not exhibit a change in taste relevant to classroom experiments. Understanding chalk’s behaviour connects the general definitions of physical and chemical changes (nodes 001, 002) to concrete, observable phenomena using a familiar material.
steps: Chalk is a ready‑made sample of calcium carbonate that lets you see both physical and chemical changes in one material.
Here is why: chalk’s physical changes are easy to spot — snapping a stick, grinding it to powder, or watching it dissolve slightly in water — because the substance stays chemically the same.

Its chemical changes are dramatic: adding dilute acid produces vigorous fizzing as carbon dioxide escapes, and strong heating makes the solid lose mass and turn into a different white solid (quicklime).
Consider a classroom demonstration: first, break a chalk stick into two pieces — size and shape change, no new substance, so physical.
Next, drop a piece into a test tube with dilute HCl — bubbles rise, the solid vanishes, and the solution becomes calcium chloride; gas evolution and irreversibility signal a chemical change.

Finally, heat a fresh piece in a hard‑glass test tube over a Bunsen burner — the tube becomes hot (heat absorbed), the chalk crumbles to a finer powder, and if you weigh before and after, the mass drops because CO₂ has…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “calcium sulphate” or “magnesium carbonate”) reveals the misconception that all white powders used for writing are chemically identical, confusing chalk with gypsum or other minerals.
remember: What is the main chemical constituent of chalk used in school laboratories.
A student grinds a piece of chalk into fine powder. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain your reasoning.
When chalk is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, bubbles of gas appear. Evaluate whether this observation alone is sufficient to conclude a chemical change has occurred.

cards.title: Iron is a grey, hard, magnetic metal used in this chapter as a case material…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Iron is a grey, hard, magnetic metal used in this chapter as a case material for studying physical and chemical changes. Its physical properties — metallic grey lustre, hardness, high density, the ability to be drawn into wires (ductility) and beaten into sheets (malleability), good conduction of heat and electricity, and attraction to a magnet — can all be observed without creating any new substance. Its physical changes are equally reversible in identity: heating an iron rod makes it expand and glow, and on cooling it returns to the same iron; magnetising and demagnetising an iron nail, or bending it, change only form and behaviour. Its chemical changes, however, create new substances and are central to Class 7 study. Rusting is the slow combination of iron with oxygen and moisture of the air, producing brown hydrated iron oxide (rust) that is brittle, non-magnetic in behaviour and quite different from the metal; it needs both air and water together, which is why oiled or painted iron does not rust. Burning iron in oxygen, or heating iron with sulphur, gives entirely new substances (iron oxide; iron sulphide, a black non-magnetic solid unlike the grey magnetic metal). Iron also reacts with dilute acids such as dilute hydrochloric acid, giving hydrogen gas bubbles and an iron salt in solution. Thus iron neatly demonstrates every indicator met earlier in the chapter — state, colour, size, shape, heat, light, gas evolution — on one familiar metal, and shows that physical changes leave the metal itself intact while chemical changes consume it into new materials.
steps: Iron is the chapter's complete teaching metal: the same grey material undergoes physical changes that leave it iron and chemical changes that turn it into something else entirely.
First argument: the untouched metal is a bundle of physical properties.
It is grey, hard, heavy for its size, magnetic, and can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires — which is exactly why India's tools, rails, and utensils are iron.
None of these observations creates matter that was not there; the substance stays iron.
Second argument: iron's physical changes are changes of form or condition.
Heat a rod and it lengthens slightly and glows; cool it and the same rod remains.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any visible alteration, even reversible expansion, counts as a chemical change, instead of asking whether a new substance has formed.
remember: Which observation proves that a change in iron is chemical rather than….
Two iron nails are set up for a week: nail 1 in a dry covered dish, nail 2 half-dipped in open….
After heating iron filings with sulphur powder, a student brings a magnet near the black product and it is not attracted, although the magnet had attracted the original filings….

cards.title: Sulphur (symbol S, atomic number 16) is a non‑metallic element that exists at…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Sulphur (symbol S, atomic number 16) is a non‑metallic element that exists at room temperature as a yellow crystalline solid (rhombic sulphur). Its key physical properties include a melting point of 115 °C, a boiling point of 444 °C, and a tendency to sublime slowly, which makes it ideal for demonstrating changes of state, colour, and size without altering its chemical identity. When heated gently, sulphur undergoes physical changes: it melts (solid → liquid), vaporises (liquid → gas), and the colour shifts from yellow to amber to reddish‑brown, yet the substance remains S₈ molecules. In contrast, strong heating in air causes combustion, a chemical change where sulphur reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide (SO₂), a colourless gas with a pungent odour. Sulphur also reacts with metals such as iron (Fe) to form iron(II) sulfide (FeS), a black solid, illustrating the formation of a new compound. These observations link directly to the chapter’s sub‑topics: change of state (melting, sublimation), colour change, evolution of gas, evolution of heat and light, and the distinction between reversible physical processes and irreversible chemical reactions. Understanding sulphur’s behaviour provides a concrete reference for classifying any observed change as physical or chemical.
steps: The one thing to remember: Sulphur is a versatile substance that clearly shows both physical changes (melting, sublimation, colour shift) and chemical changes (burning to SO₂, reacting with iron to form FeS) without any…
Here is why: 1.
Physical changes are reversible and conserve composition.
When sulphur is heated to 115 °C it melts; the liquid is still S₈ molecules.
Further heating makes it vaporise, yet cooling the vapour returns yellow crystals — no new substance appears. 2.
Colour and state changes alone do not prove a chemical reaction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “white” or “grey”) reveals the misconception that all powdered chemicals are white, confusing sulphur with common salt or chalk.
remember: What is the colour of solid sulphur at room temperature.
When sulphur is heated gently, it melts into an amber liquid. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain.
A student claims that burning sulphur in a spoon is a physical change because the sulphur disappears. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Copper (symbol Cu, atomic number 29) is a transition metal with a density of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Copper (symbol Cu, atomic number 29) is a transition metal with a density of 8.96 g cm⁻³, melting point 1085 °C and boiling point 2562 °C. It is malleable (can be hammered into thin sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires) and an excellent conductor of heat and electricity. In the context of physical and chemical changes, copper serves as a model substance: Physical changes – bending, cutting, melting or dissolving copper in nitric acid (the copper remains Cu²⁺ ions, no new element forms). Chemical changes – heating copper in air produces black copper(II) oxide (2 Cu + O₂ → 2 CuO); heating with sulphur gives copper(I) sulphide (2 Cu + S → Cu₂S); reacting with concentrated nitric acid yields nitrogen dioxide gas and copper(II) nitrate (Cu + 4 HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2 NO₂ + 2 H₂O). The colour change from reddish‑brown to black or green, evolution of gas, and heat release are observable indicators of chemical change. Copper sulphate solution (blue) used in displacement reactions with iron (Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu) further demonstrates a chemical change where copper metal is deposited. These behaviours link directly to the chapter’s experimental criteria: change of state, colour, size, shape, evolution of heat, light, gases and change of taste.
steps: Copper is a reddish‑brown metal that shows both physical changes (like bending or melting) and chemical changes (like turning black when heated in air) making it an ideal material to demonstrate the difference between…

First, copper’s physical properties — malleability, ductility, high thermal and electrical conductivity — allow students to see shape and size changes without any new substance forming; bending a copper wire or…

Second, when copper turnings are heated strongly in a test tube, the surface turns black because copper reacts with oxygen to form copper(II) oxide; the colour change and heat evolution are clear chemical‑change…
Third, heating copper with sulphur produces a black solid copper(I) sulphide, again a new substance with different properties.

Fourth, placing an iron nail in blue copper sulphate solution causes the solution to fade and a reddish deposit of copper to appear on the nail — a displacement reaction that demonstrates chemical change through colour…

Finally, everyday examples such as copper vessels developing a green patina (basic copper carbonate) over months connect classroom observations to real life, reinforcing that chemical changes are often slow but…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “silver‑white”) reveals the misconception that all metals look alike, confusing copper with aluminium or iron.
remember: What is the colour of pure copper metal at room temperature.
When copper turnings are heated in air, they turn black. Identify the product formed and the type of change.
A student claims that dissolving copper in nitric acid is a physical change because the copper disappears. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: An element is a pure chemical substance consisting of only one kind of atom…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: An element is a pure chemical substance consisting of only one kind of atom, each atom having the same number of protons in its nucleus. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means. Each element is represented by a unique one‑ or two‑letter symbol derived from its English or Latin name (e.g., Fe for iron from ferrum, Al for aluminium, Cu for copper from cuprum). The symbols are written with the first letter capitalised and the second letter, if present, in lower case. In the periodic table, elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, which equals the number of protons. Identification of an element therefore involves recognising its symbol, its name, and its position in the periodic table. For Class 7, the focus is on a few common metals — iron (Fe), aluminium (Al), copper (Cu) — and on distinguishing these symbols from those of compounds (e.g., H₂O, NaCl). The concept builds on the earlier idea that matter can be classified into pure substances (elements and compounds) and mixtures.
steps: Takeaway: An element is a pure substance made of only one type of atom, and each element has a unique one‑ or two‑letter symbol that identifies it worldwide.
Supporting arguments: 1.
Pure substance – Just as a bag of only red marbles contains a single colour, an element contains only one kind of atom. 2.
Atomic identity – The number of protons (atomic number) fixes the element; changing it creates a different element. 3.
Universal symbols – Chemists agreed on symbols (Fe, Al, Cu) so that a scientist in Mumbai and one in London write the same code for iron. 4.
Symbol rules – First letter capital, second letter small; derived from English or Latin names. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing H₂O) reveals the misconception that any chemical formula with letters is an element, confusing compounds with elements.
remember: Which of the following symbols represents an element? A) H₂O B) Fe C) NaCl D) CO₂.
A student writes the symbol for aluminium as “AL”. Explain why this is incorrect and give the correct symbol.
Evaluate the statement: “Because copper has the symbol Cu, it must contain carbon and uranium.”.

cards.title: A chemical symbol is a one‑ or two‑letter code assigned to each element by…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical symbol is a one‑ or two‑letter code assigned to each element by IUPAC; the first letter is always capitalised and the second, if present, is lower‑case (e.g., Fe for iron, Al for aluminium, Cu for copper). A chemical formula combines symbols of the constituent elements with subscript numbers to show the fixed ratio of atoms in a compound. The subscript applies only to the symbol immediately preceding it; if no subscript appears, the implied number is one. Parentheses group polyatomic units, and a dot followed by a number (or fraction) indicates water of crystallisation. Reading a formula from left to right identifies every element present and their relative atom counts. For example, Na₂SO₄ contains two sodium atoms, one sulphur atom and four oxygen atoms; CaSO₄·½H₂O shows calcium sulphate with half a water molecule per formula unit (plaster of Paris). This symbolic language is universal, allowing scientists worldwide to communicate composition without ambiguity.
steps: A chemical symbol or formula is a concise code that tells you exactly which elements are present and in what proportion.
First, symbols are universal abbreviations: Fe always means iron, never something else.
Second, formulae combine these symbols with subscripts to show fixed ratios; the subscript belongs only to the preceding symbol.
Third, reading left to right lists every element in the compound.
Fourth, parentheses group atoms that act as a unit, and a dot with a number shows water of crystallisation.
Fifth, the same element can appear in many different compounds, each with its own ratio.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “carbon” because C is the first letter) reveals the misconception that symbols are always the first letter of the English name, ignoring Latin origins and the two‑letter convention.
remember: What element does the symbol “Cu” represent.
In the formula Na₂SO₄, how many atoms of each element are present.
A student writes the formula for water as H₂O₂. Is this correct? Explain.

cards.title: A mixture is a material formed when two or more substances
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A mixture is a material formed when two or more substances (elements, compounds, or both) are combined in any proportion by mass or volume such that their particles remain in intimate contact without undergoing a chemical reaction. The components retain their individual physical and chemical properties, and no new substance with a fixed composition is created. Because the proportion is not fixed, the same mixture can have varying compositions — for example, a sugar solution can be dilute or concentrated. Mixtures are classified by the uniformity of particle distribution: homogeneous mixtures (solutions, alloys, sugar solution, acetic acid in water, milk) have particles so finely dispersed that the mixture appears uniform throughout; heterogeneous mixtures (sand and salt, sand and water, kerosene and water, chalk powder in water) show visibly distinct phases or particles. The intimate contact of particles allows physical separation methods (filtration, evaporation, chromatography, magnetic separation) to recover the original components unchanged. This definition distinguishes mixtures from compounds, where elements combine in fixed stoichiometric ratios, often with heat exchange, to form a new substance with properties different from its constituents (e.g., iron + sulphur → iron sulphide).
steps: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are combined in any proportion so that their particles remain in close contact without undergoing a chemical change.
Here is why: first, the proportion of components is not fixed — you can add a pinch or a cup of sugar to water and still have a sugar solution.
Second, the particles of each substance stay in intimate contact, meaning they mingle at the particle level but do not bond chemically.
Third, because no new chemical bonds form, each component keeps its original properties — sugar still tastes sweet, sand still feels gritty.
Fourth, this lack of chemical change allows the mixture to be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation, or magnetic attraction.
Fifth, depending on how finely the particles are dispersed, the mixture appears either uniform (homogeneous) or visibly non‑uniform (heterogeneous).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “a mixture is a new substance formed by fixed ratio”) reveals the misconception that mixtures have fixed composition like compounds.
remember: Define a mixture in one sentence.
Why can a mixture be separated by physical methods while a compound cannot.
A student says that mixing iron filings and sulphur powder in any ratio always forms iron sulphide. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Revisiting previous concepts means systematically recalling and connecting the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Revisiting previous concepts means systematically recalling and connecting the foundational ideas of matter classification learned in earlier classes. An element is a pure substance consisting of only one type of atom, represented by a unique chemical symbol (e.g., Fe for iron, Al for aluminium, Cu for copper). A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass; its composition is expressed by a chemical formula that shows the exact ratio of atoms (e.g., H₂O, NaCl, CaO, Na₂SO₄, NaHCO₃, CaSO₄·½H₂O for plaster of Paris). A mixture results when two or more substances are physically combined in any proportion without chemical bonding; the components retain their individual properties. Mixtures are classified as homogeneous (uniform throughout, such as alloys, sugar solution, acetic acid in water, milk) or heterogeneous (non‑uniform, such as sand + salt, sand + water, kerosene + water, chalk powder + water). Separation techniques like chromatography exploit differences in physical properties (adsorption, solubility) to separate mixture components. The reaction of iron powder with sulphur on heating to form iron sulphide (FeS) illustrates how a compound with new properties arises from a fixed stoichiometric ratio, unlike a mere physical mixture. This node reinforces the symbolic language (symbols, formulae) and the conceptual distinction between fixed‑ratio compounds and variable‑ratio mixtures, preparing students for deeper classification and quantitative work.
steps: Revisiting the symbols, formulae, and classification of matter connects your earlier learning to the systematic chemistry you will now build.
First, symbols and formulae are the universal language of chemistry; they let us communicate composition precisely without ambiguity.
Second, each element has a unique one‑ or two‑letter symbol (Fe, Al, Cu) that stands for a single type of atom, reinforcing the idea of purity at the atomic level.
Third, compounds are represented by formulae that show the exact, unchanging ratio of atoms (e.g., NaCl always 1:1, Na₂SO₄ always 2:1:4), which distinguishes them from mixtures where ratios can vary.

Fourth, mixtures can be homogeneous — like brass (copper‑zinc alloy), sugar solution, or milk — where the components are intimately mixed at the particle level and appear uniform, or heterogeneous — like sand‑salt…

Fifth, separation techniques such as chromatography rely on differences in how components interact with a stationary and a mobile phase, a principle that only works because mixtures lack chemical bonds.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Ir for iron”) reveals the misconception that symbols always match the English name’s first letters, ignoring historical origins.
remember: Name the chemical symbols for iron, aluminium, and copper.
Given the formula NaCl, explain why it represents a compound and not a mixture.
A student says milk is a pure compound because it has a fixed composition. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are combined in any proportion…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are combined in any proportion so that their particles remain in intimate contact without chemical bonding. The components retain their individual properties and can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation, or chromatography. Mixtures are classified as homogeneous (uniform throughout, e.g., sugar solution, alloys, acetic acid in water, milk) or heterogeneous (non‑uniform, e.g., sand and salt, sand and water, kerosene and water, chalk powder in water). A compound results when elements chemically combine in a fixed, definite proportion by mass (stoichiometric quantities), often requiring energy such as heat. The new substance has properties different from its constituent elements and cannot be separated by physical means. For example, iron powder and sulphur heated together form iron sulphide (FeS) in a 1:1 atomic ratio; the product is magnetic unlike iron, and the reaction is irreversible without chemical treatment. Common daily‑life examples: honey (mixture of sugars, water, enzymes), milk (emulsion of fat, protein, lactose), water (H₂O, fixed 2:1 H:O ratio), rust (Fe₂O₃·nH₂O, fixed Fe:O ratio). Understanding the distinction rests on recognizing variable composition for mixtures versus constant composition for compounds.
steps: The key idea is that mixtures have variable composition while compounds have a fixed composition.
Here is why: when you stir sugar into tea, you can add one spoon or three — the tea remains a mixture because the sugar particles simply disperse.
In contrast, water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 atom ratio; you cannot make “water with extra oxygen” without creating a different substance.
Consider honey: it is a natural blend of fructose, glucose, water, and enzymes.
Bees collect nectar from different flowers, so the exact sugar ratio varies from hive to hive — that variability marks honey as a mixture.
Milk behaves similarly; its fat, protein, and lactose percentages change with the cow’s diet, breed, and stage of lactation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any combination of two substances is homogeneous — confusing “mixture” with “uniform mixture”.
remember: Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture? A) Sand and salt B) Kerosene and water C) Sugar solution D) Chalk powder in water.
Explain why iron sulphide (FeS) is classified as a compound and not a mixture.
A student claims that milk is a compound because it always contains water, fat, and protein. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Water (chemical formula H₂O) is a pure chemical compound formed when two atoms…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Water (chemical formula H₂O) is a pure chemical compound formed when two atoms of hydrogen combine chemically with one atom of oxygen in a fixed 2:1 atomic ratio. The combination occurs through covalent bonds, giving water distinct properties — such as a boiling point of 100 °C and a density of 1 g cm⁻³ at 4 °C — that differ from those of its constituent elements. Unlike mixtures (e.g., salt‑water), water cannot be separated into hydrogen and oxygen by physical means; it requires a chemical reaction (electrolysis). In the CISCE Class 7 curriculum, water serves as the primary example to illustrate the difference between elements (hydrogen, oxygen), compounds (water), and mixtures (e.g., honey, milk). Its fixed composition, definite melting/boiling points, and inability to be separated physically are the key criteria used to classify it as a compound.
steps: Water is a compound because its atoms combine in a fixed 2:1 ratio and cannot be separated by physical means.
Here is why: first, the formula H₂O shows two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, a ratio that never changes in pure water.
Second, water has unique properties — such as a sharp boiling point at 100 °C — that differ from hydrogen (a gas) and oxygen (a gas).
Third, mixtures like salt‑water can be separated by evaporation, but water requires electricity (electrolysis) to split into its elements.
Consider a glass of tap water: you see a clear liquid, but at the particle level it is billions of H₂O teams.
If you pass an electric current through it using two pencils as electrodes, bubbles appear — hydrogen at the negative pencil, oxygen at the positive — proving water is chemically bonded.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “HO” or “H₂O₂”) reveals the misconception that the formula can vary like a mixture’s composition, confusing compounds with mixtures where proportions are not fixed.
remember: What is the chemical formula of water and what does it tell you about the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen atoms.
Explain why water is classified as a compound and not a mixture, using at least two distinguishing properties.
A student claims that boiling water separates it into hydrogen and oxygen gases. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Milk is a natural, opaque, white liquid secreted by mammals…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Milk is a natural, opaque, white liquid secreted by mammals; in chemistry it serves as a classic example of a homogeneous mixture known as a colloid (specifically an emulsion). In milk, the dispersed phase consists of microscopic fat globules (0.1–10 µm) stabilized by a phospholipid membrane, while the continuous phase is an aqueous solution containing lactose (a disaccharide), whey proteins (β‑lactoglobulin, α‑lactalbumin), casein micelles (colloidal calcium‑phosphate‑protein complexes), minerals (calcium, phosphorus, potassium) and vitamins. Because the particles are small enough to remain suspended for long periods and do not settle under gravity, milk appears uniform to the naked eye and does not separate on standing (unless cream rises due to density difference). The composition varies with species, breed, diet and stage of lactation, but typical cow milk contains approximately 87 % water, 3.5 % fat, 3.3 % protein, 4.8 % lactose and 0.7 % minerals by mass. Milk illustrates the concept that a mixture can have a fixed appearance yet variable composition, unlike a compound which has a definite stoichiometric formula. It also demonstrates the Tyndall effect — a beam of light becomes visible when passed through milk because the colloidal particles scatter light. Understanding milk as a colloid links to the broader classification of mixtures into homogeneous (solutions, colloids) and heterogeneous (suspensions, coarse dispersions) and prepares students for separation techniques such as centrifugation, filtration and chromatography.
steps: Milk is a homogeneous colloidal mixture because its tiny fat globules and protein micelles stay evenly dispersed in water, giving a uniform appearance without settling.
Here is why: first, the particle size (1 nm–1 µm) is small enough to remain suspended for days, unlike sand in water which settles in seconds.
Second, the phospholipid membrane around each fat globule prevents coalescence, so the emulsion is stable without chemical bonding — this is a physical mixture, not a compound.

Third, milk scatters a beam of light (Tyndall effect), a hallmark of colloids, whereas true solutions like salt water do not. Consider a glass of fresh cow milk: you see a white, opaque liquid; if you shine a flashlight…
Now compare with a spoon of sugar dissolved in water: the solution is clear and shows no beam.
Finally, note that milk’s composition can vary (buffalo milk has more fat), but water (H₂O) always has a fixed 2:1 hydrogen‑to‑oxygen ratio — milk is a mixture, water a compound.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “milk is a heterogeneous mixture because you can see cream on top”) reveals the misconception that visible cream separation means the original milk is heterogeneous, ignoring that fresh milk is uniform and cream rises only due to density…
remember: What type of mixture is milk classified as in the ICSE Class 7 chemistry curriculum.
Explain why milk exhibits the Tyndall effect while a sugar solution does not.
A student claims that milk is a compound because it always contains water, fat, protein, lactose and minerals in fixed proportions. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Rust is the common name for hydrated iron(III) oxide…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Rust is the common name for hydrated iron(III) oxide, a compound with the approximate formula Fe₂O₃·nH₂O. It forms when elemental iron (Fe) reacts with oxygen (O₂) from the atmosphere and water (H₂O) in a fixed stoichiometric ratio: 4 Fe + 3 O₂ + 6 H₂O → 4 Fe(OH)₃, which dehydrates to Fe₂O₃·nH₂O. Because the reactants combine in definite proportions, rust is a compound, not a mixture. Its properties (colour, brittleness, non‑magnetism) differ completely from those of iron, oxygen, or water. The reaction is a chemical change — irreversible under normal conditions — and illustrates the concept that compounds have a constant composition, unlike mixtures such as sand‑salt or milk where components retain their identities and can be present in any proportion.
steps: Rust is a compound formed only when iron, oxygen, and water meet in fixed proportions.
Here is why: the reddish layer on a wet nail cannot be separated into iron and oxygen by simple physical means, proving a new substance with its own properties has been created.
Consider an iron nail left on a damp windowsill during the Kerala monsoon.
After a few days the nail is coated with a flaky brown crust.
If you scrape the crust, you cannot recover shiny iron filings and oxygen gas; the original iron has chemically combined with oxygen from the air and water from the humidity.
The reaction follows the balanced equation 4 Fe + 3 O₂ + 6 H₂O → 4 Fe(OH)₃, which loses water to give Fe₂O₃·nH₂O.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only iron and oxygen”) reveals the misconception that water is merely a catalyst rather than a reactant that becomes part of the hydrated oxide product.
remember: What are the three substances that must be present for iron to rust.
A student says, “Rust is just a mixture of iron powder and oxygen gas stuck together.” Evaluate this statement.
If 56 g of pure iron completely rusts to form Fe₂O₃ (ignoring water of hydration), what mass of rust is produced? (Molar masses: Fe = 56 g mol⁻¹, Fe₂O₃ = 160 g mol⁻¹).

cards.title: This concept node extends the illustration of mixtures and compounds (node) by…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: This concept node extends the illustration of mixtures and compounds (node) by examining additional everyday substances: honey, butter, cough syrup, a salt‑sugar mixture, and a sand‑salt mixture. Each example demonstrates that a mixture forms when two or more substances combine in any proportion, their particles remain in intimate contact, yet each component retains its original chemical identity and properties. Honey is a homogeneous mixture (solution) of fructose, glucose, water, and minor constituents; its composition varies with floral source. Butter is a water‑in‑fat emulsion — microscopically heterogeneous — formed by churning cream. Cough syrup is a homogeneous solution of active pharmaceutical ingredients in a concentrated sugar syrup base. A salt‑sugar mixture is a heterogeneous solid blend where both components are visibly distinct crystals. A sand‑salt mixture is also heterogeneous, with insoluble sand grains mixed with soluble salt crystals. In all cases the components can be separated by physical methods (evaporation, filtration, chromatography, fractional crystallisation) without any chemical reaction. This node reinforces the key relationships: mixtures have variable composition, no fixed stoichiometry, and retain component properties; compounds (like water, rust, iron sulphide) have fixed composition, new properties, and require chemical change for separation. The node builds on the mixture definition (node) and the specific examples of water, milk, and rust (nodes‑008) and prepares learners for the symbolic representation of elements and compounds in node.
steps: Everyday substances like honey, butter, cough syrup, and simple mixes of salt with sugar or sand are mixtures because their ingredients keep their own properties and can be separated without chemical reactions.
Here is why: first, mixtures have no fixed proportion — the ratio of sugars to water in honey changes with the flowers bees visit.
Second, each component retains its identity — the fat in butter still behaves as fat, the medicine in cough syrup keeps its medicinal effect.
Third, mixtures can be homogeneous (uniform throughout, like honey and cough syrup) or heterogeneous (visibly non‑uniform, like butter, salt‑sugar, sand‑salt).
Fourth, physical methods such as evaporation, filtration, or heating can separate the parts because no new chemical bonds form.
Consider honey: bees collect nectar, which is mostly water and sucrose; enzymes break sucrose into glucose and fructose, and water evaporates, leaving a thick solution.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing butter) reveals the misconception that a smooth appearance guarantees homogeneity — butter is actually a water‑in‑fat emulsion, microscopically heterogeneous.
remember: Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture? A) Butter B) Honey C) Sand and salt D) Salt and sugar.
Explain why butter is classified as a heterogeneous mixture even though it looks uniform to the naked eye.
A student claims: “Cough syrup is a compound because it has a fixed composition of medicine and sugar.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A chemical symbol is a one‑ or two‑letter abbreviation that uniquely identifies…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical symbol is a one‑ or two‑letter abbreviation that uniquely identifies an element. The first letter is always capitalised; a second letter, if present, is lower‑case (e.g., Fe from Latin ferrum, Al from English aluminium). A chemical formula represents a compound by showing the symbols of its constituent elements and using subscripts to indicate the fixed number of atoms of each element in one formula unit. For example, water is H₂O because two hydrogen atoms combine with one oxygen atom. The list for this chapter includes the element symbols: iron (Fe), aluminium (Al), copper (Cu); and the compound formulae: water (H₂O), plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O), sodium chloride (NaCl), calcium oxide (CaO), sodium sulphate (Na₂SO₄), sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO₃). Symbols derive from either English or historic Latin names, while formulae follow the law of definite proportions — elements combine in simple whole‑number ratios. Recognising these representations allows students to read and write chemical information accurately, a prerequisite for later work on equations and reactions.
steps: Every element has a unique one‑ or two‑letter symbol and every compound has a fixed formula that shows the types and numbers of atoms.
Here is why: first, symbols are standardised worldwide so chemists in Mumbai, London, or Tokyo read “Fe” and know it means iron.
Second, the capitalisation rule (first letter upper‑case, second lower‑case) prevents confusion — “Co” is cobalt while “CO” would be carbon‑oxygen.
Third, formulae use subscripts to lock in the exact atom ratio; water is always H₂O, never HO or H₃O.
Fourth, the nine substances in this node are the building blocks for the chapter’s experiments and later chapters.
Consider the list: iron (Fe), aluminium (Al), copper (Cu) — each symbol comes from its Latin or English root.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Ir”) reveals the misconception that symbols always follow the English spelling, confusing iron with iridium.
remember: What is the chemical symbol for iron.
Why is the symbol for aluminium written as Al and not AL.
A student writes the formula for water as HO. Evaluate this formula.

cards.title: Iron is a chemical element with symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum) and atomic number…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Iron is a chemical element with symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum) and atomic number 26. It belongs to Group 8, Period 4 of the periodic table and is a transition metal. Its standard atomic weight is 55.85 u. Iron is a lustrous, ductile, malleable, silver‑grey metal that conducts heat and electricity well. It is ferromagnetic at room temperature, meaning it is strongly attracted to magnets and can be magnetised. Chemically, iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly called rust (Fe₂O₃·nH₂O). It also reacts with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas and iron(II) salts. In nature, iron occurs mainly as ores such as haematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄). The element is extracted in a blast furnace, but the extraction process is taught in higher classes. In the ICSE Class 7 curriculum, the focus is on recognising Fe as the symbol for iron, stating its atomic number, and identifying it in simple compounds like FeO, Fe₂O₃, and FeS. This node builds on the previous concept node where students learned to read symbols and formulae, and it prepares them for the next element, aluminium.
steps: Iron is a fundamental element identified by the symbol Fe and atomic number 26, and it serves as a classic example of a magnetic, high‑density metal used daily in Indian homes.
Here is why: 1.
Symbol origin – Fe comes from the Latin ferrum, not from the English name.
This historical naming convention appears for many elements (e.g., Na from natrium, K from kalium). 2.
Periodic table position – Iron sits in the d‑block, Group 8, Period 4.
