Its location tells us it is a transition metal with typical metallic properties and the ability to form coloured compounds. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Ir”) reveals the misconception that symbols always come from the first two letters of the English name, confusing iron with iridium (Ir).
remember: What is the chemical symbol for iron.
Why is iron represented by Fe instead of Ir or In.
A student writes the formula for iron(III) oxide as FeO₂. Evaluate this formula.

cards.title: Aluminium (symbol Al, atomic number 13) is a metallic element belonging to…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Aluminium (symbol Al, atomic number 13) is a metallic element belonging to Group 13 of the periodic table. It has three valence electrons, giving it a common valency of 3 and forming the cation Al³⁺ in compounds. The element exists as a solid at room temperature with a density of 2.70 g cm⁻³, making it about one‑third the density of iron. Its high electrical and thermal conductivity, combined with low weight, makes it valuable for wiring, utensils, and transport. Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a protective oxide layer Al₂O₃ (aluminium oxide) which prevents further corrosion. In compounds it shows a +3 oxidation state; typical compounds include aluminium oxide, aluminium chloride (AlCl₃), and aluminium sulphate (Al₂(SO₄)₃). The element is extracted from bauxite ore by the Hall‑Héroult electrolytic process, a concept introduced in higher classes. For Class 7 the focus is on recognising its symbol, valency, physical properties (lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductor), and its distinction from mixtures — aluminium is a pure substance with a fixed composition, unlike alloys such as duralumin which are homogeneous mixtures.
steps: Aluminium is a light, corrosion‑resistant metal with symbol Al and atomic number 13.
Here is why: it has three electrons in its outer shell, so it readily loses them to form Al³⁺, giving it a valency of 3.
This valency determines the formulae of its compounds, such as Al₂O₃ (two Al³⁺ ions balance three O²⁻ ions).
The metal’s low density (2.70 g cm⁻³) makes it ideal for aircraft bodies and kitchen foil — everyday Indian examples include the foil wrapping your roti and the frame of a school bus window.
When exposed to air, aluminium instantly forms a thin, transparent layer of aluminium oxide that sticks tightly and stops further reaction; this is why aluminium utensils do not rust like iron tawa.
In contrast, an alloy such as duralumin (Al + Cu + Mg + Mn) is a homogeneous mixture — its composition can vary, and it does not have a fixed chemical formula.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “symbol Al, atomic number 27”) reveals the misconception that atomic number equals mass number — confusing protons with total nucleons.
remember: What is the chemical symbol and atomic number of aluminium.
Why does aluminium not rust like iron when exposed to moist air.
A student writes the formula of aluminium oxide as AlO. Evaluate this formula.

cards.title: Copper (symbol Cu, from Latin cuprum) is a chemical element classified as a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Copper (symbol Cu, from Latin cuprum) is a chemical element classified as a transition metal. It consists solely of copper atoms, each with 29 protons. As an element, copper cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions; it retains its identity in all physical and chemical processes. Water is a chemical compound with the molecular formula H₂O, indicating each molecule comprises two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a fixed 2:1 atom ratio (mass ratio 1:8). Unlike mixtures, the composition of water is invariant — every sample of pure water contains hydrogen and oxygen in this exact proportion. In the framework of elements, compounds, and mixtures, copper exemplifies a pure elemental substance, while water exemplifies a pure compound. Their symbols and formulae provide a universal shorthand: Cu represents one atom of copper; H₂O represents one molecule of water. This node builds on the recognition of element symbols (e.g., Fe, Al) and compound formulae (e.g., NaCl) to reinforce that elements are represented by one or two letters (first capitalized) and compounds by formulae showing constituent elements and their ratios. Copper and water are common Indian household examples — copper vessels, wiring, and drinking water — making the abstract concept tangible.
steps: Copper is an element made of only copper atoms, while water is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically bonded in a fixed 2:1 ratio.
Here is why: an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means, whereas a compound can be decomposed into its constituent elements.
Copper, with symbol Cu, is found in nature as a metal and in ores; it consists entirely of Cu atoms.
Water, with formula H₂O, is formed when hydrogen and oxygen react in a fixed proportion — two volumes of hydrogen combine with one volume of oxygen to give two volumes of water vapour.
This fixed ratio is the hallmark of a compound.
Consider a copper wire: no matter how small you cut it, each piece is still copper.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Co” or “CP”) reveals the misconception that symbols are arbitrary abbreviations of the English name rather than standardized international codes, often confusing cobalt (Co) with copper.
remember: What is the chemical symbol for copper and what does it represent.
A student writes the formula of water as HO. Explain why this is incorrect and give the correct formula.
Evaluate the statement: “Since copper is a metal and water is a liquid, copper is an element and water is a compound.” Is the reasoning valid.

cards.title: Plaster of Paris is the common name for calcium sulphate hemihydrate…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Plaster of Paris is the common name for calcium sulphate hemihydrate, a compound with the chemical formula CaSO₄·½H₂O. It is produced by the controlled thermal dehydration of gypsum (calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO₄·2H₂O) at about 150 °C, which removes one and a half molecules of water per formula unit. The resulting hemihydrate is a fine white powder that, when mixed with water, undergoes an exothermic hydration reaction to re‑form the dihydrate gypsum, creating a rigid interlocking crystal network that gives the material its setting property. Unlike a mixture, plaster of Paris has a fixed composition and definite stoichiometric proportions; its particles are chemically bonded, not merely in intimate contact. It is classified as a compound because it consists of calcium, sulphur, oxygen and hydrogen in a fixed ratio, and it exhibits properties distinct from its constituent elements or from the original gypsum. In the context of the chapter, plaster of Paris serves as a classic example of a compound with a known formula, contrasting with mixtures such as salt‑sugar or sand‑salt where components retain their individual identities and can be separated by physical means.
steps: Plaster of Paris is a compound with a fixed formula CaSO₄·½H₂O that hardens when water is added because it re‑forms gypsum.
Here is why: first, gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is a naturally occurring mineral that contains two water molecules for every calcium sulphate unit.
Second, heating gypsum to about 150 °C drives off one and a half water molecules, leaving the hemihydrate — plaster of Paris — a fine white powder.

Third, when this powder meets water, the hemihydrate crystals absorb water and recrystallise as the dihydrate, creating a dense network of needle‑like crystals that lock together and give the material its strength.
Fourth, this transformation is a chemical change, not a simple physical mixing, so the product has properties (hardness, exothermic heat release) that neither the powder nor water alone possess.
Fifth, because the composition is fixed, plaster of Paris is a compound, unlike a mixture of sand and salt where each component keeps its own properties and can be separated by sieving or dissolving.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., CaSO₄·2H₂O) reveals the misconception that plaster of Paris is the same as gypsum, confusing the dihydrate with the hemihydrate.
remember: What is the chemical formula of plaster of Paris.
Explain why plaster of Paris hardens when mixed with water.
A student claims that plaster of Paris is a mixture because it contains calcium, sulphur, oxygen and hydrogen. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Sodium chloride, formula NaCl, is a compound of the elements sodium and…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Sodium chloride, formula NaCl, is a compound of the elements sodium and chlorine, in which one atom of sodium is chemically joined to one atom of chlorine in a fixed 1: 1 partnership — the strictness of this join is what makes it a compound and not a mixture. It exists as a white, crystalline, brittle solid with cubic crystals, is soluble in water, has a fairly high melting point, and in solution (or when molten) conducts electricity — behaviour that reflects its ionic character: the particles in NaCl are charged units (sodium particles carrying a positive charge and chloride particles carrying a negative charge) held together by strong mutual attraction. Sodium chloride is formed by chemical combination of its two elements — a vigorous reaction in which the dangerous soft metal sodium unites with the green reactive gas chlorine to give the stable, edible salt, a transformation that dramatically illustrates how a compound's properties differ utterly from those of its components. It occurs abundantly in nature: dissolved in sea water (which is why India has salt pans along the coasts, where sea water is trapped and evaporated by the sun), and as rock salt (halite) mined from underground deposits. Its solubility gives a classroom-proof way to distinguish the compound from its solutions: dissolving salt in water of any chosen proportion gives a mixture (salt solution), while evaporating the water recovers the same NaCl, unchanged, because the chemical join was never broken by the physical process. Uses span food (taste, preservation of pickles, papads and fish), health (ORL/ saline solutions), and industry (making other sodium and chlorine products). Within this chapter's chain of compound case studies, NaCl stands beside plaster of paris and calcium oxide as an everyday compound whose formula, fixed join, and compound-versus-mixture behaviour can all be verified at home.
steps: Sodium chloride is the compound that proves the compound concept with a kitchen dabba: one sodium particle joined to one chlorine particle, in a partnership so fixed that no power on the bench can quietly stretch it.
First argument: the formula tells the whole story.
NaCl means one atom of sodium joined to one atom of chlorine — no subscripts, because one of each is the recipe.
This is exactly the notation grammar practised with Fe and FeS, now applied to the substance every Indian child handles daily.
The two letters stand for two elements (sodium, a metal; chlorine, a non-metal), while NaCl as a whole is neither — it is the compound they form together.
Second argument: the compound is nothing like its components.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "NaCl means a mixture of sodium and chlorine") reveals the misconception that formulas describe blends, ignoring that a joined formula records chemical combination in a fixed ratio — the very definition of a compound.
remember: What does the formula NaCl state about the composition of sodium chloride.
Sodium is a dangerous reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet table salt is safe to eat. Explain what this contrast teaches about compounds.
A student dissolves 5 g of salt in 100 g of water; a friend dissolves 20 g of salt in 100 g of….

cards.title: Calcium oxide, formula CaO, commonly called quicklime or unslaked lime…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Calcium oxide, formula CaO, commonly called quicklime or unslaked lime, is a white, powdery, caustic compound in which one atom of the metal calcium is chemically joined to one atom of the non-metal oxygen — a fixed 1: 1 join recorded by its subscript-free formula. It is manufactured by strongly heating limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) in a lime kiln: the heat drives the decomposition, calcium carbonate breaks into calcium oxide, and carbon dioxide gas escapes — a chemical change in which the solid product weighs less than the starting limestone precisely because the gas has flown away. Quicklime's defining property is its violent thirst for water: when water is added, it reacts vigorously — hissing, crackling, releasing a great deal of heat, sometimes enough to make the mixture steam or even crack the vessel — and converts into calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, called slaked lime. This slaking is a chemical change (a new substance forms), not mere dissolving, and the heat released is evidence of the energetic chemical join being made. Slaked lime, mixed into a paste with more water, is the traditional Indian whitewash: painted on walls, it slowly combines with carbon dioxide of the air to give back a hard white coating of calcium carbonate, which is why freshly whitewashed walls shine after drying. Quicklime thus takes part in a complete chemical circle: limestone → quicklime (by heat) → slaked lime (by water) → back to calcium carbonate (by air's carbon dioxide). Other uses include mixing into mortar for masonry, drying moist gases (it absorbs water greedily), and treating acidic soil. Because it is caustic, handling quicklime demands care — dry hands or gloves, no eye contact, and never touch it with wet skin. Within the chapter's compound chain, CaO demonstrates that a compound's fixed join (1: 1) can be violent in behaviour even while its formula looks as simple as table salt's.
steps: Calcium oxide is the compound case study where the fixed 1: 1 join announces itself with hissing steam: CaO is modest on paper and violent in the bucket.
First argument: the formula's simplicity hides an industrial origin.
CaO states one calcium atom joined to one oxygen atom — the same subscript-free grammar as NaCl.

The compound is born in a lime kiln, where limestone (CaCO₃) is roasted strongly; the heat splits the carbonate, quicklime stays behind as the solid product and carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air. Every gram of gas…
Second argument: slaking is the loudest demonstration of chemical change in this chapter.
Pour water onto quicklime and it hisses and crackles, swells and crumbles, and pours out heat — wet steam rises from the bucket.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "CaO is a mixture of calcium and oxygen") reveals the misconception that two symbols in one formula describe a blend, ignoring that a single formula records a fixed chemical join — the compound's defining feature.
remember: What does the formula CaO indicate about the composition of calcium oxide.
Water is poured on quicklime. List three observations, name the product formed, and justify why this is a chemical change.
A kiln charges 12 g of limestone and collects 5.3 g of carbon dioxide gas that escapes during….

cards.title: Sodium sulphate, formula Na₂SO₄, is a white, crystalline…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Sodium sulphate, formula Na₂SO₄, is a white, crystalline, water-soluble compound of sodium and the sulphate group. Its formula records a new notation idea: two atoms of sodium (subscript 2 on Na) are joined to one sulphate unit — a group of one sulphur atom with four oxygen atoms, written SO₄, that behaves as a single team inside the compound. Counting atoms, one unit of Na₂SO₄ contains 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms. The compound is formed in the classic reaction of neutralisation: sodium hydroxide (an alkali, NaOH) reacts with sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) to give sodium sulphate and water — the acid's character and the alkali's character are both cancelled, and the salt plus water are the products. In symbol-display form: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, where the two NaOH units supply the two sodium atoms that the single sulphate group demands. Sodium sulphate dissolves readily in water, giving a neutral solution, and crystallises as colourless/white crystals; its most familiar hydrate holds ten water molecules per unit (Glauber's salt), which is why the substance has historically been famous for unusually large, glassy crystals. Uses centre on industry rather than the kitchen: as a filler in detergent powders, in glass-making, and in paper manufacture — so unlike sodium chloride, the student will rarely meet it at the dining table, but its formula appears on every serious detergent packet. Within the chapter's compound chain, Na₂SO₄ completes the progression: one-to-one joins (NaCl, CaO), then a compound whose formula joins atoms to a multi-atom group — preparing the ground for the radical concept that the Atomic Structure chapter will formalise as charged groups acting as single units.
steps: Sodium sulphate is the compound that upgrades the student's reading eye: after two 1: 1 formulas, Na₂SO₄ introduces the group that stays together — and the arithmetic that keeps a formula honest.
First argument: the formula is read in two tiers.
Tier one, the subscript: the 2 after Na multiplies only sodium — two sodium atoms per unit; the 4 after O multiplies only oxygen — four oxygen atoms per unit.
Tier two, the grouping: S and its four oxygens form the sulphate unit, written SO₄, one team of five atoms.
So Na₂SO₄ reads: two sodium atoms joined to one sulphate team — 7 atoms in all per unit.
The misreading to kill early is "2 × everything": the 2 belongs to Na alone.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "2 sodium, 2 sulphur, 2 oxygen — the 2 multiplies all") reveals the misconception that a leading subscript multiplies every symbol in the formula, ignoring that each subscript attaches only to the symbol (or grouped unit member)…
remember: State exactly what the formula Na₂SO₄ records, and give the total number of atoms in one unit.
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) react to form sodium sulphate and water. Explain, using atom teams, why TWO units of NaOH are needed for every ONE unit of H₂SO₄.
8 g of sodium hydroxide reacts completely with 9.8 g of sulphuric acid, producing 14.2 g of sodium….

cards.title: Sodium hydrogen carbonate
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Sodium hydrogen carbonate (systematic IUPAC name: sodium hydrogencarbonate) is an ionic compound with the chemical formula NaHCO₃. It consists of sodium cations (Na⁺) and hydrogencarbonate anions (HCO₃⁻) held together by electrostatic forces in a crystalline lattice. The hydrogencarbonate ion itself is a polyatomic anion derived from carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) by loss of one proton; it contains one hydrogen, one carbon, and three oxygen atoms. In the solid state the compound is a white, odourless, crystalline powder that is sparingly soluble in water (≈ 9 g / 100 mL at 20 °C) and decomposes on heating above 50 °C to give sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), water vapour, and carbon dioxide gas. It is a weak base (pK_b ≈ 7.6) and reacts readily with acids to produce CO₂, water, and the corresponding sodium salt. Because it releases CO₂ on mild heating or acidification, it is widely used as a leavening agent in baking, as an antacid, and in fire‑extinguishing powders. Its systematic place in the chapter is as a compound with a fixed stoichiometric ratio (1 Na: 1 H: 1 C: 3 O), contrasting with mixtures where components retain their individual proportions.
steps: Sodium hydrogen carbonate is a single pure compound with a fixed composition of one sodium, one hydrogen, one carbon and three oxygen atoms.
Here is why: the formula NaHCO₃ shows a definite 1:1:1:3 ratio that never changes, unlike a mixture where you can vary the amounts of salt and sugar.
First, recognise that the sodium ion (Na⁺) and the hydrogencarbonate ion (HCO₃⁻) combine in a 1:1 ratio to form a neutral crystal lattice.
Second, the hydrogencarbonate ion itself is a group of atoms that behaves as a unit; it contains hydrogen, carbon and oxygen covalently bonded, but the overall charge is –1.
Third, when you heat the solid, it breaks down in a predictable way: 2 NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, proving its composition is fixed.

Fourth, in the kitchen, adding a pinch of this powder to idli batter makes it rise because the acid in the batter (from fermentation) reacts with HCO₃⁻ to give CO₂ bubbles — a clear sign of a chemical reaction, not just…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Na₂CO₃) reveals the misconception that the “hydrogen” in the name means two sodium atoms, confusing sodium hydrogen carbonate with sodium carbonate.
remember: What is the chemical formula of sodium hydrogen carbonate.
Why is sodium hydrogen carbonate classified as a compound and not a mixture.
A student heats 10 g of sodium hydrogen carbonate and collects 4.4 g of carbon dioxide. Does this result support the decomposition reaction 2 NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

cards.title: An atom is defined as the smallest particle of an element that retains the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: An atom is defined as the smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical identity and properties of that element. It is the fundamental building block of matter; all elements — such as hydrogen, carbon, iron — consist of their respective atoms. Atoms of a given element are alike in mass and chemical behaviour, while atoms of different elements differ in these properties. Atoms combine in simple whole‑number ratios to form molecules (the smallest particles of a compound capable of independent existence) and radicals (charged groups of atoms that behave as a single unit). The concept of atomicity — mono‑atomic, di‑atomic, tri‑atomic, poly‑atomic — describes how many atoms constitute a molecule of an element or compound. Each element is represented by a unique symbol (e.g., H for hydrogen, O for oxygen) and occupies a specific position in the periodic table, which arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Valency, the combining capacity of an element, arises from the tendency of atoms to achieve a stable electron configuration. Understanding the atom as the indivisible unit in chemical reactions (though divisible in nuclear processes) links the macroscopic properties of substances to their microscopic composition.
steps: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still behaves like that element.
Here is why: first, every element such as gold, oxygen, or iron is made up of only one kind of atom, and that atom carries all the chemical characteristics of the element.
Second, atoms cannot be broken down further by ordinary chemical means without losing those characteristics; splitting an atom of gold yields sub‑atomic particles that no longer act like gold.
Third, atoms join together in fixed ratios to form molecules — for example, two oxygen atoms form an O₂ molecule — and the properties of the resulting substance depend on how the atoms are arranged.

Consider a familiar Indian kitchen: a single grain of salt (NaCl) contains many sodium and chlorine atoms bonded together; the smallest piece that still tastes salty is a molecule, but the smallest piece that is still…
In class, we can model this with LEGO bricks — each brick is an atom, a specific colour represents a specific element, and snapping bricks together makes molecules.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “an atom is a molecule”) reveals the misconception that the smallest unit of an element is a molecule, confusing the particle that represents an element with the particle that represents a compound.
remember: What is an atom.
Why can we not see atoms with the naked eye.
A student says, “An atom of gold can be divided into smaller pieces and still be gold.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The properties of an element — such as melting point, density, reactivity…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The properties of an element — such as melting point, density, reactivity, and electrical conductivity — are determined by the atoms that constitute it. Every atom of a given element has the same number of protons (its atomic number), which fixes its identity and governs its chemical behaviour. The arrangement of these atoms in the solid state (e.g., crystal lattice) influences physical properties; for example, carbon atoms arranged in a tetrahedral network form diamond, while the same atoms in layered sheets form graphite. Isotopes of an element have identical proton numbers but different neutron numbers, leading to nearly identical chemical properties but slightly different physical properties such as density and rate of diffusion. Thus, both the nuclear composition (proton count) and the spatial arrangement of atoms dictate the observable characteristics of an element.
steps: The properties of an element depend on the atoms that make it up. Here is why: first, each element has a unique number of protons in its nucleus, called the atomic number, which decides which element it is and how it…

Second, atoms of the same element can pack together in different ways; carbon atoms in a tight 3‑D network give diamond its extreme hardness, while the same atoms in flat sheets give graphite its slippery feel.

Third, atoms of an element may have different numbers of neutrons, forming isotopes; these isotopes behave almost identically in chemical reactions but can have slightly different densities or diffusion rates.

Consider a simple Indian kitchen example: copper vessels conduct heat quickly because copper atoms are arranged in a metallic lattice that lets electrons move freely, whereas clay pots (made of silicon‑oxygen compounds)…
In class, you can model this with coloured beads: same colour beads (same element) arranged in a line versus a triangle give different shapes, just as atomic arrangement changes material properties.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the number of neutrons decides chemical properties”) reveals the misconception that nuclear mass controls chemistry, confusing isotopes with different elements.
remember: What determines the chemical properties of an element.
Two samples of carbon — diamond and graphite — have very different hardness. Explain why, given they consist of the same atoms.
A student claims: “Changing the number of neutrons in an atom changes the element.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that can exist…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that can exist independently and still show all the properties of that substance. Divide any matter far enough and the molecules are the final stop at which the substance's identity survives: a molecule of water is wet-forming water in miniature; split that molecule further and the pieces are atoms of hydrogen and oxygen — real particles, but no longer water, with none of water's properties. For an ELEMENT, the molecule is built of atoms of one kind only — a molecule of oxygen holds two oxygen atoms joined together, so the element's smallest independent particle is already a partnership of identical atoms. For a COMPOUND, the molecule holds atoms of different kinds joined in a fixed ratio — a water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, always, which is why the compound's formula (H₂O) reads as the molecule's own signature. The deeper lesson of this node is the dependence of properties on constituting atoms: the properties of a substance flow from the atoms that make up its molecules and from the way those atoms are joined. Oxygen's two-atom molecule gives a reactive gas that supports burning; nitrogen's two-atom molecule gives a far less reactive gas; water's three-atom join gives a liquid that extinguishes burning — the same atoms (H and O) rearranged with others behave entirely differently, which is why the join, not just the list of atoms, decides the properties. Every substance the student has handled in this course — salt, sugar, chalk, iron (as atoms packed in metal), water — is ultimately a vast crowd of these tiny identity-keepers. Molecules are far too small to see: a single drop of water holds more water molecules than there are people on Earth many times over, which is why we learn about them through their collective behaviour rather than by direct sighting.
steps: The molecule is matter's smallest memory: cut matter down far enough and the molecule is the last particle that still knows which substance it belongs to.
First argument: the definition has two blades — independent existence and kept identity.

A water molecule can exist alone (in steam, drifting free) and it is still water in every property that matters at particle scale; that is why it, and not a smaller piece, deserves the name "particle of water".
Second argument: further division destroys identity.

Split the water molecule and you hold two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom — genuine particles, but nothing about them is wet, clear or drinkable; hydrogen alone burns fiercely and oxygen alone feeds burning, while…

Third argument: elements have molecules too. Oxygen's independent particle is not a single O atom but a joined pair, O₂; nitrogen drifts as N₂; some rare gases exist as single independent atoms (helium, neon) — their…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a molecule is the smallest particle of matter, period") reveals the misconception that molecules are defined only by smallness, missing the identity-keeping condition that decides why the molecule is the final stop for the substance.
remember: What is a molecule, in one complete definition.
A water molecule is split into its atoms. Are the products still water? Give the reasoning using properties.
Classify each as an elemental molecule or a compound molecule, and give the atom membership: (i) O₂, (ii) H₂O, (iii) N₂, (iv) CO₂.

cards.title: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that is capable…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that is capable of independent existence. It consists of one or more atoms of the same or different elements chemically bonded together. Molecules of elements contain only one type of atom (e.g., O₂, N₂, P₄), while molecules of compounds contain two or more different types of atoms in a fixed ratio (e.g., H₂O, CO₂, CH₄). The number of atoms in a molecule determines its atomicity: monoatomic (one atom, e.g., noble gases), diatomic (two atoms), triatomic (three atoms), or polyatomic (more than three atoms). A molecule retains the chemical properties of the substance it represents and can exist freely under normal conditions, unlike radicals which are charged and highly reactive. This concept builds on the idea that atoms are the basic building blocks (node) and that the properties of an element depend on its atoms (node). The previous node introduced the molecule as the smallest particle of an element or compound; this node emphasises its independent existence and atomic composition.
steps: A molecule is the smallest unit of an element or compound that can exist independently and is made of one or more atoms of the same or different elements.
Here is why: first, molecules can be formed from a single type of atom, like the oxygen (O₂) we inhale during pranayama, or from different atoms, like water (H₂O) in a glass of nimbu pani.
Second, the atoms in a molecule are held together by chemical bonds, giving the molecule a fixed composition — every water molecule always has two hydrogen and one oxygen atom.

Third, because they can exist on their own, molecules move freely in gases, liquids, and solids; for instance, the fragrance of incense spreads because its molecules travel through air. Fourth, the number of atoms in a…
Consider a classroom activity: give students molecular model kits — red balls for oxygen, white for hydrogen — and ask them to build O₂, H₂O, and CO₂.

They will see that O₂ uses two same-coloured balls, while H₂O uses two white and one red. This hands‑on experience connects the abstract definition to tangible models, reinforcing that a molecule’s identity comes from…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "A molecule is just a group of atoms") reveals the misconception that any collection of atoms qualifies, ignoring the requirement of independent existence and fixed composition.
remember: What is the definition of a molecule according to the ICSE Class 7 curriculum.
Explain why ozone (O₃) is considered a triatomic molecule while oxygen (O₂) is diatomic.
Evaluate the statement: "All molecules are compounds.".

cards.title: A radical is a single atom of an element or a group of atoms of different…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A radical is a single atom of an element or a group of atoms of different elements that behaves as a single charged unit in chemical reactions. It carries a net positive or negative charge because it has lost or gained electrons. Radicals are of two types: cationic radicals (positively charged, e.g., Na⁺, NH₄⁺) and anionic radicals (negatively charged, e.g., Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, OH⁻). Unlike neutral molecules, radicals do not exist independently for long; they combine with oppositely charged radicals or ions to form stable compounds. The concept of radicals links directly to valency — the charge on a radical equals its combining capacity — and to atomicity, because a radical may be mono‑atomic (one atom) or poly‑atomic (more than one atom). Understanding radicals is essential for writing correct chemical formulae and balanced ionic equations.
steps: A radical is a charged group of atoms that always moves together like a single team in a chemical reaction.
Here is why: first, radicals carry a net charge because they have lost or gained electrons, making them reactive partners.
Second, whether it is a single atom like Na⁺ or a cluster like SO₄²⁻, the whole unit keeps its identity and charge during combination.
Third, the charge on a radical tells us its valency — how many opposite charges it can neutralise.
Fourth, radicals are the building blocks of ionic compounds; for example, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ join to give NaCl, while Ca²⁺ and two NO₃⁻ give Ca(NO₃)₂.
Fifth, recognising radicals helps us write correct formulae without memorising every compound.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “a radical is a neutral molecule”) reveals the misconception that radicals are uncharged, confusing them with stable molecules.
remember: Define a radical and give one example each of a cationic and an anionic radical.
Why does the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) act as a single unit in reactions rather than as separate N and H atoms.
A student claims that Cl⁻ is not a radical because it consists of only one atom. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Atomicity is the number of atoms present in one molecule
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Atomicity is the number of atoms present in one molecule (or one independent entity) of a substance. The classification runs from the smallest upward. A mono-atomic entity has atomicity 1 — its molecule is a single atom that exists independently, as with the rare gases helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar), whose atoms need no partners; the same count applies to single-atom charged units such as the sodium radical Na⁺ or the chloride radical Cl⁻, which travel as one-atom teams. Di-atomic entities have atomicity 2 (O₂, N₂, H₂, Cl₂) and are treated fully in the next node; tri-atomic (ozone, O₃) and higher poly-atomic entities follow the same counting rule — phosphorus exists as P₄ (atomicity 4) and sulphur as S₈ (atomicity 8), which is why the same element can present different atomicities in different molecular forms. A radical is a group of atoms of different elements that behaves as a single charged unit — it carries one electric charge as a whole, travels together, and enters and leaves reactions as one team; examples are the sulphate radical SO₄²⁻ (five atoms: 1 sulphur + 4 oxygen), the nitrate radical NO₃⁻ (four atoms), the carbonate radical CO₃²⁻ (four atoms), the hydroxide radical OH⁻ (two atoms) and the ammonium radical NH₄⁺ (five atoms). A radical therefore also has an atomicity — the number of atoms in its group — and reading a formula like Na₂SO₄ correctly means seeing the radical as ONE unit joined to the sodium atoms, not as separate atoms floating loose. Atomicity thus gives chemistry its first counting grammar: every independent entity — atom, molecule or radical — has a head-count, and formulas record those head-counts precisely.
steps: Atomicity is chemistry's head-count: every independent entity — lone atom, joined molecule, or travelling radical team — has a definite number of members, and formulas record that number exactly.
First argument: the smallest head-count is one. Helium, neon and argon are complete, contented single atoms — no molecule-building needed; their atomicity is 1, and their atom IS their molecule.
The same count applies to charged loners: the sodium radical Na⁺ and chloride radical Cl⁻ are one-atom teams that carry a single charge each.
Mono-atomic does not mean unimportant — these loners fill balloons with birthday-floating gas and light our city signs with glow.
Second argument: the head-count depends on the company the element keeps.
Oxygen travels as a pair (O₂, atomicity 2) in air, but in the strange-smelling ozone layer it travels as a trio (O₃, atomicity 3); sulphur builds eight-member rings (S₈); phosphorus foursomes (P₄).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving O₃ the atomicity 1 because "it is one substance") reveals the misconception of counting substances instead of atoms — atomicity counts ATOMS inside ONE entity, never the number of substances.
remember: Define atomicity and give the atomicity of: He, O₂, O₃, S₈.
What is a radical? State the atomicity of the sulphate radical and of the hydroxide radical, with their atom membership.
In one unit of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), what is joined to what? Give the reading in words and the total number of atoms per unit.

cards.title: A di‑atomic entity is a molecule or elemental form that contains precisely two…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A di‑atomic entity is a molecule or elemental form that contains precisely two atoms chemically bonded. The term “di‑atomic” comes from the Greek di (two) and atomic (relating to atoms). In the context of atomicity — the number of atoms constituting a discrete particle — di‑atomic species have an atomicity of 2. Key relationships: - Elemental di‑atomic molecules: Seven non‑metal elements exist naturally as di‑atomic gases at room temperature — hydrogen (H₂), nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), fluorine (F₂), chlorine (Cl₂), bromine (Br₂, liquid) and iodine (I₂, solid). Their molecules consist of two identical atoms joined by a covalent bond. - Compound di‑atomic molecules: Some binary compounds also contain only two atoms, e.g., carbon monoxide (CO), hydrogen chloride (HCl), nitric oxide (NO). These are heteronuclear di‑atomic molecules because the two atoms are different elements. - Atomicity classification: Atomicity = 1 → mono‑atomic; = 2 → di‑atomic (this node); = 3 → tri‑atomic; >3 → poly‑atomic. - Properties: Di‑atomic gases are typically colourless, odourless (except Cl₂, Br₂, I₂), and have relatively low melting/boiling points because only weak van der Waals forces act between molecules. Their chemical reactivity depends on bond strength; for example, the H–H bond (436 kJ mol⁻¹) is strong, making H₂ relatively inert at room temperature, whereas the F–F bond (158 kJ mol⁻¹) is weak, so F₂ is extremely reactive. Understanding di‑atomic species is essential for writing correct chemical formulae, balancing equations, and later learning about molecular geometry and bond enthalpies.
steps: Di‑atomic molecules are the simplest stable molecules made of two atoms.
Here is why: two atoms can share electrons to achieve a full outer shell, forming a covalent bond that holds them together as a single particle.
Consider the oxygen we breathe: each oxygen atom has six valence electrons and needs two more; by sharing two electrons each, two O atoms form a double bond (O=O) and become O₂, a di‑atomic molecule.
First, recall that atomicity counts atoms in one particle.

Mono‑atomic particles (like He, Ne) contain one atom; di‑atomic contain two. The seven elemental di‑atomic gases are often remembered by the mnemonic “HONClBrIF” (Hydrogen, Oxygen, Nitrogen, Chlorine, Bromine, Iodine…
All exist as X₂ at standard conditions except bromine (liquid) and iodine (solid), but they are still di‑atomic molecules.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “He, Ne, Ar”) reveals the misconception that noble gases are di‑atomic; they are mono‑atomic because they have complete valence shells and do not form X₂ molecules under normal conditions.
remember: Name three elemental di‑atomic gases at room temperature and write their chemical formulae.
Explain why chlorine (Cl₂) is a gas at room temperature while bromine (Br₂) is a liquid, even though both are di‑atomic halogens.
A student writes the formula for hydrogen gas as “H”. Evaluate this error and state the correct representation.

cards.title: A triatomic molecule is a discrete chemical species composed of exactly three…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A triatomic molecule is a discrete chemical species composed of exactly three atoms that are chemically bonded together. The term “atomicity” refers to the number of atoms present in one molecule of an element or compound; for triatomic species the atomicity is three. The three atoms may be of the same element, as in ozone (O₃), or of different elements, as in water (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and hydrogen sulfide (H₂S). Triatomic molecules are distinct from monoatomic (single atom, e.g., noble gases), diatomic (two atoms, e.g., O₂, N₂) and polyatomic (more than three atoms, e.g., P₄, S₈) species. They can exist as stable gases, liquids or solids under normal conditions and participate in chemical reactions as whole units. The concept of atomicity helps in writing correct chemical formulas, balancing equations and understanding stoichiometric relationships. In the periodic table, the first 20 elements include several that form triatomic molecules (e.g., O₃, CO₂, H₂O, SO₂). Recognising triatomic species is a stepping stone to classifying molecular substances by atomicity.
steps: A triatomic molecule consists of exactly three atoms chemically bonded together, giving it an atomicity of three.
Here is why: atomicity counts atoms in a molecule, not the number of different elements.
Consider ozone (O₃) — three oxygen atoms share electrons to form a single molecule that protects us from ultraviolet radiation.
Next, water (H₂O) has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; it is the liquid we drink and the steam that rises from a hot cup of chai.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) contains one carbon and two oxygen atoms; it is the gas we exhale and the fizz in a cold soda.
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) are other triatomic gases with distinct smells.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “atomicity is two because there are two elements”) reveals the misconception that atomicity counts distinct elements rather than total atoms.
remember: What is the atomicity of a triatomic molecule.
Which of the following is a triatomic molecule: O₂, CO₂, N₂, H₂.
A student says ozone (O₃) is diatomic because it contains only oxygen atoms. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A polyatomic entity is a molecule or ion that consists of four or more atoms…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A polyatomic entity is a molecule or ion that consists of four or more atoms chemically bonded together, behaving as a single unit during chemical reactions. The term “polyatomic” literally means “many atoms”. In the context of atomicity, entities are classified as mono‑atomic (1 atom), di‑atomic (2 atoms), tri‑atomic (3 atoms) and polyatomic (≥ 4 atoms). Polyatomic molecules may be composed of atoms of the same element (e.g., P₄, S₈) or different elements (e.g., H₂SO₄, NH₄⁺, CO₃²⁻). When a group of atoms carries an overall charge and acts as a single charged unit, it is called a polyatomic radical or polyatomic ion (e.g., nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺). The properties of a polyatomic entity — such as its reactivity, solubility, and the type of bonds it forms — depend on the arrangement and nature of its constituent atoms and the overall charge if it is an ion. Understanding polyatomic species is essential for writing correct chemical formulae, balancing equations, and predicting the products of reactions involving acids, bases, and salts.
steps: Polyatomic entities contain four or more atoms bonded together and behave as a single unit in chemical reactions.
Here is why: the definition of atomicity extends naturally from mono‑, di‑, and tri‑atomic species; once we pass three atoms we simply use the prefix “poly‑” (many).
Consider the element phosphorus — it exists as P₄, a tetra‑atomic molecule where four phosphorus atoms form a tetrahedral ring.
Sulphur forms S₈, an eight‑atom crown.
Both are polyatomic molecules because they are neutral and contain only one element.
Now look at sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄: it has two hydrogen, one sulphur, and four oxygen atoms — seven atoms in total — making it a polyatomic molecule of a compound.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing CO₂) reveals the misconception that any compound with more than one element is automatically polyatomic, ignoring the atom‑count rule.
remember: Which of the following species is polyatomic? A) O₂ B) CO₂ C) NH₄⁺ D) He.
Explain why the sulfate ion (SO₄²⁻) is classified as a polyatomic ion rather than a polyatomic molecule.
A student writes the formula of phosphorus tetramer as P₄ and says “this is a tri‑atomic molecule because it has four atoms”. Evaluate the statement.

cards.title: The first twenty elements of the periodic table are the building blocks most…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The first twenty elements of the periodic table are the building blocks most often encountered in Class 7 chemistry. Each element has a unique name and a one‑ or two‑letter symbol derived from its English or Latin name (e.g., hydrogen → H, helium → He, sodium → Na from natrium, potassium → K from kalium). The symbols are universally accepted by chemists and appear in every chemical formula, equation, and periodic‑table chart. Knowing these twenty name‑symbol pairs allows a student to identify elements in compounds, write correct formulas, and begin to understand valency and bonding. The list proceeds in order of increasing atomic number: 1 H, 2 He, 3 Li, 4 Be, 5 B, 6 C, 7 N, 8 O, 9 F, 10 Ne, 11 Na, 12 Mg, 13 Al, 14 Si, 15 P, 16 S, 17 Cl, 18 Ar, 19 K, 20 Ca. Mastery of this set is a prerequisite for writing balanced equations, interpreting the periodic table, and applying valency rules in later chapters.
steps: The one thing to remember is that each of the first twenty elements has a fixed, internationally agreed symbol that never changes.
Here is why: symbols act as a universal shorthand so chemists worldwide can communicate without language barriers.
First, notice that most symbols are the first one or two letters of the English name (H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne).
Second, a few come from Latin roots: Na (natrium), K (kalium), and the two‑letter symbols always have the first letter capitalised and the second lower‑case (Mg, Al, Si, Cl, Ar, Ca).
Third, the order of the elements follows increasing atomic number, which is the number of protons in the nucleus; this order is the backbone of the periodic table.
Fourth, once you know the symbols, you can read any simple formula: H₂O tells you two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “So” or “S”) reveals the misconception that symbols are always derived from the English name, ignoring the historical Latin origins for several elements.
remember: What is the chemical symbol for sodium.
If you see the symbol “K” on a periodic table, which element does it represent and why is the symbol not “P”.
A student writes the symbol for magnesium as “Mg” and for manganese as “Mn”. Are both symbols correct? Evaluate.

cards.title: Valency is the combining capacity of an element…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Valency is the combining capacity of an element — the number of hydrogen atoms with which one atom of the element combines, or which it replaces. Hydrogen, the reference element, has valency 1; chlorine combines with one hydrogen (HCl), so chlorine's valency is 1; oxygen combines with two hydrogens (H₂O), so its valency is 2; nitrogen with three (NH₃) gives valency 3; carbon with four (CH₄) gives valency 4. Some metals are measured by replacement instead: zinc displaces two hydrogens from dilute acid, marking valency 2. The valency ladder for the first twenty elements runs: H 1; He 0; Li, Na, K 1; Be, Mg, Ca 2; B, Al 3; C, Si 4; N, P 3 (phosphorus also 5); O, S 2; F, Cl 1; Ne, Ar 0 — with the noble gases at 0 because their atoms combine with nothing. Radicals carry group valencies: hydroxide (OH) 1, nitrate (NO₃) 1, ammonium (NH₄) 1, sulphate (SO₄) 2, carbonate (CO₃) 2. Valency is the key that unlocks formula-writing: since the total holding-hands must balance, formulas are built by exchanging valencies — aluminium (3) with oxygen (2) gives Al₂O₃, calcium (2) with chlorine (1) gives CaCl₂, sodium (1) with the sulphate team (2) gives Na₂SO₄ — each formula reading as a balanced trade of holding-hands. A few elements show variable valency: iron 2 and 3 (giving FeS-type and Fe₂O₃-type joins), copper 1 and 2, phosphorus 3 and 5; the name often signals which valency is at work (ferric versus ferrous). Valency thus connects this chapter's earlier ideas: atoms (the holders), molecules (the joins), radicals (the teams) — and hands over to the periodic table, where the valency pattern reappears as a column-wise rhythm.
steps: Valency is the holding-hands number: every atom (or radical team) brings a fixed number of hands to chemistry's marriage market, and every formula is a handshake ledger that must balance.
First argument: hydrogen is the measuring stick.

One hydrogen holds one hand; so an atom that pairs with exactly one hydrogen (chlorine in HCl) has valency 1, an atom that holds two (oxygen in H₂O) has 2, three (nitrogen in NH₃) has 3, four (carbon in CH₄) has 4.
The same scale works by replacement: drop a zinc strip into dilute acid and each zinc atom yanks two hydrogens out — zinc's valency is 2.
Second argument: the first twenty elements arrange themselves on a small ladder.
One-hand elements: Li, Na, K (and F, Cl).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "oxygen's valency is 1 because one oxygen atom joins the molecule") reveals the misconception of counting atoms-in-the-formula instead of counting the hydrogen-holding hands that define the measure.
remember: Define valency and state the valency of chlorine, oxygen and nitrogen using their hydrogen compounds.
Write the formula of the compound of aluminium (valency 3) and oxygen (valency 2) by exchanging valencies, and verify the balance by the hands-product check.
An element X combines with exactly two hydrogen atoms per atom of X. (i) State X's….

cards.title: The periodic table is a systematic arrangement of all known chemical elements…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The periodic table is a systematic arrangement of all known chemical elements in order of increasing atomic number (the number of protons in the nucleus). It consists of horizontal rows called periods and vertical columns called groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, which gives them similar chemical properties and valency trends. The first 20 elements (hydrogen to calcium) occupy the first three periods and groups 1, 2, and 13‑18. Metals appear on the left and centre, non‑metals on the right, and metalloids lie along a stair‑step line. The table reflects the periodic law: properties of elements repeat at regular intervals when arranged by atomic number. This node links the atomic structure concepts (atom, molecule, atomicity, valency) to a visual framework that predicts reactivity, bonding, and compound formation. Sibling nodes cover the names and symbols of the first 20 elements and the definition of valency; this node focuses on the table’s layout, period/group significance, and how position guides valency and metallic character.
steps: The periodic table is a map that places every element in a unique box determined by its atomic number, and this position instantly tells you its group, period, and likely valency.

Here is why: the atomic number fixes the number of protons and electrons, which decides how many electrons occupy the outermost shell; elements with the same outer‑electron count fall in the same vertical group and…
Consider the first three periods: Period 1 has only H and He (1 shell), Period 2 adds Li to Ne (2 shells), Period 3 adds Na to Ar (3 shells).
In Group 1 (alkali metals) each element has one valence electron, giving valency 1; in Group 17 (halogens) each has seven valence electrons, typically gaining one electron to show valency 1.
The stair‑step line from B to At separates metals (left) from non‑metals (right); elements touching the line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) are metalloids with mixed properties.
To use the table, first find the atomic number, then read across to the period (row) and up/down to the group (column).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "elements are arranged by atomic mass") reveals the misconception that Mendeleev’s original mass‑based ordering is still used, ignoring the modern definition based on proton count.
remember: What is the fundamental basis for the arrangement of elements in the modern periodic table.
Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table exhibit similar chemical properties.
A student claims, "The periodic table has only eight groups because there are eight columns." Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A valency card is a concise learning tool that displays three essential pieces…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A valency card is a concise learning tool that displays three essential pieces of information for an element: its name (e.g., Carbon), its chemical symbol (C), and its valency (4). Valency is defined as the combining capacity of an element, measured by the number of hydrogen atoms (valency 1) with which one atom of the element can combine or replace. For the first 20 elements of the periodic table, valencies are typically fixed and follow the pattern of group number for main‑group elements (e.g., Group 1 → 1, Group 2 → 2, Group 13 → 3, Group 14 → 4, Group 15 → 3, Group 16 → 2, Group 17 → 1, Group 18 → 0). The card format reinforces the link between an element’s position in the periodic table, its atomicity (mono‑, di‑, tri‑, poly‑atomic), and its behaviour in forming molecules and radicals. By creating a physical or digital deck of these cards, students internalise the periodic trends and can later use the cards to predict formulas of simple binary compounds (e.g., using H valency 1 and O valency 2 gives H₂O). This node focuses solely on constructing and interpreting the cards; writing chemical formulas using the cards is covered in the next node.
steps: A valency card is a compact reference that shows an element’s name, symbol, and valency, letting you quickly see how it combines with others.
Here is why: the periodic table arranges elements so that their valencies follow a clear pattern; a card makes that pattern portable and memorable.
First, the card format mirrors the way we learn cricket stats — name, jersey number, batting average — so the analogy sticks.
Second, the first 20 elements cover all the main‑group patterns needed for Class 7 chemistry.
Third, knowing the valency of each element lets you predict formulas without memorising each compound.
Consider you are given a blank card template.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “atomic number, mass number, valency”) reveals the misconception that a valency card is a periodic table entry rather than a focused combining‑capacity tool.
remember: What three pieces of information must appear on a valency card for an element.
If an element is in Group 16 of the periodic table, what is its typical valency and why.
Evaluate the statement: “A valency card for neon should show valency 8 because it is in Group 18.”.

cards.title: A chemical symbol is a one- or two-letter abbreviation that uniquely identifies…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical symbol is a one- or two-letter abbreviation that uniquely identifies an element; the first letter is always capitalised and the second, if present, is lowercase (e.g., H, He, Na). Symbols often derive from the English name (O for oxygen) or the Latin name (Na for natrium, Fe for ferrum). Valency is the combining capacity of an element, defined as the number of hydrogen atoms (valency = 1) that one atom of the element can combine with or replace. For the first 20 elements, typical valencies are: H = 1, He = 0, Li = 1, Be = 2, B = 3, C = 4, N = 3, O = 2, F = 1, Ne = 0, Na = 1, Mg = 2, Al = 3, Si = 4, P = 3/5, S = 2/4/6, Cl = 1, Ar = 0, K = 1, Ca = 2. Valency arises from the tendency to achieve a stable electron configuration (usually an octet). When writing formulas, the total positive valency must balance the total negative valency; the simplest whole‑number ratio gives the empirical formula. Radicals (e.g., OH⁻, NO₃⁻) also possess a net valency equal to their charge magnitude. This node links each element’s symbol to its common valency, enabling formula writing for binary compounds and simple radicals.
steps: The symbol and valency of an element together act as its chemical identity card, allowing us to predict how it will combine with other elements.

Here is why: a symbol is a universal shorthand that avoids language barriers; valency quantifies the element’s bonding power; and the cross‑multiplication rule translates these two pieces of data into a correct formula.
Consider the first 20 elements arranged in the periodic table.
Each has a unique symbol — H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca — and a typical valency derived from its group number (for main‑group elements) or common chemistry.
For instance, carbon (group 14) shows valency 4, nitrogen (group 15) shows 3, oxygen (group 16) shows 2, and halogens (group 17) show 1.
Noble gases have valency 0 because they rarely combine.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P” or “Po”) reveals the misconception that symbols always follow the English name’s initial letters, ignoring Latin derivations.
remember: What is the chemical symbol for potassium.
Why does oxygen typically exhibit a valency of 2.
A student writes the formula of calcium chloride as CaCl. Is this correct? Explain.

cards.title: A chemical reaction occurs when two or more reactants come into physical…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical reaction occurs when two or more reactants come into physical contact, allowing their particles (atoms, ions, or molecules) to collide and rearrange. During this process, chemical bonds break and new bonds form, resulting in products with different properties. Energy is always transferred: reactions may release energy (exothermic, e.g., combustion of methane) or absorb energy (endothermic, e.g., dissolving ammonium nitrate in water). The transfer can appear as heat, light, sound, or electrical energy. For a reaction to start, reactants must be close enough for effective collisions (collision theory) and possess at least the minimum activation energy. In Class 7 ICSE Chemistry, we observe simple reactions such as dilute hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium carbonate to evolve carbon dioxide gas, noting colour change, gas evolution, temperature change, and precipitate formation as evidence. The concept links to the law of conservation of mass — total mass of reactants equals total mass of products — and introduces the idea that energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed.
steps: A chemical reaction only happens when reactants touch each other and energy moves between them.
Here is why: reactants must collide to break old bonds and form new ones; without contact, no collision occurs.
Energy is needed to start the rearrangement (activation energy) and is released or absorbed as bonds change.
Consider the classic classroom demonstration: a teacher adds dilute hydrochloric acid to solid sodium carbonate in a test tube.
Immediately, bubbles of carbon dioxide rise, the tube feels warm, and a clear solution forms.
The acid and carbonate were separate solids and liquids; only when poured together did they contact, react, and transfer heat to the surroundings.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “reactants just need to be in the same room”) reveals the misconception that spatial closeness alone is enough, ignoring the necessity of actual particle‑level contact and energy input.
remember: What must happen for a chemical reaction to start between two substances.
During the reaction of dilute HCl with Na₂CO₃, a student observes bubbles, a temperature rise, and a clear solution. Which observation directly indicates gas evolution.
A student claims that mixing solid salt and solid sugar in a bowl will cause a chemical reaction because they are in contact. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A chemical reaction occurs when reactants come into contact and energy is…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical reaction occurs when reactants come into contact and energy is transferred, leading to the formation of new substances called products. The occurrence of a reaction is recognised by specific observable characteristics. The most common characteristics are: (1) evolution of a gas, seen as bubbles or effervescence; (2) change in colour of the reaction mixture; (3) formation of a precipitate, an insoluble solid that separates from the solution; (4) change in temperature, either a rise (exothermic) or a fall (endothermic); (5) emission of light or flame. These signs indicate that bonds in reactants have broken and new bonds have formed in products. The transfer of energy may be in the form of heat, light, or electricity. Not every contact between substances produces a reaction; the reactants must have sufficient energy (activation energy) and proper orientation. The characteristics listed are qualitative indicators used in the laboratory to confirm that a chemical change has taken place. They are distinct from physical changes, which do not produce new substances and usually show only changes of state or shape without the above signs. Understanding these characteristics builds the foundation for writing chemical equations and for quantitative study of reactions in later chapters.
steps: A chemical reaction announces itself through clear, observable changes such as gas bubbles, colour shifts, precipitate formation, temperature variation, or light emission.

Here is why: each characteristic reflects a specific molecular event — gas evolution shows a gaseous product forming; colour change indicates a new coloured species; precipitate formation means an insoluble product…
Consider the classic test‑tube demonstration where dilute hydrochloric acid is added to solid sodium carbonate.
Immediately, colourless gas bubbles rise (carbon dioxide), the solution may turn slightly cloudy if a fine precipitate forms, and the test tube feels warm — an exothermic temperature rise.
In another activity, mixing potassium iodide solution with lead nitrate solution yields a bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide, a vivid colour change from colourless to yellow.

A third example: adding water to quicklime (calcium oxide) produces a vigorous hiss, the mixture becomes hot, and a white solid (calcium hydroxide) forms — showing both temperature rise and precipitate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any visible change like bubbling must be chemical, confusing physical effervescence (e.g., boiling water) with chemical gas evolution.
remember: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic sign of a chemical….
A student mixes two colourless solutions and observes a yellow solid….
During a reaction the test tube becomes noticeably….

cards.title: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction that…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction that uses element symbols, compound formulae, and state symbols (s, l, g, aq) to show the transformation of reactants into products. The reactants are written on the left of an arrow (→) and the products on the right. Coefficients (whole numbers placed before formulae) balance the equation so that the number of atoms of each element is identical on both sides, obeying the law of conservation of mass. State symbols indicate the physical state of each substance at reaction conditions. Observational skills — noting gas evolution, precipitate formation, colour change, temperature change — allow the learner to infer the identities of products before writing the equation. Practice with word equations, skeleton equations, and fully balanced equations builds fluency in translating laboratory observations into precise chemical language.
steps: A balanced chemical equation is the concise, universal language that turns what you see in a test tube into a precise statement of mass conservation.
Here is why: the law of conservation of mass demands that every atom present before the reaction appears again after it, so the equation must show equal numbers of each element on both sides.
First, write a word equation from the observation — e.g., “magnesium + dilute hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen gas”.
Second, replace each name with its correct chemical formula, adding state symbols (Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)).

Third, count atoms on each side; if they differ, place the smallest whole‑number coefficients in front of formulae until every element balances — never change subscripts because that would alter the substance itself.
Fourth, double‑check: magnesium 1→1, hydrogen 2→2, chlorine 2→2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “zinc + sulphuric acid → zinc oxide + water”) reveals the misconception that acids always produce oxides or water, confusing acid‑metal reactions with combustion.
remember: Write the word equation for the reaction observed when a strip of zinc metal is placed in dilute sulphuric acid, producing a colourless gas and a colourless solution.
Given the skeleton equation Fe(s) + H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + H₂(g), explain why the coefficient 3 must be placed before Fe on the reactant side.
A student writes the balanced equation for the reaction of sodium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid as Na₂CO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O +….

cards.title: The demonstration involves adding a dilute acid
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The demonstration involves adding a dilute acid (commonly dilute hydrochloric acid) to solid sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) in a test tube. Upon contact, a chemical reaction occurs: sodium carbonate reacts with the acid to produce sodium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide gas. The evolution of gas is observed as vigorous bubbling (effervescence). The reaction is exothermic, so the test tube may feel warm. A burner may be used to gently heat the mixture to accelerate the reaction, though the reaction proceeds readily at room temperature. The gas evolved can be identified by passing it through lime water (calcium hydroxide solution), which turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate. This demonstration illustrates key characteristics of a chemical reaction: gas evolution, temperature change, and formation of new substances. It also provides a concrete context for writing word equations and, later, balanced chemical equations. The apparatus includes a test tube, a dropper or pipette for adding the dilute acid, and optionally a Bunsen burner for heating. Safety precautions include wearing eye protection and handling acids carefully. The demonstration links prior knowledge of reactants and products (from earlier nodes) to observational skills and the language of chemistry.
steps: The demonstration of adding dilute acid to solid sodium carbonate in a test tube is a classic, reliable way to see a chemical reaction in action because it produces obvious gas bubbles and a temperature change.
Here is why: first, the reactants are a solid carbonate and an aqueous acid, which are easy to handle and safe in small quantities.
Second, the reaction is fast at room temperature, so students see immediate effervescence without needing strong heating.
Third, the gas produced is carbon dioxide, which has a simple, confirmatory test (lime water turns milky) that reinforces observational skills.
Fourth, the reaction is exothermic, letting students feel the test tube warm up, linking energy transfer to chemical change.
Fifth, the word equation uses familiar names (sodium carbonate, hydrochloric acid, sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide), bridging everyday language to chemical language.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “oxygen” or “hydrogen”) reveals the misconception that any gas from an acid reaction must be oxygen or hydrogen, confusing acid–carbonate reactions with acid–metal or decomposition reactions.
remember: What gas is evolved when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to solid sodium carbonate in a test tube.
Why does the reaction produce bubbles when dilute acid is added to sodium carbonate.
A student claims the gas evolved is oxygen because it supports combustion. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Solid sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) is an ionic crystalline compound composed of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Solid sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) is an ionic crystalline compound composed of two sodium cations (Na⁺) and one carbonate anion (CO₃²⁻). Its molar mass is 106 g mol⁻¹. In the solid state it appears as a white, odourless powder that is readily soluble in water, forming an alkaline solution. As a carbonate, it follows the general acid–carbonate reaction pattern: when it contacts a dilute acid (e.g., HCl), a double‑displacement reaction occurs producing a salt (NaCl), water, and carbon dioxide gas. The balanced chemical equation is Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). The evolution of CO₂ bubbles provides a clear, observable indication that a chemical reaction has taken place, linking directly to the characteristics of chemical reactions (gas evolution, temperature change, colour change) and to the practice of writing chemical equations from observations. In the classroom demonstration the teacher adds dilute HCl to a small amount of solid Na₂CO₃ in a test tube; the immediate fizzing and the subsequent milky lime‑water test confirm the identity of the gas. This node focuses on the properties of the solid reactant, its role in the demonstration, and the stoichiometric relationships that allow quantitative predictions of product amounts.
steps: Solid sodium carbonate reacts with dilute acids to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and a salt, providing a clear observable sign of a chemical reaction.
First, Na₂CO₃ is a carbonate; all carbonates react with acids in a predictable pattern, releasing CO₂.
Second, the gas evolution (fizzing) is one of the classic characteristics of a chemical reaction taught earlier.
Third, the balanced equation Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ shows a 1:1 mole ratio between Na₂CO₃ and CO₂, enabling quantitative work.
Fourth, the lime‑water test (Ca(OH)₂ turning milky) confirms the gas is CO₂, reinforcing observational skills.
Fifth, the demonstration uses only a test tube, a burner for gentle heating if needed, and dilute acid, making it safe and repeatable.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., NaCO₃) reveals the misconception that the carbonate ion carries a –1 charge, confusing it with bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻).
remember: What is the chemical formula of solid sodium carbonate.
Why does solid Na₂CO₃ fizz when dilute HCl is added.
Compare the reaction of Na₂CO₃ with dilute HCl and with dilute H₂SO₄. Which observation would be the same and which would differ.

cards.title: Sodium acetate, formula CH₃COONa (written compactly as NaCH₃COO or NaOAc)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Sodium acetate, formula CH₃COONa (written compactly as NaCH₃COO or NaOAc), is the sodium salt of acetic acid — the white crystalline, highly water-soluble solid that remains in solution after the famous vinegar-plus-baking-soda reaction has spent its fizz. Its formation equation tells its origin story: acetic acid (CH₃COOH, the acid in vinegar) reacts with sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃, baking soda) to give sodium acetate, water, and carbon dioxide gas — CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ — so the dramatic effervescence that fills the classroom is only the departure of the gas, while the quiet, important product is the salt left dissolved in the liquid. The atom audit certifies the equation: CH₃COOH holds 2 carbons and NaHCO₃ holds 1 — 3 carbons on the left; the right side holds 2 carbons in CH₃COONa and 1 in CO₂ — 3 carbons, with hydrogens (4 + 1 = 5 left; 3 + 2 = 5 right), oxygens (2 + 3 = 5 left; 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 right) and the sodium (1 = 1) all matching. As a substance, sodium acetate is a white, odourless crystalline solid, strongly soluble in water, with a mildly alkaline reaction in solution (the opposite character to the acid that made it). Its celebrated party trick and industrial virtue is supersaturation: a hot concentrated solution cooled carefully holds MORE dissolved salt than cold water should allow, and a single seed crystal or a sharp tap makes the excess crystallise instantly — a chain of white "needles" spreading through the liquid while heat is given out. This is why sodium acetate fills reusable hand-warmers and is used in textile dyeing and as a food additive. Within this chapter, sodium acetate completes the vinegar-baking-soda story begun in the demonstration nodes: every fizz the student has watched was the birth-cry of a salt they can now name, write, and audit.
steps: Sodium acetate is the quiet hero of the loudest experiment in school chemistry: while everyone watches the gas escape, the salt is born and stays.
First argument: read the reaction as a birth record, not a fireworks show.

Acetic acid from vinegar meets sodium bicarbonate; the acid's hydrogen and the bicarbonate's carbonate-hydrogen pair off into water, the carbonate's carbon and oxygens leave as carbon dioxide gas, and the sodium joins…
The fizz is the by-product's exit; the salt is the product's arrival.
Second argument: the equation is audited like any other.
Carbons: 2 in the acid + 1 in the bicarbonate = 3; right side 2 in the salt + 1 in the gas = 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the only product is the gas, since that is all that is seen") reveals the misconception of equating the most dramatic observation with the most important product; the gas is the by-product that leaves, and the salt is what the reaction…
remember: Name the three products of the vinegar-baking-soda reaction, and state which one remains in the liquid after the fizzing stops.
Run the complete atom audit on: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
A hand-warmer pouch is boiled to dissolve all its sodium acetate, cooled to room temperature, and then….

cards.title: A test tube is a cylindrical piece of borosilicate glass…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A test tube is a cylindrical piece of borosilicate glass, typically 10–20 cm long and 1–2 cm in internal diameter, with a rounded bottom and an open top. Borosilicate glass (low coefficient of thermal expansion) resists thermal shock, so the tube can be heated directly over a Bunsen burner or in a water bath without cracking. The open top allows gases to escape and lets a student observe colour changes, precipitate formation, or effervescence. Test tubes are used for qualitative reactions (e.g., adding dilute acid to solid Na₂CO₃ to see CO₂ evolution), for small‑scale heating, and for temporary storage of reagents. They are held with a test‑tube holder or clamped to a retort stand; never held by hand while heating. After use they are rinsed with water, then with distilled water, and placed upside‑down on a rack to dry. The test tube’s simple geometry makes it ideal for demonstrating the characteristics of a chemical reaction — gas evolution, colour change, temperature change — while keeping the quantities small enough to be safe for a Class 7 laboratory.
steps: A test tube is a small, heat‑resistant glass tube that lets us safely hold, heat, and observe tiny amounts of chemicals during a reaction.

Here is why: first, its borosilicate glass expands very little when heated, so sudden temperature changes do not shatter it. Second, the rounded bottom distributes heat evenly and prevents a solid from lodging in a…
Third, the open top gives a clear view of any gas bubbles, colour shifts, or precipitate forming — exactly the observational skills the chapter emphasises.
Fourth, the narrow diameter means only a few millilitres of reagent are needed, keeping the experiment safe and economical.
Consider the teacher’s demonstration: a pinch of solid sodium carbonate is placed in a clean test tube, a few drops of dilute acetic acid are added, and carbon dioxide bubbles rise instantly.
The student watches the effervescence, notes the gas evolution, and later writes the word equation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “soda‑lime glass”) reveals the misconception that any clear glass can be heated directly — soda‑lime glass shatters under thermal shock.
remember: What material is a standard laboratory test tube made of.
Why is borosilicate glass preferred over ordinary glass for test tubes.
A student wants to heat a solid sample strongly in a test tube. Evaluate whether a plain test tube held with bare hands is safe.

cards.title: A burner is a laboratory device that burns fuel to produce a steady…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A burner is a laboratory device that burns fuel to produce a steady, controllable flame used for heating, boiling, and carrying out reactions that need warmth — the heat source on which every "gently warm" instruction in practical chemistry depends. Two burners matter at this level. The spirit lamp (spirit burner) is the simplest: a small glass or metal reservoir holding methylated spirit (denatured alcohol), a metal collar at the mouth from which a wick rises, and a tight cap to extinguish the flame and stop evaporation. Lighting it means lighting the tip of the wet wick; putting it out means capping it (starving the flame of air), never blowing it, which can push flame down into the reservoir. The Bunsen burner is the precision instrument: a heavy base for stability, a gas inlet joined to the bench gas tap through rubber tubing, a needle valve (or screw) controlling how much gas flows, a collar with an adjustable air hole that controls how much air mixes with the gas, and a vertical metal barrel (chimney) where the mixture burns. The air hole is the burner's personality switch.
