cards.title: Row and column operations are the structural edits of the grid…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Row and column operations are the structural edits of the grid: INSERT (a new empty row or column appears at the chosen position, and everything beyond slides down or right to make room), DELETE (a whole row or column and its every cell are removed, and everything beyond slides up or left to close the gap), and RESIZE (a row's height or a column's width is changed — widened to show a long name, auto-fitted to its widest entry, or set by drag). THE MECHANICS, precisely: insertion happens ABOVE the selected row or LEFT of the selected column (select row 5, insert — a new row 5 appears and the old row 5 becomes row 6); deletion removes the ENTIRE row or column (chosen by clicking its header — the numbered strip for rows, the lettered strip for columns), not merely its cells; and after either operation every address in the grid RE-NUMBERS — the register's geography shifts to stay gapless, because a spreadsheet's rows and columns are always contiguous. THE DEEP CONSEQUENCE — formulas survive intelligently, usually: a total reading C2:C31 stretches to C2:C32 when a student-row is inserted inside its span, and shrinks honestly when a row inside it is deleted — the references track their CONTENT. But delete a column that a formula points at DIRECTLY (its own operand, not inside a range) and the formula's subject is gone: the cell shows #REF! — the invalid-reference error, the eraser's echo — and every cell reading THAT cell inherits the cry. THE HONEST PRACTICE that precedes every structural edit: select the header (whole row/column), pause, and know what reads what (the dependency thought: "who references me?") — because in a wired grid, structure is shared by every formula that lives on it. THE VISUAL OPERATIONS complete the set: column width and row height set by drag or by auto-fit (the command that sizes a column to its widest entry), and hidden rows/columns — a display trick that hides data from view but not from calculation. What these operations are NOT: they are not cell clearing (Delete key empties cells; delete row removes the row and renumbers the world), and they are not reordering (sorting rearranges rows' contents — a later sibling's territory).
steps: The takeaway first: rows and columns are the register's load-bearing walls — insert slides the world down or right and renumbers every address; delete removes a wall and its echo (#REF!) rings through every formula that…
Supporting argument 1 — the grid is always contiguous, and that is the design decision behind everything.
There are no gaps in a spreadsheet: delete row 7 and row 8 becomes row 7 at once; the world slides to stay seamless.

The consequences follow mechanically: addresses renumber (a cell you knew as B9 may be B8 by the time you look), ranges keep naming their corners (which are now different cells), and every operation is undoable…
Students who internalise contiguity stop being surprised by the grid's shape-shifting — the grid never has holes; it has fewer rows.
Supporting argument 2 — references track content, until they cannot.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "insert row adds a row at the bottom of the sheet") reveals append-confusion — insertion is positional (above/left of the selection), not appended; the exam answer must state the slide directions as part of the operation's meaning.
remember: Recall: Define insert and delete for rows and columns, state the direction a new row appears relative to the selection and the direction things slide, and name the header strips….

cards.title: Copy and paste duplicate cell contents to a new location while the original…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Copy and paste duplicate cell contents to a new location while the original stays put: select the source, COPY (Ctrl+C), select the destination's top-left cell, PASTE (Ctrl+V) — the destination's old contents are replaced. Cut and paste (move) relocates instead: CUT (Ctrl+X) lifts the source, and paste replants it — the original place is emptied (for whole rows/columns, the neighbours slide shut, the mechanics). THE CLIPBOARD is the staging shelf between the two acts: the copied or cut selection waits there (invisible, remembered by the program) until a paste spends it — and a clipboard's copy can be pasted MANY times, while a cut's contents move once. THE MAGIC CLAUSE — formulas translate: when a formula is COPIED to a new position, its relative references shift by the same offset as the copy — =C7+D7+E7 (Meera's total, row 7) copied one row down arrives reading =C8+D8+E8 (the next student's total); copied right, it shifts columns; the relationship ("sum my row's three subjects") travels while the addresses translate — which is why a register's forty row-totals are written ONCE and copied THIRTY-NINE times. THE FIT RULE and its honesty: the destination must be shaped like the source (a 2×3 copy needs a 2×3 clear stage), or the paste overwrites whatever sits in its footprint — the replaced contents are gone (undo net standing beneath, as ever). Copying NUMBERS and TEXT is simpler: they travel unchanged — a copy of 45 is 45 anywhere. MOVING (cut-paste) carries references intact in this course's scope: the formula lands as it was. THE CRAFT DISCIPLINES: paste onto the destination's TOP-LEFT cell (the paste grows down-right from there); check the paste's footprint before pressing; and copy formulas only after one copied instance has been verified — the first copy is the pattern's proof. What copy/move is NOT: it is not autofill (the fill handle EXTENDS series — next node's magic, built on this node's copy machinery), and it is not delete-and-retype (copy relocates structure and relationships wholesale; retyping rebuilds them by hand, with hands' error rates).
steps: The takeaway first: copy duplicates with the original staying and formulas translating their references to the new address; cut moves and empties the source — the clipboard shelves the selection between the acts — and…
Supporting argument 1 — the pair is one verb with two remainders.
Copy and move differ in exactly one fact: what is left behind.
Copy leaves the source intact (a twin exists); cut empties it (a migration happened).

Every classroom confusion about the two dissolves into this one question — "what remains at the source?" — and every shortcut (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V) hangs on the same shelf: the clipboard, which remembers the…
Students who hold the remainder-question never mix the pair again.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "copy removes the original to the new place") reveals remainder-confusion — that is cut's behaviour; copy's defining fact is the surviving original; the exam answer must state the remainder for each verb.
remember: Recall: Define copy-paste and cut-paste, give their shortcuts, and state for each exactly what remains at the source after the paste.
Reasoning: A cell holds =C7+D7+E7 (a row's three subject….
Evaluate: "I cut my table from Sheet1 and pasted to Sheet2, then found I still needed it on Sheet1 — I'll just copy it back from Sheet2." Evaluate the plan: what actually happened….

cards.title: AutoFill is the spreadsheet's pattern-extension command…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: AutoFill is the spreadsheet's pattern-extension command: the small square at the corner of a selection (the FILL HANDLE) is dragged, and the program extends the selection's pattern into the new cells — copying, or (its real magic) CONTINUING SERIES. WHAT IT EXTENDS: (1) THE OBVIOUS SERIES — numbers with a step: select 1 and 2, drag, and 3, 4, 5... arrive; select 2 and 4, and the drag continues 6, 8, 10 — two cells are enough to teach the step; (2) THE CALENDAR LISTS — days (Monday, Tuesday...) and months (January, February...) are built into the program as known sequences: one entry dragged fills the week, the month, the year, wrapping around automatically; (3) DATES — a date dragged fills the next dates (and day-steps or month-steps are available from the fill options); (4) FORMULAS — dragging a formula's fill handle is copy-down: the translated references of per row, which is exactly how a register's totals column is built in one gesture; (5) PLAIN TEXT WITHOUT PATTERN — copies verbatim (a name dragged stays a name). THE MACHANICS AND THE CHOICE: the fill handle's drag FILLS by default (series where a pattern exists, copy where none does), and the fill-options button that appears after the drag lets the filler switch intentions (fill series versus copy cells) — while holding Ctrl while dragging forces copy-only. THE VERIFICATION DISCIPLINE (the node's one commandment): autofill is CONFIDENT, not correct — it extends whatever pattern it detected, so the dragged result is read against the intended pattern before trusting it; the classic surprise is the single-number drag (select 5 alone, drag: five 5s arrive — one cell teaches no step), cured by selecting two cells that state the step. THE LADDER OF THIS CHAPTER COMPLETES HERE: the grid (05_001) named its cells (05_003), typed its types (05_005), wrote its formulas (05_006), netted its mistakes (05_007), moved its walls (05_008) and twinned its patterns (05_009) — and autofill is the gesture that does the last mile: forty totals, a year of weekdays, a term's date column, each a drag away. What autofill is NOT: it is not intelligence about meaning (it knows Monday comes after Sunday, not what your marks mean), and it is not a substitute for the anchor-and-verify craft of the copy node — it is that craft, accelerated, with the same duties at the end.
steps: The takeaway first: autofill is the fill handle's pattern-extension — drag and the grid continues what it detected: number steps from two witnesses, calendar lists from one entry, formulas translated row by row — and…
Supporting argument 1 — two witnesses state a pattern; one states nothing.

The fill handle's first question is "what repeats here?" — and for numbers the honest answer needs TWO cells: 1 then 2 declares a step of 1; 2 then 4 declares 2; 5 alone declares nothing, and the drag fills with 5, 5, 5…
The calendar lists are the exception that proves the machinery: Monday is a KNOWN sequence's member, so one witness suffices — the program carries the list internally.
Supporting argument 2 — the calendar lists are the grid's first taste of knowledge.
Days and months wrap (Sunday loops to Monday;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "autofill invents the missing numbers in any list — type 3 and 8 and it fills 4 to 7") reveals mind-reading — autofill extends DETECTED patterns (two cells teach the step 5: 13, 18...); it does not interpolate intentions; the exam answer…

Reasoning: A student selects the single cell containing 5 and drags the fill handle down five….

cards.title: This chapter's territory: databases and the programs that manage them.
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: This chapter's territory: databases and the programs that manage them. A database is an organised COLLECTION of related data — the school's students, a library's books, a railway's trains — stored so that entries can be added, found, changed, counted and reported quickly and reliably. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the SOFTWARE that houses and operates a database — the storekeeper, the librarian and the accountant in one program: it defines the structure (tables made of rows and columns), stores the records, retrieves answers to questions (queries), prints neat outputs (forms and reports), and guards the data's rules (like no two students sharing one roll number). THE CHAPTER'S EIGHT-STATION JOURNEY: (1) THIS OVERVIEW — the map; (2) THE INTRODUCTION — what a database means, its everyday uses, and why "organised" is the operative word; (3) HANDS-ON CREATION — creating and saving a database file in a real DBMS; (4) THE PRIMARY KEY — the rule that makes every record uniquely findable; (5) QUERIES — asking the database questions and getting exact answers; (6) FORMS AND REPORTS — the friendly face for entering data and the tidy printout for reading it; (7) MANAGING RECORDS — sorting, filtering and keeping the collection orderly as it grows; (8) THE SYNTHESIS — the whole machinery assembled and drilled against CISCE exam patterns. THE WHY THAT RUNS UNDER ALL EIGHT: organised data is findable data — and findable data is what every institution runs on; the difference between loose papers and a database is the difference between searching a drawer and asking a question. The chapter's supporting vocabulary — TABLE, RECORD (one complete entry: one student), FIELD (one kind of fact: the roll number column), DATA TYPE (what kind of fact a field holds) — is introduced where each station needs it. What this chapter is NOT: it is not the spreadsheet chapter re-run — a spreadsheet is a flexible calculating grid, while a database is a disciplined collection built for finding, integrity and scale (the comparison is drawn honestly at station 2); and it is not about programming — the DBMS does the machinery, the student designs and asks.
steps: The takeaway first: this chapter travels eight stations — from what a database means, through building one and giving it a primary key, to querying it, dressing it with forms and reports, managing its growth, and…

Supporting argument 1 — the journey is built like construction, because that is what it is. The eight stations are ordered as a building is: conception (what is a database and why), foundation (create and save the…
The order is not syllabus cosmetics: each station's skill is the next station's tool — one cannot query what one has not structured, and cannot structure what one has not created.
Supporting argument 2 — the DBMS is a staff, not a shelf.

The definition that survives the chapter is division of labour: the DATABASE is the collection itself (the organised facts); the DBMS is the managing software — the storekeeper that shelves (stores), the librarian that…

Students who carry this two-noun distinction — collection versus manager — are fluent for every exam question the chapter asks, because every later skill is one of the manager's duties applied to the collection.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a database and a DBMS are the same thing — both mean the software") reveals two-noun fusion — the chapter's first and most-examined distinction; the exam answer must keep collection and manager apart in one clean sentence.
remember: Recall: Define database and DBMS, state the difference between them, and name the chapter's eight stations in order.
Reasoning: Explain why the chapter's stations are ordered creation → primary key → queries → forms/reports → sorting/filtering, reasoning from what each station needs that an….

cards.title: A database is an organised collection of related data stored in a way that…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A database is an organised collection of related data stored in a way that supports fast finding, safe changing, and exact reporting — and its organisation has a fixed shape: data lives in TABLES; each table holds RECORDS (the rows — one complete entry: one student, one book); each record is built of FIELDS (the columns — one kind of fact each: Roll_Number, Title); and every field holds data of one declared TYPE (numbers here, text there, dates in their place) so the machine can compare, count and sort honestly. Its USES are every institution that must answer questions about many facts: SCHOOL — student records, marks, fees, attendance; the term report is a report over this data; LIBRARY — the catalogue of books, members and issues; "is this book on the shelf?" is a query; BANKING — accounts, transactions, balances; an ATM balance-check is a query with the bank's whole weight behind it; RAILWAYS AND AIRLINES — trains, flights, seats, bookings; a reservation is a record inserted into a table that a lakh others are reading; HOSPITALS — patients, doctors, appointments, prescriptions; TELEPHONE AND SHOPPING — call records, customer accounts, stock and orders. The common anatomy of every use: MANY records, FEW kinds of facts, QUESTIONS asked all day, and RULES that must never break (no two accounts with one number; no seat sold twice). The manager beside it — the DBMS (Database Management System), with everyday examples LibreOffice Base and Microsoft Access at school scale, and server systems like MySQL behind websites — is what turns the collection into a service: it stores, retrieves, adds, updates, guards, prints. The honest border with the spreadsheet: a spreadsheet is a flexible CALCULATING page — brilliant for totals, charts and what-if marks on a few hundred rows; a database is a disciplined COLLECTION — built for thousands of records, many users at once, enforced uniqueness, and joint questions across tables; for a one-class mark list, the spreadsheet wins; for the school's whole memory, the database is the tool the job demands. What a database is NOT: it is not a pile of files (organisation and shared rules are the definition's spine), and it is not the DBMS (the collection versus its manager — the chapter's first distinction, held from the overview).
steps: The takeaway first: a database is a collection with a shape — tables holding records, records built of typed fields — and it earns its place wherever many records meet daily questions and unbreakable rules; the…
Supporting argument 1 — the shape is the definition; the rest is consequence.

"Organised collection" is made concrete by four words: TABLE (all the facts of one kind), RECORD (one complete entry — one whole student, not one fact about them), FIELD (one kind of fact, the same for every record)…

Once the shape is held, every institution's database is readable at sight: the library's Books table is a thousand records of five fields; the railway's Trains table is a national register of a dozen fields.
Students who can name a record and a field in a live table have the chapter's vocabulary for life.
Supporting argument 2 — the uses share one anatomy, which is why they are one subject.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a record is one cell — Meera's roll number") reveals cell-level confusion — a cell is one field of one record; the RECORD is the whole row, the complete entry; the exam answer must keep the three levels (table, record, field) in their…
remember: Recall: Define a database through its shape, naming tables, records and fields — and identify all three in a school Students table.
Reasoning: Every database use — school, bank, railway — shares one….
Evaluate: "Spreadsheets and databases do the same thing — one is old, one is new." Evaluate the claim: what each tool's DESIGN optimises for, the two jobs where the spreadsheet….

cards.title: Creating and saving a database is the process of using a Database Management…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Creating and saving a database is the process of using a Database Management System (DBMS) to allocate a new logical container for structured data, define its file name and storage location, and persist it on secondary storage. The DBMS presents a graphical interface or command line where the user selects “New Database”, chooses a template or blank database, specifies a file name with the appropriate extension (e.g.,.accdb for Microsoft Access,.odb for LibreOffice Base), and confirms the save operation. The system then creates the underlying system tables, metadata catalogs, and an empty schema ready for tables, queries, forms, and reports. Saving writes the file to disk, ensuring durability across sessions. This node focuses on the procedural steps: launching the DBMS, initiating a new database, naming it, selecting a folder, and confirming the save. It does not cover table design, primary keys, or querying, which are addressed in subsequent nodes.
steps: Creating and saving a database is the first concrete action that turns the idea of a database into a usable file on your computer.
Here is why: the DBMS needs a container file to hold all future objects; without saving, any work would disappear when the program closes.
Consider the analogy of a new school register: you first buy a blank register (create), write the school name on the cover (name), and place it in the staff room cupboard (save).

The steps are: 1) Open the DBMS application (e.g., Microsoft Access). 2) On the start screen, click “Blank database”. 3) In the “File Name” box, type a descriptive name such as “LibraryDB” — avoid spaces, use…
This sequence mirrors the workflow students will repeat for every project, reinforcing the habit of saving early and often.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “.mdb”) reveals the misconception that the older extension is still the default, confusing legacy versions with current ones.
remember: What is the default file extension for a database created in Microsoft Access 2016 and later.
Why must a database be saved before any tables are added.
A student names a new database “My Database” (with a space) and saves it on a Windows PC. Will the DBMS accept this name.

cards.title: A primary key is a column (or a set of columns) in a relational database table…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A primary key is a column (or a set of columns) in a relational database table that uniquely identifies each row. It must contain distinct values for every record and cannot hold NULL values. The primary key enforces entity integrity, guaranteeing that no duplicate rows exist and that each row can be referenced reliably by other tables through foreign keys. In practice, a primary key is often an auto‑incrementing integer (e.g., `StudentID`), a natural identifier such as an Aadhaar number, or a composite key formed by combining two columns (e.g., `ClassID` + `RollNo`). The database management system (DBMS) uses the primary key to build an index, which speeds up search, join, and update operations. Relationships between tables — such as linking a `Students` table to a `Marks` table — rely on the primary key of the parent table appearing as a foreign key in the child table. Understanding primary keys is essential before learning querying, because queries that filter, join, or aggregate data depend on the certainty that each row is uniquely addressable.
steps: A primary key is the single most important rule that keeps a database table trustworthy: it guarantees every row has a unique, non‑empty identifier.
Here is why: without a unique ID, the DBMS cannot tell two identical‑looking rows apart, leading to ambiguous updates or deletions.
First, uniqueness means no two rows may share the same key value; think of a school where each student gets a distinct admission number — even twins receive different numbers.
Second, the key cannot be NULL because an empty identifier would break the guarantee of uniqueness and make joins impossible.
Third, the DBMS automatically creates an index on the primary key, so finding a row by its key is as fast as looking up a word in a dictionary.
Fourth, other tables refer to this key as a foreign key, forming relationships; for example, a `Marks` table stores `StudentID` to link each mark sheet to the correct student.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “primary key must be numeric”) reveals the misconception that data type determines primary‑key eligibility, confusing implementation detail with logical requirement.
remember: What are the two mandatory properties that every primary key must satisfy in a relational database.
Why can a column containing student names not serve as a primary key in a `Students` table.
Evaluate the statement: “A composite primary key made of `Class` and `RollNo` is always better than a single auto‑increment `StudentID`.”.

cards.title: Querying is the process of requesting specific information from a database by…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Querying is the process of requesting specific information from a database by stating criteria that the desired records must satisfy. In a relational database, a query is expressed using a query language (commonly SQL) or a visual query‑design tool. The main components of a query are: the SELECT clause (which fields to display), the FROM clause (which table(s) to search), the optional WHERE clause (filter conditions such as `Class = 7 AND Sport = 'Cricket'`), and optional ORDER BY (sorting the result). Queries can also perform calculations (e.g., `COUNT`, `AVG`) and join multiple tables using primary‑key/foreign‑key relationships. The result of a query is a temporary recordset (a virtual table) that can be viewed, printed, or used as the source for forms and reports. Querying does not modify stored data; it only retrieves and presents a subset that matches the given logic.
steps: A query is a precise question you ask the database, and the database answers with only the rows that match your conditions.
Here is why: a database can hold thousands of records, but you rarely need all of them at once; querying lets you pull out exactly what you need for a task.
Consider the school register example: the table Students has fields `AdmNo`, `Name`, `Class`, `Sport`.
To list Class 7 cricket fans you write `SELECT Name, Sport FROM Students WHERE Class = 7 AND Sport = 'Cricket' ORDER BY Name;`.
The database engine scans the table, keeps rows where both conditions are true, projects only the two requested columns, sorts them alphabetically, and returns the recordset.
If you omit the WHERE clause, every row appears; if you omit ORDER BY, the order is undefined.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “FROM”) reveals the misconception that the table name determines the output columns, confusing the source with the projection.
remember: What keyword is used to specify the columns you want to see in a query result.
Explain why a query without a WHERE clause returns every row of the table.
A student writes `SELECT FROM Students WHERE Class = '7' OR Sport = 'Cricket'`. Evaluate whether this query will show a Class 6 student who likes cricket.

cards.title: A form is a database screen that presents ONE RECORD AT A TIME through…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A form is a database screen that presents ONE RECORD AT A TIME through labelled, ordered boxes — the friendly face for entering, viewing and editing data. Its service over raw tables: the entry clerk sees exactly the fields in a sensible order (Name, then Class, then Roll) instead of a wide grid's sea of columns; the tab key walks the boxes in order, so no field is skipped; and the form can be fed by a QUERY, so the clerk edits only the records that matter (today's issue-desk books, not the whole catalogue). A report is the database's formatted OUTPUT — selected fields, arranged and usually SORTED, dressed with titles, headings and (where asked) SUMMARIES (counts, totals, averages), laid out for PRINTING or presenting: the overdue-books list for the library wall, the term's fee summary for the principal's desk, the class-wise strength for the notice board. THE DIVISION OF LABOUR, the node's spine: the TABLE STORES (the truth, in the raw), the QUERY SELECTS (the right records, by question), the FORM ENTERS (one record at a time, guided), and the REPORT PRESENTS (many records, dressed and ordered) — input faces and output faces built over the storage and the questions beneath them. THE STATION-5 TIE that makes forms and reports more than decoration: both take a QUERY as their source — a form bound to "today's overdue books" shows the clerk only those records, and a report bound to "Class 7B by roll number" prints exactly that question's answer; the query asked once in the last station now feeds every face the school sees. THE CRAFT RULES OF EACH: a form's fields follow the ENTRY order of the real world (the way the paper form lies on the desk), its labels are full words, and one record fills one screen; a report's fields follow the READING order of its audience (sorted the way the reader will look: by class, then roll), its title states the question it answers, and its summary row answers "how many/how much" so the reader need not count. What forms and reports are NOT: they are not the data (deleting a form deletes the door, not the rooms — the table stands); and they are not two words for printing (the form is INPUT machinery; the report is OUTPUT dressing — the exam's favourite distinction).
steps: The takeaway first: a form is the database's door — one record at a time, labelled and ordered, fed even by a query so the clerk meets only the records that matter — and a report is its window: the right records, sorted…
Supporting argument 1 — the raw table is a store, not a workplace.
A wide table shows forty fields a-scatter and a hundred records at once: the entry clerk's eye wanders, the tab lands anywhere, a roll number lands in the Phone column.
The form fixes the workplace: ONE record, fields in the order the desk actually works (the paper admission form's order), labels in full words, the tab walking a straight line.
Errors are prevented by geography — the clerk cannot type into the wrong column because there are no columns, only named boxes in a chosen order.
Supporting argument 2 — the query-bound form is focus made mechanical.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a form and a report are both printouts — one is smaller") reveals input-output fusion — the form is ENTRY machinery (it never prints), the report is PRESENTATION machinery (it never edits); the exam answer must place them on opposite…
remember: Recall: Define a form and a report, and state the four-part division of labour — table, query, form, report — with one line on each office.
Reasoning: Explain why entering records directly into a wide table produces more errors than entering through a form — reasoning from what the clerk's eye and tab key meet in each.
Evaluate: "Our reports are fine — the clerk copies the query's results into a word processor and formats them there." Evaluate the claim: what the copy-and-dress method delivers….

cards.title: Sorting is the database operation that ARRANGES RECORDS IN A PARTICULAR ORDER…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Sorting is the database operation that ARRANGES RECORDS IN A PARTICULAR ORDER — ascending or descending — based on one or more chosen fields, called the SORT KEYS. Ascending order (A to Z, smallest to largest number, oldest to newest date) climbs up; descending order (Z to A, largest to smallest, newest to oldest) walks down. When two records tie on the primary sort key, a SECONDARY SORT KEY breaks the tie — Class 7B sorted by section (primary) and then by roll number (secondary) puts every student in exactly one unarguable position. The crucial comfort: records move as WHOLE ROWS — a student's marks travel with her name; only the order of records changes, never the contents of any record. Filtering is the operation that DISPLAYS ONLY THE RECORDS THAT MEET A STATED CONDITION (the FILTER CRITERION) — marks greater than 80, class equal to "7B", fee-due greater than zero — and TEMPORARILY HIDES the rest. The hidden records are not deleted, damaged or lost: the filter is a lens, not an eraser; remove it and every record walks back on stage. A filter with one condition is the quick, un-saved cousin of the QUERY from station 5 — the same selection idea, done in one click for a moment's question, where a query is designed once to be re-run forever. THE DIVISION OF LABOUR, this node's spine: SORTING answers "in WHAT ORDER should I read them?" and FILTERING answers "WHICH records matter now?" — and the two compose: filter first (narrow the crowd), then sort (line up the survivors), which is exactly how every good report from the last station was built — the query selected, the report's sort ordered, the reader read. What sorting and filtering are NOT: neither one changes the data — sorting changes POSITION, filtering changes VISIBILITY, and the table underneath keeps every record whole through both.
steps: The takeaway first: sorting puts records IN ORDER — ascending or descending, on a key you choose — and filtering puts records IN SIGHT — only those that pass the criterion, the rest hidden and safe; neither touches the…
Supporting argument 1 — order is information the raw table does not have.
A table in entry order answers nothing a human asks: "who topped?" hides in row 212.
Sort on Marks descending and the topper is row one — the SAME rows, re-arranged, now carrying their answer on their face.
The sort key is the promise: pick the field the reader will search by, and the search ends before it begins.
This is why station 6 insisted the report's sort match the reader's search — the operation behind that craft rule is this station's first tool.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "filtering removes the records that do not match") reveals the deletion fear — the filter is a lens, not an eraser; the exam answer must state the hiding as temporary and reversible, because that reversibility is precisely the…
remember: Recall: Define sorting and filtering in a….
Reasoning: The result sheet of 250 students is in entry….

cards.title: A database is an ORGANISED COLLECTION OF RELATED DATA stored so that it can be…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A database is an ORGANISED COLLECTION OF RELATED DATA stored so that it can be easily accessed, managed and updated — and the DBMS (Database Management System) is the SOFTWARE that keeps that collection: the tool through which tables are created, records entered, questions asked and answers presented. The chapter's machine, assembled station by station: the TABLE stores the truth — related records built from fields, every row a complete entry (one student, one book); the PRIMARY KEY identifies — a field (or combination) whose value is never empty and never repeated, so every record owns exactly one identity (Admission_No, Accession_No); the QUERY selects — a saved question stated as conditions, returning each time a fresh record-set of exactly the matching rows; the FORM enters and the REPORT presents — the input face showing one record at a time through labelled boxes, the output face dressing selected, sorted records with a title and a summary; and SORT and FILTER manage — arranging all records into ascending or descending order on a key, or showing only those that pass a criterion, changing position and visibility and never the data. THE ONE TRUTH beneath every face: the table is the only place data lives; key, query, form, report, sort and filter are all VIEWS and DOORS over it — each reads the vault, none duplicates it, so a correction made once is correct everywhere. THE USES that justify the machine: a school's admissions and fees, a library's catalogue and issues, a hospital's patient records, a railway's reservations — anywhere data is too big, too shared and too questioned for paper registers. What the synthesis node ADDS to its seven siblings: the ability to see the machine whole — to route any task to its station's tool, to narrate the chain in exam prose, and to design a small database end-to-end without missing a station.
steps: The takeaway first: the eight stations are one machine with one truth — the table stores, the key identifies, the query selects, the form enters, the report presents, sort and filter manage; every part reads the same…

Supporting argument 1 — the chain has a grammar, and exam questions speak it. Every question this chapter can ask is one of five verbs: DEFINE (what is a table/key/query/form/report?), IDENTIFY (why this primary key?…

The synthesis student hears the verb in the question and reaches for the right station's vocabulary — the definitions from one, the never-empty-never-repeated clause from another, the criterion discipline from a third.
Supporting argument 2 — the one-truth principle is the chapter's deepest sentence.

Seven tools, one storage: the query does not copy the overdue books, it points at them; the report does not freeze the fee defaulters, it re-asks the query at print time; the form is a door in the vault wall, not a room…
Consequence two: nothing but the table needs backing up first, and nothing but the table can lose data.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing "spreadsheet, folder, backup" as stations) reveals chapter-blindness — the chain is the chapter's own stations in their own order; the exam answer must narrate the machine, not invent a filing system.
remember: Recall: Name the eight stations of the database chapter in order, with the one-line job of each, and state the one-truth principle that binds them.
Reasoning: An exam question asks, "The librarian corrected a member's phone number through the….
Evaluate: A teacher says, "We already keep everything in spreadsheets — this database chapter is a big word for the same thing." Evaluate the claim: what the spreadsheet does….

cards.title: HTML provides two list elements for grouping related items.
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: HTML provides two list elements for grouping related items. The ordered list element `<ol>` creates a numbered sequence; each child `<li>` (list item) receives an automatic counter that can be styled with the `type` attribute (1, A, a, I, i) and the `start` attribute to set the initial number. The unordered list element `<ul>` creates a bulleted sequence; each `<li>` receives a bullet whose shape can be changed with the CSS `list-style-type` property (disc, circle, square, none). Both `<ol>` and `<ul>` are block‑level containers that may be nested — a list item can contain another `<ol>` or `<ul>` to show sub‑steps or categories. The relationship between the two is purely presentational: they share the same `<li>` child semantics but differ in default marker rendering. Attributes such as `reversed` on `<ol>` reverse the numbering order, while `compact` (deprecated) once reduced spacing. Modern practice relies on CSS for spacing and marker styling. Understanding these elements is prerequisite for later nodes covering images, links, tables, marquee, and forms, because lists often structure navigation menus, form option groups, and tabular data summaries.
steps: The one thing to remember: `<ol>` gives you automatic numbers or letters, `<ul>` gives you bullets, and both use `<li>` for each item.
Here is why: browsers read the tag name and apply a built‑in counter for `<ol>` or a bullet character for `<ul>`.
Consider a simple recipe page.

First, create an ordered list for steps: `
  1. Boil water
  2. Add tea leaves
  3. Steep three minutes
`.
The `type="1"` tells the browser to use decimal numbers; `start="1"` begins at one. If you wanted Roman numerals you would write `type="I"`.

Next, create an unordered list for ingredients: `
  • Water
  • Tea leaves
  • Sugar
`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `<ul>` creates numbers) reveals the misconception that both list tags behave identically — confusing unordered bullets with ordered counters.
remember: What tag pair creates a numbered list in HTML.
If you write `<ol type="A" start="3">`, what will be the label of the first list item.

A student writes `
  • Apple
  • Banana
` and expects numbers. Evaluate the output.

cards.title: The `` element is a void (self‑closing) HTML tag that embeds a raster…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition:
The `` element is a void (self‑closing) HTML tag that embeds a raster image directly into the document flow. It requires a `src` attribute containing a URL — either a relative path such as `images/mango.jpg` or an absolute address like `https://example.com/photos/mango.jpg` — that the browser fetches and renders at the tag’s position. The `alt` attribute supplies alternative text; it is read by screen readers, indexed by search engines, and displayed when the image cannot be loaded, making it essential for accessibility and SEO. Optional `width` and `height` attributes accept positive integers (pixels) and reserve layout space before the image downloads, preventing reflow. If only one dimension is given, the browser scales the other proportionally to preserve the intrinsic aspect ratio. Unlike container tags (`

`, `

`), `` never wraps content and therefore has no closing tag; in HTML5 the trailing slash is optional (`` or ``). The element is inline‑replaced, so it behaves like a single character in text flow unless CSS changes its display property. Understanding `` prepares students for later nodes where images become clickable links (``), appear inside table cells, or serve as form controls.
steps: The `` tag is the only HTML element that inserts a raster picture directly into a page, and it must always include a `src` attribute pointing to the image file and an `alt` attribute describing the picture for…
Supporting argument 1: `` is an empty, self‑closing element; it never wraps content, so the syntax ends with `/>` (or just `>` in HTML5).

This distinguishes it from container tags like `

` or `

`.
Supporting argument 2: The `src` attribute accepts a URL — either a relative path such as `images/mango.jpg` or an absolute address like `https://example.com/photos/mango.jpg`.
The browser follows this address, downloads the file, and paints it where the tag appears.
Supporting argument 3: The `alt` attribute is not optional decoration; screen readers read it aloud, search engines index it, and browsers display it when the image cannot load.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “`src` and `width`”) reveals the misconception that sizing attributes are required — they are optional and only affect layout, not the ability to display the image.
remember: What are the two mandatory attributes of the `` tag in HTML.
If an `` tag has `src="photo.jpg"` but no `alt` attribute, what will a screen reader announce.
