cards.title: A hyperlink (link) is the HTML element that connects the current page to…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A hyperlink (link) is the HTML element that connects the current page to another resource — another page of the same site, a page on a different site, or any addressable file — so that one click carries the reader there; the `` (anchor) tag builds it, and is a CONTAINER tag: an opening ``, the clickable content between, and a closing ``. The `href` attribute (hypertext reference) holds the DESTINATION — the address the browser travels to when the link is clicked — and the content between the tags is the SIGN the reader actually sees and clicks: text, or an `` element from the previous station wrapped by the anchor (`` makes a picture-link). THE TWO ADDRESS FORMS `href` accepts: an absolute URL — the complete address including the protocol, used to reach OTHER websites (e.g. `India Post`) — and a relative URL — the address measured from the current page's own folder, used to reach pages of the SAME site (`Next`, `Results`, `Home`); the same-site pages travel light by relative path, and the whole site can move to a new domain without one link breaking, because the doors were never written with the house's street address. THE BROWSER'S SIDE OF THE DEAL: by default a link's text renders BLUE and UNDERLINED (violet once visited), the mouse pointer becomes a hand over it, and the destination replaces the current page — the visual promise that this text is a door. THE RULES THAT KEEP DOORS HONEST: the sign should say where the door leads ("Class 7 syllabus", not "click here"), every attribute value sits in quotes, and no anchor is left unclosed — an unclosed `` swallows the rest of the page into one giant link. What links are NOT: they are not images or lists (sibling stations) — the `` builds only the door; the sign it shows may borrow any element as its face.
steps: The takeaway first: a link is a door built of two parts — the address hidden in `href` and the visible sign between the tags; the anchor is a container (open, content, close), its address is absolute for other sites and…
Supporting argument 1 — the two-part anatomy explains every link question. `Track your parcel` — the browser renders only "Track your parcel", blue and underlined; the address…
Students who fuse the parts write the URL as the sign or expect the href to display; the anatomy — ADDRESS IN THE TAG, SIGN BETWEEN THE TAGS — answers every such error before it is made.
And because `` is a container, the sign can be ANY element: text, or an `` — the previous station's picture becomes this station's doorway face.
Supporting argument 2 — the address form follows the relationship, not the habit.
A door to ANOTHER house carries the full street address: absolute URL, protocol and all, for every destination outside your site.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "href is the blue text the user clicks") reveals part-fusion — the href is the hidden address, the between-tags content is the visible sign; the exam answer must keep the two parts separate and name which one shows.
remember: Recall: Name the tag that creates a hyperlink, the attribute that holds its destination, and the two forms that destination can….
Reasoning: A school site has pages `index.html`, `pages/about.html` and….
Evaluate: A classmate's page has three links, all reading "click….

cards.title: An HTML table is a structured grid used to display tabular data on a web page.
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: An HTML table is a structured grid used to display tabular data on a web page. The `<table>` element acts as the container for the entire grid. Inside it, each row is defined by a `<tr>` (table row) tag. Within a row, individual cells are created using `<td>` (table data) for regular data or `<th>` (table header) for column or row headings; browsers typically render `<th>` content in bold and centred. Cells can span multiple columns with the `colspan` attribute or multiple rows with the `rowspan` attribute, allowing complex layouts such as merged headers. Optional attributes like `border`, `cellpadding`, and `cellspacing` control visual spacing, though modern practice prefers CSS for styling. Tables can be nested, but excessive nesting harms accessibility and maintenance. The relationship between these tags is strictly hierarchical: `<table>` > `<tr>` > `<td>`/`<th>`. This node focuses on the core markup; styling, scripting, and advanced accessibility features belong to later topics.
steps: The one thing to remember: a table is built layer by layer — first the outer `<table>`, then rows with `<tr>`, then cells with `<td>` or `<th>` — and every cell must sit inside a row. Here is why: browsers read HTML top…
First, start with `<table>` and optionally add a `border="1"` attribute so you can see the grid while learning.
Second, add a header row using `<tr>` and inside it place `<th>` tags for each column title; this makes the headings bold and centred automatically.
Third, for each data row, open a `<tr>`, then add as many `<td>` tags as there are columns, filling each with text, images, or even links from the previous node.
Fourth, if a cell needs to stretch across two columns, add `colspan="2"` to that `<td>`; if it must stretch down two rows, use `rowspan="2"`.
Fifth, close every tag in reverse order: ``, ``, ``.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `<td>`) reveals the misconception that the cell tag itself creates the row, confusing the container with the content.
remember: Which tag defines a single row in an HTML table.
What happens if you write `Data` directly inside `` without a surrounding ``.
Compare `<td>` and `<th>`: which one is intended for column headings and how does the browser render it by default.

cards.title: The `<marquee>` element is a container tag that displays its content — text…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: The `<marquee>` element is a container tag that displays its content — text, an image, or both — MOVING ACROSS THE SCREEN continuously: a scrolling banner built for announcements and headlines; an opening `<marquee>`, the moving content between, and a closing `</marquee>` bound the movement to exactly its own content. THE FOUR DIALS THAT SHAPE THE WALK: `direction` — the way the content travels: `left` (the default: enters from the right edge, marches leftward), `right`, `up`, or `down`; `behavior` — the travel's manner: `scroll` (the default: crosses fully, vanishes, re-enters — the endless parade), `slide` (enters once, stops at the far edge and STAYS — a notice that walks in and sits down), or `alternate` (bounces back and forth between the edges, never leaving the screen — a door-swing); `scrollamount` — the step size in pixels per move: a LARGER number moves the banner FURTHER each step, so the march is FASTER (scrollamount="10" strides, scrollamount="2" crawls); `scrolldelay` — the pause in milliseconds between steps: a LARGER number waits LONGER between moves, so the march is SLOWER (delay 100 hurries, delay 500 ambles) — the two dials work together, step size and pause, and either one alone retimes the walk. THE SUPPORTING DIALS: `loop` — how many times the banner crosses before resting (a number; unending by default); `bgcolor` — a background colour strip behind the moving content so the banner reads as a band; `width` and `height` — the size of the stage the banner walks across. THE ANATOMY RULE: marquee MOVES its content, it does not restyle it — bold, colour and font inside the banner come from their own elements; marquee's only job is the walk. THE HONEST FOOTNOTE the syllabus keeps and the student should know: marquee is an older element that modern standards retire in favour of CSS animation — but browsers still render it, ICSE asks it, and its four dials remain the clearest first lesson in motion on a page. What marquee is NOT: it is not a table (the previous station's grid) and not a form (the next station's inputs) — it is the page's one walking announcement.
steps: The takeaway first: the `<marquee>` element is a container that makes its content walk — `direction` picks the way, `behavior` picks the manner (scroll endlessly, slide in once, alternate between edges), and the two…
Supporting argument 1 — marquee is a stage with a walker, and the anatomy decides what moves.
Only the content between the tags walks: `<marquee>PTM on Saturday</marquee>` marches the sentence, and everything outside stands still.
The container rule, learned at links, repeats here with motion — an unclosed `</marquee>` claims the rest of the page into the parade.
The stage's size is settable (`width`, `height`, `bgcolor`), so the banner can be a full-width news band or a small boxed ticker.
Supporting argument 2 — the four dials answer the four questions every banner asks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "scrollamount makes it slower because it is a delay") reveals dial-sense inversion — stride and rest are opposite dials; the exam answer must attach each dial to its sense with the walker image: stride length versus standing still.
remember: Recall: What is the `<marquee>` element? Name its default direction and default behavior, the two speed dials with their opposite senses, and the container rule about what moves.
Reasoning: Two banners run on the reception….
Evaluate: The principal rejects the club's banner — "It keeps sliding away before I finish….

cards.title: An HTML form is a container element (`<form>`) that groups interactive controls…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: An HTML form is a container element (`<form>`) that groups interactive controls so a visitor can enter data and send it to a server. The `action` attribute specifies the URL that receives the data, while the `method` attribute chooses HTTP GET (data appended to URL) or POST (data in request body). Inside the form, `<input>` elements create fields: `type="text"` for single‑line text, `type="password"` for hidden characters, `type="radio"` for single choice, `type="checkbox"` for multiple choices, `type="submit"` for the send button, and `type="reset"` to clear the form. The `<select>` element with nested `<option>` tags builds a dropdown list. `<textarea>` provides a multi‑line text area. Each control should have a `name` attribute so the server can identify the value. The `required` attribute forces the user to fill the field before submission. Labels (`<label for="id">`) improve accessibility by linking descriptive text to controls. Forms can contain other HTML content (lists, images, links, tables) but those are covered in earlier nodes. The form itself does not process data; it only collects and transmits it.
steps: A web form collects information from a visitor and sends it to a server using the `<form>` element with input controls.
Here is why: first, a form mirrors a paper form that Indian students fill for school admission or railway reservation.
Second, each input type is designed for a specific kind of data — text for names, password for secrets, radio for one‑of‑many, checkbox for many‑of‑many.
Third, the `action` and `method` attributes decide where the data goes and how it travels, just as a letter needs an address and a postage type.
Fourth, linking a `<label>` to an input with the `for` attribute helps screen readers and makes clicking the label focus the field.
Fifth, the `required` attribute ensures mandatory fields are not left empty before the form is sent.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `<input>` or `<div>`) reveals the misconception that any block‑level tag can act as a form, confusing a container with a control.
remember: Which HTML tag defines a form that can collect user input.
Explain the difference between `method="get"` and `method="post"` in a form.
A student writes `<input type="text" name="email" required="true">`. Is this correct HTML5? Evaluate.

cards.title: Listening and viewing comprehension is the active skill of receiving spoken or…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Listening and viewing comprehension is the active skill of receiving spoken or visual-oral texts — a talk, an announcement, a story read aloud, a documentary, an interview, a radio bulletin — and reconstructing their meaning accurately: the main idea (what the speaker is basically saying), the supporting details (the facts, names, numbers, and reasons that hold the idea up), the speaker's purpose (to inform, persuade, entertain, or instruct), and the tone (the attitude behind the words — serious, amused, worried, proud). It is called active because it is done on purpose, with the listener's mind doing four jobs at once: predicting (guessing where the talk is going from its first sentences), attending (holding attention on the words rather than wandering), interpreting (linking new information to what is already known — the way a talk on the monsoon connects to last year's flooded street), and recording (catching key words in a notebook, because spoken words vanish the moment they are said, unlike the words on this page which wait for you). Viewing comprehension extends the same discipline to texts that speak through pictures as well as voice — a news clip, a documentary on the Western Ghats, a classroom video — where the listener must also read images: what the camera shows, what it repeats, what it never shows. The skill rests on a distinction every listener must hold: gist (the one-sentence heart of the text) and detail (the evidence around the heart); strong listeners take the gist first and hang details on it, weak listeners chase every detail and lose the shape of the whole. In the CISCE framework this skill is examined through heard-and-answered exercises: passages read aloud (often twice), with questions on content, vocabulary in context, and inference.
steps: Listening is a skill with a method, and its first law is that the gist comes before the details.

Picture the school assembly where the headgirl announces the sports-day schedule: the student who tries to remember every date as it falls forgets all of them by lunch, while the student who first catches the shape …
About what?
What is the point? — and the second for the flesh — the names, the numbers, the exceptions.
Note-taking is the second pillar, and its rule is keys, not copies.

The notebook that tries to transcribe the speaker always loses, because writing is slower than speech; the notebook that catches key words — "monsoon — late this year — 14% less rain — farmers wait" — wins, because five…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "there is no difference; if the sound is loud enough you will remember it") reveals the misconception of listening as volume, ignoring that comprehension fails from inattention, not from quietness — the loudest announcement in the world…
remember: What is the difference between hearing and listening, and why does the difference matter in an examination that reads a passage aloud only twice.
A radio bulletin says: "The monsoon has arrived three days early over….
Why does the trained listener take key words instead of full sentences in….

cards.title: A discussion is a structured exchange of views in which a small group examines…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: A discussion is a structured exchange of views in which a small group examines a question together — weighing reasons, testing examples, disagreeing politely — with the aim of reaching deeper understanding or a shared conclusion rather than winning. Its unit is not the speech but the turn: each member's short, focused contribution that either opens a new point, supports a point with evidence, or responds to a previous speaker. Discussion differs from debate in aim and manner: debate assigns sides and rewards demolition, while discussion assigns a question and rewards the group's progress on it — the good discusser is not the loudest voice but the one whose turns move the circle forward. The skill rests on five disciplines. Turn-taking: speaking when the floor is free, yielding when it is not, and using courteous entry phrases ("May I add something?", "If I may come in here") instead of interruption. Building: attaching one's point to another's — "building on what Meera said..." — so the discussion grows connective tissue instead of a row of unjoined monologues. Reasoned agreement and disagreement: every position carried by a because — "I agree because...", "I see it differently, because..." — where the disagreement attacks the point, never the person. Clarifying: asking genuine questions ("Do you mean the whole school, or only the senior wing?") that sharpen vague claims, and answering questions asked of oneself without taking offence. Summarising and concluding: at intervals, one member gathers what the circle has agreed so far, so the group does not walk in circles — and at the end, states the conclusion reached, including the points left unresolved. In the CISCE classroom this skill is trained through group discussions on familiar topics — school rules, mobile phones, festivals, environment — and assessed on the quality of listening shown (from the previous node), the relevance of each turn, the courtesy of the manner, and the evidence carried by the arguments.
steps: A discussion succeeds or fails on its turns — the first law of the circle is that every turn must carry the group somewhere.

Break a good turn open and you find three parts in under a minute: the point (one clear claim — "Homework should be lighter on festival days"), the reason ("because the evening belongs to the family, and tired children…
Meera's turn in the Class 7 discussion on school uniforms follows exactly this shape, and its discipline is what makes the circle lean in: nobody must unpack a paragraph to find her meaning.
The second law is that disagreement is a duty, done cleanly.
A circle where everyone nods is not discussing — it is echoing; the value of "I see it differently, because..." is that it forces both speakers to sharpen their reasons.
But the because must bite the claim and never the claimant: "I disagree, because the survey only asked the senior wing" is a discussion;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a discussion is just a friendly debate where nobody keeps score") reveals the misconception of the two as the same activity at different volumes, ignoring that the aim itself differs — the debater must defend a side even against his own…
remember: How does a discussion differ from a debate in aim and in manner? Give one situation where each is the right form.
Break a good discussion turn into its three parts, and show the parts in a turn on the topic "Should the school day begin with ten minutes of silence?".
Rohan says: "You always say silly things — homework can't possibly be lighter during festivals." Write the two defects in his disagreement, and rewrite his turn so it obeys the….

cards.title: A presentation is a prepared talk delivered by one speaker to an audience…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: A presentation is a prepared talk delivered by one speaker to an audience — two minutes to ten — in which meaning is carried on three channels at once: the words (the script and its structure), the voice (tone, pace, pitch, pauses — together called voice modulation), and the body (posture, eye contact, gesture, and facial expression). Voice modulation is the speaker's control over how something is said: pace — the speed of delivery, slowed for important points and at ends of sentences, quickened for excitement or listing; pitch — the highness or lowness of the voice, rising for questions and surprise, falling for conclusions and certainty; volume — projected to the last row without shouting, dropped to a near-whisper to draw the audience in; and the pause — the most powerful tool of all, the one- or two-second silence before a key point that makes the hall lean forward, and after it, that lets the point land. Tone is the attitude the voice displays — enthusiastic, solemn, warning, amused — and must match the matter: a cheerful voice on a pollution report destroys the message faster than any wrong fact. The body's channel works the same way: eye contact that moves across the audience in small honest holds (two or three seconds per face, never a roving blur and never a glued stare at one friend or at the ceiling) makes each listener feel addressed; gesture — the hand that counts the three reasons, opens the palm at the big claim, points at the imagined map — should be few, large, and deliberate, because small busy hands distract and frozen hands bore; posture stands tall and still, weight on both feet, no swaying, pockets, or pacing. The three channels must agree — this agreement is called congruence — because an audience believes the tone and the body over the words when the two conflict: say "I am confident" while swaying and staring at your shoes, and the audience hears the shoes. In the CISCE framework, presentations are trained and assessed on exactly these mechanics — clarity, modulation, audience contact, and organisation — through show-and-tell, explanatory talks, and short speeches on given topics.
steps: A presentation is won before the first word — in the plan of the talk and the rehearsal of the channels.
The structure first, because the voice has nothing to modulate until the matter stands: a strong presentation runs opening hook — body — closing line.

The hook is one sentence that earns the audience's ears — a question ("How much water does your school use before lunch?"), a surprising number ("one dripping tap wastes forty-five litres a day"), or a picture in words…

The body carries two or three points — never more, in a Class 7 talk — each announced by a signpost the audience can follow ("the first reason...", "which brings me to...", "and now the part nobody expects"), because…
The closing line is written out word for word and learnt — the last sentence is what the hall carries out, and "so... yeah, that's all" is a wasted exit.
Then the voice channel, tool by tool.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "only the words matter if the content is well prepared, since the audience came to learn, not to watch") reveals the misconception of the presentation as an essay read aloud, ignoring that speech is received through three senses at once…
remember: Name the three channels that carry a presentation, and state the congruence rule that binds them.
A student opens a talk with: "How much water does your school use... before lunch?" written to be….
Why are pauses called the most powerful tool of voice modulation? Give the two placements of a pause in a presentation and the effect of each.

cards.title: A multimedia-supported talk is a presentation — the structure, voice…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: A multimedia-supported talk is a presentation — the structure, voice, and body skills of the previous node — joined by a fourth channel: projected visuals (slides, photographs, charts, maps, short video clips) that the speaker controls and speaks to. Its home in this chapter is the social-issue talk: a two-to-five-minute presentation on a public concern — water scarcity, plastic waste, road safety, child labour, saving a city lake — where the multimedia channel does three honest jobs. Evidence: the photograph of the choked storm drain shows what the statistic claims; the chart of rising temperatures shows the trend the words describe; the map of the ward's garbage-collection points shows the geography of the problem. Simplification: a single slide with five words ("One tap. Forty-five litres. Every day.") lands a number that the ear alone forgets; the visual is the talk's memory anchor. Emotion and urgency: the image of a child carrying water cans makes an audience feel the issue's human weight before any argument begins. But the fourth channel carries the talk's greatest dangers, and the craft is mostly restraint. The slide is not the script: text-heavy slides steal the audience's eyes from the speaker, and once the audience reads, it stops listening — words on screen and words in ears compete and both lose. The image must be spoken to, not past: the presenter turns, gestures at the visual, reads it aloud with the audience ("see how the line climbs after 2015"), and turns back — the visual is a co-witness to be questioned, not wallpaper. And visuals are claims, not truth: a photo can be cropped, a chart's axis stretched to exaggerate a trend, a clip edited to remove context — so the ethical presenter chooses honest images, admits their limits ("this photo is from last summer, not this week"), and checks sources. The talk's structure follows the presentation's — hook, signposted points, closing line — with slides designed as single-idea cards: one image or one line of figures per slide, readable from the last bench, and never read out word for word by the speaker.
steps: A multimedia talk on a social issue is planned in two documents, and the order matters: first the speech, then the slides — never the reverse.

The speech first, because the issue must survive as an argument before it deserves pictures: the hook (the question or startling fact that earns the hall's ears — "how many of you drank bottled water today? now, how…
Only when the speech stands does the slide plan begin, and its law is the single idea: one slide per point, one idea per slide.

The size-point gets the chart — the ward's waste figures climbing year by year, axis honestly labelled, five words at the top ("our ward's waste, 2015–2024"); the causes-point gets the photograph — the single choked…

Delivery then follows the speak-to-the-slide rule: the slide appears and the speaker turns to it, gesture including it in the talk — "look at the year 2020, see the jump" — reads the visual aloud with the audience, and…
The social-issue frame adds the talk's ethical weight, and its test is honesty.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "slides first is fine, because strong pictures will inspire better words than planning could") reveals the misconception of the talk as an illustrated mood, ignoring that inspiration without structure produces association rather than…
remember: Why must the speech be planned before the slides? Show what goes wrong in reverse, with the example of a talk on plastic waste.
State the single-idea rule for slides and apply it: redesign this terrible slide for the causes-point of a plastic-waste talk: "PLASTIC WASTE — CAUSES: Plastic is cheap and….
Describe the speak-to-the-slide technique — the exact sequence of a presenter's moves when a slide appears — and why each move matters.

cards.title: Reading comprehension in this chapter begins with a classification every reader…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Reading comprehension in this chapter begins with a classification every reader must carry: texts divide into literary and non-literary by what they are built to do. A literary text — the short story, the novel extract, the poem, the play scene, the personal essay — is built to create an experience: it invents characters, scenes, and events (fiction), or shapes feeling into pattern (poetry), and it works through the resources of language itself — imagery (word-pictures appealing to the senses), figurative speech (simile, metaphor, personification), dialogue, and narrative point of view. Its test is not "is this true?" but "does this ring true, and what does it make me see and feel?". A non-literary text — the news report, the article, the biography, the letter, the diary entry, the advertisement, the notice, the instructions, the speech of information — is built to convey: information, opinion, argument, or direction about the real world; it works through organisation — headings, dates, named sources, sequence, facts — and its test is "is this accurate, clear, and reliable?". The chapter's first theme, self and family, runs through both kinds: the literary version gives the family story — a grandmother's kitchen, a brother's rivalry, a rainy-day power-cut conversation — where the reader watches character and feeling unfold; the non-literary version gives the family document — the diary entry, the personal letter, the memoir extract, the interview — where a real or realistic voice records a life. Reading either well demands the same first moves, which this node trains: identifying the text type before reading closely (because a poem's statement is not a report's claim), grasping the main idea, following sequence and character, and retelling accurately in one's own words. These moves are the floor on which every later node of the chapter stands — theme by theme from family to community to nation, then the reading crafts of summarising and evaluation.
steps: The first skill of reading is knowing what kind of thing you have been handed — and the test takes ten seconds.
Ask: does this text invent, or does it report?

The family story opens "When the power failed that May evening, Amma lit the old kerosene lamp and the veranda filled with cousins" — invented people, an imagined evening, imagery doing the work: literary.
The diary entry begins "15 June.
Papa's transfer order finally came today" — a dated, first-person record of a life: non-literary, however personal.
Neither is better; they are different instruments.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the interview is literary because it is about a person's life, and poems are only about nature") reveals the misconception of literary as a subject-matter label, ignoring that the classification is about the text's construction — an…
remember: State the single test that classifies a text as literary or non-literary, and apply it to: (a) a poem about a grandmother grinding spices at….
A story shows this scene: "When the lights failed, Chacha continued shelling peas in the dark, and the children gathered around the sound alone." What does this scene show without….
The same power-cut evening at a family home is written up three times: as a diary entry by the daughter, as a letter from the mother to a cousin, and later as a story by the son.….

cards.title: A community text is any literary or non‑literary piece — story, poem, article…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: A community text is any literary or non‑literary piece — story, poem, article, speech, graphic novel, or documentary excerpt — that centres on a group of people bound by geography, culture, interest, or circumstance. The theme explores how members interact, negotiate identity, resolve conflict, and create shared norms. Sub‑concepts include: (1) collective rituals (festivals, meetings, sports), (2) social roles (elders, youth leaders, volunteers), (3) conflict and consensus (disputes over resources, decision‑making), and (4) change over time (migration, technology, policy). In the ICSE Class 7 curriculum, community texts appear across genres — folk tales from Kerala’s Theyyam, a newspaper report on a Mumbai housing‑society water‑sharing scheme, a graphic memoir of a tribal village in Odisha — allowing students to compare how form shapes the portrayal of communal life. The node also introduces the reading skills of summarising (capturing the main communal issue and resolution) and evaluating the author’s argument (judging whether the text presents a balanced view of the community’s challenges). These skills are developed further in sibling nodes 008 and 009, but here they are applied specifically to community‑focused material.
steps: The key takeaway is that community texts reveal how groups negotiate shared life, and reading them well means spotting the collective problem, the voices involved, and the author’s stance.

Here is why: every community text, whether a folk song from Rajasthan or a news article about a Bengaluru residents’ association, follows a pattern — a triggering event (water shortage, festival planning, migration), a…
First, students locate the trigger by asking “What disrupts the normal routine?” In a story about a village panchayat meeting, the trigger is a proposed road that cuts through communal grazing land.
Second, they map stakeholders: the sarpanch, the herders, the women who fetch water, the contractor.
Third, they note resolution cues — votes, compromises, protests — and ask whether the text shows all sides.

Fourth, they practice a concise summary: “The village debates a road project; herders fear loss of grazing, women worry about longer water walks; the panchayat votes for a bypass after women’s petition.” Finally, they…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to memorise facts about different Indian festivals”) reveals the misconception that community texts are merely informational catalogues rather than vehicles for analysing social dynamics and authorial perspective.
remember: What is the primary purpose of a community‑focused text in the ICSE Class 7 reading curriculum.
In a short story about a coastal fishing village deciding whether to allow a tourism resort, which textual element most directly shows the community’s conflict.
A student writes a 70‑word summary of a newspaper article on a residents’ welfare association meeting but includes the phrase “I think the association should have acted faster.”….

cards.title: Nation-themed texts are the literary and non-literary writings whose central…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Nation-themed texts are the literary and non-literary writings whose central character is the nation itself — its identity, its history, its diversity, its struggles, and its aspirations. The literary side gives the nation a face and a voice: the poem in which the mother tongue itself is the speaker pleading for its life; the story of a Hindu family's Muslim friend staying back during Partition nights; the folk-song of a boatman on the Brahmaputra; the school-tale where a Chennai child and a Kashmiri child discover they both call the same rain by different names. It works through the resources already met in this chapter — invented characters, imagery, shown-not-told feeling — but points them at collective experience: belonging, freedom, sacrifice, unity in diversity, and the quiet ordinary patriotism of daily work. The non-literary side gives the nation its record and its argument: the news report on the Republic Day parade; the biographical extract on a freedom fighter; the speech — historic or school-made — that asks citizens for something; the letter, the memoir extract, the article on the Constitution or the census. It works through dates, named sources, sequence of events, and stated claims. Reading nation-themed texts demands the chapter's classification habit (is this a shaped experience or a report?) plus two moves that grow sharper at this scale: reading symbolically (the flag, the river, the train, the mother tongue functioning as more than themselves — a literary device the reader must catch without over-reading every object) and reading perspective (whose nation is this text describing, from which vantage — the soldier's letter and the farmer's poem describe the same country differently, and neither is the whole of it). The node sits third in the chapter's widening circle: self and family, community, and now the nation — the biggest "we" a text can carry — before the chapter turns to environment, science, peace, and adventure.
steps: A nation is too big to see — and that is exactly why texts are built about it: the poem and the report are the only ways a country can fit inside a classroom.
The first habit remains the ten-second classification.
The story of the train journey where a Partition refugee shares his last roti with a stranger is literary: invented people, shaped scene, feeling shown through action.
The biographical extract on the same period is non-literary: dated, sourced, built to convey what happened.
The national theme changes the cargo, not the classification — and the reader who knows the kind knows which questions to carry.
In the literary text, the new skill is reading symbols.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "(a) is non-literary because language death is a real, documented problem, so the poem reports it") reveals the misconception of the classification as topic-testing, ignoring that build, not subject, decides — the poem reports nothing…
remember: Classify and justify: (a) a poem in which the mother tongue, personified, begs its speakers not to abandon….
In a Partition-era story, a train recurring through the narrative is described as "carrying whole villages in one….
Two texts describe the same Himalayan border region: a soldier's letter home ("we held the post; the cold took two of Bhandari's fingers") and a farmer's poem from the same valley….

cards.title: The environment sub‑topic in Class 7 ICSE Reading covers literary and…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: The environment sub‑topic in Class 7 ICSE Reading covers literary and non‑literary texts that explore the natural world and humanity’s interaction with it. Texts may be poems describing a forest, newspaper articles on air‑quality in Delhi, diary entries of a child planting saplings, or scientific reports on the Western Ghats’ biodiversity. The sub‑concepts include: (1) genre variety — poetry, prose, reportage, speeches; (2) thematic focus — ecosystems, pollution, conservation, climate change, sustainable living; (3) author’s perspective — descriptive, persuasive, reflective, or argumentative; (4) language features — imagery, factual data, rhetorical devices, cause‑effect structures. Students learn to identify the main idea, distinguish fact from opinion, trace the author’s argument, and summarise the text in their own words. This node builds on the “nation” node where students examined texts about national identity, and prepares them for the “science & tech” node where environmental data meets technological solutions.
steps: The environment node teaches you to read any text about nature — whether a poem about a river or a news report on smog — by spotting the central message, the evidence the writer uses, and the way the argument is built.
Here is why: 1.
Genre signals purpose.
A poem uses imagery to evoke feeling; a newspaper article uses data to inform; a speech uses rhetoric to persuade.
Recognising the genre tells you what to expect. 2.
Theme anchors the content.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Poems never argue because they are not essays”) reveals the misconception that argumentation only appears in prose, ignoring persuasive language in verse.
remember: A student reads a poem describing a monsoon river and says, “This poem is just a description; it has no argument.” Is the student correct? Explain.
In a newspaper article about Delhi’s air‑quality index, the author writes, “The AQI crossed 400 yesterday, proving that government policies have failed.” Identify the claim, the….

cards.title: Science and technology texts are the non-literary
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Science and technology texts are the non-literary (and occasionally literary-adjacent) writings whose job is explanation: the article on how the Chennai desalination plant turns sea water into drinking water; the instructions for assembling a rain-gauge; the report on India's solar mission; the profile of a scientist; the manual page on a phone camera's settings; the school-lab experiment write-up. Their build is specific and learnable. Precision of vocabulary: technical terms (condensation, algorithm, voltage) are used with fixed meanings, and near-synonyms are not interchangeable — a "current" is not a "voltage", and the reader who lets a term blur has lost the explanation while still understanding every individual word. Definition-then-expansion structure: most good explanatory writing defines its core term early, then unfolds it with classification (three types of...), process (first, then, finally), or cause-effect (because this, therefore that). Sequence and process language: the ordered connectors — first, subsequently, meanwhile, as a result — carry the logic, and a reader who skips them reads a heap of sentences where a machine was described. Visual and numerical anchoring: figures, diagrams, tables, and numbers do half the explaining, and the text's claims lean on them ("efficiency rose to 22 per cent" is nothing without the question "from what, measured how?"). The literary-adjacent form — the science profile or narrative popularisation (a day in the life of the ISRO tracking station; the story-shaped account of the Mars orbiter's midnight launch) — borrows story's warmth but keeps explanation's duties: nothing in it may be vague, however delightful. Reading this genre trains four moves: term-control (fixing every technical word's meaning on first meeting, from context or glossary), process-tracing (rebuilding the steps in order, often as a flow diagram in the margin), claim-number checking (attaching every quantity to its comparison and unit), and purpose-spotting (what is this text trying to make me able to do or understand — assemble, choose, or merely comprehend). The node sits in the chapter's theme sequence — after environment, before peace — and feeds the later crafts of summarising and argument evaluation, where its precision habit becomes the spine.
steps: An explanatory text is a machine made of sentences — every part has a job, and the reader who reads it like a story has brought a fork to a socket.
The first discipline is term-control.
Technical writing succeeds or dies on its terms, and the reader's first meeting with one is a checkpoint: "condensation" — do I know this exactly, or roughly?

Roughly is not good enough, because the explanation will build on it: three lines later, "as the vapour condenses on the cold coil" demands a precise picture (gas to liquid, releasing heat, on a surface), and the reader…

The fix is mechanical: on first meeting, fix the term — from the text's own definition ("condensation: the change of a gas into a liquid as it cools"), from the glossary, or from context plus dictionary — and write it…
Explanations of how-things-work are ordered, and their order travels on connector words: "First the sea water is filtered...
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "there is no difference — careful reading is careful reading") reveals the misconception of reading skill as one uniform diligence, ignoring that attention must be aimed: the explanation keeps its meaning in sequence, terms, and numbers…
remember: Why is reading a science explanation like reading a story forbidden? State the two different jobs of the two genres and the different success test each sets its reader.

cards.title: Peace-themed texts are the literary and non-literary writings whose subject is…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Peace-themed texts are the literary and non-literary writings whose subject is conflict and its unmaking: quarrels between people, divisions between communities, wars between nations — and the exchanges, gestures, forgiveness, and agreements that hold or restore what anger breaks. The literary side shows conflict as lived experience: the story of two neighbourhood cricket gangs whose war over one ground ends in a shared eleven; the poem spoken by a border fence itself, tired of keeping people apart; the tale where a Hindu family's shop is saved in the riots by the Muslim family two lanes over, and neither ever says why. It works through shown-not-told feeling — the clenched fist, the unreturned gaze, the hand that finally opens — and through symbols paid for in the text (the fence, the shared ball, the unbroken lamp at the window). The non-literary side gives conflict its record and its craft: the news report of a ceasefire; the extract from a peace agreement or a historic speech (Gandhi's, or a school captain's after a wall-painting feud); the letter exchanged across a divide; the account of a mediation — in the UN chamber or the Class 7 corridor. Reading peace texts trains the chapter's standing skills at their sharpest: classification (is this shaped experience or record?), symbol-reading paid for in quotations ('s discipline), and — the node's own emphasis — reading the anatomy of conflict and de-escalation: how a text shows a quarrel escalating (words hardening, sides forming, the small provocation magnified) and how it shows peace being built (the initiative, the apology, the third party, the compromise that lets both faces stay whole). Because peace writing is persuasive by nature, the reader also learns to weigh its claims: a peace text argues for something — reconciliation, understanding, the end of a feud — and the reader must feel the pull of that argument while still asking how its picture was built. The node sits between science and technology and adventure, and feeds the chapter's evaluative endgame.
steps: Peace texts are anatomy lessons in feeling — they cut open a quarrel and show its working, and the reader's job is to trace the working, not just mourn or cheer the ending.
Trace first the escalation, because every quarrel in every text has a ladder, and the writer marks each rung.

In the cricket-ground story: the first rung is the dispute itself (one ground, two gangs — a real conflict of interest, not yet a war); the second rung is the hardening of words ("their ground now" — the pronoun does…
The skilled reader quotes the rung-lines as they climb — because escalation in text is always in the language, and "their ground" is a colder sentence than it looks.

Then trace the de-escalation, which is the genre's real interest: peace in texts is never a mood, it is a sequence of doable acts, and the writer plants them like rungs of the ladder down — the initiative (the smallest…

The reader who traces these rungs learns the genre's deepest lesson: in peace writing, as in life, peace is engineered, not wished — and every act on the ladder down is a thing a reader could do in her own corridor on…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., taking "the fish theft" as the rung where the quarrel became serious and the rest as mere detail) reveals the misconception of escalation as event-size, ignoring that the theft is the smallest sentence on the ladder — what escalates is…
remember: Trace the escalation ladder in this four-sentence extract, quoting the line that marks each rung: "The two lanes had shared the pond for….
In the same pond story, the writer adds a final scene: "Then the drought….

cards.title: Adventure-themed texts are the literary (and factual-report) writings whose…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Adventure-themed texts are the literary (and factual-report) writings whose engine is risk in an indifferent physical world: the sea passage through a storm; the cave descent with a rising trickle of water; the night walk out of a flooded village; the balloon over the Deccan in a shifting wind; the trek where the map and the ground disagree. Their machinery is precise and learnable. Risk with a clock: the danger is physical, concrete, and time-bound — the tide turns at four, the rope holds "for now", the storm is "twelve miles off and closing" — and the text's tension is built almost entirely from clocks and counts, not from villains; the antagonist, where one exists, is the environment itself, which cannot be argued with, bribed, or reformed. Sequence as survival: adventure plots are chains of decision — each act (turn back? push on? send the light signal?) narrows what remains possible, and the reader must hold the current state of the risk (water level, light left, distance gone) the way a chess player holds a board. Competence and its display: the genre's heroes are not the strongest but the most prepared — knots, weather-signs, the discipline of counting food — and the text teaches by showing knowledge used, which is why adventure is the most quietly instructional of all the story genres. The factual branch — the expedition report, the Everest dispatch, the sailor's log, the survivor's account — carries the same structure with real names, dates, and figures, and demands the chapter's non-literary tools (sequence-tracing, claim-checking, vantage-catching). Reading adventure trains specific moves: tracking the risk-state (maintaining a running inventory of danger: how high, how dark, how long left), decision-mapping (pausing at each choice-point to state the options and the cost of each, before reading on), and separating luck from judgement (which outcomes were earned by preparation and which were gifts of chance — the genre's own moral ledger). The node sits between peace and the chapter's two craft nodes — summarising and evaluating the author's argument.
steps: Adventure texts are suspense machines, and their fuel is a single trick: the reader is made to hold a running calculation.

Every good adventure passage keeps a set of live numbers — the water is at the third rung, the torch has an hour, the cave mouth is four hundred metres back — and the reader who does not track them is reading a travel…

This is risk-state tracking, and it is a skill with a method: as you read, maintain the inventory — what is rising (the tide, the water in the cave, the wind), what is falling (light, food, the temperature), what is…
The second skill is decision-mapping.

Adventure plots are not things that happen to people; they are choices people make, and the writer marks each choice-point deliberately — the fork in the passage, the moment the sail must be reefed or not. The…

This habit does two things: it converts suspense into judgement (the reader stops merely fearing and starts choosing, which is the genre's real pleasure), and it trains the moral instrument the genre exists to sharpen …
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the risk-state is just that they are wet and will get wetter") reveals the misconception of danger as sensation, ignoring that the genre's danger is quantitative — the terror of this extract lives in three numbers (four o'clock…

cards.title: Summarising is the craft of compressing a text into a shorter faithful version…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Summarising is the craft of compressing a text into a shorter faithful version — usually one third of the original's length or less — that preserves the skeleton of its meaning: the main idea, the essential supporting points, and the outcome, while discarding the flesh of example, repetition, illustration, and ornament. It is a craft with rules, not an art of vibes. Own words: the summary must recast, not copy — copied sentences bypass understanding and defeat the exercise's diagnostic purpose (the rule inherited from the chapter's first node). Fidelity: nothing added (no comment, no opinion, no outside knowledge, no invented connections) and nothing distorted (the claims kept at their original strength — "may" stays "may", "all" stays "all"); the summary's reader must be able to trust it as the text in miniature. Selection by structure: what stays is decided by the text's own architecture — for a narrative, the spine of events (who, the problem, the key turn, the outcome); for an explanation, the process's stages or the argument's moves (claim, reason, evidence, conclusion); for an argumentative piece, thesis, main grounds, and verdict. Proportion: the summary's space must mirror the text's — a point that took half the original gets roughly half the summary, so the miniature keeps the original's shape and does not silently promote a footnote into a headline. The disciplined method runs in passes: first read for the global shape (what is this, and what is it for); then mark — underline the sentence or clause that carries each stage's meaning and cross out the recognisable discards (repetitions, examples, asides, direct speech reduced to reported gist); then draft from the marks in own words; then verify against the original — the checklist run: length, fidelity (added? distorted? own words?), proportion, and coverage (does every paragraph's contribution appear somewhere?). Summary differs from its neighbours: paraphrase keeps the length and changes the words; précis (the older term in CISCE tradition) is the formal summary with a stated word-limit and a single paragraph; and the book-report is not a summary at all when it adds judgement. The node stands after the six theme nodes ( to), forging their reading habits into one tool, and feeds directly into the chapter's last node, evaluating the author's argument.
steps: A summary is a building demolished to its frame — and the first law of demolition is that you must know which walls carry the roof.

That knowledge is structural, and it comes before any cutting: read once through for the global shape, asking the classifier's question (narrative? explanation? argument?) because the skeleton differs by kind — the…
Then the marking pass, which is where summaries are actually won or lost.

Underline the carrier-clauses: in each paragraph, the sentence or clause that holds the stage's meaning — not necessarily the first sentence (writers bury mains mid-paragraph exactly where skim-readers lose them, a…

Cross out the discards, and name them as you cross: repetition (the point made second time in different words), example (the three instances after the general statement — keep the general statement, one instance at most…
The draft pass then writes from the marks in own words — the old floor rule — connecting the kept stages with the text's own logical order, not the arbitrary order of your remembering.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "they are all just saying the text again in shorter or different words, so the names hardly matter") reveals the misconception of the trio as one activity at volumes, ignoring that each combination of the two duties serves a different…

cards.title: Evaluating an author's argument is the critical skill of judging how well a…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Evaluating an author's argument is the critical skill of judging how well a text supports what it wants you to believe — separating the claim (what the author asserts), the grounds (the reasons, examples, and evidence offered), and the assumptions (the unspoken beliefs the argument leans on), and then testing the joints: does the evidence actually bear on the claim, is it sufficient, is it representative, is the reasoning valid? The evaluation toolkit has named instruments. Claim-spotting: arguments often state their claim as if it were fact, and the reader's first task is the one learnt on the nation and science nodes — finding the verdict-sentences inside report-clothes ("a spectacle that finally showcased the nation's unity"). Evidence-testing: for each ground, three questions — Is it relevant (does it bear on this claim, or on a neighbouring one)? Is it sufficient (enough instances, enough data — one corridor does not a law make, as the peace node showed)? Is it representative (drawn fairly from the whole field, or cherry-picked — the forty happiest students consulted about the timetable)? Assumption-hunting: the unexamined beliefs beneath the reasoning ("improvement proves the cause" assumes nothing else changed; "everyone agrees" assumes the people consulted are everyone). Fallacy-noticing at Class 7 level: the loaded word (adjectives doing the arguing — "flawless", "common-sense reform"), the false either-or ("either we ban phones or the school decays"), the appeal to popularity ("everyone knows"), the hasty generalisation (one incident branded a trend), and the attack on the person standing in for an answer to the point. Counter-consideration: the mature evaluation asks what a fair-minded opponent would say, and whether the text acknowledges the other side — an argument that has never heard its opposition is weaker than its confidence. Balance in the verdict: the evaluation's conclusion is calibrated, not tribal — "the claim is partly supported: the evidence is real but narrow, the sample small, the counter-arguments unaddressed" — and it, too, must give its own reasons, because the evaluator's essay is an argument and stands in the dock it constructed. The node completes the chapter: reading classified, themed (002–007), and summarised (008) now meets its final office — the reader as judge.
steps: Every argument is a bridge from evidence to claim, and the evaluator's job is to walk it — testing every plank, not admiring the far bank.
The inspection begins with the anatomy, and the anatomy is found by question: What does this text want me to believe?
(the claim — often the loudest sentence, sometimes never stated outright but visible as the direction every paragraph pushes).
What does it offer me to believe it?
(the grounds — reasons, examples, figures, authorities).
And what must I already accept for the grounds to reach the claim?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., taking "even the sceptics arrive refreshed" as the argument's claim because it is the most vivid sentence) reveals the misconception of claims as emphasis, ignoring that the claim is what the text wants adopted — a policy, not an image…

Test this ground against the three evidence tests: claim — "the composting project should be extended to the whole city"; ground — "our school's three bins have worked perfectly….

cards.title: Creative composition is the disciplined art of producing a short, complete…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Creative composition is the disciplined art of producing a short, complete, original piece of continuous prose — at the CISCE Class 7 level, 200 to 250 words on a given topic, picture, or opening line — within a fixed skeleton and a controlled word budget. The skeleton has four stations. The title: short, pointed, drawn from the composition's central impression, not a paraphrase of the question. The opening paragraph: two to four sentences that set scene or state the controlling idea, hook the reader with one concrete detail, and make clear what the composition will be about — the examiner's first and strongest impression forms here. The body: two or three paragraphs, each built on ONE main idea or stage of the incident, each opening with its idea in a topic sentence and developing it with specific detail (sights, sounds, small true actions — never a general list), paragraphs joined by linkers (however, therefore, meanwhile, at last) so the prose walks instead of lurching. The conclusion: two or three sentences that close the incident, return to the controlling impression, and stop — no new incident, no apology, no moral bolted on unless it grows from the story. Around the skeleton run the disciplines that make it work. Planning first: a five-minute outline (one line per station) decided before drafting, because a composition is built twice — once in the outline, once in the draft — and the outline is where mistakes are cheapest. One-incident discipline: a short composition cannot carry a month; it carries one afternoon, one market visit, one power cut — and its power comes from depth (what the light did on the wet road) rather than breadth (everything that happened that year). Word-budget discipline: 200–250 words is not a cage but a contract — long enough to develop one impression fully (about 12 to 18 sentences), short enough to draft, revise, and polish in the examination hour; the writer who respects the budget chooses details, and choosing is thinking. Register discipline: compositions are written in continuous connected prose — full sentences, standard grammar, past tense for narration held steady — the formal-but-living register of the good school essay, neither the chumminess of chat nor the deadness of the memorised paragraph. The node opens the Writing chapter: reading (chapter 02) trained the eye on other writers' architecture; this node turns the builder's tools around, and the siblings that follow — story, poem (003), dialogue (004) — are this same craft in special dresses.
steps: A good composition is decided before it is written: the five minutes spent on an outline do more for the final mark than twenty minutes of unplanned writing, because the examination composition fails at the planning…
The craft therefore runs in three movements.
Movement one, the five-minute plan.
Read the topic twice and convert it into one question: what is the ONE incident or impression this composition will develop?

("A Visit to a Book Fair" — not the whole fair's history: the hour you got lost between two stalls and found a book you still own.) Then rule four lines: TITLE (chosen now — it forces the central impression to the…
OPENING (one line: scene plus hook);

cards.title: Story-writing is the craft of shaping one trouble into a complete short…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Story-writing is the craft of shaping one trouble into a complete short narrative — at the CISCE Class 7 level, typically expanding a given outline of five to seven points into a story of 150–250 words with a title — and its difference from the general composition is the engine: a story must contain a problem, because a sequence of events is a report, while a trouble that tightens and resolves is a story. The skeleton has five stations. The title: short, loaded with the story's centre ("The Last Bus" promises deadline and loss before line one). The opening: a few sentences that fix place, time, and the main character in motion, and plant the want that the trouble will block — Ravi oversleeps on the morning that matters. The rising trouble: the middle station where the problem tightens through two or three beats, each making things worse or the clock shorter, developed in shown action (hands, voices, objects) rather than summary. The climax: the turning point where the trouble peaks and the character makes the choice or takes the action that decides everything — the story's most expensive sentences belong here. The resolution: the landing that shows how the world sits after the choice, drawing the meaning out of the action without lecture. Around the stations run the craft rules. Outline-expansion discipline: the CISCE outline's points are stations, not paragraphs — each point expands into three to six sentences of scene at roughly one-to-three ratio, and points that cannot carry a beat are joined or dropped within the budget. Character-through-action discipline: a short story cannot analyse a person; it shows one deciding — the boy who wipes the tomato juice on his shirt and keeps pushing the cart has been characterised more deeply than a paragraph of adjectives could. The fair-twist discipline: surprise is permitted, coincidence is not — a resolution must grow from seeds the story has already planted (the listener, the planted object, the earlier choice), and a rescue that arrives from outside the story ("suddenly the teacher drove up") cheats the reader of the ending her attention earned. Narration discipline: narrator chosen at the start (first person "I" for closeness, third person for freedom to roam) and tense held in the past; dialogue, if used, is brief and in the format of the dialogue node's cousin — two or three lines at most, each doing plot-work. The moral question: a Class 7 story may carry a lesson, but the lesson must grow inside the events and be felt at the resolution — "Thus we learn" is the sound of a writer abandoning her story. The node sits second in the Writing chain: the composition node built the floor (plan, budget, revision), and this node installs the engine — trouble — which the poem node will then compress into stanzas.
steps: A story is one trouble, told at the speed of its own tightening — and the examiner can identify a real story in the first thirty words, because a real story has already begun to go wrong.
The craft begins before the first sentence, with the reading of the outline.
The CISCE story task supplies five to seven points; the untrained writer copies each point as a paragraph and produces a stretched report.

The trained writer reads the points as stations of a single trouble: which point contains the want (Ravi must reach the exhibition), which the block (the bus leaves without him), which the tightening beats (the blocked…
Marking the stations on the outline costs two minutes and is the difference between a story and a list.
Then the expansion, and here the ratio rules: each chosen point becomes three to six sentences of scene — not because length is virtuous but because plot-work needs bodies;

cards.title: Poem-writing is the craft of compressing one impression — a moment, a scene…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Poem-writing is the craft of compressing one impression — a moment, a scene, a feeling — into a few stanzas of concentrated language, where the build-unit is the image (a word-picture the reader can see, hear, or feel) rather than the sentence, and where sound — rhythm and rhyme — is a working part of the meaning, not decoration. At the CISCE Class 7 level the task is typically a poem of three or four stanzas on a given topic, or the completion of a begun poem, and the standard skeleton is: a TITLE that names the poem's centre-promise; three or four QUATRAINS (four-line stanzas), each built on ONE impression, so the poem walks in steps like the story's stations but at higher compression; and a LAST STANZA whose job is the landing — an image that leaves the reader inside the feeling, never a lecture about it. The RHYME SCHEME is the skeleton's sound-pattern, marked in letters: AABB (paired couplets, the marching scheme — the model's "hill/still", "feet/street"), ABAB (alternating, the swaying scheme), ABCB (the loose scheme that rhymes only lines two and four and leaves the poet's hands free), and free verse (no scheme at all — sound made by rhythm and repetition instead), each a legitimate choice declared by writing, not announced. Around the skeleton run the craft disciplines. Image-first discipline: the poem is planned as pictures before sounds — an image bank of four to six specific sights, sounds, and touches collected in the plan, because "the brass pot filled with a plink" carries the rain that "rain is very nice" cannot; rhyme-last discipline: the rhyme scheme is fitted after the images exist, since a rhyme hunted first enslaves the sense — the disease called forced rhyme (inverted syntax to reach a chime, dead pairs like "fine/pine", and padding like "very divine"), which is the commonest fault in Class 7 verse; the read-aloud discipline: a poem is an oral machine and is tested with the mouth — any line the tongue stumbles on or the breath cannot finish is rewritten, because the ear catches the false rhyme, the broken rhythm, and the filler word that the eye forgives; and the compression discipline: articles and connectives may be trimmed, adjectives rationed (two per image at most), and every "very" evicted, since a poem is the one form where word-count is felt as weight. Figurative tools — the simile, the metaphor, the personification the model uses ("clouds came walking... grey as buffaloes") — are named and used here as image-makers, while their formal identification and fuller taxonomy belong to the grammar-and-vocabulary strand later in this course; the analysis of set poems belongs to the literature strand. The node sits third in the Writing chain: the composition node built the skeleton habit, the story node built the one-trouble compression, and the poem compresses further still — a story's best moment, carried by a bicycle built for it.
steps: A poem is planned in pictures and only then in sounds — the writer who collects images before hunting rhymes writes a poem, and the writer who hunts rhymes first writes rhymed sentences and calls the padding poetry.
The craft begins with the choosing of the parcel.

A poem cannot carry a rainy day; it carries the first drop on the tin roof, the brass pot's plink, Grandmother's wink — one impression, stated in the plan as a single line ("the arrival of rain heard from inside a…

Then the image bank: four to six specifics, gathered under the impression-line in the plan's first minute — sights (buffalo-grey clouds, water sheeting the lane), sounds (the drum on the tin, the gutter finding its…
"Beautiful", "nice", "lovely" are not images but verdicts, and a poem made of verdicts is a comment on a poem nobody wrote.

The stanza map comes third: three or four stations, ONE impression each, ordered like the story's trouble — Stanza one, the arrival (the first drop); stanza two, the full rain (the world answering); stanza three, the…

cards.title: Dialogue is a literary device that presents direct speech between characters…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Dialogue is a literary device that presents direct speech between characters, allowing readers to hear their voices without narrator mediation. In the CISCE Class 7 English curriculum, dialogue writing is a sub‑skill of creative composition (200‑250 words) and is assessed for: (1) correct formatting — speaker tag, colon, line break; (2) punctuation — commas, question marks, exclamation marks inside the spoken line; (3) characterisation — vocabulary, tone, and idiom appropriate to age, region, and situation; (4) purpose — advancing plot, revealing conflict, or conveying information; and (5) integration with narrative — seamless shifts between dialogue and descriptive prose using linkers such as “however” or “therefore”. Dialogue differs from monologue (single speaker) and from reported speech (indirect narration). It also connects to the notice and poster formats taught in the same chapter because all require concise, purpose‑driven language, but dialogue uniquely demands interactive exchange and dramatic tension.
steps: A well‑crafted dialogue reads like a real conversation while serving the story’s purpose.
Here is why: dialogue must reveal character, advance plot, and sound authentic, all within the strict formatting rules CISCE expects.
First, decide the speakers and their relationship — a grandmother and grandson at a Mumbai local train station will use different diction than two classmates planning a science project.
Second, give each speaker a distinct voice: the grandmother may sprinkle Marathi words (“Aai”, “kaay”) while the grandson uses school slang (“cool”, “lit”).
Third, use line breaks and speaker tags (e.g., “Rohan:”) so the examiner can instantly see who speaks.
Fourth, punctuate inside the spoken line — commas before tags, question marks for questions, exclamation for strong feeling.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Write the name in brackets before the speech”) reveals the misconception that dialogue uses parentheses like a script, confusing stage‑script conventions with prose dialogue formatting.

cards.title: This node establishes the structural framework for grammar and vocabulary in…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: This node establishes the structural framework for grammar and vocabulary in context. A phrase is a group of words lacking a finite verb (e.g., “in the garden”, “very quickly”). A clause contains a subject and a finite verb; it can be independent (expresses a complete thought) or dependent (needs an independent clause). Simple sentences have one independent clause; compound sentences join two or more independent clauses with coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or); complex sentences combine one independent clause with at least one dependent clause introduced by subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when). Active voice places the agent as subject (“The chef cooked the meal”); passive voice makes the patient the subject (“The meal was cooked by the chef”), using a form of “be” + past participle. Synonyms are words with similar meanings (happy–joyful); antonyms are opposites (hot–cold); analogy shows a relationship between two pairs (bird:nest:: dog:kennel). Figurative language includes: simile (explicit comparison using like/as), metaphor (implicit comparison), personification (giving human traits to non‑human), alliteration (repetition of initial consonant sounds), assonance (repetition of vowel sounds), onomatopoeia (words imitating sounds), irony (contrast between expectation and reality). Domain vocabulary refers to subject‑specific terms (e.g., “photosynthesis” in science, “latitude” in geography) that enable precise communication within a discipline. These sub‑concepts interlink: clauses build sentences; voice changes clause focus; synonyms/antonyms/analogy expand lexical choice; figurative devices operate at phrase/clause level; domain vocabulary supplies the content words that fill those structures.
steps: Understanding the building blocks of sentences — phrases, clauses, voice, and figurative devices — lets you write clearly and read deeply.
First, phrases are like ingredients (flour, sugar) while clauses are the baked goods (cookies, cakes) because a clause has both a subject and a verb and can stand alone.

Second, sentence types are like connecting train cars: a simple sentence is a single engine; a compound sentence couples two engines with a conjunction; a complex sentence attaches a trailer (dependent clause) to the…
Third, active and passive voice are camera angles: active zooms on the doer (“The monsoon flooded the streets”), passive zooms on the receiver (“The streets were flooded by the monsoon”).
Fourth, synonyms, antonyms, and analogies are a thesaurus toolkit — they let you swap words for precision or variety, just as a chef substitutes spices.

Fifth, figurative language adds flavour: simile (“as busy as a bee”), metaphor (“time is a thief”), personification (“the wind whispered”), alliteration (“silent snakes”), assonance (“high tide”), onomatopoeia (“buzz”)…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “The bright sun rose” as a phrase) reveals the misconception that any word group is a phrase — confusing a clause (which has a subject and verb) with a phrase.
remember: Identify the phrase in the following sentence: “The bright sun rose over the hills.”.

cards.title: Grammar and vocabulary in context is the study of how language structures…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Grammar and vocabulary in context is the study of how language structures — phrases, clauses, sentence types (simple, compound, complex), voice (active–passive), and word relationships (synonyms, antonyms, analogies) — combine with figurative devices (irony, personification, alliteration, metaphor, simile, assonance, onomatopoeia) and domain‑specific vocabulary to create appropriate register (formal, informal, persuasive, descriptive) for a given purpose and audience. A phrase lacks a finite verb; a clause contains a subject and a finite verb. Simple sentences have one independent clause; compound sentences join two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction; complex sentences link an independent clause with one or more dependent clauses. Active voice places the doer as subject (“Rohit hit the ball”); passive voice makes the receiver the subject (“The ball was hit by Rohit”). Synonyms share meaning; antonyms oppose; analogies show relational similarity (“bat: cricket:: racket: badminton”). Figurative language adds layers: irony contrasts expectation and reality; personification gives human traits to non‑human; alliteration repeats initial sounds; metaphor equates unlike things; simile compares with “like/as”; assonance repeats vowel sounds; onomatopoeia mimics sounds. Mastery of these elements lets a writer shift register precisely — formal for a notice, conversational for a diary entry — while maintaining grammatical correctness.
steps: The one thing to remember: register is the match between your grammatical choices, vocabulary, and figurative language to the purpose and audience of your writing.
Here is why: every piece of writing — a notice, a story, a letter — demands a specific tone; using the wrong clause type, voice, or figure of speech makes the message sound off‑key.

Consider a school notice about a clean‑up drive: it needs formal register, so you use passive voice (“The playground will be cleaned by volunteers”), complex sentences (“Because the monsoon is approaching, we must act…

In contrast, a diary entry about the same event can be informal: active voice (“I joined the clean‑up”), simple sentences (“It was fun.”), and figurative language like personification (“The broom danced across the…
Step 1: Identify the purpose (inform, persuade, narrate) and audience (principal, friend, public).
Step 2: Choose sentence structures — simple for clarity, compound for balance, complex for cause‑effect.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is a clause because it has a verb ‘running’”) reveals the misconception that any verb form makes a clause — confusing non‑finite verb forms with finite verbs.
remember: Identify the underlined group of words as a phrase or a clause: “Running down the lane, the boy waved at his mother.”.
