Why are the first five ideals grouped together and the last four grouped together in the Preamble.
Assess the impact of the 42nd Amendment on the Preamble’s vision.

cards.title: The chapter introduces the concept of a welfare state and the Directive…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The chapter introduces the concept of a welfare state and the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution of India. A welfare state is a system where the government assumes responsibility for the basic well‑being of its citizens — providing health care, education, employment, and social security. The DPSP are guidelines for the central and state governments to frame laws and policies that promote social and economic justice. They are divided into general principles (such as securing a living wage, equal pay, and protection of children) and Gandhian principles (such as promoting village panchayats, cottage industries, and prohibition of intoxicating drinks). Unlike Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable and enforceable by courts, DPSP are non‑justiciable; courts cannot compel the government to implement them, yet they serve as a moral compass for governance. The chapter also highlights the relationship between the two: Fundamental Rights protect individual liberty, while DPSP aim at collective welfare, and together they embody the Constitution’s vision of a just society. Understanding this overview helps students see how constitutional goals translate into everyday policies like mid‑day meals, rural employment schemes, and public health programmes.
steps: The chapter shows that the Directive Principles are the Constitution’s roadmap for turning India into a welfare state where the government actively works for citizens’ basic needs.

Here is why: first, a welfare state commits the state to provide health, education, and livelihood security, which students already see in programmes like the Mid‑Day Meal Scheme and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural…

Third, unlike Fundamental Rights, these principles are non‑justiciable; courts cannot order the government to fulfil them, yet they shape legislation because governments ignore them at political cost.
Fourth, the chapter sets up the comparison: Fundamental Rights protect individual freedom (e.g., speech, equality), while Directive Principles pursue collective welfare (e.g., nutrition, housing).
Fifth, understanding this overview prepares students to examine each principle in detail and to evaluate how far India has progressed toward the welfare ideal.

Consider a village where a new panchayat builds a health centre — the panchayat acts on a Gandhian directive, the centre fulfills a general directive for public health, and the funding comes from a law inspired by the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles”) reveals the misconception that the classification mirrors the two parts of the Constitution rather than the thematic grouping within Part IV.
remember: Recall: What are the two broad categories of Directive Principles of State Policy mentioned in the chapter.
Reasoning: Why are Directive Principles described as non‑justiciable, and what practical effect does this have on governance.
Evaluate: “Fundamental Rights are more important than Directive Principles because they are enforceable.” Assess this statement using the chapter’s perspective.

cards.title: A welfare state is a system of governance in which the state assumes primary…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: A welfare state is a system of governance in which the state assumes primary responsibility for the social and economic well‑being of its citizens. In the Indian constitutional framework this idea is embedded in the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36‑51). The key features of a welfare state, as reflected in these principles, are: (1) Social Justice – the state strives to eliminate inequalities of status, opportunity and income; (2) Economic Justice – it seeks to secure the right to an adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, and fair distribution of material resources; (3) Provision of Basic Needs – the state aims to provide nutrition, housing, health care, education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disability; (4) Promotion of Human Dignity – policies are directed toward raising the standard of living and ensuring humane conditions of work; (5) Participatory Governance – the state encourages institutions like village panchayats and cooperatives so that citizens can take part in decision‑making. Together these features translate the abstract ideal of a “welfare state” into concrete policy directions that guide legislation and executive action, even though the Directive Principles themselves are non‑justiciable.
steps: A welfare state means the government actively works to secure every citizen’s basic well‑being, not just protect liberties.
Here is why: the Constitution’s Directive Principles turn the moral promise of the Preamble — “social, economic and political justice” — into actionable policy goals.
First, social justice requires the state to reduce gaps between rich and poor, which appears in Article 38’s call to promote a social order based on justice.
Second, economic justice is spelled out in Article 39, directing the state to ensure adequate livelihood, equal pay, and prevent concentration of wealth.
Third, provision of basic needs is captured in Articles 41 (right to work, education, public assistance), 42 (just and humane conditions of work) and 47 (nutrition, public health).
Fourth, human dignity is advanced by Article 43, urging a living wage and decent standard of life for workers.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Article 39”) reveals the misconception that economic directives alone define the welfare state, ignoring the broader social‑justice mandate of Article 38.
remember: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to promote a social order based on justice — social, economic and political.
Explain why the provision of midday meals in government schools is an example of a welfare‑state feature.
Evaluate the statement: “A welfare state guarantees every citizen a job.”.

cards.title: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (DPSP) — MEANING — this node's lesson…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (DPSP) — MEANING — this node's lesson: what the Directive Principles are, where they sit, what makes them "directives" rather than "rights", and why the Constitution calls unenforceable principles "fundamental". THE PLACEMENT AND TEXT: Part IV of the Constitution of India, ARTICLES 36 to 51 — the longest single part of the Constitution's instructions to government; Article 36 defines "the State" for this part (the Central Government, the state governments, and all local and other authorities within India's territory), and Article 37 states the two rules that make the part unique: the provisions "shall NOT BE ENFORCEABLE BY ANY COURT", but the principles laid down are "NEVERTHELESS FUNDAMENTAL IN THE GOVERNANCE OF THE COUNTRY and it shall be the DUTY OF THE STATE to apply these principles in making laws". THE MEANING IN THREE LOADS: (1) DIRECTIVES — the DPSPs are INSTRUCTIONS TO GOVERNMENT (the Centre, the states, all public authorities): not commands to citizens and not rights held against the government, but goals the government must pursue — secure livelihoods, distribute resources, run village panchayats, educate children, protect the environment, promote cottage industries, support the weak; they are the STATE'S JOB DESCRIPTION for building a welfare state. (2) PRINCIPLES — they are stated as principles, not detailed laws: broad, continuing goals (Articles 36–51) from which PARLIAMENT AND THE STATE LEGISLATURES draw specific laws — the mid-day meal in schools, pensions for the aged, legal aid for the poor are particular laws made under particular principles; the principles themselves stay in the Constitution as the permanent direction. (3) POLICY — they govern POLICY-MAKING, not litigation: their force is political and moral — voters, parties, courts interpreting laws, and every government's own conscience measure budgets and statutes against them. THE TWO UNIQUENESS-FACTS, stated exactly: (a) NON-JUSTICIABILITY — if a government ignores a Directive Principle, no citizen can sue to enforce it in court; the remedy is political (elections, debate), not judicial; (b) FUNDAMENTAL-IN-GOVERNANCE — Article 37's own words declare them "fundamental in the governance of the country": the Constitution refuses to let non-enforceability slide into unimportance — it puts a DUTY on the State to apply them in law-making. THE ANCESTRY: the DPSPs were borrowed from the CONSTITUTION OF IRELAND (1937), which itself carried the idea of directive principles of social policy; the framers also knew the "INSTRUMENTS OF INSTRUCTIONS" issued under the Government of India Act 1935 — directions to governors — and converted that device into a democratic, people-facing charter; the framers' intent is the chapter's own: political democracy (one person, one vote) is not enough without ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEMOCRACY (a life worth voting for) — the DPSPs are the engine of the WELFARE STATE (the chapter's opening nodes,–002). THE CHARACTER IN FOUR ADJECTIVES: POSITIVE (they direct the State to DO — build, protect, provide — where fundamental rights mostly direct it to REFRAIN), CONTINUING (no expiry: each government inherits them), FLEXIBLE-IN-METHOD but FIXED-IN-GOAL (the how is each era's choice; the what is permanent), and SUPPLEMENTARY (they complete the Fundamental Rights — the shield and the promise, Part III and Part IV, the two wheels of the same vehicle; the full comparison is the later sibling node's work,). THE EXAMINATION LINE: Part IV, Articles 36–51; directives to the State; Article 37's two rules (not enforceable, yet fundamental in governance and a duty in law-making); Irish ancestry; welfare-state aim; positive-continuing-supplementary character.
steps: The Directive Principles are the Constitution's to-do list for the State — unenforceable in court, yet called fundamental by the Constitution itself, and the paradox is the design, not a defect.
First load: DIRECTIVES — who is being addressed.

A right is held BY a citizen AGAINST the State ("the State shall not abridge..."); a directive is held BY the Constitution UPON the State ("The State shall... secure, promote, organise, protect"): Part IV addresses the…
Second load: PRINCIPLES — the form the instructions take.

The DPSPs are stated as PRINCIPLES, not as statutes: "secure adequate means of livelihood", "promote cottage industries", "raise the level of nutrition" — broad, permanent goals that no single law can exhaust and no…
Third load: POLICY — the force the instructions carry.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing the DPSPs in Part III "with the rights", or dating the Irish source to 1950) reveals the misconception of part-confusion — Part III holds Fundamental Rights, Part IV holds Directive Principles, and the examiner marks the boundary…
remember: Recall: In which part and articles do the Directive Principles….
Reasoning: A student objects: "If no court can enforce the Directive Principles, they are just advice — and advice can be….
Evaluate: A student claims: "Article 37 contradicts itself — the same article says the principles cannot be enforced and then calls them….

cards.title: CLASSIFICATION OF THE DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES — GENERAL AND GANDHIAN…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: CLASSIFICATION OF THE DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES — GENERAL AND GANDHIAN — this node's lesson: how the principles of Part IV (Articles 36–51) are grouped for study, and what each group contains. THE FRAME: the Constitution itself sets out the principles as one list; the grouping into categories is the STUDENT'S MAP, a convention of textbooks and teaching that collects the articles by the vision each serves; the two shelves this syllabus names are the GENERAL principles and the GANDHIAN principles. THE GENERAL PRINCIPLES — the modern welfare state's programme, articles that direct the State to build social and economic fairness across the whole economy: ARTICLE 38 (secure a social order for the promotion of welfare — social, economic and political justice — and minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities); ARTICLE 39 (secure adequate means of LIVELIHOOD for all; distribute material resources for the common good; prevent CONCENTRATION of wealth; EQUAL PAY for equal work for men and women; protect workers' health and childhood from abuse and exploitation); ARTICLE 39A (equal justice and FREE LEGAL AID to the poor — a later insertion); ARTICLE 41 (the right to work, to education and to PUBLIC ASSISTANCE in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement); ARTICLE 42 (just and humane conditions of work and MATERNITY RELIEF); ARTICLE 45 (early childhood care and education for children below six years); ARTICLE 47 (raise the level of NUTRITION and the standard of living; improve PUBLIC HEALTH); ARTICLE 48 (organise AGRICULTURE and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines); ARTICLE 48A (PROTECT and improve the environment, forests and wildlife); ARTICLE 51 (promote INTERNATIONAL PEACE and security; honour international law; settle disputes by arbitration). Alongside these, some textbooks list a further "liberal" cluster — ARTICLE 44 (strive for a UNIFORM CIVIL CODE for all citizens) and ARTICLE 50 (SEPARATE the judiciary from the executive in the public services) — and a careful answer may note the grouping-convention without forcing it. THE GANDHIAN PRINCIPLES — the articles that carry Mahatma Gandhi's programme of village-centred reconstruction into the Constitution: ARTICLE 40 (organise VILLAGE PANCHAYATS and endow them with enough powers to work as units of self-government); ARTICLE 43 (secure a LIVING WAGE and a decent standard of life to all workers; promote COTTAGE INDUSTRIES in rural areas, individually or through co-operatives); ARTICLE 46 (promote the educational and economic interests of the SCHEDULED CASTES, SCHEDULED TRIBES and other WEAKER SECTIONS and protect them from social injustice and exploitation); the PROHIBITION clause of ARTICLE 47 (endeavour to bring about PROHIBITION of intoxicating drinks and drugs — Gandhi's cherished reform); the CATTLE clause of ARTICLE 48 (prohibit the slaughter of COWS and calves and other milch and draught cattle — the rural-economy and sentiment principle). THE POINT OF THE MAP: the two shelves answer the two inheritances the republic chose to honour — the general shelf builds the MODERN state (welfare economics, labour protection, environment, internationalism), the Gandhian shelf builds the VILLAGE republic (decentralised self-government, cottage economy, the weakest first, the social reforms of the freedom movement) — and both shelves are the same Part IV: directives to the State, non-enforceable, fundamental in governance (the frame of the previous node,). A HONESTY-FLAG: Article 47 carries one clause on each shelf (nutrition in general, prohibition in Gandhian) and Article 48 similarly straddles (scientific agriculture and cattle protection), because the articles were not written for the map — the map serves the memory; and Article 43B (workers' CO-OPERATIVES, a later addition) belongs to the Gandhian shelf's co-operative spirit. THE EXAMINATION LINE: the general group with its article-numbers and one-line contents (38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 45, 47-nutrition, 48-agriculture, 48A, 51 — and 44, 50 as liberal entries); the Gandhian group (40, 43, 46, 47-prohibition, 48-cattle, 43B); the straddling-flag; the same-Part-IV frame.
steps: The Constitution wrote one list of directives; the student's map draws two shelves — the general shelf for the modern welfare state and the Gandhian shelf for the village republic — and reading the shelves in order is…
First shelf: THE GENERAL PRINCIPLES — the programme of a modern welfare state.

Begin at ARTICLE 38, the shelf's anchor: the State shall secure a SOCIAL ORDER for the promotion of welfare — social, economic and political justice — and shall MINIMISE INEQUALITIES of income, status, facilities and…
ARTICLE 39A turns it into the courtroom — equal justice and FREE LEGAL AID so the poor are not silenced by the fee;
ARTICLE 41 turns it into the life-cycle — support in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and the rights to work and education;
ARTICLE 42 turns it into the workplace — just and humane conditions and MATERNITY RELIEF;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing Article 40 under "general" because panchayats exist everywhere today, or pairing Article 48A with Gandhi) reveals the misconception of shelf-drift — the map's whole point is the vision each article serves, and the examiner marks…
remember: Recall: Name the two groups of the Directive Principles. List four general principles with article numbers, and four Gandhian principles with article numbers, one line each.
Reasoning: A student asks: "Why are the panchayat, cottage-industry and prohibition articles called….
Evaluate: A student claims: "The Gandhian shelf is outdated — panchayats and cottage industries belong to the village past; the general shelf is the future." Assess the claim….

cards.title: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are guidelines in Part IV of the…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36‑51) that direct the Union and State governments to frame laws and policies for a welfare state. They cover social, economic, and political goals such as securing a living wage, promoting cottage industries, and protecting the environment. Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12‑35) are justiciable guarantees — citizens can approach courts if these rights are violated. The key relationship: DPSP are non‑justiciable (Article 37), while Fundamental Rights are enforceable; however, the Supreme Court has held that the two are complementary and the State must harmonise them when making laws. DPSP include general principles (e.g., Article 38 – social order) and Gandhian principles (e.g., Article 40 – village panchayats, Article 43 – cottage industries). Understanding the distinction helps students see why some policies become laws immediately (rights) while others remain aspirational targets (principles).
steps: The one thing to remember: Fundamental Rights are legally enforceable guarantees, while Directive Principles are moral‑political guidelines that the government strives to fulfil but cannot be sued for. Here is why: the…
DPSP were placed in Part IV and declared non‑justiciable by Article 37, reflecting the reality that socio‑economic goals need resources and time.
Yet the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) said the two are “equally fundamental” and the State must balance them.
Consider a village that lacks a primary school.
Article 45 (originally a DPSP) urged the State to provide free education; later, the 86th Amendment turned it into a Fundamental Right under Article 21A, making it enforceable.
This shift shows how a directive can become a right when political will and resources align.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Part III”) reveals the misconception that all important provisions are in the same part, confusing the location of rights with that of directives.
remember: Which part of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy.
Explain why a citizen cannot file a writ petition to enforce Article 40 (organisation of village panchayats).
Evaluate the statement: “Directive Principles are inferior to Fundamental Rights because they cannot be enforced.”.

cards.title: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES IN ACTION — this node's lesson…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES IN ACTION — this node's lesson: the principal laws and programmes by which the State has converted Part IV's principles (the frame of, the shelves of) into enforceable reality — the designed pathway called PRINCIPLE-TO-LAW CONVERSION. THE MECHANISM, once and for all: a Directive Principle cannot be sued on (Article 37), but the legislature can turn it into a STATUTE or a SCHEME — and the statute is then fully enforceable in court; the conversion is how non-justiciable goals grow justiciable wings. THE EXHIBITS, arranged by shelf. THE GENERAL SHELF IN ACTION: (1) ARTICLE 38/39 (livelihood, no concentration, fair shares) — LAND REFORMS after Independence: abolition of the ZAMINDARI system (the intermediaries between the cultivator and the state removed), tenancy reforms securing cultivators, and LAND CEILING laws capping holdings, redistributing surplus to the landless; and the NATIONAL RURAL EMPLOYMENT GUARANTEE — the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, guaranteeing 100 DAYS of wage employment each year to every rural household that demands work — the largest work-guarantee in the world; (2) ARTICLE 39(d) (equal pay for equal work) — the EQUAL REMUNERATION ACT, 1976, forbidding unequal wages for men and women in the same work; (3) ARTICLE 41 (assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness) — the NATIONAL SOCIAL ASSISTANCE PROGRAMME (1995): old-age, widow and disability pensions for the poor; (4) ARTICLE 42 (maternity relief, humane work) — the MATERNITY BENEFIT ACT (1961, with paid leave extended to 26 weeks in 2017) and the Factories Acts' work-condition rules; (5) ARTICLE 39A (free legal aid) — the LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITIES ACT, 1987, creating the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and LOK ADALATS (people's courts of conciliation) that settle disputes free of cost; (6) ARTICLE 45/47 (education, nutrition) — the school MID-DAY MEAL programme (now PM POSHAN), serving cooked lunches to children in government schools — a Supreme Court order of 2001 made hot cooked meals compulsory, converting the nutrition directive into a daily entitlement; and (7) the greatest conversion — ARTICLE 45's education directive became a FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT: the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, and the RIGHT OF CHILDREN TO FREE AND COMPULSORY EDUCATION ACT (RTE), 2009, made free schooling a legal right for children aged 6 to 14, in force from 1 April 2010. THE GANDHIAN SHELF IN ACTION: (8) ARTICLE 40 (panchayats) — the 73rd CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1992): panchayats given constitutional status in a new Part of the Constitution — three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions, direct elections, five-year terms, seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and (one-third) women — the directive's greatest victory; the journey began with the BALWANT RAI MEHTA COMMITTEE (1957) recommending three-tier Panchayati Raj and the first launch at Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959; (9) ARTICLE 43 (cottage industries) — the KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION (KVIC, 1956), planning and funding village crafts, handlooms and rural workshops; (10) ARTICLE 46 (weaker sections) — scholarships, hostels and skill programmes for Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and first-generation learners, and protective land and moneylending laws for tribal communities; (11) ARTICLE 48A (environment) — the WILDLIFE (PROTECTION) ACT, 1972, the WATER and AIR pollution Acts (1974 and 1981), the FOREST (CONSERVATION) ACT, 1980, and the ENVIRONMENT (PROTECTION) ACT, 1986 — the whole green statute-book born of one directive; and (12) ARTICLE 47's PROHIBITION clause — states that chose it: GUJARAT (prohibition since 1949 under the Bombay Prohibition Act) and BIHAR (prohibition from 2016). THE EXAMINATION LINE: the mechanism (principle-to-law conversion) + the paired exhibits (article → law, with years): 39/38-land reforms and MGNREGA 2005; 39(d)-Equal Remuneration Act 1976; 41-NSAP 1995; 42-Maternity Benefit 1961/2017; 39A-Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and Lok Adalats; 45/47-mid-day meals and the RTE 2009 (with the 86th Amendment 2002 and Article 21A); 40-the 73rd Amendment 1992 with the 1957 committee and the 1959 Nagaur launch; 43-KVIC 1956; 48A-the environment acts 1972-1986; 47-prohibition in Gujarat and Bihar.
steps: Part IV's principles were written as directions; sixty years of legislatures have answered them in statutes and schemes — and the record is the proof that non-justiciable does not mean dormant.
First: THE MECHANISM.

Remember the hinge — Article 37 bars the courtroom but lays the duty on law-making; the duty's product is the CONVERSION: the legislature takes a broad directive ("equal pay for equal work") and writes a specific…
Second: THE GENERAL SHELF'S CONVERTED RECORD.

Land: ARTICLE 38/39's fair-shares instruction drove the post-Independence LAND REFORMS — zamindari abolition ended the intermediaries, tenancy reforms secured the cultivator, ceilings redistributed surplus land;

Work: ARTICLE 41's assistance-in-unemployment became the boldest conversion in the world — MGNREGA (2005), the legal guarantee of 100 DAYS of paid rural work on demand, a directive grown into an enforceable right…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dating the RTE to the 73rd Amendment or pairing Article 40 with the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee alone) reveals the misconception of pairing-drift — each article has exactly one headline conversion and the examiner marks the pair — and of…
remember: Recall: State the conversion mechanism.….
Reasoning: A student asks: "If MGNREGA and the RTE are so enforceable, why were they not written as Fundamental Rights in 1950 — why route them through Part IV first?" Unravel the….
Evaluate: A student claims: "The 73rd Amendment is the greatest DPSP conversion because it gave the directive a structure; the RTE is only a bigger scheme." Assess the comparison….

cards.title: The Liberal‑Intellectual Principles form one of the four classifications of the…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Liberal‑Intellectual Principles form one of the four classifications of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV of the Indian Constitution. They reflect a liberal democratic outlook and emphasize individual liberty, rule of law, and international cooperation. Key articles include Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code), Article 45 (early childhood care and education), Article 48 (organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry on modern lines), Article 49 (protection of monuments), Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), and Article 51 (promotion of international peace and security). Unlike Fundamental Rights, these principles are non‑justiciable — courts cannot enforce them — but they serve as moral and political guidelines for law‑making. They differ from Socialistic Principles (which focus on economic equality) and Gandhian Principles (which stress village self‑governance and prohibition). Together, the four categories — General, Socialistic, Gandhian, and Liberal‑Intellectual — constitute the complete DPSP framework that aims to establish a welfare state.
steps: The Liberal‑Intellectual Principles are the Constitution’s liberal democratic wish‑list, guiding the state toward rule of law, individual freedom, and global harmony.
Here is why: they translate abstract liberal ideals into concrete policy directions that governments should pursue.
First, Article 44 urges a Uniform Civil Code to replace personal laws based on religion, promoting legal equality — like having one school dress code for all students regardless of background.
Second, Article 50 mandates separation of judiciary from executive, ensuring courts remain independent — just as a referee must not be a player.
Third, Article 51 directs the state to foster international peace, respect treaties, and settle disputes by arbitration — similar to a class agreeing to resolve fights through a peace committee.
Fourth, Articles 45, 48, and 49 focus on education, modern agriculture, and heritage protection, reflecting a progressive, knowledge‑based society.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Article 45”) reveals the misconception that education‑related articles also cover personal law — confusing the subject matter of different articles.
remember: Which Article of the Constitution directs the state to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens.
Why are the Liberal‑Intellectual Principles considered non‑justiciable.
Evaluate the statement: “Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive) has been fully implemented in India.”.

cards.title: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36‑51) of the Indian Constitution, are non‑justiciable guidelines that direct the State to establish a welfare state — a system where the government actively promotes social, economic, and political justice. They are classified into General Principles (e.g., Article 38: secure a social order; Article 39: equitable distribution of resources; Article 44: uniform civil code) and Gandhian Principles (e.g., Article 40: village panchayats; Article 43: cottage industries; Article 47: prohibition of intoxicants). Unlike Fundamental Rights (Part III), which are justiciable, negative obligations on the State, and protect individual liberty, DPSP are positive obligations, collective in nature, and morally binding but not legally enforceable. Judicial interpretation (e.g., Champakam Dorairajan, Kesavananda Bharati, Minerva Mills) has harmonised conflicts, holding that Fundamental Rights prevail in case of inconsistency, yet DPSP inform legislative policy and constitutional amendment. Understanding this interplay is essential for analysing how India balances individual rights with collective welfare goals.
steps: The Directive Principles are the Constitution’s roadmap for turning India into a welfare state, guiding governments to pursue social and economic justice alongside political freedom.
Here is why: they translate the Preamble’s promises of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity into actionable policy goals.
First, the General Principles (Articles 38‑48, 50‑51) set broad targets: Article 38 asks the State to minimise inequalities;
Article 39 directs equitable distribution of wealth;
Article 44 envisions a uniform civil code;
Article 51 promotes international peace.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Part III”) reveals the misconception that both rights and directives share the same Part, confusing justiciable rights with non‑justiciable guidelines.
remember: Which Part of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy.
Explain why Directive Principles are described as “non‑justiciable” but “fundamental in governance.”.
Evaluate the statement: “Fundamental Rights are superior to Directive Principles in all circumstances.”.

cards.title: A ratio compares two quantities of the SAME kind and SAME unit by division…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A ratio compares two quantities of the SAME kind and SAME unit by division: the ratio of a to b is a: b or a/b, read "a is to b". Three properties make it lawful: (1) the quantities must carry the same unit before the ratio is written (45 minutes against 2 hours must become 45: 120); (2) a ratio has NO units — after dividing like by like, the units cancel; (3) a ratio is written in lowest terms by cancelling the common factor (8: 12 = 2: 3), exactly as a fraction is reduced — the comparison is unchanged because both parts were scaled by the same number. The two terms have names: a and b are the antecedent and the consequent; order matters, since 2: 3 and 3: 2 tell opposite stories. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal: a: b:: c: d (read "a is to b as c is to d"). The outer terms a and d are the extremes, the inner terms b and c are the means, and the test that decides everything is the cross-product rule: the proportion holds exactly when a × d = b × c (product of extremes equals product of means). This rule both CHECKS a proportion and SOLVES one — if three terms are known, the fourth follows. A continued ratio a: b: c compares three quantities at once, and a whole quantity can be divided in a given ratio by counting total parts: each share = (its parts ÷ total parts) × whole amount. These ideas chain together: ratio compresses comparison, proportion extends a known comparison to a new pair, and division in a ratio distributes — the three moves this revision node consolidates before the unitary method builds on them.
steps: A ratio is a fraction wearing comparison clothes — same units first, cancel to lowest terms, no units left — and a proportion is simply two equal ratios whose cross-products must match; master those two sentences and…
Comparing 25 paise with ₹1 demands conversion before comparison: ₹1 = 100 paise, so the ratio is 25: 100 = 1: 4, never 25: 1.

The rule exists because a ratio divides one quantity by the other, and division of paise by rupees divides different families; once both sides speak the same unit, the units cancel and the ratio is born unit-less.

The Class 7 habit to rehearse: before writing any colon, ask "what unit is the smaller side in, and can I upgrade both sides to the bigger one?" — minutes to hours, paise to rupees, grams to kilograms — and only then…

Argument two: simplification is inherited from fractions, and order is everything. 8: 12 simplifies to 2: 3 because both terms divide by 4 — the comparison "for every 8, there are 12" is the same comparison as "for…
But 2: 3 and 3: 2 are different comparisons entirely: if 2: 3 is boys to girls in a class of cricket players, then 3: 2 claims there are MORE boys, and the sentence flips its meaning.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "boys: girls = 40: 16 = 5: 2" or "girls are 2/3 of the class") reveals the confusion of comparing with the WHOLE instead of with the other term in the first case, and the error of reading a ratio 2: 3 as the fraction 2/3 instead of 2…
remember: Define a ratio and state its two essential….
Express the ratio 45 minutes: 2 hours in its lowest terms, showing the unit conversion at the correct place. Then state why "45: 2" is unlawful.
A student writes "the ratio of 25 paise to ₹1 is 25: 1". Evaluate the claim, give the correct ratio, and state the general conversion principle the student missed.

cards.title: The unitary method is a systematic technique for solving problems involving…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The unitary method is a systematic technique for solving problems involving direct proportion. It consists of two steps: (1) determine the value of a single unit by dividing the given total quantity by the number of units; (2) obtain the required quantity by multiplying the unit value by the desired number of units. Symbolically, if Q total corresponds to n units, then unit value u = Q / n and required value R = u × m for m units. The method assumes a constant ratio between the two varying quantities (e.g., cost ∝ number of items, distance ∝ time at constant speed). It extends the concept of ratio and proportion by providing an algorithmic route to find unknowns without explicitly writing a proportion equation. The unitary method applies to any pair of directly proportional quantities — price‑quantity, speed‑distance, work‑time — and forms the basis for later topics such as percentage, profit‑loss, simple interest, and speed‑distance‑time calculations.
steps: The unitary method always works by first finding the value of one unit and then scaling to the required number of units.
Here is why: the relationship between the two quantities is constant, so the per‑unit value stays the same no matter how many units we consider.
Consider a shopkeeper who sells 12 notebooks for ₹360.
To find the cost of 7 notebooks, we first divide ₹360 by 12 to get ₹30 per notebook — this is the invariant unit rate.
Then we multiply ₹30 by 7 to obtain ₹210.

The same logic applies if a car travels 180 km in 3 hours; the unit distance per hour is 60 km/h, so in 5 hours it covers 300 km. In each case we (1) identify the given total and its corresponding units, (2) compute the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹8) reveals the misconception that the unit cost is obtained by subtracting the number of pens from the total cost instead of dividing.
remember: If 8 pens cost ₹96, what is the cost of 1 pen.
A car covers 240 km in 4 hours. How far will it travel in 7 hours at the same speed.
Evaluate: “If 5 kg of wheat costs ₹200, then 12 kg will cost ₹480.” Is the statement correct.

cards.title: The unitary method solves problems about equal groups by first finding the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The unitary method solves problems about equal groups by first finding the value of ONE unit and then scaling to the required number of units. Its two directions: FORWARD (cost of many → cost of one → cost of the asked number) and REVERSE (cost of many → cost of one → "how many can I buy with this much?"). Its quiet foundation is uniformity: the method is lawful only when every unit is identical and the rate is the same throughout — 5 identical notebooks at one price, a train running at a steady speed, rice at one rate per kilogram. If the units differ (5 notebooks and 3 pens for ₹100) the method cannot touch the problem until the mixture is separated. The method's signature is a two-line working: "cost of 1 unit = total ÷ number of units; cost of asked units = unit value × asked number" — with a quotient that must come out sensible (a whole rupee or an exact paisa; a half-notebook is a signal of an error or an ill-posed question). This node consolidates the method across its problem families: single-rate purchases, uniform-speed distances, wage-per-day earnings, price-per-gram comparisons and the reverse "how-many" form. It also fixes the method's checking habits — re-multiply to recover the given total, and sanity-check that more units cost more (the seed of direct proportion that the chapter's later nodes formalise). The general LETTER expression of the method is reserved for the next node; here the skill must become automatic in numbers alone.
steps: The unitary method is one move wearing many costumes — find the ONE, then multiply or divide out — and consolidation means the move runs in both directions, across mixed kinds, and with its own verification switched on…
Argument one: the forward direction is a division followed by a multiplication, and the two lines must both be visible.
"7 identical water bottles cost ₹217 — find the cost of 12." Line one: cost of 1 = 217 ÷ 7 = ₹31.
Line two: cost of 12 = 31 × 12 = ₹372.
Students who jump straight to "×12/7" often get the right number and lose the method mark — the unit line is the method; the multiplication is bookkeeping.
The visible working also self-checks: 31 × 7 must rebuild 217, and any slip in the division is caught before it spreads.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "96 × 13 = ₹1,248" or "96 ÷ 13 ≈ ₹7.38 each") reveals the multiply-everything habit — applying the given count's operation to the asked count without first dividing down to the unit; the unit line is not decoration, it IS the method, and…
remember: State the unitary method in your own words and the one condition that must hold for it to be….
A box of 6 soap bars costs ₹198.….
Evaluate this student's solution, find the error, and write the correct solution: "12 pens cost ₹90, so 1 pen costs 12 ÷ 90 = ₹0.133; therefore 20 pens cost 0.133 × 20 = ₹2.66.".

cards.title: The general expression for the unitary method states…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The general expression for the unitary method states: if m identical units have a total value c, then the value of n such units is (c ÷ m) × n, and the number of units affordable with an amount A is A ÷ (c ÷ m), which is the same as (A × m) ÷ c. The expression is DERIVED, not memorised: value of one unit = c/m (the unit line, written in letters); value of n units = (c/m) × n (rebuild by multiplication); re-substituting n = m must return c itself — (c/m) × m = c ✓ — which is the expression's built-in proof that it never loses the given data. The letters have fixed meanings: m counts the units whose value is KNOWN (the given count), c is that known total value, n counts the asked units, and A is the amount available in reverse questions. The expression is lawful under the same uniformity condition as the numerical method: identical units, one rate throughout. Its two powers over the numerical method: (1) it is INDEPENDENT of the particular numbers — one derivation serves every future problem; (2) it exposes STRUCTURE — (c/m) × n can be read as c × (n/m), showing the answer scales with n and inversely with m, so doubling the asked count doubles the cost and doubling the given count halves the unit rate. These structural reads are the student's first sight of direct proportion in letters. This node keeps the expression in one-letter arithmetic; the proportion statement a: b:: c: d of is the same content wearing its ratio costume, and the chapter's percentage work ( onwards) will reuse this scaling habit with denominator 100.
steps: The general expression (c ÷ m) × n is the unitary method promoted to a law — derived once, self-checking, substitutable, and structurally transparent about what makes costs grow and shrink — and learning it is learning…
Argument one: the derivation is two lines the class already owns, now in letters.
Known: m units cost c. Unit line: one unit costs c/m.

Rebuild: n units cost (c/m) × n. There is no new idea — only the numbers 216, 8 and 19 have been replaced by c, m and n — and the promotion's value is that the two lines now hold for EVERY problem simultaneously.

The derivation ends with the self-check that makes the expression trustworthy: put n = m, and (c/m) × m = c — the expression hands back exactly the given total, so no information was bent on the way. Argument two…

With m = 12, c = 1,560, n = 25: (1560 ÷ 12) × 25 = 130 × 25 = ₹3,250 — the bracket FIRST, because the bracket IS the unit line; computing 1560 × 25 ÷ 12 happens to give the same number here, but only the bracketed form…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "(m ÷ c) × n = (8 ÷ 344) × 14 ≈ 0.33") reveals the letter-blind inversion — copying the expression's shape while swapping its division's direction; the letters mean fixed things (c is the TOTAL over m UNITS), and the self-check n = m…
remember: Write the general expression for the unitary method in letters, name every letter, state the condition of validity, and verify the expression by….
Derive the reverse form "number of units affordable with amount A" from the general expression, showing every algebraic….
Evaluate this student's claim, find the error, and repair it: "If 6 chairs cost ₹2,160, then 10 chairs cost (6 × 10) ÷ 2160 × 100... roughly ₹2.78 — wait, chairs can't cost….

cards.title: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100: x per cent…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100: x per cent, written x%, means x/100, or x hundredths of the whole. The word descends from the Latin "per centum" — per hundred — and the symbol % is the compressed picture of that idea: the whole (the circle of 100) with the part marked in it. Three readings of x% must live together in the student's mind: (1) as a FRACTION — 35% = 35/100 = 7/20 of the whole; (2) as a POSITION on the hundred-scale — 35 of the 100 small squares of the percent-grid are shaded; (3) as a RATE OF COMPARISON — "35% of the class walks to school" means if the class had exactly 100 students, 35 would walk, whatever its real size. The hundred-denominator is percentage's whole purpose: fractions with different denominators (17/20, 4/5, 3/4) are hard to rank by eye, but all of them become hundredths (85%, 80%, 75%) and hundredths rank instantly. Percentage is therefore not a new kind of number — it is a common DRESS in which fractions, decimals and ratios can meet and be compared: the fraction-with-denominator-100 that this chapter's next node states precisely, and whose two-way conversion mechanics drills. What belongs to this introductory node: the MEANING of the symbol, the hundred-grid picture, reading and interpreting percentages from daily life (test scores, cricket statistics, battery indicators, sale boards), estimating with friendly percentages (50%, 25%, 10%), and the idea that percentages can exceed 100 or fall below 1 when the part outgrows or shrinks against the hundred-whole. Finding "x% of a quantity" by the unit-value route (x hundredths of it) is touched here in its simplest cases and consolidated through the chapter's applications.
steps: Percentage is a common currency for fractions — every part is quoted against the same whole of 100 — and once a quantity is spoken in this currency, comparison, estimation and "how much of it" questions all become…
Argument one: the symbol is a definition, not a decoration. 35% IS 35/100 — not "like" it, not "about" it: the sign means hundredths, exactly as cm means hundredths of a metre.

This single identity does the node's work: reading any percentage as a fraction is copying it over a 100 bar; shading it on the 10 × 10 grid is filling 35 small squares (each square one hundredth, each ROW ten percent)…
Argument two: the hundred-grid is percentage's home picture, and reading it is a two-count skill.
The 10 × 10 grid holds 100 squares; a shaded patch of 23 squares announces 23%, a half-shaded grid 50%, and the whole grid 100% — the grid MAKES "whole = 100" visible.

Two counts run on it: by squares (each square 1%) and by rows-and-columns (each row or column 10%, each small strip 1%) — so 47% is four rows and seven squares, and a student who can move between these counts has…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "38% needs 38 half-squares" or "2 rows + 8 squares = 2 + 8 = 10%") reveals the grid-unit confusion — treating the square as half a percent or reading rows as 1% instead of 10%; the grid's grammar is fixed: one square = 1%, one row or…
remember: State what "per cent" means and what the symbol %….
Meera scores 34 out of 40 in Mathematics and Arjun scores 52 out of 65 in….
Estimate each mentally using the friendly-percentage set, stating the composition you used, then verify exactly: (a) 50% of….

cards.title: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is 100…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is 100: the statement "r%" and the fraction r/100 are two names of one number, and this node's work is to make the naming bidirectional wherever the denominator-100 route is natural. Two laws organise the formulation. Law of the fixed denominator: to SAY any part as a percentage, the part must first be written as a number of hundredths of its own whole — either because the fraction's denominator divides or extends to 100 exactly (2/5 = 40/100 by multiplying top and bottom by 20, the equivalent-fraction route), or because the part and whole are re-expressed so that the whole becomes 100 units (the re-unitising route: 18 marks out of 60 — make the whole 100 by scaling 60 → 100, factor 5/3, so 18 → 30; hence 30%). Law of the named whole: "a is p% of b" is the full sentence; p = (a ÷ b) × 100 read as "a is that many hundredths of b" — and the sentence is incomplete, and usually wrong, until b is named. This node also fixes the boundary vocabulary: a fraction whose denominator does NOT reach 100 neatly (2/3) still has an honest percentage — 66 2/3% — kept exact as a mixed number rather than murdered into 66.66; and a percentage larger than 100 (5/4 = 125/100 = 125%) is lawful whenever the part outgrows the whole. What this node adds beyond the introduction is FORM: the denominator-100 statement as a working definition, the equivalent-fraction and re-unitising routes as the two standard methods, and "express one quantity as a percentage of another" as a solved sentence-pattern. The mechanical conversion ALGORITHMS for arbitrary decimals and the reverse direction (percentage → fraction → decimal at speed) are the next node's territory.
steps: Percentage is the fraction family's standardised dress — denominator fixed at 100 — and dressing a fraction in it takes exactly two lawful routes: scale the denominator to 100 when it agrees, or re-unitise the whole…
Argument one: the definition is bidirectional, and both directions are laws, not tricks.
Reading: r% IS r/100 — 45% is the number forty-five hundredths, reducible to 9/20 when a simpler fraction serves.
Writing: a fraction whose denominator can honestly be replaced by 100 becomes a percentage by scaling BOTH terms by the same factor — 7/20 × (5/5) = 35/100 = 35%.

The scaling is the equivalent-fraction law of Class 6 (multiply or divide both terms by the same non-zero number), and its guarantee is that nothing about the comparison changes: 7/20 of a class and 35% of a class are…

The forbidden move is equally instructive: adding 80 to a denominator to force 100 (3/20 → "3/100") breaks equivalence — only MULTIPLICATION or division by a common factor preserves the fraction's value, which is why 20…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer in (b) (e.g., "5/8 = 0.625 ≈ 63%" by the decimal route with rounding) reveals the premature-decimal habit — reaching for the shift-the-decimal shortcut (next node's tool) and Rounding where the fraction route is exact; 62½% and 63% are…
remember: State the denominator-100 definition of percentage.….
Using the friendly-denominator table, convert exactly (no decimals): (a) 3/5 to a….
Express: (a) 24 as a percentage of 64….

cards.title: Percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100, denoted by the symbol %. A fraction represents a part of a whole using a numerator and denominator (e.g., 3/4). A decimal represents the same value in base‑10 notation (e.g., 0.75). The three forms are interchangeable: to convert a fraction to a percentage, multiply the fraction by 100 and attach the % sign; to convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply the decimal by 100 and attach %; to convert a percentage to a fraction, write the percentage over 100 and simplify; to convert a percentage to a decimal, divide the percentage by 100 (or move the decimal point two places left). These conversions rely on the definition that “percent” means “per hundred”. The relationship is linear: Percentage = Fraction × 100 = Decimal × 100. Understanding this equivalence allows students to switch between representations depending on the context — such as interpreting test scores, discounts, or data in graphs — and forms the foundation for later applications in profit‑loss, simple interest, and speed‑distance‑time problems.
steps: The key takeaway: To move between fractions, decimals, and percentages, always use 100 as the bridge — multiply by 100 to go to percentage, divide by 100 to leave percentage.

Here is why: percentage literally means “per hundred”, so any fraction can be scaled to a denominator of 100 by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same factor; any decimal can be shifted two places right…
Consider a pizza cut into 8 equal slices.
If you eat 3 slices, the fraction is 3/8.
To express this as a percentage, multiply 3/8 by 100: (3 × 100)/8 = 300/8 = 37.5%.
The same value as a decimal is 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 34%) reveals the misconception that the numerator and denominator are simply written together as digits instead of performing the multiplication by 100.
remember: What is 3/4 expressed as a percentage.
Convert 0.625 to a percentage.
A student says 45% = 0.045. Is this correct? Explain.

cards.title: This node applies the chapter's percentage machinery (–007) to a single…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node applies the chapter's percentage machinery (–007) to a single transaction: one article (or one identical lot) bought once and sold once. The vocabulary is fixed: the cost price (CP) is everything the seller pays to acquire the article ready for sale — purchase price plus, where stated, expenses such as transport, repair or packing; the selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays the seller. Two subtractions decide the story: profit = SP − CP when SP > CP (the seller gained), loss = CP − SP when CP > SP (the seller lost); when SP = CP the transaction breaks even — neither row applies. The headline rule of the topic: profit% and loss% are ALWAYS calculated on the CP (profit% = profit/CP × 100, loss% = loss/CP × 100), because the CP is the seller's investment and the market's fair base for "how much did I make on what I put in". The four standard problems, all single-step chains of the same two quantities: (1) given CP and SP, find profit/loss and its percentage; (2) given CP and profit%/loss%, find the SP (SP = CP + profit = CP × (100 + p)/100, or SP = CP − loss = CP × (100 − l)/100); (3) given SP and profit%/loss%, find the CP by reversing the same link; (4) compare two transactions through their percentages, never through raw profits. What "single transaction" excludes: successive buy-sell chains, discounts computed on marked price, overheads beyond those stated in the CP, and mixture lots of different articles — those wait for later classes; here every problem has exactly one CP, one SP and one honest subtraction.
steps: Profit and loss is percentage arithmetic with a fairness law bolted on: the subtraction says HOW MUCH was gained or lost, the percentage on CP says how WELL the money worked — and every problem in this node is those two…
Argument one: the subtraction is the story; the percentage is the verdict.
A vendor buys a crate for ₹480 and sells it for ₹552: profit = 552 − 480 = ₹72.
The subtraction is finished — but "₹72 profit" means different things on different investments: ₹72 on ₹480 (a strong day) and ₹72 on ₹4,800 (a weak one).
The percentage converts the story into a verdict: profit% = (72/480) × 100 = 15% — fifteen rupees earned per hundred rupees invested, the market's standard sentence.
This division-by-CP is the node's ONE percentage computation, and its base is fixed by law: CP, the seller's own money, never the SP, the buyer's.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "profit% = (115/1035) × 100 ≈ 11.1%") reveals the SP-base error — the single most penalised slip of this topic; the percentage of profit is measured on the seller's INVESTMENT (CP), never on the buyer's payment (SP), and the difference…

A shopkeeper sells a saree for ₹1,530 and loses….
A dealer buys a bicycle for ₹2,400, spends ₹180 on repairs, and sells it for….

cards.title: Simple interest is the extra money paid or earned on a principal amount when…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simple interest is the extra money paid or earned on a principal amount when the time period is expressed in whole years. The principal (P) is the original sum of money lent or borrowed, measured in rupees (₹). The rate of interest (R) is the percentage charged per annum (per year). The time (T) is the number of complete years the money is used. The simple interest (SI) is calculated by the formula SI = (P × R × T) / 100. The total amount (A) returned at the end of the period is A = P + SI. This concept builds directly on the percentage work in the previous node (profit and loss) and the unitary method: finding interest for one year (unitary step) and then multiplying by the number of years. Only whole‑year periods are considered; fractional years are reserved for higher classes. The relationship between the sub‑concepts is linear: doubling the time doubles the interest, doubling the rate doubles the interest, and doubling the principal doubles the interest, all other factors staying constant.
steps: The one thing to remember: Simple interest grows linearly with time — each complete year adds the same interest amount.
Here is why: interest is a fixed percentage of the principal charged every year.
Consider a principal of ₹500 at 6 % per annum.
For the first year the interest is (500 × 6 × 1)/100 = ₹30.

Because the rate and principal do not change, the second year also adds ₹30, the third year another ₹30, and so on. This is exactly the unitary method: find the interest for one year (unit), then multiply by the number…
Step 1 – Identify the three quantities: Principal (P) in rupees, Rate (R) in percent per year, Time (T) in complete years.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., SI = P × R × T) reveals the misconception that the percentage does not need division by 100, confusing the rate expressed as a percent with a decimal multiplier.
remember: What is the formula for simple interest when time is given in complete years.
If the principal is ₹1 500, the rate is 8 % per annum, and the time is 3 years, what is the simple interest? Show the substitution steps.
Evaluate the statement: "If the time period is doubled, the simple interest also doubles, provided principal and rate stay the same." Is this always true for complete years.

cards.title: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time: speed = distance ÷ time…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time: speed = distance ÷ time, with standard units metres per second (m/s) in the SI system and kilometres per hour (km/h) in daily life. The definition is a rate — the same "value of one unit" architecture as the unitary method (–004) with distance as the value and time as the unit-count — so its two rearrangements are the method's two directions: distance = speed × time (forward) and time = distance ÷ speed (reverse). The unit names read as the formula: "60 km/h" means 60 kilometres PER one hour, and any speed sentence is incomplete without its per-unit tag. Uniform speed — the constant rate this chapter works with — means equal distances in equal successive times; real traffic rarely holds it, so computed speeds are really average speeds (total distance ÷ total time), a distinction the problems state or assume. The unit bridge is exact and must be memorised as fractions: 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s = 5/18 m/s, and inversely 1 m/s = 18/5 = 3.6 km/h; so 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 90 km/h = 25 m/s, 20 m/s = 72 km/h — multiply km/h by 5/18 to descend to m/s, multiply m/s by 18/5 to climb to km/h. What this node owns is the CONCEPT and the two-way unit machinery: the distance and time directions get their own sibling nodes ( and).
steps: Speed is the chapter's unit-rate idea driving on a highway: distance divided by time, named with its per-unit tag, converted between the two lawful unit families by the exact 5/18 and 18/5 bridges — and every problem is…
Argument one: the definition reads the unit aloud.
"72 km/h" is a sentence: seventy-two kilometres for every hour of travel.

This is why the formula has no mystery — speed = distance ÷ time IS the sentence compressed: (72 km) ÷ (1 h) = 72 km per h. The rate grammar inherited from the unitary method does the teaching: find what happens in ONE…

A train covering 240 km in 5 hours at uniform speed covers 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km in the one-hour unit — its speed, 48 km/h — and then 48 × 8 = 384 km in 8 hours is merely the parts-machine (–003) rolling on rails.
Argument two: the two rearrangements are the two directions of one rate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "40 × 18/5 = 144 m/s" or "260 ÷ 6.5 = 4 km/h" by mis-placing the decimal) reveals the flipped-bridge or division slip; the flipped bridge inflates by 12.96× — a train at 144 m/s outruns sound-adjacent speeds and fails the magnitude sense…

cards.title: Distance is a scalar quantity that represents the total length of the path…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Distance is a scalar quantity that represents the total length of the path travelled by an object, irrespective of direction. In the context of speed–time–distance relationships, distance (d) is the product of speed (s) and time (t): d = s × t. Speed is the rate at which an object covers distance (distance per unit time), and time is the duration of travel. The three quantities are interdependent: knowing any two allows calculation of the third. In the SI system, distance is measured in metres (m), speed in metres per second (m/s), and time in seconds (s). In everyday Indian usage, kilometres (km) and kilometres per hour (km/h) with time in hours (h) or minutes (min) are common. Distance differs from displacement, which is the straight‑line vector from start to finish; distance accumulates every segment of the actual route. This node builds on the concept of speed and prepares students for calculating time and solving real‑life problems involving travel, logistics, and simple motion.
steps: Distance is found by multiplying speed by time, and this single formula unlocks every travel‑related calculation.
Here is why: speed tells you how many kilometres (or metres) are covered in one unit of time; if you travel for several such units, you simply repeat that coverage.
Consider a train leaving Mumbai at 60 km/h.
After 1 hour it has gone 60 km, after 2 hours 120 km, after 3.5 hours 210 km. The pattern is linear: distance = speed × time.
First, identify the known quantities.
If speed is given in km/h and time in minutes, convert time to hours (divide by 60) before multiplying.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 25 km) reveals the misconception that distance is speed divided by time, confusing the formula with speed = distance/time.
remember: What is the distance covered by a car travelling at a constant speed of 50 km/h for 2 hours.
A cyclist rides for 30 minutes at 12 km/h. Explain why converting 30 minutes to 0.5 hours is necessary before using d = s × t.
Evaluate the statement: “If a bus travels 150 km in 3 hours, its speed is 45 km/h.” Is the statement correct? Justify.

cards.title: Time, in the rate triangle of this chapter…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Time, in the rate triangle of this chapter, is the quantity found by time = distance ÷ speed — the reverse direction of's formula family and the denominator-partner of's distance: at a uniform rate, the time taken grows in direct proportion to the distance and in inverse proportion to the speed (double the distance, double the time; double the speed, halve it). The unit law governs every computation: hours with km/h, seconds with m/s — and the conversion ladder inside time itself is base-60, NOT base-10: 1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 2 h 30 min = 2.5 h but 2 h 30 min ≠ 2.30 h — the single most punished slip of the topic. The same base-60 machinery runs elapsed-time problems: durations between clock readings are computed by the hop-to-the-hour method (from 9:45 hop 15 minutes to 10:00, then count whole hours, then add the tail), across a.m./pm boundaries and across midnight, where the 24-hour clock (00:00 to 23:59) removes the am/pm ambiguity that railway timetables, airline schedules and hospital shifts cannot afford: 18:45 is 6:45 pm, and 06:20 is 6:20 am. Duration answers are stated in h-min form with the arithmetic carried in one unit (hours as decimals, or minutes as wholes) and converted only at the line where the answer is spoken. This node owns the TIME face of the triangle — t = d ÷ s with unit-carried working, the minutes-into-hours ladder, elapsed time by hopping, and 24-hour reading; the concepts of speed and distance belong to the sibling nodes and are used, not re-taught.
steps: Time is the triangle's reverse face: divide the distance by the speed and the hours fall out — but only if the base-60 ladder is climbed honestly, the clock's midnight is respected, and every duration is closed by…
Argument one: the time formula is division, and its proportionality directions are feel-able before they are nameable.
A bus covering 180 km at 45 km/h spends 180 ÷ 45 = 4 hours — the distance dealt out in per-hour bundles.

The two directions: more distance at the same speed takes MORE time (300 km at the same 45 needs 300 ÷ 45 = 20/3 = 6 h 40 min — more bundles, more hours); more speed over the same distance takes LESS time (180 km at 60…
These are the direct and inverse instincts that the unitary nodes trained — nothing new, only the travel costume.

The verification is division's own echo: distance ÷ time must hand back the speed (180 ÷ 4 = 45 ✓), and the three quantities check each other like the parts of a sum. Argument two: the base-60 ladder is the topic's toll…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "294 km takes 6 hours because the train is the same" or "294 ÷ 42 ≈ 7.002") reveals the fixed-time assumption or the division wobble — same speed does not mean same time when the distance changed, and the bundle picture (each 42 km buys…

cards.title: This node consolidates the chapter as ONE connected system by tracing its…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node consolidates the chapter as ONE connected system by tracing its single spine: comparison by division. The chain runs: ratio fixed the grammar — same units, lowest terms, order matters; the proportion test (cross-products equal) certified when two comparisons agree; the unitary method (–004) turned comparison into computation — find the value of one unit, scale to many, with the general expression (c ÷ m) × n and its reverse (A × m) ÷ c; percentage (–007) fixed the unit at one-hundredth — a fraction with denominator 100, the fairness machine that lets different wholes meet on one scale; profit and loss applied the percentage verdict to the market with its base-law (percent on CP); simple interest added the third factor, time, at a fixed per-year rate; and the rate triangle (–012) closed the chapter with distance, speed and time as one divisible family. The consolidation's central claims: (1) every tool in the chapter reduces to "find the one, scale to the many" or "put both on the same base, then compare"; (2) every tool carries a named BASE or WHOLE whose identity decides the answer (the unit in unitary work, the 100 in percentages, the CP in profit, the principal in interest, the per-hour in speed); (3) every tool closes with a rebuild check — the parts re-sum, the percentage re-applies, the rate re-multiplies. The node's job is to make the spine visible through mixed problems that force the tools to work together, so the chapter leaves as one memory, not ten.
steps: The chapter's ten tools are one tool in ten costumes — compare on a common base by finding the value of one — and a student who can NAME the base, CHOOSE the tool, and REBUILD the joints owns the whole chapter in a…
Argument one: the spine is visible in the chapter's own vocabulary trail.

Read the chapter's key phrases in order: "same unit before the colon" (ratio), "cost of ONE notebook" (unitary), "per cent — per hundred" (percentage), "percent on the COST price" (profit), "per annum — per year…
Every phrase fixes a BASE: the common unit, the one unit, the hundred, the cost, the year, the hour.
The chapter never changed subjects; it changed only what played the role of "the one".
A student who underlines the base in every problem statement has already solved half of it — because the base is where the division lands, and the division is where every answer is born.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "profit percent divides on the selling price" or "speed divides on the total journey") reveals the unnamed-base habit — the chapter's most repeated conviction; the base is not decoration, it is the divisor, and every wrong answer this…

Solve the chained problem, naming the tool used at each step: A panchayat splits a ₹72,000 grant among water, schooling and roads in the ratio 5: 3….
