cards.title: A rational number is any number that can be expressed in the form (p)/(q) where…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A rational number is any number that can be expressed in the form (p)/(q) where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. The set of rational numbers is denoted by Q. It includes all integers (since n = (n)/(1) ), all fractions (proper, improper, mixed), and all decimals that either terminate (e.g., 0.375 = 3/8) or repeat (e.g., 0.3 = 1/3). Two fractions (a)/(b) and (c)/(d) represent the same rational number if ad = bc (cross‑multiplication). Every rational number has a unique standard form where the denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1 (i.e., they are coprime). On the number line, rational numbers are dense: between any two distinct rationals there exist infinitely many other rationals. Comparison of two rationals (a)/(b) and (c)/(d) (with b,d > 0 ) is done by cross‑multiplication: (a)/(b) > (c)/(d) iff ad > bc. Conversion between fraction and decimal forms is achieved by long division of the numerator by the denominator; the process either terminates or enters a repeating cycle.
steps: Every rational number can be written as a fraction (p)/(q) with integers p, q ( q ≠ 0 ) and it occupies a unique point on the number line.
First, rational numbers extend the fractions and decimals you already know: integers like –3 become –3/1, terminating decimals like 0.125 become 1/8, and repeating decimals like 0.6 become 2/3.
Second, many fractions represent the same rational number; for example, 2/4, 3/6, and 1/2 are all equivalent.
The standard form chooses the version with a positive denominator and no common factors — here 1/2.
Third, the number line shows that rationals are dense: between 1/3 and 1/2 you can always find another rational, say 5/12, and between those two yet another, ad infinitum.
Fourth, to compare two rationals you cross‑multiply: to decide whether 3/5 > 4/7, compute 3 × 7 = 21 and 4 × 5 = 20; since 21 > 20, 3/5 is larger.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing 0.333… because “it never ends”) reveals the misconception that any non‑terminating decimal is irrational, confusing repeating decimals with non‑repeating ones.
remember: Which of the following is NOT a rational number? (a) 0.333… (b) √2 (c) –7/3 (d) 4.
Express 0.125 as a rational number in standard form.
A student says –3/4 is greater than –2/3 because 3/4 > 2/3. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The four operations on rational numbers combine the fraction arithmetic of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The four operations on rational numbers combine the fraction arithmetic of Class 6 with the integer sign rules of node, applied to numbers written in standard form p/q (q > 0, coprime). Addition and subtraction: give the numbers a common positive denominator — preferably the LCM of the denominators — convert each to an equivalent form over that denominator, and add or subtract the numerators by the integer rules, keeping the common denominator: a/c ± b/c = (a ± b)/c. Multiplication: multiply numerators together and denominators together, no common denominator needed, letting sign rules govern the product: (p/q) × (r/s) = (pr)/(qs); cancelling common factors before multiplying keeps the arithmetic small. Division: multiply by the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of the divisor — dividing by r/s means multiplying by s/r, defined because r ≠ 0; the sign travels with the reciprocal. Properties hold throughout: closure (results stay rational), commutativity and associativity of addition and multiplication, the identities 0 (additive: a + 0 = a) and 1 (multiplicative: a × 1 = a), and the inverse pairs a + (−a) = 0 and a × (1/a) = 1 (a ≠ 0). Distributivity ties the two structures together: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. The order of operations (brackets, of, division/multiplication left to right, addition/subtraction left to right — BODMAS) governs every mixed computation, and negative signs distribute over brackets: −(a − b) = −a + b. Every final answer is reported in standard form. This node completes the arithmetic layer of the Number System chain; the exponents node (007) then compresses the repeated multiplication this node performs explicitly.
steps: Every rational-number computation is two skills stacked — fraction machinery on top, integer sign rules underneath — and writing each number in standard form first is what makes the stack work.
Addition and subtraction share one method.
Compute 2/3 + (−1/4): the LCM of 3 and 4 is 12; convert — 2/3 = 8/12 and −1/4 = −3/12; add numerators by the integer rule: 8 + (−3) = 5, so the sum is 5/12, already standard.
The subtraction case 5/6 − 7/9 runs identically: LCM 18, giving 15/18 − 14/18 = 1/18; note that the deciding work 15 − 14 = 1 is pure integer arithmetic, which is why node 003 had to come first.
When the numerators disagree in sign and size — 3/4 + (−5/6) — the LCM is 12: 9/12 + (−10/12) = (9 − 10)/12 = −1/12, and the negative answer is legitimate, not a mistake to be re-tried.

Multiplication needs no common denominator at all: multiply tops, multiply bottoms, and let signs follow the integer rules — like signs give a positive product, unlike signs a negative one. Compute (−2/3) × (−9/4)…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., adding numerators and denominators separately: (2 + (−1))/(3 + 4) = 1/7) reveals the misconception that fractions add "part over part"; the denominator counts the size of the parts and must be unified by the LCM before the parts can be…
remember: State the rule for adding two rational numbers with unlike denominators, and compute 2/3 + (−1/4) showing every step.
Compute (−2/3) × (−9/4) and (5/8) × (4/15), using pre-cancellation and stating the sign rule used in each.
Compute (−7/12) ÷ (−21/8), stating what is flipped and why, and verify the answer by multiplying it back.

cards.title: An exponent (or index/power) records repeated multiplication…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An exponent (or index/power) records repeated multiplication: aⁿ means the base a multiplied by itself n times — a × a × … × a with n factors — where n is a positive integer. Reading aⁿ as "a raised to the power n" or "a to the n": 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32; 3⁴ = 81; (−2)³ = −8. The base may be any rational number, and the sign rules of the previous node decide the sign of the result: a negative base to an odd power stays negative ((−2)³ = −8), to an even power turns positive ((−2)⁴ = 16); a fractional base powers both numerator and denominator ((2/3)² = 4/9). The laws of exponents govern computation without expansion: product rule aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷); quotient rule aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (3⁵ ÷ 3² = 3³); power-of-a-power rule (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ ((2²)³ = 2⁶); power of a product (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ; and the zero exponent a⁰ = 1 for every non-zero a, justified by the quotient rule (a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ must equal 1 since any number divided by itself is 1). Standard form (scientific notation) writes a large number as a product c × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ c < 10 and n a positive integer: 149,600,000 = 1.496 × 10⁸ — the decimal point slid 8 places. Prime factorisations are recorded compactly with exponents: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Exponents compress the multiplication that node performed explicitly, and they set up squares (index 2) and cubes (index 3) — the special cases the next two nodes study through their inverses, the square root and cube root.
steps: Exponents are a compression device: aⁿ packs n identical factors into one symbol, and the laws of exponents let you compute with the packed forms directly.
Start with evaluation, where the only new skill is counting factors. 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2: multiply in pairs — 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, 16 × 2 = 32.
Fractional bases power top and bottom separately: (2/3)² = (2 × 2)/(3 × 3) = 4/9;

Negative bases follow the sign rules of multiplication: (−2)³ = (−2) × (−2) × (−2) — two like signs make +4, times the third (−2) gives −8; but (−2)⁴ = 16, because an even number of negatives cancels pairwise.
The rule to own: odd power of a negative base is negative, even power is positive — and the magnitude is the base's absolute value raised to the index.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3⁴ = 3 × 4 = 12, or (1/2)³ = 3/2) reveals the misconception that the exponent multiplies the base; the exponent counts identical factors, which is why powers grow so much faster than multiples.
remember: Define aⁿ and evaluate 3⁴ and (1/2)³, showing the factor rows.
Evaluate (−3)⁴ and (−3)⁵, and explain the parity rule for negative bases. Also evaluate −3⁴ and contrast it.
Simplify 2³ × 2⁴ and 3⁵ ÷ 3² using the laws, then verify each by full expansion.

cards.title: The square of a number a is a² = a × a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The square of a number a is a² = a × a; a is a perfect square if it is the square of an integer (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, …). The square root of a number is the inverse quantity: √N is the number whose square is N; every positive perfect square has two square-root candidates, +√N and −√N, and the √ symbol by convention names the positive one (the principal root). Squares obey visible patterns: the square of a number ending in 5 ends in 25, with the leading part n(n + 1) — 85² = 8 × 9 hundreds + 25 = 7225; the sum of the first n odd numbers is n² (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25 = 5²); squares alternate in parity and their last digits can only be 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 — so any number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 (or an odd number of trailing zeros) is certainly not a perfect square, a screening test that needs no computation. Between consecutive squares (n² and (n + 1)²) there are 2n non-square integers, so squares thin out as numbers grow. Finding square roots: (i) by prime factorisation — write N as a product of prime powers and halve every exponent: 1296 = 2⁴ × 3⁴ gives √1296 = 2² × 3² = 36; the method doubles as a test, since a perfect square's exponents must all be even; (ii) by repeated subtraction — subtract the successive odd numbers 1, 3, 5, … until 0 is reached; the count of subtractions is the root (36 needs six: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36); (iii) by estimation between known squares, refined by the last-digit screen. Square roots extend to decimals by the factor rule: √1.44 = 1.2 since 1.2² = 1.44, and √0.09 = 0.3. This node's material is the index-2 special case of the exponent node, consumed directly by mensuration (areas of squares, Pythagorean work) and completed for index 3 by the cubes node (009).
steps: Squaring is the index-2 power and square-rooting is its undoing, and the pair is best learned through the patterns squares leave behind.

Build the table by addition, not multiplication: each square is the previous square plus the next odd number — 1, 4 (= 1 + 3), 9 (= 4 + 5), 16 (= 9 + 7), 25 (= 16 + 9) — because 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
That identity is why repeated subtraction works as a root-finder: 36 sheds 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 in six subtractions to reach 0, so √36 = 6.

The last digits of squares march through a fixed set: 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9 — computed from the last digit of the base (0→0, 1→1, 2→4, 3→9, 4→6, 5→5, 6→6, 7→9, 8→4, 9→1) — so 2,3,7,8-ending numbers are eliminated without any…
The ending-in-5 pattern is a two-second calculator: for a number written n5, the square is n(n + 1) followed by 25 — 85²: n = 8, 8 × 9 = 72, so 7225; 115²: n = 11, 11 × 12 = 132, so 13225.

Squares also sit in a lattice: 20² = 400 and 21² = 441, so √415 lies strictly between 20 and 21 — an estimate the last digit of 415 (5 is legal) cannot refine without computation, which is exactly the honest answer…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "−7 is not a square root of 49 because roots are positive") reveals the misconception that the convention erases the second root; the convention only fixes which one the symbol prints, not which ones exist.

cards.title: The cube of a number a is a³ = a × a × a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The cube of a number a is a³ = a × a × a; a is a perfect cube if it is the cube of an integer (1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000, …). The cube root ∛N is the number whose cube is N; unlike square roots, every integer has exactly one real cube root — negative numbers have real cube roots (∛(−64) = −4, since (−4)³ = −64), because an odd number of negative factors stays negative: odd powers of a negative base are negative, even powers positive. Cubes inherit the sign of their base and keep its parity: the cube of an even number is even, of an odd number odd. Last digits of cubes follow a fixed map — 0→0, 1→1, 2→8, 3→7, 4→4, 5→5, 6→6, 7→3, 8→2, 9→9 — so 2s and 8s swap, as do 3s and 7s, while the rest are preserved. Finding cube roots by prime factorisation: write N as a product of prime powers; N is a perfect cube exactly when every exponent is a multiple of 3, and ∛N is obtained by dividing every exponent by 3 — 216 = 2³ × 3³ gives ∛216 = 2 × 3 = 6; 1728 = 2⁶ × 3³ gives ∛1728 = 2² × 3 = 12. Adjusting to a perfect cube: to make a number a perfect cube by multiplication, multiply by the primes whose exponents are short of the next multiple of 3 (72 = 2³ × 3² needs ×3 to become 216 = 6³); by division, remove the primes with non-multiple exponents (81 = 3⁴ ÷ 3 → 27 = 3³). Cubes model volume: a cube of side a holds a³ unit cubes, which is why the word "cube" fits, and why this node feeds the mensuration of solids. The chapter's Indian landmark is 1729, the Hardy–Ramanujan number: the smallest number expressible as a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways — 1729 = 12³ + 1³ = 10³ + 9³ — from Ramanujan's famous remark to Hardy in 1919 (an anecdote retold in this node's diagnostics as cultural context, with the mathematics verified).
steps: Cubing is the index-3 power, and its root machine is the square machine with one change: exponents must be even for squares but multiples of 3 for cubes, and division by 3 replaces the halving.
Build the cube table and its behaviour first. 1³ = 1, 2³ = 8, 3³ = 27, 4³ = 64, 5³ = 125, 6³ = 216, 7³ = 343, 8³ = 512, 9³ = 729, 10³ = 1000.
Signs: cubing preserves sign — (−4)³ = −64, since three negative factors multiply to a negative — which is why every integer, unlike the square case, has a genuine cube root: ∛(−1000) = −10.

Parity is preserved too (even³ even, odd³ odd), and the last digit obeys the swap map: a cube ending in 8 came from a base ending in 2, one ending in 7 from a base ending in 3, and the others (0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9) preserve…
These facts make cube-root questions half-answerable at sight: a perfect cube's last digit immediately limits the root's last digit.
The main machine is prime factorisation with exponent division.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "∛(−64) is not allowed, like √(−4)") reveals the misconception that the square rule (no real roots of negatives) transfers to cubes; the odd index is exactly what permits the negative root.

cards.title: The synthesis node converts the chapter's nine content nodes into examination…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The synthesis node converts the chapter's nine content nodes into examination competence. A CISCE-style mathematics paper at this level is built from a small set of question shapes: short-answer items (1–2 marks) testing one fact or one computation — a sign rule, a standard form, a single root; structured long answers (3–4 marks) testing a chained computation — a rational-number simplification with BODMAS, a multiplier-adjustment problem, a factorisation-based root with justification; word/application problems (4–5 marks) testing translation from a situation (tank volumes, garden areas, temperatures, money) into the chapter's machinery; and HOTS items (higher order thinking skills) that mix two or more nodes in one question — a cube that must be recognised through a square, an exponent comparison hiding a rational comparison. Every shape is answered by the same discipline: identify the node that owns the question (family first: integer? rational? power?), write the formula or rule being applied, compute with one operation per line, and verify — by re-substitution, by the last-digit screen, by estimation, or by the sum-check. The chapter's content ladder (integers → operations → decimals → rationals → operations → exponents → squares/roots → cubes/roots) maps onto the paper as four question families: signed-number and rational arithmetic; decimal and fraction–decimal conversion; the power family including roots; and mixed applications. This node's practice set walks each family from recall to HOTS, and its marking schemes show how marks are earned line by line — the meta-skill of this chapter's endgame is knowing what the examiner's marks buy.
steps: Examination success in this chapter is a classification skill before it is a computation skill: every question belongs to a node, every node owns one verifying habit, and the mark scheme pays for both.
The paper's four shapes each demand a different rhythm.

Applications (4–5 marks) pay for the translation: a cubical tank of volume 13,824 litres... converting litres to cubic metres (1 m³ = 1000 litres) gives 13.824 m³, whose side is ∛13.824 — the honest route recognises…

cards.title: Motion is the change in position of an object with respect to time and its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Motion is the change in position of an object with respect to time and its surroundings — an object is in motion if it occupies a new position at every succeeding moment, judged by watching it against objects that stay put. Rest is its partner-state: an object is at rest if its position does not change with time. Both statements hide the chapter's most powerful idea — the reference point (also called the reference object): motion and rest are never absolute properties, they are COMPARISONS against something chosen as stationary — the lamp post, the platform, the school gate — and a different reference can flip the verdict. The passenger asleep in a running bus is at rest with respect to (w.r.t.) the seat and the co-passenger beside her, because her position among them never changes; she is in motion w.r.t. the road's milestones and the passing shops, because against them her position changes every second. Both answers are correct physics — each names its reference. THE TWO INGREDIENTS, ALWAYS BOTH: position — the object's location described by naming it against the reference (20 m past the gate, opposite the tea stall) — and time — the change must be tracked as moments succeed each other; a shifted stone that now lies still has CHANGED position but is not IN motion: motion lives in the changing, not in the change. THE DESCRIPTION DISCIPLINE: a motion statement is complete only when it says what moved, compared to what, and how position changed as time passed — "the bus is moving" is shorthand for "the bus changes position w.r.t. the road and the buildings as time passes". What this node does NOT yet do: it does not classify motions into types (translatory, rotatory, oscillatory — the next station's work), does not measure them as uniform or non-uniform with average speed (a later station), and does not time them with apparatus (the stopwatch and pendulum stations); it builds the one sentence every later station will quantify: an object is in motion when its position changes with respect to a reference point as time passes.

The reference point is usually an obvious stay-put object — the lamp post, the platform edge, the school gate — and the watching of the mover AGAINST it is the whole act of detecting motion.

cards.title: Types of motion is the classification of motion by the path a body traces and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Types of motion is the classification of motion by the path a body traces and the way that path is traced — the same position-change-with-time that the first station defined, now sorted into named families. TRANSLATORY MOTION: the body as a whole changes its place, and every particle of the body travels the same distance in the same direction at the same instant — a line drawn on the body stays parallel to itself throughout. Its two sub-types follow the path's shape: rectilinear motion (the path is a straight line — a drawer sliding shut, a goods train on a straight track, a mango falling from the branch) and curvilinear motion (the path is a curved line — a javelin after the throw, a stone from a slingshot, a car rounding a bend while holding its heading). When the curved path is a circle traced about an axis that does NOT pass through the body, the motion gets its own name, circular motion (the Earth's yearly journey around the Sun, a stone whirled on a thread). ROTATORY MOTION is spin: the body turns about a fixed axis that passes THROUGH the body itself — every particle traces a circle around that axis while the body holds its place (the ceiling fan's blades, a spinning top, the potter's wheel, the Earth turning on its axis once a day, a clock's minute hand). THE AXIS TEST separates the two round families: the circle-path alone proves nothing — WHERE the axis sits decides; axis outside the body → circular; axis through the body → rotatory. OSCILLATORY MOTION is to-and-fro motion about a mean (central) position — the pendulum of a wall clock, a jhoola, a branch swaying in the breeze. Its rapid cousin, vibratory motion, is the same to-and-fro with tiny amplitude and fast repeats — the plucked sitar string, a drum's skin, a ringing bell. PERIODIC MOTION is any motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time — every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (the Earth's yearly revolution repeats, yet swings about no mean position). RANDOM MOTION has no fixed path and no fixed direction — the housefly, the dribbling footballer, monkeys leaping through a tree. And the counting rule: multiple motion — one body often executes two or more types at once, each named against its own axis or reference (a bus wheel: rotatory about its axle, translatory with the bus). What this node does NOT do: it does not measure how the position-change is distributed in time — uniform versus non-uniform motion and average speed belong to; it only names the shape of the change.

Same family, split only by the path's shape — straight versus curved.

cards.title: Uniform motion is motion in which a body covers equal distances in equal…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniform motion is motion in which a body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals — the position-change per interval never varies, so the body's table of positions (the lamp-post table of) shows the same advance in every row: the minute hand of a clock, a machine belt running steadily, a train holding its pace on a clear straight track. Non-uniform motion is motion in which equal time intervals are covered in unequal distances — the city bus creeping between signals, the mango speeding up as it falls, the cyclist tiring on the last stretch; the table's rows now disagree, and the disagreement is the signature. This classification judges HOW the position-change is distributed in time — the question the previous station could not yet ask, having only named the paths. Speed is the distance covered by a body in unit time — SPEED = DISTANCE COVERED / TIME TAKEN — the measure of how fast the position changes along the path. SI unit: metre per second (m/s); the practical unit is kilometre per hour (km/h), with 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s and 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h = 3.6 km/h. Average speed is the single honest speed for a journey whose pace kept changing: AVERAGE SPEED = TOTAL DISTANCE COVERED / TOTAL TIME TAKEN — total meaning the whole journey's distance (every kilometre, even those walked pushing a bicycle) divided by the whole journey's time (every minute, including halts at signals and tea stalls, when the distance added is zero but the clock runs). The rule that guards every computation: average speed is NOT the casual mean of the leg speeds — the legs' times, not their bare numbers, decide the average; the casual mean agrees with total/total only by accident (equal-time legs). What this node does NOT do: it does not give speed a direction (that is velocity — senior work), does not distinguish distance from displacement (senior classes), does not plot distance-time graphs (senior stations), and does not explain WHY pace changes (force — senior work); it measures and classifies the pace, on the rectilinear paths the previous station named.

cards.title: Measuring time in physics means counting the repetitions of a motion that…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Measuring time in physics means counting the repetitions of a motion that repeats itself identically — every clock ever built is a repeating motion wearing numbers (the pendulum's swing, the balance wheel's twitch, the quartz crystal's vibration, the Earth's rotation). The classroom's repeating motion is the simple pendulum: a bob — a heavy weight, here a metal ball with a hook — suspended from a rigid support by a light thread, free to swing. Its anatomy names the stations of its motion: the mean position (the vertical rest position the bob returns to when left alone), the two extreme positions (the farthest points of the swing, left and right), and the amplitude — the maximum displacement of the bob from the mean position (kept small in laboratory work). One complete oscillation is the bob's full to-and-fro: from the mean position to one extreme, back through the mean to the other extreme, and back again to the mean (equivalently, from one extreme to the other and back to the same extreme). The time period (T) is the time taken for ONE complete oscillation — the pendulum's fixed, personal unit of time. The laboratory discipline for finding it: time the pendulum through N complete oscillations (conventionally 20), then TIME PERIOD = TOTAL TIME FOR N OSCILLATIONS ÷ N — dividing the reaction-time error of the stopwatch across many swings instead of trusting one hastily counted swing. WHAT THE PERIOD OBEYS: the time period is governed chiefly by the thread's LENGTH — a longer thread swings slower (bigger T), a shorter thread swings faster — and is, for small amplitudes, practically INDEPENDENT of the bob's mass and of the size of the swing; these two independences are the pendulum's faithfulness, and the apparatus stations ahead ( — the ball as bob; — the thread and its length) verify each by experiment. This node builds the concept every apparatus station will instrument: the pendulum of's oscillatory family is also its most faithful periodic member (equal-interval repetition —), and its period is the first TIME the chapter measures precisely, after measured pace. What this node does NOT do: it does not operate the stopwatch (station 006), does not assemble the bob-and-hook or the stand (stations 007 and 009), does not tabulate the length-versus-period experiment (station 008), and gives no formula connecting T to length (senior work) — only the qualitative rule: longer is slower.

cards.title: The bob is the heavy weight at the lower end of a pendulum — in the classroom…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The bob is the heavy weight at the lower end of a pendulum — in the classroom, a metal ball fitted with a small hook to which the thread is tied — and this station establishes what the ball must be and what, surprisingly, it must not be blamed for. THE THREE QUALIFICATIONS OF A GOOD BOB: (1) heavy for its size — a dense ball (iron, brass) rather than a light one (cork, paper): the bob's weight keeps the thread taut (a slack thread swings like noodles, wobbling out of its plane) and makes air resistance a negligible guest compared with the swing; (2) round and smooth — a sphere's centre is fixed and known, it presents the same face to the air all round, and it does not tumble (an irregular lump spins and wobbles, spoiling the count); (3) fixed at a single point — the hook lets the thread attach at one definite spot, so the bob pivots about one fixed suspension point and the knot cannot slip mid-swing (a slipping loop quietly changes the thread's working length and corrupts every timing). THE LENGTH RULE THAT COMES WITH THE BOB: the pendulum's length is measured from the point of suspension to the CENTRE of the bob — not to its top or bottom — because the centre is where the bob's swing behaves as if its whole weight were gathered (the full-length measurement becomes the working number at the thread station,). THE GREAT UNIMPORTANCE — the station's experiment: hang bobs of different masses and materials (an iron ball, a heavier brass ball, a light wooden ball of similar size) on the SAME thread at the SAME length, release each with the SAME small amplitude, and time twenty oscillations of each: the periods AGREE within trial noise — the time period of a pendulum does NOT depend on the bob's mass or material; the bob is the pendulum's faithful weight, not its pace-setter. This verifies experimentally the mass-independence that stated qualitatively, and it sharpens the control-of-variables discipline: change ONE thing at a time (here, only the bob), keep the rest (thread, length, amplitude, counting) identical, or the comparison proves nothing. What this node does NOT do: it does not operate the stopwatch, does not detail the hook-and-knot assembly, does not study how the thread's length changes the period, and does not build the full stand setup.

cards.title: A stop watch is a hand-held timing instrument that can be STARTED and STOPPED…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A stop watch is a hand-held timing instrument that can be STARTED and STOPPED at will by the experimenter, and then reset to zero for the next reading — unlike an ordinary wall clock, which runs day and night whether or not anything is happening, the stopwatch runs only when the event it is hired to time is running. THE TWO KINDS the laboratory knows: (1) the mechanical stopwatch — a small drum wound up by turning its knob (the crown), with a LONG SECOND HAND sweeping a main dial (often 0–30 s per turn, divided into small divisions of 0.1 s or 0.2 s) and a SMALL MINUTE HAND on a little subsidiary dial counting the turns; one press of the button starts it, a second press stops it, and a third (or the crown) snaps the hands back to zero; (2) the digital stopwatch — a button-operated watch whose liquid-crystal display shows the elapsed interval in figures, reading typically to 0.01 s. THE LEAST COUNT — the instrument's confession: the least count of a stopwatch is the value of the SMALLEST DIVISION it can display (mechanical: usually 0.1 s or 0.2 s; digital: 0.01 s); no reading taken from it can be trusted finer than its least count, and when a hand stops between two divisions the reading is recorded to the nearest division — the least count is the finest grain of truth the instrument can offer. THE ZERO ERROR: a stopwatch that does not return exactly to zero when reset lends a constant gift (or steals a constant tax) from every reading — if the hands stand at 0.2 s at the instant of starting, every reading is 0.2 s too big, and the honest reading is the observed one MINUS the zero error. THE TWO HONESTIES OF TIMING: even a perfect instrument is worked by an imperfect finger — human reaction time is about 0.2 s, so the instant the watch starts and stops wobbles by that much; and the chapter's defence is arithmetic, not machinery — time TWENTY oscillations in one block and divide by twenty (the discipline laid down at), and the reaction wobble is spread across twenty swings, shrinking the error per swing from a fat 0.2 s to a thin 0.01 s. IN THIS CHAPTER'S BENCH: the stopwatch is the scorekeeper of the pendulum experiments — it times the twenty-swing blocks whose agreement or disagreement delivers the verdicts (the bob station has just depended on it); the stations that follow — the hook-and-knot assembly, the thread and the laboratory stand — complete the apparatus, and every one of them will send its numbers through this watch. What this node does NOT do: it does not compute speeds from times ('s territory), does not study how the thread's length sets the period, and does not teach any formula beyond the divide-by-N rule.

cards.title: A bob with hook is a compact, dense mass
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A bob with hook is a compact, dense mass (typically brass, steel, or lead) equipped with a rigid metallic loop (the hook) that allows a thread or string to be attached securely. In the context of Class 7 Physics, the bob serves as the oscillating mass of a simple pendulum when suspended from a laboratory stand using a thread (see node). The hook ensures the point of suspension is well‑defined and the length of the pendulum (distance from the point of suspension to the centre of mass of the bob) can be measured accurately with a metre rule. The bob’s mass does not affect the period of small‑amplitude oscillations (as per the simple‑pendulum approximation), but its density minimises air‑resistance effects. The bob‑hook assembly is therefore a standard apparatus component for experiments on periodic motion, uniform and non‑uniform motion, and measurement of acceleration due to gravity (g). It connects directly to the concepts of motion as change in position with time (node), types of motion (node), and uniform/non‑uniform speed (node). The stop watch (node) is used to time the oscillations, while the laboratory stand (node) provides a rigid support.
steps: A bob with a hook is the essential swinging mass that turns a thread and stand into a simple pendulum.
Here is why: the hook gives a fixed, repeatable point of suspension so the length of the pendulum stays constant during each swing.
Consider a brass bob of 50 g with a small steel loop; you tie a 1 m cotton thread to the hook, clamp the other end on a laboratory stand, and pull the bob aside a few centimetres.
When released, the bob swings back and forth in a regular arc — this is periodic motion, a type of non‑uniform motion because its speed changes (fastest at the bottom, zero at the ends).
The stop watch measures the time for, say, 20 complete oscillations; dividing gives the period.
Because the bob is dense and small, air drag is minimal, so the measured period closely matches the ideal simple‑pendulum model.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the hook makes the bob heavier”) reveals the misconception that the hook contributes to the oscillating mass rather than serving as an attachment point.

cards.title: The thread is the light, strong…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The thread is the light, strong, non-stretching cord that joins the bob (hung at its hook, the assembly of) to the point of suspension, and in this chapter it plays two roles at once: it is the pendulum's CONNECTION — the arm from which the bob hangs and swings — and it is the pendulum's TIMER-SETTING LEVER, because the pendulum's length lives in the thread. THE FOUR QUALIFICATIONS OF A GOOD THREAD: (1) strong — it must carry the bob's weight through every pass without snapping mid-trial; a snapped thread loses not only the bob but the whole twenty-swing block; (2) non-stretching — cotton or a similar non-elastic cord, NOT a rubber band or a stretchy nylon: a thread that creeps longer under the bob's steady pull silently re-writes the length between the measuring and the timing, and every period recorded after the stretch belongs to a longer pendulum than the one measured; (3) light and thin — the thread's own weight must be a negligible guest beside the bob's, so the swing is honestly the bob's swing and the measured length (suspension point to the bob's CENTRE, the rule fixed at) is the whole story; (4) smooth and untwisted — a kinked or twisted cord unwinds as it swings, spinning the bob, wasting the swing's energy and quietly changing its own working length turn by turn. THE LENGTH LAW THIS STATION VERIFIES: lengthen the thread and the period grows; shorten it and the period shrinks — and the growth is STEADY but SLOW: the bench ladder (25 cm → 50 cm → 100 cm) gives periods of about 1.0 s → 1.4 s → 2.0 s, so doubling the length does NOT double the period (it multiplies it by only about 1.4), and quadrupling the length doubles it (25 cm → 100 cm carries 1.0 s → 2.0 s); the period climbs more gently than the length — read as an experimental table at this level, with the full formula behind it reserved for senior classes. THE KNOT RULE: the thread is fixed at both ends — tied at the bob's hook and held at the support's clamp — and the length must be measured AFTER both knots are tied and the bob hangs free, because the knots consume thread and a measured-then-tied length is not the swinging length. What this node does NOT do: it does not fit the hook or tie the bob, does not provide the rigid support and the full setup protocol, does not time the swings ( owns the stopwatch), and does not derive any period formula (senior work).
steps: The takeaway first: the thread is the pendulum's true clockmaker — the bob supplies the weight and the stopwatch merely listens, but the LENGTH of the thread sets the period: lengthen it and the swing slows, shorten it…
Supporting argument 1 — the thread is hired twice: as arm and as tuning lever.

As arm, it holds the bob away from the pivot and lets it swing in one clean plane; as lever, its length IS the pendulum's length — the one quantity the experimenter can change at will to change the period.

STRONG: the thread carries the bob through thousands of passes; a snap mid-block loses the trial and the twenty-count with it. NON-STRETCHING: the bob pulls the thread taut all day, and an elastic cord answers that pull…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "any strong thread will do — nylon fishing line is the strongest, so it is best") reveals strength-only selection — strength is one of four qualifications, and stretchy nylon fails the non-stretching test that protects the data; the exam…

cards.title: The laboratory stand is the rigid support that holds the upper end of the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The laboratory stand is the rigid support that holds the upper end of the pendulum's thread and provides the point of suspension — the single fixed point about which the whole pendulum swings. ITS THREE PARTS: (1) the base — a heavy, flat slab (cast metal) whose weight and wide footprint anchor the assembly; it exists to be harder to move than anything the experiment can push; (2) the rod — the vertical metal pillar bolted at the base's centre, which carries the working height; (3) the clamp (tightened through its boss head on the rod) — the jaw that grips the thread at a definite spot, so that the suspension point is not "somewhere on the stand" but ONE place that can be pointed at, measured from, and returned to. THE STAND'S TWO CERTIFICATES: RIGIDITY — the point of suspension must not move while the bob swings: a swaying stand adds its own motion to the bob's, so the period timed belongs to pendulum-plus-stand, the measured length (suspension point to the bob's centre, the rule of) stops describing the true swing arm, and the swing plane drifts; STABILITY — the assembly must not topple or slide: a swinging bob pulls sideways at the top of the rod every pass, and a tall, light, loose stand is a lever waiting to fall (the base's mass and footprint, and clamping the rod or base to the bench, are the defences). THE HEIGHT RULE: the stand must be planned for the LONGEST length in the experiment — the suspension point must sit higher than the longest thread by the bob's clearance: suspension height above the bench must be at least (thread length + a comfortable margin, about 10 cm), because at the mean position the bob hangs at its lowest and must sweep clear of bench, books and knees. THE COMPLETE ASSEMBLY the stand completes: bob at its hook (, hung per the bob's qualifications of), thread tied at both ends with length measured after tying, gripped in the clamp of this station, timed by the stopwatch — the stand is the last apparatus station and the first one touched in setup, because the assembly order begins with the root. What this node does NOT do: it does not qualify the bob or re-teach the hook (,), does not qualify the thread or re-teach the ladder, does not time anything, and does not teach why the length sets the period beyond the table already read (the formula is senior work).
steps: The takeaway first: the laboratory stand is the pendulum's fixed point made physical — the one thing in the experiment that must be perfectly still while everything else moves; its base buys stability, its rod buys…
Supporting argument 1 — the pivot is a promise.

Every measurement in this chapter is anchored to one point: the length runs from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob, the swing turns about the suspension point, and the counting card's "same-way pass…

A thread knotted to a doorknob has a suspension point that is "wherever the knot settled"; a thread in a tightened clamp jaw has one the class can point to. The experiment can only be as definite as its pivot.
Supporting argument 2 — rigidity is a measurement, not a mood.

When the stand sways with each pass, three corruptions enter at once: the pivot moves (the swing's turning point is no longer fixed), the working length changes (the measured number described a still support), and the…

cards.title: The video on motion and types of motion is the chapter's review station…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The video on motion and types of motion is the chapter's review station — a moving-picture consolidation of what defined (motion as change of position with respect to time) and what classified (the families of motion), watched with a scientist's discipline rather than a viewer's idle eye. THE FAMILIES THE VIDEO MONTAGES, each with its deciding test: translatory motion — the body shifts so that every line drawn through it stays parallel to itself (the rectilinear case: a bus on a straight road; the curvilinear case: a ball on a curved path); circular motion — a body (or a point on it) travels a round path about an axis OUTSIDE the body (a coin on a turntable, a merry-go-round horse); rotatory motion — the body spins about an axis THROUGH itself (a ceiling fan, a spinning top); the AXIS TEST separates the two round families — ask where the axis of rotation lives; oscillatory motion — to-and-fro swinging about a mean position (the pendulum the class has just finished assembling and timing — stations 004 through 009); its rapid cousin is vibratory; periodic motion — any motion repeating at equal intervals of time, the umbrella under which oscillation sits (the pendulum is both); random motion — no fixed path, no repeat (a flying housefly). THE THREE TESTS THE VIEWER CARRIES: the AXIS TEST (where is the axis — through the body: rotatory; outside it: circular), the MEAN-POSITION TEST (is there a middle the motion swings about: oscillatory), the REPETITION TEST (does it repeat at equal intervals: periodic). WHAT THE VIDEO ADDS OVER THE STILL PAGE: motion is shown IN TIME — slow motion reveals what the eye cannot slice (the fan's blades, the swing's turnaround), and one scene can hold SEVERAL motions at once (the cyclist: the cycle translates, the wheels rotate about their own axles, a pedal travels a circle about the crank axis — classification attaches to a BODY and its REFERENCE, never to "the whole picture"). What this node does NOT do: it does not re-derive the definitions (they live at 001 and 002 — this station exercises them), does not touch uniform and non-uniform motion or speed (, and the next review station), does not re-teach the pendulum apparatus (004–009 — the video's pendulum scene is quoted, name-only, as an old friend), and does not compute speed from any scene (that is's finale).
steps: The takeaway first: a motion video is not something you watch — it is something you interrogate: every scene asks "which family, and by which test?", every classification must survive its test's prediction, and the…
Supporting argument 1 — classification attaches to a body, never to a scene.

The cyclist scene is not "a motion": the cycle's frame translates along the road, each wheel rotates about its own axle, a pedal travels a circle about the crank axis, and the rider's chest translates.

The trained viewer asks "WHICH BODY, with respect to WHAT?" before naming anything — the discipline inherited from 001's reference-point rule — and then one scene yields several honest answers, one per body.
The habit this builds is larger than video-watching: it is the habit of never classifying a fog. Supporting argument 2 — the tests are predictions, not labels.
Naming a family is only half the exercise; the other half is letting the name PREDICT something checkable: "rotatory" predicts every marked point on the fan blade circles the same axle;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "circular and rotatory are the same thing, just words for spinning") reveals the axis-blindness the axis test exists to cure — the two round families differ in WHERE the axis lives, through the body or outside it; the exam answer must…

cards.title: Uniform motion occurs when an object travels equal distances in equal intervals…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniform motion occurs when an object travels equal distances in equal intervals of time, meaning its speed (magnitude of velocity) remains constant. Non‑uniform motion is the opposite: the object covers unequal distances in equal time intervals, so its speed changes continuously or in steps. Speed is defined as the rate of change of distance with respect to time, v = (s)/(t), with SI unit metre per second (m s⁻¹). Average speed for a whole journey is total distance travelled divided by total time taken, v = S_totalT_total. In uniform motion the instantaneous speed equals the average speed at every instant; in non‑uniform motion they differ. The video illustrates these ideas with a ball rolling on a track, a pendulum bob swinging, and a stopwatch measuring time intervals, linking the visual evidence to the mathematical definitions.
steps: The one thing to remember: Uniform motion means constant speed; non‑uniform motion means speed changes.
Here is why: when a ball rolls on a smooth horizontal track without friction, it covers the same length of track every second — this is uniform motion.

Consider a pendulum bob on a thread attached to a laboratory stand: as it swings, it moves fastest at the bottom and momentarily stops at the extremes, so its speed varies — this is non‑uniform motion.
The video shows both side by side, using a stopwatch to time each segment.
You see the ball’s positions marked at equal time intervals forming equally spaced dots, while the pendulum’s dots bunch up near the ends and spread out in the middle.
From these dots you can compute speed: distance between successive dots divided by the fixed time interval.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “yes, because the car moves each hour”) reveals the misconception that any regular motion is uniform, confusing regularity of observation with constancy of speed.
remember: A student says, “If a car travels 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the second hour, its motion is uniform because it moves every hour.” Is the student correct? Explain.
A ball rolls 10 m in 2 s, then another 10 m in the next 2 s, then 10 m in the following 2 s. What type of motion does it exhibit? Calculate its speed.
A pendulum completes one full oscillation in 2 s. The length of its path for one oscillation is 1 m. What is its average speed? Is its motion uniform.

cards.title: The video on speed of objects in daily life is the chapter's closing review…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The video on speed of objects in daily life is the chapter's closing review station: a moving catalogue of how fast the world's familiar movers move, watched with the conversion arithmetic and the comparison habits that turn a parade of numbers into an ordered, usable map. WHAT THE CATALOGUE HOLDS (approximate, everyday values — the point is the scale, not the decimal): a snail about 1 mm per second; a walking person about 1.4 m/s (about 5 km/h); a cyclist about 4 m/s (about 15 km/h); a city bus about 10 m/s (36 km/h); an express train about 25 m/s (90 km/h); a passenger jet about 250 m/s (900 km/h); SOUND in air about 340 m/s; LIGHT about 300,000 km/s — the unbeatable head of the parade. THE TWO UNITS AND THE BRIDGE BETWEEN THEM: speed in m/s (metres each second — the laboratory's unit, the one the distance-time arithmetic runs in) and speed in km/h (kilometres each hour — the road's unit, the one every vehicle's dial reads); the bridge is the factor 3.6, because 1 km = 1000 m and 1 h = 3600 s: m/s → km/h MULTIPLY by 3.6, km/h → m/s DIVIDE by 3.6 (10 m/s = 36 km/h; 90 km/h = 25 m/s). WHAT THE VIDEO TRAINS, THREE HABITS: (1) the UNIT QUESTION — asked before any comparison: which unit is this number wearing? (comparing 25 m/s of a train with 90 of a bus is meaningless until the bridge is crossed — and after crossing, they are the SAME speed); (2) the ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE FEEL — knowing that each step up the parade (walk → cycle → bus → train → jet → sound → light) jumps by several times, not a little; (3) the DISTANCE-TIME READ — speed answers "how far in how long?": at 25 m/s the train covers 25 m each second, 1.5 km each minute, and the video's favourite question "how long to cross this bridge?" is one division away. THE CHAPTER'S HOME COMING: speed itself was defined at, and the steady-versus-changing question belongs to the previous review — this station closes the chapter by putting NUMBERS on the moving world the class has been classifying (001, 002, 010) and timing (004–009). What this node does NOT do: it does not re-define speed or average speed (003, 011 — name-only), does not re-teach the uniform/non-uniform distinction, does not derive anything (senior kinematics), and does not touch the pendulum's apparatus except as an old friend at the farewell.

A student with the shape can place anything new: a crow flies between the bus and the train; a scooter between the cycle and the bus; a river current near the walk.
The catalogue is a ruler, not a phone book.
Supporting argument 2 — the 3.6 bridge is not a magic number; it is 1000 divided by 3600.

One metre per second means 1 m each second, so in one hour (3600 s) it covers 3600 m = 3.6 km: hence 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, and the bridge runs both ways — multiply by 3.6 to climb from m/s to the road's km/h, divide by 3.6…

cards.title: Work, in physics, is said to be done when a force acting on a body makes the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work, in physics, is said to be done when a force acting on a body makes the body move through a distance in the direction of the force. It is measured by the product of the force applied and the displacement produced: WORK = FORCE × DISPLACEMENT (W = F × s), where F is the force in newtons and s is the displacement in the direction of the force in metres. The SI unit of work is the joule (J): one joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves a body through one metre in the direction of the force (1 J = 1 N·m). Larger amounts are measured in kilojoules (1 kJ = 1000 J). TWO CONDITIONS must both hold before we may say work is done: (1) a force must act on the body, and (2) the point of application of the force must move — if a body does not move through any distance, the work done is ZERO, whatever the size of the force. Pushing a heavy trunk that refuses to budge, pressing against a wall, or holding a loaded bag motionless in your hand are all cases of ZERO work, because the displacement is zero — the effort is real, but physics work is not done. When a body is LIFTED, the force needed equals its weight (weight = mass × g; at this level g ≈ 10 m/s²), so the work done against gravity = weight × height raised. Work is a scalar quantity at this level of study — it has a size but we do not attach a direction to it in numericals. Work is the OPENING idea of the Energy chapter: it is the currency in which every later station — the law of conservation, the meaning of energy (003), the work–energy relation (004), the forms (005, 006) and their conversions (007–012) — will be counted. What this node does NOT do: it does not define "energy" itself (003's station), does not prove that work done equals energy spent (004's station), and does not treat force as a concept afresh — force and its effects were the previous chapter's territory and are used here as tools, name-only.
steps: The takeaway first: in physics, work is force that succeeds — a force multiplied by the distance it moves its point of application — W = F × s, counted in joules — and the whole discipline of this station is the ZERO…
Supporting argument 1 — the definition is a pair of conditions, not a feeling.
The daily word "work" pays for effort; the physics word pays only for MOVED FORCE.
Both tests must pass: a force must act, and the body must move through a distance in the direction of that force.
Fail either test and the work ledger reads zero.

This is why the same trolley can cost the pusher zero joules (stuck in mud, wheels locked, no displacement) and then sixty joules (rolling freely, 20 N × 3 m) — the force may not change, but the displacement does, and…

cards.title: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, and the TOTAL amount of energy in a closed system remains constant through every change. In the joule bookkeeping installed by, the law is one balanced sentence: the sum of all the energies present BEFORE any transformation equals the sum of all the energies present AFTER it — every joule is traceable from one form to another, and no ledger line is ever lost, however complicated the machine. THREE PARTS of the law must be understood together: (1) NO CREATION — no device, animal or process manufactures energy from nothing; a fan does not make energy, it only converts electrical energy delivered to it into motion, heat and sound; (2) NO DESTRUCTION — when energy seems to "disappear" (a swinging cradle stops, a moving cycle coasts to rest), it has not died; it has LEFT the visible account as heat (friction), sound (air and surfaces) — energy passed to the surroundings, where it still exists; (3) ONLY CONVERSION — every energy event is a change of costume: chemical to electrical in a cell, electrical to light and heat in a lamp, mechanical to heat when hands are rubbed. The law also explains why an "energy crisis" is never a shortage of energy itself — the Earth is not running out of energy, it is running out of energy in USABLE, concentrated forms (fuels, stored charge, food), which is why will define energy carefully and later stations (004–012) will trace conversions through machines, roller coasters, dams and pendulums — each one a demonstration of this single balanced law. What this node does NOT do: it does not define the term energy itself (003's station, name-only), does not prove work equals energy spent (004), does not catalogue the forms (005, 006), and does not demonstrate the law on apparatus — the roller-coaster demonstration (008), the hydroelectric ledger (009) and the pendulum (010) each own one demonstration; this station owns the LAW and its bookkeeping.
steps: The takeaway first: the law of conservation of energy is a bookkeeping rule for the whole universe — energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only change form, so in every event the joules before exactly equal the…
Supporting argument 1 — the law is easiest to believe as an accounting audit, not as a slogan.

Take any device and write what goes in and what comes out. A torch: the cell delivers 600 J of chemical energy converted to electrical; the lamp turns it into 100 J of light and 500 J of heat — 600 J in, 600 J out…
A table fan: 2000 J electrical in; 1200 J of motion of the blades, 700 J of heat in the motor, 100 J of sound out — balanced again.

The audit never fails; when a column seems short, the missing joules are hiding as unlisted heat or sound, and the FIX for the ledger is always "add the overlooked entry", never "the energy vanished".
Supporting argument 2 — "disappearance" is transfer in disguise.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "energy is never wasted" or "energy always decreases with use") reveals the misconception of reading the law as a moral slogan about thrift or as a claim of gradual loss — the law is a strict balance: the TOTAL never changes at all; only…

cards.title: Energy is defined as the capacity of a body to do work.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy is defined as the capacity of a body to do work. A body that can exert a force and move something through a distance possesses energy, and the AMOUNT of energy a body possesses is measured by the TOTAL work it can do — which is why energy is counted in exactly the unit work is counted in: the joule (J), with the kilojoule (1 kJ = 1000 J) for larger amounts. The definition carries three consequences the class must hold together: (1) ENERGY IS A CAPACITY, NOT AN EVENT — a stretched catapult, a charged battery and a loaded trolley on a slope all sit QUIETLY possessing energy; the work happens only when the capacity is spent, and between the storing and the spending nothing need move at all; (2) ENERGY IS MEASURED BY WORK DONE — to find how much energy a body has, let it (or ask what went into it) and count the joules of work it can perform: a hammer that can drive a nail through 2 cm against an average resistance of 500 N carries 500 N × 0.02 m = 10 J of capacity; (3) ENERGY IS A PROPERTY OF THE BODY; WORK IS A TRANSFER BETWEEN BODIES — the hammer HAS energy; the nail RECEIVES work. The daily-life experiences that make the term real fall into a small set of recurring families, each rehearsed with examples in this station: MOVING bodies (a rolling ball, blowing wind, flowing water — anything moving can push or turn something); RAISED bodies (the stored clockwork of height — a raised hammer, tank water, a book on a shelf); CHANGED-SHAPE or CONFIGURED bodies (a wound toy spring, a stretched rubber band, a bent bow); FUELS and FOOD (stored chemical capacity — kerosene, wood, cooking gas, chapati and rice); and READY-TO-DELIVER stores (a charged cell, a full water tank above the house). The term defined here is the chapter's CENTRE: the law of conservation governs how energy shifts between these families, the work–energy relation (004) pins the counting, and the forms catalogue (005, 006) names the costumes — this station owns the DEFINITION and the daily-life feel. What it does NOT do: it does not name the full formal catalogue of energy forms (005–006), does not compute any form's size by formula (senior work), and does not demonstrate conversions on apparatus (007–012, name-only).
steps: The takeaway first: energy is the capacity to do work — possessed quietly, spent loudly, and counted in the same joules as work — so the whole station reduces to one sentence spoken correctly: the more work a body CAN…

Supporting argument 1 — the definition is read twice, and each reading does a different job. Read as CAPACITY: "this wound toy can pull its wheels through 5 m against 4 N of resistance — it holds 20 J." Read as EVENT…
The cure is the tense test — CAN do work (energy present) versus IS doing work (energy being transferred) — and a still body that can act is fully charged.
Supporting argument 2 — the daily-life families make the abstraction unavoidable, because EVERY one of them is met before breakfast.
The moving family: the wind that turns the paddy-field pump, the stream that spins a flour mill's wheel.
The raised family: the water tank on the terrace whose height lets it gush down every morning; the pressure-cooker weight lifted by steam.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "energy is the force of a body" or "energy is measured in newtons") reveals the misconception of confusing energy with force — force is the pusher (newtons), work is the push acting through distance (joules), and energy is the CAPACITY…

cards.title: The relation between work and energy is the chapter's counting bridge…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The relation between work and energy is the chapter's counting bridge, and it has two complementary halves. FIRST HALF — WORK DONE BY A BODY SPENDS ITS ENERGY: when a body does work, it loses an amount of energy exactly equal to the work done; the moving air that turns a windmill gives the mill as many joules of work as it gives up of its own energy; a horse pulling a cart spends energy equal to the force × distance it delivers. SECOND HALF — WORK DONE ON A BODY GIVES IT ENERGY: when work is done on a body, the body gains an amount of energy exactly equal to that work; the work done in lifting a 5 kg load 2 m (weight 50 N × 2 m = 100 J) is stored by the load as exactly 100 J of raised-position capacity; the wound spring holds exactly the work the winding hand spent on it. Together the halves form one conservation-friendly sentence: ENERGY SPENT = WORK DONE, and WORK DONE ON A BODY = ENERGY GAINED BY THE BODY — work is the TRANSFER, energy is the HOLDING, and the joule is the common currency (both counted in joules, 1 kJ = 1000 J). Two precision points belong to the definition: (1) the equality is EXACT, not approximate — a body cannot gain 40 J from 40 J of work, nor spend 40 J of energy by doing 35 J of work; any ledger gap means an uncounted output (heat, sound), never a broken equality; (2) the relation runs THROUGH bodies — the energy leaves one body as work and arrives in another as capacity, which is why the same joules appear once as "work done" (in the giver's account) and once as "energy gained" (in the receiver's): they are the SAME joules seen from two doors. This relation formalises the bridge 003 built between the two words, uses the conservation law of 002 as its guarantee, and equips every later station — the forms catalogue (005, 006), the conversions (007–012) — with its only needed arithmetic. What this node does NOT do: it does not re-define work (001) or energy (003), does not restate the conservation law (002), and does not assign energy to named forms with formulas (005–006, senior treatment).
steps: The takeaway first: work and energy are one currency at two doors — energy spent by the giver equals work done; work done on the receiver equals energy gained — both counts in joules, both exact — and the entire skill…

Every scene has a GIVER and a RECEIVER joined by a joule-pipe through which work flows: the horse (giver) pays; the cart (receiver) gains; the falling hammer (giver) pays; the nail (receiver) gains; the winding hand…
The student's first question in any numerical is therefore not "what formula?" but "which direction?" — is work being done BY the body under study (its energy falls) or ON it (its energy rises)?

The same arithmetic answers both: force × displacement either leaves the giver's account or enters the receiver's, and misreading the direction is the source of nearly every sign error this station ever sees.

cards.title: The forms of energy are the distinct costumes in which energy is held and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The forms of energy are the distinct costumes in which energy is held and delivered, and the Class 7 catalogue names six: (1) MECHANICAL energy — the energy of moving or positioned objects — which has TWO sub-forms: KINETIC energy, the energy a body possesses because of its motion (a rolling ball, blowing wind, flowing river water — anything moving can do work by pushing or turning something); and POTENTIAL energy, the energy a body possesses because of its POSITION (a raised body — its raised capacity counted by the lifting arithmetic weight × height) or its SHAPE/CONDITION (a wound spring, a stretched rubber band, a compressed ball — strained bodies ready to do work); (2) HEAT energy, the energy of a hot body — flowing from a hotter body to a colder one, able to do work by expanding, boiling or lifting (steam raising a cooker's vent-weight, the Sun warming the sea); (3) LIGHT energy, the energy of the Sun, a flame, a glowing filament or a LED — visible energy that lets us see, warms what it falls on, drives photosynthesis and powers solar cells; (4) SOUND energy, the energy of a vibrating body carried to our ears — a drum's skin, a plucked string, a ringing bell: small in joules, but genuinely able to rattle a windowpane and shake a diaphragm; (5) CHEMICAL energy, the energy stored IN substances and released when they change — fuels (wood, kerosene, cooking gas), food (rice, dal, roti), the chemicals of a cell or battery: the body's own running currency and the kitchen's cooking currency; (6) ELECTRICAL energy, the energy of electric current — the most DELIVERABLE costume, arriving through wires to become light in bulbs, heat in irons, motion in fans, sound in speakers. TWO classification habits hold the catalogue together: kinetic and potential are the two sub-forms of MECHANICAL energy (motion versus position/strain), and every form is still just energy — the same joules of 001–004 — so the catalogue names COSTUMES, not different stuff. This station NAMES and DEFINES the wardrobe; fills each costume with daily-life examples, 007 shows the quick-changes between them, and 008–012 demonstrate the wardrobe on apparatus. What this node does NOT do: it does not compute any form by formula (no kinetic-energy formula — senior treatment; raised-position capacity only through the weight × height lifting work already owned), and it does not catalogue the conversions (007).

cards.title: Forms of energy with examples is the inventory station…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Forms of energy with examples is the inventory station: each costume named at is here filled with the daily-life examples that make it unmistakable, and every example is pinned by its one-line holding-condition test. KINETIC energy — every mover: the monsoon gale drying clothes and bending the banana trees; the river current that turns a floating mill; a rolling marble, a moving bus, the kicked football, the falling coconut, the blades of a running fan, the bullet of water from a hand-pump's spout. POTENTIAL energy — every raised or strained body: the terrace tank's water; the coconut hanging on the palm; the drawn bucket at the well; the wound clock and toy springs; the stretched catapult and slingshot bands; the bent bow; the compressed squeeze of a foam ball; the straining rope in tug-of-war's frozen pull. HEAT energy — every hot body: the cooker's steam lifting its vent-weight; the morning sun warming the terrace; the idli pot; the iron pressing the school uniform; the cup of chai; the friction-warmed palms rubbed in winter; the match head's first flame. LIGHT energy — every visible delivery: the Sun — the great original; the bulb and tube-light; the candle and the diya at Diwali; the firefly in the monsoon evening; the laser pointer's dot; the glow of a hot ember. SOUND energy — every heard vibration: the temple and school bells; the tabla's struck skin; the whistle of the pressure cooker; the shout across the courtyard; the lorry's horn; the hum of the transformer; a lizard's chirp at dusk. CHEMICAL energy — every store-in-substance: the LPG cylinder, kerosene, firewood and cow-dung cakes of the kitchen; petrol and diesel in vehicles; the cell and inverter battery; medicines' subtle stores; and above all FOOD — rice, roti, dal, groundnut, ghee — the body's own chemical wardrobe. THE CATALOGUE'S CROWN is the source arc: nearly every example on the list traces back to the SUN — its light grew the plants that became firewood, food, coal-over-ages and the wind itself (sun-warmed air moving), and even the rain that fills the terrace tank climbed up as sun-evaporated vapour — so the day's inventory is, at one remove, sunlight re-costumed. This station maps and drills; the conversions between costumes belong to 007–012. What this node does NOT do: it does not re-define the forms (005, name-only), does not demonstrate inter-conversion on apparatus (007), and adds no formulas — the only arithmetic is the raised-count (weight × height) where a potential example is numbered.
steps: The takeaway first: the six forms are learned for good not by reciting the wardrobe but by hanging the whole day on it — twenty tags from waking to sleep, each defended by its test — because a form that can be FOUND in…
Supporting argument 1 — the inventory is walked in time, not listed in tables.

MORNING: the alarm's wound spring (potential-strain) buzzes its small sound; the geyser and the chai pot pour heat; the sunlight on the study table is light; the gale snaps the clothesline — kinetic; the idlis going…
NOON: the noon-meal's rice is the body's refuelling; the tin roof's heat shimmers; the hand-pump's spout is a kinetic rope of water raised from potential stores below.

EVENING: the courtyard cricket ball flies kinetic, lands where the neem's shadow is deep; the tube-light converts electrical to light (and its heat share); the temple bell sends sound over the rooftops.
NIGHT: the inverter (chemical store) carries the fan through the cut; the body, on its day's chemical fuel, closes the ledger in sleep.

cards.title: Inter-conversion of energy is the process by which energy passes from one form…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Inter-conversion of energy is the process by which energy passes from one form to another — the six-costume wardrobe of read in motion instead of at rest. Every conversion happens AT a device or process, which acts as the changing room: energy enters at one door wearing one form and leaves at the other wearing another, and the device itself holds nothing back (its own temperature may rise a little — the heat line of every real ledger). The demonstration shelf of this chapter pins one arrow per device: the cycle dynamo (mechanical/kinetic energy of the turning wheel → electrical energy in the lamp circuit); the windmill (kinetic energy of moving air → electrical energy, or → potential energy when it pumps water up); the burning candle or burner (chemical energy → heat energy + light energy); the electric bulb (electrical → light + heat); the microphone (sound → electrical); the loudspeaker (electrical → sound); the solar cell (light → electrical); and the electric fan or mixer motor (electrical → kinetic + heat + sound). Two grammar rules govern every arrow. THE LEDGER RULE: input joules = useful output joules + the heat (and thin sound) exit lines — nothing is created or destroyed at the changing room, exactly as the transfer bookkeeping of 002 required with its giver-receiver pairs and its two doors. THE SEQUENCE RULE: conversions chain — the candle's chemical came from plants that captured sunlight, so its flame is sunlight re-costumed twice; the dusk cycle's lamp light traces legs → kinetic → dynamo's electrical → lamp's light in three arrows. This node demonstrates and drills the arrows; the statement that the TOTAL stays constant through every change is the law of conservation, unpacked with its applications at, and the great hydroelectric diagram that assembles the chains belongs to — both name-only here. What this node does NOT do: it does not re-teach the six forms or their tests (005–006, assumed fluent), introduces no efficiency percentages or power ratings (senior work), and adds no new formula — the only arithmetic is the familiar raised-count wherever a conversion ends with water or a load lifted.
steps: The takeaway first: inter-conversion of energy is the wardrobe put in motion — at every device one costume goes in at the input door and another comes out at the output door, the joule ledger balancing exactly with its…
Supporting argument 1 — every conversion is a TWO-DOOR event with a device between the doors.
The grammar has exactly three parts: the giver's form, the device, the receiver's form(s).

The cycle dynamo is the cleanest exhibit: the wheel's KINETIC presses the little spindle; inside, that turning becomes ELECTRICAL in the wires; the lamp wears it as LIGHT (and the classic warmth of every bulb).
Two doors, three costumes, one device — and the ledger closes: joules of motion in = joules of electricity out + the small heat at the stiff hub and the filament.
The two-doors bookkeeping of 002 never changes; conversion only adds the middle term, the changing room.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing "the bulb converts electricity into brightness" as if brightness were a form) reveals the misconception of naming appearances instead of catalogue forms — the exit costume must be one of the wardrobe's six (here light, with its…

cards.title: Conservation of energy is the law that governs every arrow drilled at…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conservation of energy is the law that governs every arrow drilled at: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes from one form to another, so the TOTAL energy of a system — all its costumes counted together — stays constant through every change. The ledger sentence of the conversions ("input = useful output + heat/sound lines") was this law read locally; the law is the same bookkeeping declared universally. The roller coaster is the law's demonstration exhibit: the car hauled up the first hill banks its joules as POTENTIAL (position door, counted by the raised-count weight × height); released, the bank converts to KINETIC as it thunders down; the next rise converts kinetic back to potential; and so the ride is one long see-saw between the wardrobe's two mechanical costumes. THE LAW'S SIGNATURE shows in the track's shape: every hill after the first MUST be lower, because each conversion pays its heat line — axle friction, air swirl, the rattle of the wheels — and that heat never returns to the car; the missing joules are not lost but re-costumed into the track's and air's warmth, exactly where the ledger says they went. Other everyday conservation exhibits: the playground swing (potential at the ends of the arc, kinetic at the bottom, each arc lower as the joints' friction and air drag collect their tax); the falling coconut (006's courtyard example — 120 J of waiting capacity arriving as 120 J of motion, paid out as thud-heat and sound); the trampoline jumper (chemical → kinetic → strain-potential of the stretched mesh → kinetic → potential of the rise, the bounce fading as the mesh and air warm); a stone tossed upward (kinetic → potential on the rise, potential → kinetic on the fall, returning a little short of the hand because of air drag). The law is the reason every ledger in the chapter ever balanced: nothing new is minted, nothing is destroyed, only the costume changes. What this node does NOT do: it does not re-drill the conversion arrows device by device (007), does not build the hydroelectric diagram (, name-only), does not run the pendulum's precise swing-counts, and adds no new formula — the raised-count remains the only arithmetic, now used to PROVE totals rather than to price single lifts.
steps: The takeaway first: conservation of energy says the wardrobe's total never changes — every device, every fall, every ride only re-costumes the same joules — and the roller coaster proves it in public: a first hill banks…
Supporting argument 1 — the law is the ledger grown universal.
Since 002 every transfer closed the same sentence: giver's joules = receiver's joules + exits.
Since 007 every device closed the same: input = useful output + heat lines.
The law says these were never separate lucky balances: energy simply CANNOT be minted or burnt out of existence — only re-costumed.
The student should hear the continuity: the law is not a new fact to memorise but the reason every old balance worked.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating only "energy is never wasted" as the whole law) reveals the misconception of the conservation-as-thrift reading — the law is not advice about wasting less but a strict count: no creation, no destruction, conversion only, total…

cards.title: Hydroelectric power generation is a practical application of the law of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Hydroelectric power generation is a practical application of the law of conservation of energy. Water held at a height in a reservoir possesses gravitational potential energy given by PE = mgh, where m is the mass of water, g is acceleration due to gravity, and h is the vertical head. When released, this potential energy converts into kinetic energy as water accelerates down the penstock (KE = ½ mv²). The moving water strikes turbine blades, transferring kinetic energy into mechanical rotational energy of the turbine shaft. The turbine drives a generator, where electromagnetic induction converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. At each stage, a fraction of energy dissipates as heat, sound, and turbulence, so the useful electrical output is less than the initial potential energy. An energy conversion diagram represents these transformations with labelled boxes (potential, kinetic, mechanical, electrical) and arrows showing the processes (water release, turbine, generator) and loss branches (heat, sound). By constructing such diagrams, students deduce that the sum of all output energies (electrical + losses) equals the input potential energy, confirming energy conservation. This node builds on earlier concepts of work, energy forms, and inter-conversion (nodes 001, 002, 005, 006, 007) and the roller‑coaster example (node 008), extending them to a real‑world engineering system.
steps: In a hydroelectric plant, the gravitational potential energy of stored water is converted step by step into kinetic, mechanical, and finally electrical energy, and a properly drawn energy conversion diagram proves that…
First, water at height possesses potential energy proportional to its mass, the gravitational acceleration, and the vertical head (PE = mgh).
Second, as water flows down the penstock, this potential energy transforms into kinetic energy (KE = ½ mv²).
Third, the kinetic energy of the jet drives turbine blades, converting it into mechanical rotational energy.
Fourth, the turbine shaft rotates a generator, where electromagnetic induction changes mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Fifth, at every conversion some energy escapes as heat, sound, and turbulence; these losses appear as branches in the diagram but the sum of all outputs still equals the input.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “kinetic energy”) reveals the misconception that stored water is already moving — confusing the energy of position with energy of motion.
