cards.title: A simple pendulum is a small, heavy bob (a metal ball) hung by a light…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A simple pendulum is a small, heavy bob (a metal ball) hung by a light, non-stretchable string from a fixed support — the chapter's cleanest conservation exhibit after the roller coaster. Its parts are named exactly: the point of suspension (where the string is fixed), the string (light and unstretchable), the bob (small and heavy, so the swinging belongs to it), and the length of the pendulum (from the point of suspension to the CENTRE of the bob — not to its bottom). When the bob is pulled aside and released it oscillates: one oscillation (one vibration, one to-and-fro) means the bob goes from the mean position to one extreme, back through the mean to the other extreme, and returns to the starting point — the full round trip. The mean position is the resting hang-straight-down line; the extremes are the farthest points of the swing; the amplitude is the distance (or the angle) by which the extreme lies from the mean. The time period (T) is the time for ONE complete oscillation; the frequency is the number of oscillations per second (= 1/T). Measured the classroom way: time n oscillations with a stopwatch and divide — T = total time ÷ n. The conservation story runs the swing: at each extreme the bob hangs for an instant, its energy parked as potential (it is at its highest, raised by the amplitude); through the mean it runs fastest, the bank exchanged for kinetic; back up the far side the kinetic re-costumes as potential; and so the swing is a two-costume see-saw — shrinking arc by arc, because pivot friction and air drag collect their small warmth-and-sound tax each pass, until the bob settles at the mean with the whole bank spent into warmth. One more measured truth: the time period grows with length — a longer pendulum swings slower — which is why the clock keeper shortens or lengthens the rod to hurry or slow the tick. What this node does NOT do: it does not restate the law of conservation (, name-only as the law the see-saw obeys), does not build the hydroelectric chain (, name-only), does not sort the forms into charts (, name-only), and introduces no senior timing formula — the time period stays a measured quantity (total time ÷ oscillations) and the only arithmetic remains the raised-count pricing the amplitude.
steps: The takeaway first: the simple pendulum is the conservation law made into a metronome — potential parked at each extreme, kinetic running through each mean, the arc shrinking swing by swing as pivot and air collect…
Supporting argument 1 — the pendulum's names must be worn exactly, because the exams and the physics both live in them.
The LENGTH is suspension point to the CENTRE of the bob — to the bottom would be a different, longer pendulum and a different clock.
ONE OSCILLATION is the full round trip — mean to one extreme, through mean to the other extreme, home; a half trip is a half oscillation, the beginner's classic miscount.
AMPLITUDE is the extreme's distance from the mean — the size of the swing, not its speed.
The student who can label the diagram and count the round trip owns the vocabulary the timing habit needs.

cards.title: Charts showing different forms of energy is the consolidation station…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Charts showing different forms of energy is the consolidation station: the chapter's knowledge — six forms with their holding-condition tests, their sources, their conversion arrows and the conservation law — organised into wall-chart displays that a reader can audit at a glance and a maker can defend line by line. A chart here is not decoration; it is the chapter compressed under discipline. THE FORMS CHART carries six columns (kinetic, potential, heat, light, sound, chemical), and every entry is a daily-life example with its one-line TEST beneath — because an example without its test is a picture, not physics. THE SOURCES CHART climbs the trunk built at 006: the Sun at the crown (light grew the plants that became food, firewood, coal and petroleum over ages; sun-heated air became the wind; sun-lifted vapour became the rain in the tanks), with the honest exceptions boxed separately (the Earth's own deep warmth; the vast nuclear store inside the Sun itself) — so the chart teaches the arc without pretending it has no edges. THE CONVERSIONS CHART lays the arrows of 007 with the DEVICE named at every arrowhead — dynamo, burner, bulb, microphone, speaker, solar cell, motor, windmill — each arrow doubly tested and each device's heat line signed, because a bare arrow hides the very machinery the chapter demonstrated. THE CONSERVATION CHART assembles the law's exhibits — the roller coaster's shrinking hills, the simple pendulum's timed see-saw (with its measured time period in the box), the falling coconut's exact ledger — and states the law in its two lines where every reader must pass. A chart earns wall space only if it passes the maker's audit: no entry without a test, no arrow without a device, no number without its working, no claim without the law behind it. What this node does NOT do: it does not re-teach any form, device or law (005–010 all assumed, name-only); it organises them — and the making, auditing and defending of the charts IS the new learning.

The audit rule follows: any entry whose test cannot be written in one line does not belong on the chart — it is not yet understood, and the wall must not lie. Supporting argument 2 — the conversions chart is drawn in…

cards.title: Energy interconversion is the process by which energy transforms from one form…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy interconversion is the process by which energy transforms from one form to another while the total energy in a closed system remains constant, as stated by the law of conservation of energy. Common forms include gravitational potential, kinetic, chemical, electrical, thermal, sound, and nuclear energy. A video demonstrating interconversion captures a dynamic sequence — for example, water stored at height (gravitational potential) falls, gaining kinetic energy, spins a turbine (mechanical), drives a generator (electrical), and finally lights a bulb (light and thermal). Such visualisations make abstract concepts concrete by showing real‑time transitions, allowing learners to identify each form, trace the conversion pathway, and verify that no energy is created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed. The video medium also reveals rates of conversion and the role of non‑conservative forces like friction, which appear as heat or sound, reinforcing the principle that apparent “losses” are actually conversions to less useful forms. This node builds on static charts of energy forms and prepares students for quantitative energy accounting in higher classes.
steps: Videos turn invisible energy swaps into a visible story, making the abstract law of conservation tangible for Class 7 learners.
Here is why: first, a video shows the sequence of conversions in real time — water falling, turbine spinning, bulb glowing — so students see the order of forms rather than memorising a list.

Second, it reveals rate and continuity; a pendulum video displays the smooth back‑and‑forth exchange between potential and kinetic energy, highlighting that the total stays constant if friction is small.

Third, it exposes dissipative effects: a roller‑coaster clip shows the car never quite reaching the initial height because some mechanical energy becomes heat and sound, teaching that “loss” is really transformation.
Fourth, videos allow pause‑and‑analyse moments — teachers can freeze a frame, ask “What energy forms exist right now?” and have students sketch a conversion arrow diagram.
Fifth, Indian contexts like a hydroelectric plant at Bhakra Nangal or a solar cooker in a village kitchen connect the physics to familiar surroundings, reinforcing relevance.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to entertain students”) reveals the misconception that educational videos are merely for engagement rather than for conceptual clarification.

cards.title: The normal is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular (at 90°) to the reflecting…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The normal is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular (at 90°) to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence. It serves as the reference line for measuring the angle of incidence (∠i) and the angle of reflection (∠r). The point of incidence is the exact point where the incident ray strikes the reflecting surface. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane. The normal divides the angle between the incident and reflected rays into two equal parts when the laws of reflection are obeyed. For a plane mirror, the normal is perpendicular to the plane of the mirror. For curved mirrors (concave/convex), the normal at any point passes through the centre of curvature of the mirror. The concept of the normal is essential for stating the laws of reflection precisely: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r), both measured with respect to the normal.
steps: The normal is the invisible reference line that makes the laws of reflection measurable and universal.
Here is why: without a fixed reference, "angle of incidence" would be ambiguous — measured from the surface, from the vertical, or from the horizontal?
The normal solves this by being uniquely defined at every point on any surface, flat or curved.
Consider a plane mirror placed vertically on a table.
Shine a torch at an angle.
The light ray hits the mirror at a specific point — the point of incidence.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "45°" or "0°") reveals the misconception that the normal is merely a line drawn at the point of incidence without the perpendicular constraint, confusing it with the surface itself or an arbitrary reference.

cards.title: A plane is a perfectly flat, two-dimensional surface such that a straight line…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A plane is a perfectly flat, two-dimensional surface such that a straight line joining any two points on it lies entirely on the surface. In the study of reflection of light, the plane is the geometry of the reflecting surface: a plane mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface is a plane. Because every point on a plane is oriented in exactly the same direction, the perpendicular (the normal) drawn at any point of a plane surface is parallel to the normal drawn at any other point. This single property is what makes reflection from a plane mirror so regular: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection at every point of the surface, by the same rule. Real surfaces are never perfectly plane — a sheet of paper, a wall, or even good glass has microscopic bumps — but polished glass with a silvered backing (a plane mirror), the undisturbed surface of still water, and a well-polished metal sheet come close enough that regular reflection happens and clear images form. A rough surface, even if made of the same material, has normals pointing in many random directions, so it produces diffuse (irregular) reflection instead of an image. The plane is therefore the reference surface against which curved mirrors (spherical mirrors) are later compared: a spherical mirror is a small part of a sphere's surface, while a plane mirror is a small part of an infinitely large flat surface.
steps: A plane surface is the only surface whose shape gives exactly the same reflection rule at every point, and that is why plane mirrors form clear images.
Here is the logic: reflection is governed by the normal at the point where light strikes.

On a flat (plane) surface, the direction "straight out of the surface" is identical everywhere — every normal points the same way. So if light strikes point A or point B or point C of a plane mirror at the same angle…
This regularity is called regular reflection, and it is what lets a plane mirror produce a sharp image of your face.
Now contrast this with a rough surface like the plastered wall of your house or an unpainted cement sheet.
Microscopically, the wall is a landscape of tiny hills and valleys.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a plane is any smooth or shiny surface") reveals the misconception that plane describes smoothness or polish of a material, when it actually describes the flatness (geometry) of the surface; a surface can be plane without being shiny…
remember: What is a plane surface.
Why does a plane mirror produce regular reflection while a wall usually does not, even though both obey the same law of reflection.
Evaluate this statement: "A plane mirror is called plane because it is made of a flat piece of glass, not because of its reflecting coating.".

cards.title: The point of incidence is the precise location on a reflecting surface where an…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The point of incidence is the precise location on a reflecting surface where an incident ray of light strikes. It is a geometric point — having no size — that lies on the plane of the mirror or any reflecting surface. In a ray diagram, the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface at that point) all intersect at the point of incidence. This point serves as the reference for defining the angle of incidence (between the incident ray and the normal) and the angle of reflection (between the reflected ray and the normal). Because the reflecting surface is a plane (as introduced in the previous node), the point of incidence can be located using coordinates or measured distances along the surface. It is distinct from the point of reflection, which is the same physical point but emphasises the ray after reflection. Understanding the point of incidence is essential before stating the laws of reflection, which require the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal to be coplanar and the two angles to be equal.
steps: The point of incidence is the single spot where an incoming light ray meets a mirror, and it is the anchor for every reflection diagram.
Here is why: without a fixed meeting point we cannot draw the normal, measure angles, or apply the laws of reflection.

First, recall that a plane mirror is a flat, smooth surface — like the steel plate used in a school science lab. When a ray from a torch hits that plate, the exact spot of contact is the point of incidence.
Second, imagine drawing a line perpendicular to the plate at that spot; that line is the normal.
The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray all cross at the same point, forming a neat “Y” shape.
Third, if you place a protractor at that point, you can measure the angle between the incident ray and the normal — that will later be called the angle of incidence.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the point where the reflected ray leaves the mirror”) reveals the misconception that the point of incidence is associated only with the outgoing ray, ignoring the incoming ray and the normal.
remember: What is the point of incidence in a ray diagram.
Why must the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all intersect at the same point.
A student draws a ray diagram where the normal is drawn at a point 2 cm away from where the incident ray touches the mirror. Evaluate this diagram.

cards.title: The angle of incidence is the angle formed between the incident ray and the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The angle of incidence is the angle formed between the incident ray and the normal drawn at the point of incidence on a reflecting surface. The incident ray is the ray of light that approaches the surface. The point of incidence is the exact point where the incident ray meets the surface. The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence. By convention, the angle of incidence (denoted by i) is measured from the normal to the incident ray, not from the surface. Its SI unit is the degree (°) or radian (rad), though degrees are used in school-level ray diagrams. This concept builds directly on the earlier nodes: the reflecting plane, the normal, and the point of incidence. Understanding the angle of incidence is essential because the law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and it also governs how images form in plane mirrors. In ray diagrams, the angle of incidence is always shown as the acute angle between the incident ray and the normal, measured inside the medium from which the light comes.
steps: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal drawn at the point of incidence on a reflecting surface.
Here is why: the normal provides a fixed reference that is independent of the surface orientation, making the measurement consistent for any plane or curved surface.
The incident ray is the path of light before it strikes the surface.
The point of incidence anchors both the ray and the normal.
By measuring from the normal, we ensure that the angle of incidence directly relates to the angle of reflection, which is measured on the other side of the same normal.
Consider a ray of sunlight hitting a flat mirror on a verandah in Delhi at noon.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "angle between incident ray and the mirror surface") reveals the misconception that the surface itself is the reference line, confusing the angle of incidence with the glancing angle.
remember: Define angle of incidence and state its SI unit.
A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence.
A student claims that the angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the reflecting surface. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The angle of reflection (θᵣ) is the acute angle measured between the reflected…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The angle of reflection (θᵣ) is the acute angle measured between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence on a reflecting surface. It is defined only after the normal — a line perpendicular to the plane of the mirror at the point where the incident ray strikes — has been drawn. The angle of incidence (θᵢ) is the acute angle between the incident ray and the same normal. According to the first law of reflection, θᵣ = θᵢ for any plane reflecting surface. Both angles are measured in degrees (°) or radians (rad) and lie in the same plane as the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal. This relationship holds for all wavelengths of light and for any smooth (specular) surface such as a plane mirror, still water, or polished metal. The concept links directly to the earlier nodes: the reflection normal, the plane of the mirror, the point of incidence, and the angle of incidence. Together they form the basis for the Laws of Reflection and for understanding image formation in plane mirrors.
steps: The angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence when light reflects off a plane surface.
Here is why: the law of reflection is a fundamental rule of nature that applies to every smooth surface, from a bathroom mirror to a calm pond.
First, the normal is an imaginary line drawn at 90° to the mirror exactly where the light ray hits — this point is the point of incidence.
Second, the incident ray approaches the mirror and makes an angle with the normal; that angle is the angle of incidence.
Third, the reflected ray leaves the mirror on the opposite side of the normal, making its own angle with the normal — that is the angle of reflection.
Fourth, careful experiments (and countless everyday observations like using a periscope or seeing your face in a mirror) show that these two angles are exactly equal.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror surface”) reveals the misconception that angles are measured from the surface instead of the normal — confusing the reference line.
remember: What is the angle of reflection.
If the angle of incidence is 40°, what is the angle of reflection? Explain your reasoning.
A student draws a ray diagram where the angle of reflection is 50° while the angle of incidence is 30°. Is this diagram correct? Why or why not.

cards.title: The laws of reflection are the two universal rules that describe how light…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The laws of reflection are the two universal rules that describe how light changes direction when it strikes any reflecting surface. First law: the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r), where both angles are measured between the respective ray and the normal at the point of incidence. Second law: the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. This plane is called the plane of incidence; if you hold a sheet of paper so it contains the incident ray and the normal, the reflected ray will always be found on that same sheet. Three precise conditions attach to these laws. The angles are measured from the normal, never from the surface. The two rays lie on opposite sides of the normal. And the laws hold at every point of every reflecting surface — plane or curved, smooth or rough — it is only the organisation of the many reflected rays (image-forming versus scattered) that depends on the surface quality. The second law has a practical consequence used in laboratories: if the mirror or the paper holding the incident ray is rotated, the reflected ray disappears from view unless the receiving plane also contains the normal — an elegant demonstration that all three lines are coplanar. The laws are empirical: they are verified by experiment (pins and mirror strip, or laser and protractor board), and they have no known exception for ordinary reflection of light. They are also reversible — light travelling along the reflected path reflects again along the original incident path — which is why two people can always see each other's eyes in a plane mirror.
steps: The two laws of reflection — equal angles from the normal, and coplanarity of incident ray, reflected ray and normal — are the complete rulebook that predicts the outgoing direction of every reflected ray in the world.

Here is why stating them formally matters: up to now each piece existed separately (normal, point of incidence, ∠i, ∠r); the laws bind them into one testable claim that works for every surface from a bathroom mirror to…
The first law says: measure ∠i from the normal, measure ∠r from the normal, and the two numbers come out equal — always.

The second law says: all three lines fit in one flat sheet — if the incident ray comes in tilted out of your paper, the reflected ray tilts out too, staying in the sheet that holds the ray and the normal together.

Verify it yourself the CISCE way: fix a white sheet on a board, stand a mirror strip on a drawn line, and erect the normal ON at the mid-point O. Draw an incident ray at 40° to ON and stand two pins on it. Look from the…

Repeat at 25°, 55°, 65° — every trial returns ∠r = ∠i, and every pin-alignment works only while your eye stays on the paper (the plane of incidence); lift your eye off the sheet and the images no longer line up — the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the surface, and the two rays stay parallel to each other") reveals two misconceptions at once: using the surface instead of the normal as the angle reference, and…
remember: State the two laws of reflection.
A ray is incident on a plane mirror with ∠i =….
Evaluate this statement: "The laws of reflection are valid only for plane mirrors; on rough walls, reflection does not obey them.".

cards.title: A plane mirror forms a virtual image because reflected rays diverge…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A plane mirror forms a virtual image because reflected rays diverge; their extensions behind the mirror meet at a point where the image appears. The image is erect (upright), same size as the object (linear magnification = 1), and laterally inverted (left–right reversed). The image distance v (measured behind the mirror) equals the object distance u (measured in front) in magnitude: |v| = |u|. Using the sign convention (real is positive), for a plane mirror v = −u and magnification m = −v/u = 1. The image cannot be projected on a screen because no actual light energy converges at the image location. These characteristics follow directly from the laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applied to each point on the object.
steps: A plane mirror always produces a virtual, erect, same‑size, laterally inverted image located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Here is why: when light from an object point strikes the mirror, it obeys the law of reflection — the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

If we draw two rays from the top of a pencil placed 10 cm in front of a mirror — one ray hitting the mirror perpendicularly (so it returns on itself) and another striking at an angle — the reflected rays diverge.
Extending these reflected rays backward behind the mirror makes them intersect at a point 10 cm behind the surface.
That intersection is the virtual image of the pencil tip. Because every point on the object behaves the same way, the whole image is upright and the same height as the object.

The left‑right reversal occurs because the mirror swaps the front‑back axis; your right hand’s light reaches the mirror from the right side and reflects to your eye from the left side, so the image appears to raise its…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “real because we can see it”) reveals the misconception that visibility implies a real image — confusing perception with the physical convergence of light rays.
remember: What type of image is formed by a plane mirror — real or virtual.
If an object is placed 12 cm in front of a plane mirror, what is the image distance v (using the sign convention where distances measured against incident light are negative).
A student draws a ray diagram for a plane mirror but shows the reflected rays converging in front of the mirror. Evaluate the diagram.

cards.title: The speed of light is the rate at which light travels…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The speed of light is the rate at which light travels, and in vacuum (empty space) it is a universal constant: c = 3 × 10^8 metres per second (approximately 300,000 km per second). This is the highest speed at which any signal or object can travel — nothing known outruns light. Light slows down when it enters a transparent material: in water it travels at about 2.25 × 10^8 m/s, and in ordinary glass at about 2 × 10^8 m/s, which is why a stick half-dipped in water appears bent at the surface (the light from the underwater part changes speed and direction). In air, light travels almost as fast as in vacuum (very slightly slower), so for school calculations the speed in air is taken as 3 × 10^8 m/s. Because the speed is so enormous, astronomers use a distance unit built from it: the light-year — the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10^15 metres (nearly 9.5 lakh crore kilometres). When we say a star is 4 light-years away, we mean its light took 4 years to reach us, so we see the star as it was 4 years ago — looking into the night sky is looking into the past. The basic relation used for all light-travel calculations is speed = distance ÷ time, rearranged as distance = speed × time. Typical results worth remembering: sunlight covers the Sun-to-Earth distance (about 150 million km) in about 500 seconds (8 minutes 20 seconds); moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us; and lightning's flash reaches you almost instantly while its thunder, carried by much slower sound, lags behind — the flash arrives at roughly three lakh kilometres in one second of travel.
steps: Light travels at 3 × 10^8 m/s in vacuum — the fastest speed in nature — and every "instant" thing you see still took measurable time to reach your eye. Here is how to make that number concrete: light covers about 7.5…
Yet the distances of space dwarf even this speed.
The Sun stands about 150 million km away; light crossing that gulf takes 150,000,000 km ÷ 300,000 km/s = 500 seconds — 8 minutes 20 seconds.
The sunrise or sunset you admire is therefore an 8-minute-old message; if the Sun somehow switched off now, we would enjoy eight more minutes of daylight before knowing.

The Moon, at about 3,84,000 km, sends its light in about 1.3 seconds — close enough that the delay is imperceptible, but real enough that laser beams bounced off the Moon's reflectors take about 2.6 seconds for the…
The calculation tool is the plain speed formula rearranged: time = distance ÷ speed for travel times, distance = speed × time for how far light gets.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "light travels faster in glass because glass is transparent and smooth") reveals the misconception that transparency and smoothness speed light up; transparency lets light through, but the material's density always slows it below its…
remember: State the speed of light in vacuum. How does the speed change when light enters glass.
The Sun is about 150 million km from the Earth. Calculate the time taken by sunlight to reach the Earth.
Evaluate this statement: "Since light is so fast, we always see everything exactly as it is at this very moment.".

cards.title: Primary colours of light are the three additive colours — red (R), green (G)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Primary colours of light are the three additive colours — red (R), green (G), and blue (B) — that cannot be produced by mixing other colours of light. When combined in pairs they form the secondary colours of light: red + green = yellow, green + blue = cyan, blue + red = magenta. When all three are superimposed with equal intensity they produce white light. This additive mixing follows the principle that the human eye contains three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to one of these wavelength bands (≈ 620–750 nm for red, 495–570 nm for green, 450–495 nm for blue). The RGB model is the basis of electronic displays (televisions, monitors, smartphones) where each pixel consists of three sub‑pixels emitting red, green, and blue light at variable intensities. By varying the intensity of each sub‑pixel from zero to maximum, the display can reproduce a large gamut of colours. The concept of primary colours of light is distinct from the subtractive primary colours (cyan, magenta, yellow) used in pigments and printing, where mixing removes wavelengths rather than adding them.
steps: The one thing to remember: Red, green, and blue light are the additive primary colours; mixing them in pairs gives yellow, cyan, magenta, and mixing all three gives white.
Here is why: 1.
Human eyes have three cone types, each tuned to a different wavelength band; stimulating two cone types simultaneously creates the perception of a secondary colour. 2.
Light adds energy — when two beams overlap, their intensities add, so the eye receives both wavelength ranges at once. 3.
Electronic screens exploit this by placing tiny red, green, and blue sub‑pixels side by side; the brain blends them into a single colour. 4.
A simple classroom demonstration uses three torches covered with red, green, and blue cellophane; overlapping the beams on a white sheet shows the secondary colours and white. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “red, yellow, blue”) reveals the misconception that the primary colours of pigments (subtractive mixing) apply to light as well.
remember: Name the three additive primary colours of light.
Why does mixing red light and green light produce the sensation of yellow.
A student claims that because mixing red and blue paint gives magenta, mixing red and blue light must also give magenta. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Additive colour mixing combines beams of coloured light.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Additive colour mixing combines beams of coloured light. The three primary colours of light are red (≈650 nm), green (≈530 nm), and blue (≈460 nm). When two primary beams overlap on a white surface, the eye perceives a secondary colour: red + green → yellow, green + blue → cyan, blue + red → magenta. These secondary colours are not present in the spectrum as single wavelengths; they are physiological sensations created by stimulating two types of cone cells simultaneously. Overlapping all three primaries at full intensity stimulates all three cone types equally, producing the sensation of white. The process is governed by the principle of superposition: the resultant spectral power distribution is the sum of the individual distributions. This differs from subtractive mixing (pigments), where each pigment absorbs certain wavelengths. Additive mixing is the basis of electronic displays (televisions, smartphones) where tiny red, green, and blue sub‑pixels vary in intensity to create a full colour gamut. Understanding additive mixing also explains why a yellow object appears yellow under white light — it reflects red and green wavelengths while absorbing blue.
steps: The key takeaway is that secondary colours — yellow, cyan, and magenta — appear when two of the three primary coloured lights (red, green, blue) overlap, because the eye’s three cone types are stimulated in pairs.
Here is why: first, each primary colour targets a specific cone type (L, M, S).
Second, when two primaries combine, two cone types fire together, creating a new colour sensation that is not a single wavelength.
Third, the brain interprets this combined signal as a distinct hue — yellow for red+green, cyan for green+blue, magenta for blue+red.
Fourth, adding the third primary stimulates all three cones equally, which the brain reads as white.
Consider a dark room with three torches covered in red, green, and blue cellophane.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “orange, purple, and light blue”) reveals the misconception that secondary colours of light are the same as pigment mixing — confusing additive with subtractive processes.
remember: What are the three secondary colours produced by additive mixing of red, green, and blue light.
If a green light and a blue light overlap on a white screen, what colour will be seen? Explain why.
A student says that mixing red and blue light gives purple, which is the same as violet. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The colour of an object is determined by the light it reflects (or transmits)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The colour of an object is determined by the light it reflects (or transmits) into the observer's eye, compared with the light falling on it. White light is a mixture of colours; when it falls on an object, the object's surface absorbs some components and reflects others, and the reflected mixture is what the observer perceives as the object's colour. A red rose appears red in sunlight because its petals reflect mainly red light and absorb the other components (green, blue and the rest). A leaf appears green because chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the red and blue regions and reflects green. A white object reflects all components of white light equally, so it appears white in white light; a black object absorbs essentially all components, reflecting almost nothing, so it appears black. Opaque objects show their colour by reflection; transparent objects show their colour by transmission — a red sheet of glass transmits mainly red light and absorbs the rest, so the world seen through it looks red. The rule that ties this to the lighting: an object can only reflect colours that are present in the incident light. A red rose in pure green light reflects nothing (green is absorbed) and therefore appears black — colour is a partnership between the object's absorption properties and the light shone on it. This principle explains why cloth colours look different under yellowish street lamps than in daylight, why shopkeepers prefer daylight-style lamps in clothing sections, and why the sodium-lit road makes red cars look dull brown at night. It also connects to colour addition and subtraction: the object subtracts components from white light by absorption, and the surviving components add in the eye to give the perceived colour.
steps: An object has no colour of its own — it has absorption rules, and its colour appears only when light cooperates: the object shows the components of the incident light that it fails to absorb.

Here is the full causal chain: white light (all colours mixed) strikes the object; the surface's material absorbs some components and reflects the rest; the reflected bundle reaches your eye; the three cone types…

Take the mango: sunlight carries the full rainbow; mango skin absorbs blue and much green, reflecting red and yellow components strongly — your eye receives a red-plus-yellow mix and reports "yellow-orange mango".
The leaf beside it runs the opposite portfolio: chlorophyll needs red and blue for photosynthesis, absorbs them, and discards green by reflection — hence green leaves.
White chalk reflects all components about equally — white.
A blackboard's surface absorbs nearly everything — black.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the rose is painted red by the red part of sunlight falling on it" or "the rose makes its own red light") reveals the misconception that colour is added to the object from outside or generated by it, rather than being the survival of…
remember: Why does a rose appear red in sunlight.
A green cap is viewed first in white light, then under pure red light. State its apparent colour in each case and explain the difference.
Evaluate this statement: "Black objects are those which emit black light; white objects emit white light.".

cards.title: Colour subtraction is the formation of colours by removing (absorbing) some…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Colour subtraction is the formation of colours by removing (absorbing) some components of white light and transmitting or reflecting the remainder. It is the working principle of pigments, paints, inks, dyes and colour filters. A filter or pigment does not emit or add anything: it selectively absorbs part of the incident white light, and the colour we see is whatever survives. The subtractive primaries are cyan, magenta and yellow (CMY) — chosen because each absorbs exactly one of the additive primaries: cyan absorbs red (reflects/transmits green + blue), magenta absorbs green (reflects/transmits blue + red), and yellow absorbs blue (reflects/transmits red + green). Mixing subtractive primaries stacks their absorptions: cyan + yellow = green (red is absorbed by cyan, blue by yellow, only green survives); magenta + cyan = blue (green absorbed by magenta, red by cyan, blue survives); magenta + yellow = red (green absorbed by magenta, blue by yellow, red survives); and all three together absorb everything, giving black. Every additional pigment can only remove more light, which is why mixing many paints gives a dark, muddy black and never white — the exact opposite of colour addition, where overlapped lights brighten toward white. Complementary pairs reappear with the same sum-to-white logic viewed in reverse: a filter and its complementary filter together stop all light (e.g., a yellow filter stacked on a blue filter passes nothing, since yellow removes blue and blue removes red + green). Colour subtraction runs the entire printed world: book illustrations, currency notes, hoardings and T-shirt prints are built from CMY (plus black) ink layers, each layer subtracting its share of the white paper's reflected light.
steps: Colour subtraction is the physics of everything you read: every printed colour is white light minus whatever the inks removed.

Here is the mechanism: white paper reflects all of the white light falling on it; lay a yellow ink dot on it and the dot absorbs the blue component, returning red + green — the eye adds them and reads "yellow".
This is why a banana looks yellow in sunlight: its skin subtracts blue and returns the rest — paint and fruit obey one rule.

The three master removers are cyan (absorbs red), magenta (absorbs green) and yellow (absorbs blue); each is the complement of one additive primary, built to delete exactly one. Stack or mix them and the deletions pile…
Magenta over cyan — magenta deletes green, cyan deletes red, and blue survives.
Magenta over yellow — green and blue are deleted, red survives.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the subtractive primaries are red, green and blue") reveals the misconception of reusing the additive primaries for pigments; RGB are emitters' primaries — for absorbers (inks, filters), CMY do the deleting.
remember: Name the three subtractive primaries and state the additive primary colour each one absorbs.
A white torch beam passes through a yellow filter and then through a magenta filter. What colour emerges? Show the surviving components.
Evaluate this statement: "A green shirt and a green filter produce green in the same way, so there is no real difference between seeing and filtering.".

cards.title: This concept node focuses on designing and conducting simple classroom…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: This concept node focuses on designing and conducting simple classroom activities that let students observe and verify the laws of reflection using plane mirrors, laser beams, and everyday materials. The activities explicitly demonstrate the normal (a line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence), the plane of incidence, the angle of incidence (between the incident ray and the normal), and the angle of reflection (between the reflected ray and the normal). By measuring these angles with a protractor, students confirm the first law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and the second law (incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane). The same set‑up also reveals the characteristics of a plane‑mirror image: virtual, upright, laterally inverted, and same size as the object. These hands‑on experiences connect directly to the earlier nodes on reflection terminology (‑006) and prepare learners for the next node where they translate observations into ray diagrams. No advanced optics such as spherical mirrors, mirror formula, or colour‑mixing theory are introduced here; those belong to later chapters.
steps: The key idea is that simple hands‑on activities let students see for themselves that light follows the law of reflection, making the abstract rule concrete.
First, a plane mirror provides a perfectly flat reflecting surface, so every point on it behaves like the “plane” defined in node 002.
When a narrow laser beam (representing a single ray) strikes the mirror, the spot where it hits is the point of incidence (node 003).
Drawing a line perpendicular to the mirror at that point gives the normal (node 001).
The angle between the incoming beam and the normal is the angle of incidence (node 004); the angle between the outgoing beam and the same normal is the angle of reflection (node 005).
Second, by placing a sheet of paper behind the mirror and marking the incident and reflected beams with a pencil, students create a permanent record.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “convex lens and prism”) reveals the misconception that reflection requires refracting elements, confusing reflection with refraction.
remember: Name two common classroom materials that can be used to demonstrate the law of reflection.
Why must the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane during the activity.
A student uses a curved spoon as a mirror and claims the law of reflection still holds for each point. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A reflection ray diagram is the standard drawing that records reflection at a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A reflection ray diagram is the standard drawing that records reflection at a mirror: the reflecting surface (a straight line for a plane mirror, with short hatching on the non-reflecting side), the incident ray (a straight line with an arrowhead pointing at the mirror), the point of incidence (marked O where the incident ray meets the surface), the normal (a dashed line through O at exactly 90° to the surface, labelled N), and the reflected ray (a line with an arrowhead pointing away from O, on the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray). The two angles — ∠i between incident ray and normal, ∠r between normal and reflected ray — are marked with small arcs at O and must be equal in measure for a plane mirror. Correct drawing is a sequence of construction steps, not freehand art: (1) draw the surface line and hatch it; (2) mark the point of incidence O; (3) erect the normal with a set square (exactly perpendicular); (4) draw the incident ray at the chosen angle using a protractor centred on O with its baseline along the normal; (5) copy the same angle to the other side of the normal and draw the reflected ray; (6) add arrowheads on both rays showing the direction of travel; (7) label every element (O, N, ∠i, ∠r). The hatching convention tells the reader which side reflects; arrowheads tell the direction of light; dashes distinguish the imaginary normal from real rays. These conventions are the shared language of CISCE diagrams: an unlabelled or convention-breaking diagram loses marks even when the geometry is right, because the diagram must communicate, not merely illustrate.
steps: A correct reflection diagram is built in seven fixed steps, and the order itself prevents the classic errors.

Step 1: draw the mirror as a clean straight line — say 8 cm — and hatch short strokes along its lower side; the hatching declares "reflection happens from the smooth upper side" and instantly disqualifies any ray drawn…
Step 2: mark the point of incidence O anywhere on the line — anywhere is legal, because every point of a plane mirror is equivalent.

Step 3: stand the normal ON at O with a set square, dashed, reaching well above the line; a dashed normal is the universal sign of an imaginary reference, and its exact 90° is the single most important geometric fact of…

Step 5: swing to the other side of the normal, mark the same 40°, and draw the reflected ray from O outward; the equality is now built in by construction, which is why a diagram drawn this way can never violate the…
Self-check any diagram — yours or a textbook's — with the four-tick audit: normal perpendicular? angles equal? rays on opposite sides of the normal? arrowheads correct?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting the normal or the arrowheads as "optional decorations") reveals the misconception that diagrams need only the two rays; the normal is the reference that defines both angles, and the arrowheads carry the physics of travel…
remember: List the five elements that must appear in every plane-mirror reflection ray diagram.
Why is the normal drawn dashed while the incident and reflected rays are drawn solid.
Evaluate this diagram description: "The mirror is drawn as a thick….

cards.title: A plane mirror is a reflecting surface that is perfectly flat and polished…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A plane mirror is a reflecting surface that is perfectly flat and polished, usually made by coating one side of a glass sheet with a thin layer of silver or aluminium. When light from an object strikes the mirror, each ray obeys the laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. Because the surface is planar, the reflected rays appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror. The image formed is virtual (cannot be projected on a screen), erect (same orientation as the object), laterally inverted (left‑right reversed), same size as the object, and located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. The distance of the image from the mirror (image distance, d_i) equals the distance of the object from the mirror (object distance, d_o). Magnification is unity (m = 1). These characteristics hold for any object placed in front of a plane mirror, regardless of its shape or colour. The plane mirror does not alter the speed or wavelength of light; it only changes the direction of propagation. In everyday life, plane mirrors are used in bathrooms, dressing rooms, periscopes, and as rear‑view mirrors in vehicles. The concept of a plane mirror builds directly on the earlier nodes covering the normal, point of incidence, angles of incidence and reflection, and the laws of reflection, and it sets the stage for studying curved reflecting surfaces.
steps: A plane mirror always produces a virtual, erect, laterally inverted image that is the same size as the object and located behind the mirror at the same distance as the object is in front.
Here is why: when light rays from an object strike a flat, polished surface, each ray reflects such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Because the surface is planar, the reflected rays do not actually converge; they only appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror.
Our brain interprets these diverging rays as coming from an image located behind the mirror.
Consider a candle placed 20 cm in front of a plane mirror.
Draw a ray from the top of the candle flame perpendicular to the mirror; it reflects back along the same path.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the image is real and inverted”) reveals the misconception that a mirror works like a lens, confusing reflection with refraction and thinking the image forms on the mirror surface.
remember: What are the five characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror.
An object is placed 30 cm in front of a plane mirror. Where is the image formed and what is its size relative to the object.
A student claims that the image in a plane mirror is real because it can be seen on a screen placed behind the mirror. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A reflecting surface is any boundary that turns back incident light into the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A reflecting surface is any boundary that turns back incident light into the same medium. It obeys the laws of reflection: the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal at the point of incidence lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Reflecting surfaces are classified by their microscopic smoothness. A regular (specular) reflecting surface — such as a plane mirror, polished metal, or still water — has irregularities much smaller than the wavelength of light, so parallel incident rays remain parallel after reflection, producing clear images. A diffuse reflecting surface — such as paper, unpolished wood, or a white wall — has irregularities comparable to or larger than the wavelength, causing incident rays to scatter in many directions; no distinct image forms, but the surface becomes visible. Curved reflecting surfaces (concave and convex) are also regular reflectors but change the convergence or divergence of reflected rays; their detailed image formation is treated later. The nature of the reflecting surface determines whether we see a sharp image (specular) or just illuminated surroundings (diffuse). Colour appearance of objects depends on which wavelengths a surface reflects and which it absorbs, linking reflecting surfaces to colour subtraction and addition concepts.
steps: A reflecting surface is any surface that sends light back into the same medium, and its smoothness decides whether we see a clear image or just a bright surface.
Here is why: first, the laws of reflection hold at every point on any reflecting surface, whether it is a mirror or a mud wall.

Second, if the surface is smooth at the scale of light’s wavelength (about 500 nanometres), parallel rays stay parallel after reflection — this is specular reflection, giving sharp images like in a plane mirror or a…

Third, if the surface has bumps and pits larger than the wavelength, each tiny facet still follows the laws, but the normals point in random directions, so the reflected rays scatter — this is diffuse reflection, which…

Fourth, curved regular reflectors (like the shiny back of a stainless steel spoon) also obey the laws, but their normals vary smoothly, causing rays to converge or diverge; that behaviour is studied later.
Fifth, the colour we see depends on which wavelengths the surface reflects; a red rose reflects red and absorbs other colours, a concept linked to colour subtraction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing a mirror as diffuse) reveals the misconception that any shiny object is diffuse — confusing shininess with surface smoothness at the wavelength scale.
remember: Name two examples of regular reflecting surfaces and two examples of diffuse reflecting surfaces commonly found in an Indian household.
A ray of light strikes a smooth steel plate at an angle of incidence of 35° measured from the….
Evaluate the statement: "A curved mirror does not obey the laws of reflection because its surface is not flat.".

cards.title: Heat is a form of energy transferred between systems or objects due to a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat is a form of energy transferred between systems or objects due to a temperature difference. In the International System of Units (SI) the unit of heat energy is the joule (symbol J), defined as the work done when a force of one newton displaces an object by one metre (1 J = 1 N·m). A traditional, non‑SI unit still used in nutrition and some laboratory contexts is the calorie (symbol cal), defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of pure water by one degree Celsius at a pressure of one atmosphere. The exact conversion is 1 cal = 4.184 J. A larger dietary unit, the kilocalorie (kcal) or “Calorie” with a capital C, equals 1000 cal = 4184 J. Heat is not a substance; it is energy in transit. When heat enters a body, its internal energy increases, which may raise its temperature, cause a phase change, or do work (e.g., expansion). The direction of spontaneous heat flow is always from the region of higher temperature to the region of lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached.
steps: Heat is energy that moves because of a temperature difference — this is the single idea you must remember.

Here is why: (1) Energy can be stored in many forms (chemical, kinetic, potential) but heat is the only form that spontaneously travels from a hotter object to a cooler one. (2) The joule is the universal SI unit for…

(3) The calorie was invented for chemistry and nutrition; it is defined by water’s response to heat, making it convenient for laboratory and food‑label use. (4) The exact conversion 1 cal = 4.184 J lets us switch…
(5) Understanding the direction of heat flow explains everyday phenomena — why a metal spoon becomes hot in tea, why ice melts in your hand, and why a thermos keeps drinks hot or cold.
Consider a steel tiffin box filled with hot sambar placed on a wooden table.
The sambar (≈80 °C) is hotter than the table (≈25 °C).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “calorie” or “watt”) reveals the misconception that heat has a special unit different from other energy forms, confusing the historical calorie with the modern SI standard.
remember: What is the SI unit of heat energy.
Explain why heat flows from a hot object to a cold object and not the reverse.
A student says, “One calorie is exactly 4 J.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Heat is a form of energy transferred between bodies due to a temperature…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat is a form of energy transferred between bodies due to a temperature difference. In the International System of Units (SI) the unit of heat energy is the joule (symbol J), defined as the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre (1 J = 1 N·m). In the older centimetre‑gram‑second (CGS) system the unit is the calorie (symbol cal), defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of pure water by one degree Celsius at a pressure of one atmosphere. The two units are related by the conversion factor 1 cal = 4.184 J (commonly approximated as 4.2 J for classroom calculations). A larger dietary unit, the kilocalorie (kcal) or Calorie (capital C), equals 1000 cal = 4184 J. Understanding both units allows students to interpret scientific data (which uses joules) and everyday information such as food labels (which use calories). The relationship is linear, so any quantity in calories can be converted to joules by multiplying by 4.184, and vice‑versa by dividing by 4.184.
steps: The joule is the universal scientific unit for all forms of energy, including heat, while the calorie is a legacy unit still used for food energy.
Here is why: the SI system adopted the joule because it links directly to mechanical work (newton‑metre), making calculations consistent across physics.
The calorie was defined historically from water‑heating experiments, so it remained convenient for nutrition.
Consider a typical Indian snack label showing “200 kcal”.

To express this in joules, multiply 200 kcal × 1000 cal/kcal × 4.184 J/cal = 836 800 J. Conversely, a physics problem may give 5000 J of heat; dividing by 4.184 gives about 1195 cal. In class, we demonstrate the…
This reinforces that both units describe the same physical quantity — heat energy — just in different “languages”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “calorie” or “cal”) reveals the misconception that the calorie is the standard scientific unit, confusing the historical CGS unit with the modern SI system.
remember: What is the SI unit of heat energy and its symbol.
If 1 cal = 4.184 J, how many joules are equivalent to 250 cal? Show the calculation.
A student claims that “calorie is a larger unit than joule because food labels show numbers like 200 kcal while physics problems show thousands of joules.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. The three common scales are Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K). The Celsius scale sets 0 °C at the freezing point of pure water at standard atmospheric pressure and 100 °C at its boiling point. The Fahrenheit scale sets 32 °F at the freezing point of water and 212 °F at its boiling point, giving 180 equal divisions between them. The Kelvin scale is an absolute thermodynamic scale; its zero (0 K) is absolute zero, the theoretical point where particle motion ceases. The size of one kelvin equals one degree Celsius, so the conversion is a simple shift: K = °C + 273.15. The relationship between Celsius and Fahrenheit is linear: °F = (9/5) °C + 32 and °C = (5/9)(°F – 32). These formulas allow exact conversion between any two scales. Thermometers are calibrated in one or more of these scales; a dual‑scale thermometer shows both °C and °F markings.
steps: The key idea is that temperature can be expressed in different scales — Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin — and we can convert between them using fixed linear formulas.
Here is why: each scale was invented for a different purpose.
Celsius was designed around water’s phase changes, making it intuitive for everyday use and scientific work in most countries.
Fahrenheit was created earlier with a finer division (180 steps between freeze and boil) for precise weather reporting in the United States.
Kelvin was later introduced by scientists to have a true zero where molecular motion stops, which is essential for gas laws and thermodynamics.
Consider a laboratory thermometer marked in both °C and °F.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “freezing at 32 °C”) reveals the misconception that the numerical values are the same on both scales, confusing the scale labels with the actual temperature.
remember: What are the freezing and boiling points of water on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
If a thermometer reads 25 °C, what is the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit? Show the conversion steps.
A student claims that 100 °F is hotter than 100 °C. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The effects of heat are the changes heat produces in a body's size and state…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The effects of heat are the changes heat produces in a body's size and state: on heating, nearly all substances expand (increase in size); on cooling, they contract (decrease in size). Expansion happens because heat increases the vibrations of a body's particles, which push slightly farther apart on average — the particles themselves do not grow, only their spacing does. All three states of matter show the effect, but to different extents for the same temperature rise: solids expand the least (their particles are tightly bound), liquids expand more (their particles are freer), and gases expand the most (their particles are almost free), which is why a balloon left in the sun swells dramatically while a steel spoon barely changes. Expansion and contraction are reversible: cooling a heated body returns it very nearly to its original size. Everyday evidence surrounds an Indian student — the clanking tiffin carrier loosens when heated; an exactly-fitting steel lid stuck on a jar releases under hot water (the steel expands more than the glass); overhead power lines hang lowest in summer and pull tight in winter; railway tracks, bridges and concrete roads are built with deliberate gaps so the summer expansion has somewhere to go. The effect has industrial power too: a slightly smaller iron rim is heated till it slips over a cart wheel and, contracting on cooling, grips it in a vice-like "tyre fit". One distinguished exception — water behaving strangely between 0°C and 4°C — belongs to later study and is deliberately not treated here.
steps: Heating makes nearly everything expand and cooling makes it contract, because heat jiggles each body's particles so hard that their average spacing grows — size change, not particle growth.

First, fix the ordering: for the same temperature rise, solids expand least, liquids more, gases most — a steel rail lengthens by millimetres over a season while the air inside a sealed bottle swells enough to push a…

Third, the effect does useful work: the classic cartwheel fit heats an iron rim till it slips over the wheel, then cooling contraction locks it tight; a stubborn metal lid on a glass jar yields under hot tap water…

Fourth, watch the everyday traps — a sealed full water bottle left in a parked car can bulge or burst because both bottle and liquid expand; a taut wire fence sings in January and sags in May; a marble slab set…

Finally, connect the node to measurement: every such effect rides on a temperature change, so quantify it in the scales of — a bridge built at 15°C facing a 50°C Delhi summer endures a rise of 35°C, which is a rise of…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the ball gains extra particles when heated, making it bigger") reveals the misconception of expansion as addition of matter; mass stays constant, and expansion is purely a spreading of the same particles farther apart.
remember: What happens to the size of a solid metal ball when it is heated, and what explanation does the particle picture give.
For the same rise in temperature, arrange solids, liquids and gases by how much they expand, and justify the order using the freedom of their particles.
Evaluate this statement: "Railway engineers leave gaps between rail segments because trains lose speed at the joints.".

cards.title: Heat transfer is the passage of heat energy from a body at higher temperature…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat transfer is the passage of heat energy from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature, and it occurs by three distinct methods. Conduction is transfer through a substance without any movement of the substance itself: the hot end's vigorously vibrating particles pass energy to their neighbours along the chain, which is how a steel karchi's handle warms while its bowl sits in dal; solids — especially metals — conduct best, gases worst, which is why handles are wood or plastic and why still air is an excellent insulator. Convection is transfer by the bulk movement of the heated fluid itself: warmed liquid or gas expands, becomes less dense, rises, and cooler fluid sinks to take its place, setting up a convection current — the rolling boil in a pot, the sea breeze by day and land breeze by night, the circulation that warms a whole room from one heater. Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves needing no medium at all: it works across a vacuum, which is how the sun's heat crosses 150 million kilometres of empty space to reach the earth, and how an open flame toasts your face across cool air; dull black surfaces absorb and emit radiation best, shining polished surfaces least — the reason winter clothes are dark and fuel storage tanks are painted white or silver. Every heat event in daily life mixes the three: a cup of chai loses heat by conduction through its wall, convection in the air above it, and radiation from its surface. Insulation works by blocking all three at once — the design logic behind the thermos flask.
steps: Heat never travels without a reason or a road: the reason is a temperature difference and the road is one of exactly three methods — conduction, convection, radiation.

First, conduction: hold a steel karchi in hot dal and the handle warms though no metal flowed anywhere — each hot particle shakes its neighbour, passing energy hand to hand up the handle; metals do this brilliantly…

Third, radiation: waves that need no medium whatsoever, crossing even vacuum — the only way the sun's heat reaches earth — and travelling in straight lines that warm whatever they strike; a bonfire's face-warmth across…

The mastery habit: for every heat event, ask three questions — is something solid passing heat along (conduction), is a fluid circulating it (convection), or is it crossing space as waves (radiation)?
Most real events answer twice: chai cools by all three at once, and the thermos flask wins by beating all three together.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "conduction is when hot things flow upward") reveals the misconception of mixing conduction with convection; flow of the material itself is exactly what conduction never has and convection always has.
remember: Name the three methods of heat transfer and state the one defining feature of each.
Why is the handle of a cooking vessel made of wood or plastic although the vessel itself is metal.
Evaluate this claim: "The earth receives the sun's heat by convection, because the sun's warmth rises up to the sky.".

cards.title: A thermos flask (vacuum flask) is an insulated container designed to minimise…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A thermos flask (vacuum flask) is an insulated container designed to minimise heat transfer between its contents and the surroundings by simultaneously addressing the three modes of heat transfer: conduction, convection, and radiation. Its construction consists of a double‑walled glass or stainless‑steel vessel; the space between the walls is evacuated to create a vacuum, which eliminates the material medium required for conduction and convection. The inner surfaces of the walls are coated with a reflective metallic layer (usually silver or aluminium) that reflects infrared radiation back into the liquid, reducing radiative heat loss. A tight‑fitting stopper made of cork or plastic seals the neck, preventing convective currents from escaping or entering. The outer casing provides mechanical protection. By combining vacuum insulation, reflective surfaces, and a sealed stopper, the thermos flask achieves a very low overall heat transfer coefficient, allowing hot liquids to remain hot and cold liquids to remain cold for several hours. This application directly uses the principles of heat transfer taught in the previous concept node and demonstrates how engineering solutions exploit physics concepts.
steps: A thermos flask keeps drinks hot or cold by blocking all three heat‑transfer modes at once.

Here is why: the vacuum between the double walls removes the medium needed for conduction and convection; the shiny metallic coating reflects infrared radiation back into the liquid; the tight stopper stops air currents…
Consider a hot cup of tea poured into a thermos at 80 °C.
Without insulation, the tea would lose heat quickly through the steel walls (conduction), through the air above the liquid (convection), and by radiating infrared waves to the surroundings.
In a thermos, the inner wall touches the tea, but the vacuum gap means there are almost no molecules to conduct heat to the outer wall.
Convection cannot occur in the vacuum because there is no fluid to circulate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the vacuum reflects heat radiation”) reveals the misconception that a vacuum can reflect radiation — reflection is done by the shiny metallic coating, not by the vacuum itself.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the vacuum between the double walls of a thermos flask.
Explain why the inner surfaces of a thermos flask are silvered or coated with a reflective metal.
A student claims that a thermos flask works only because the stopper is tight. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The Fahrenheit scale (°F) is a temperature scale defined by two fixed points at…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Fahrenheit scale (°F) is a temperature scale defined by two fixed points at standard atmospheric pressure: the freezing point of pure water at 32 °F and the boiling point at 212 °F, giving 180 equal divisions between them. A thermometer marked in °F contains a liquid (usually mercury or coloured alcohol) that expands uniformly with temperature; the calibrated glass tube shows the corresponding °F value. The relationship to the Celsius scale (°C) is linear: F = (9)/(5)C + 32 and C = (5)/(9)(F - 32). Demonstrating a °F thermometer involves (1) immersing the bulb in a known reference (ice‑water mixture for 32 °F, steam for 212 °F) to verify calibration, (2) reading the meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax, and (3) converting the reading to °C when required. This node focuses on the practical use, reading technique, and conversion, not on the history of the scale or the construction of the thermometer, which are covered elsewhere.
steps: A Fahrenheit thermometer gives temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, where water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F.
Here is why: the scale was built so that the interval between these two reproducible states contains 180 equal parts, making each degree smaller than a Celsius degree.
First, place the thermometer bulb in a beaker of crushed ice and water; wait until the liquid column steadies at 32 °F — this verifies the lower fixed point.
Next, hold the bulb in steam from boiling water (100 °C) and confirm the reading reaches 212 °F.
To measure an unknown temperature, immerse the bulb, wait for equilibrium, keep the thermometer vertical, and read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Record the value, then convert if needed: subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9 to get °C; or multiply °C by 9, divide by 5, add 32 to get °F.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “0 °F and 100 °F”) reveals the misconception that Fahrenheit uses the same fixed points as Celsius, confusing the two scales.
remember: What are the two fixed points used to calibrate a Fahrenheit thermometer at standard atmospheric pressure.
A student reads a Fahrenheit thermometer as 98 °F. What is the temperature in Celsius? Show the conversion steps.
Why must the thermometer bulb be fully immersed and the reading taken at eye level.

cards.title: Measuring temperature in Fahrenheit involves using a thermometer calibrated…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Measuring temperature in Fahrenheit involves using a thermometer calibrated with the Fahrenheit scale, where the freezing point of water is 32 °F and the boiling point is 212 °F at standard atmospheric pressure. The activity requires students to (1) safely immerse a laboratory thermometer in a known volume of water, (2) allow thermal equilibrium so the mercury or alcohol column stabilises, (3) record the reading in °F, and (4) optionally convert the value to Celsius using the linear relationship F = (9)/(5)C + 32. This process reinforces the concept that temperature is a measurable physical quantity, that different scales exist, and that conversion between scales is a simple arithmetic operation. It also links to prior learning about heat as energy transfer and the use of thermometers in °C (node).
steps: Measuring water temperature in Fahrenheit is a hands‑on way to see how a different temperature scale works and to practice conversion.
Here is why: the Fahrenheit scale is still used in weather reports and some scientific contexts, so being comfortable with it broadens a student’s practical toolkit.
First, gather a clean beaker, water at room temperature, a Fahrenheit‑graduated laboratory thermometer, and a notebook.
Pour about 100 mL of water into the beaker.
Gently lower the thermometer bulb into the water without touching the sides or bottom.
Wait until the liquid column stops moving — this indicates thermal equilibrium between the thermometer and the water.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 0 °F) reveals the misconception that the Fahrenheit scale starts at zero like Celsius, confusing the two scales’ reference points.
remember: What is the freezing point of water on the Fahrenheit scale.
A student reads a thermometer at 68 °F. What is the temperature in Celsius.
Why must the thermometer bulb be fully immersed and not touch the beaker walls.

cards.title: Heat transfer is the movement of thermal energy from a region of higher…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat transfer is the movement of thermal energy from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. It occurs through three distinct modes: 1. Conduction – transfer through direct contact between particles; in solids, vibrating atoms pass kinetic energy to neighbours. The rate is given by Fourier’s law: Q = (k A Δ T)/(d), where k is thermal conductivity, A the cross‑sectional area, Δ T the temperature difference, and d the thickness. 2. Convection – transfer in fluids (liquids or gases) by bulk motion of the fluid itself. Warm fluid becomes less dense, rises, and is replaced by cooler fluid, setting up a circulation current. The rate is often expressed as Q = h A Δ T with h the convective heat‑transfer coefficient. 3. Radiation – transfer by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) that require no medium; all objects above absolute zero emit radiation. The net power radiated follows the Stefan‑Boltzmann law: Q = σ A (T^4 - T_0^4), where is emissivity, σ the Stefan‑Boltzmann constant, T the object’s absolute temperature, and T_0 the surroundings’ temperature. In this node we demonstrate each mode with hands‑on activities so students can see and feel the differences, and then identify the mode in real‑world situations such as a pressure cooker (conduction + convection), a room heater (radiation + convection), and a thermos flask (minimising all three).
steps: Heat always travels from hot to cold, and it does so through three distinct pathways — conduction, convection, and radiation — each with a characteristic “look” that we can demonstrate in class.
Here is why: 1.
Conduction needs touch.
When a metal spoon sits in hot tea, the spoon’s handle warms up because atoms at the hot end vibrate faster and pass that energy along the lattice.
We show this by heating one end of a copper rod and placing wax‑coated pins at intervals; the pins fall off sequentially as the heat front arrives. 2.
Convection needs fluid motion.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “convection because the sambar is moving”) reveals the misconception that any fluid motion automatically means convection, ignoring that the handle is solid and only conduction can operate inside it.
remember: Which mode of heat transfer is primarily responsible for the handle of a metal ladle becoming hot when the ladle is left in a pot of boiling sambar.
In a beaker of water heated from below, a drop of ink rises in a curved path. Explain why this observation demonstrates convection rather than conduction.
A student claims that a vacuum flask (thermos) keeps tea hot mainly because the vacuum stops radiation. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Conduction is the mode of heat transfer in which thermal energy passes from a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conduction is the mode of heat transfer in which thermal energy passes from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature through direct contact between particles of a material, without any bulk motion of the material. In solids, especially metals, free electrons and vibrating atoms transfer kinetic energy to neighbouring particles. The rate of heat flow by conduction is described by Fourier’s law: the heat current Q (joule per second, i.e., watt) is proportional to the cross‑sectional area A, the temperature difference Δ T across the material, and inversely proportional to the thickness L. The proportionality constant k is the thermal conductivity of the material (SI unit W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Good conductors (copper, aluminium) have high k; insulators (wood, thermocol) have low k. Conduction does not occur in vacuum because there are no particles to carry the energy. In Class 7 we focus on identifying conduction in everyday objects, comparing conductors and insulators, and using the simple relationship Q = k A Δ T / L for qualitative reasoning.
steps: Conduction moves heat through a solid by passing energy from particle to particle, like a line of students handing a baton.
Here is why: the hotter end has particles vibrating more vigorously; they knock neighbouring particles, spreading the vibration along the material.
Consider a metal rod heated at one end — the far end becomes warm even though the rod does not move.

First, the material matters: metals have free electrons that carry energy quickly, so a copper spoon heats faster than a wooden one. Second, a thicker rod (larger cross‑section) provides more parallel paths for energy…
Third, a shorter rod reduces the distance energy must travel, so heat reaches the other end sooner.
Fourth, a larger temperature difference between the ends drives a stronger flow.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “heat moves because the metal expands and carries heat”) reveals the misconception that bulk motion of the material is required, confusing conduction with convection.
remember: What is the primary mechanism by which heat travels through a solid metal rod during conduction.
Why does a copper spoon feel hotter than a wooden spoon when both are left in a pot of boiling water for the same time.
Evaluate the statement: “Increasing the length of a metal rod always decreases the rate of heat conduction through it.”.

cards.title: Convection is the transfer of thermal energy through the bulk movement of a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Convection is the transfer of thermal energy through the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas).
