This is why a liquid keeps a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container, flowing from a bucket into a glass without changing how much space it occupies. In a gas, the particles are spaced very far apart compared with their own size and move rapidly in all directions, colliding with one another and with the container walls; the forces between them are negligible at this spacing. This is why a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume — it spreads to fill every corner of whatever encloses it, like the smell of samosas reaching a whole classroom or air filling a cycle tyre. The three states therefore form a progression of particle freedom: vibrational motion only (solid), sliding motion in contact (liquid), and fast, free, random motion with large separations (gas). The same substance can exist in all three states — water as ice, liquid water and steam — with the state decided by how much energy its particles carry, the bridge to the next node.
steps: The three states of matter are one picture told three ways: the same particles, held by different strengths of grip, moving with different freedoms.
Fix the picture state by state.

In a solid — the ice cube in a lemon water glass, a chalk stick, an iron nail — particles sit shoulder to shoulder in a fixed orderly pattern, each vibrating about its own spot like students seated in an assembly row…

That locked arrangement is exactly why a solid keeps its own shape and volume, why a brick stacks, and why a solid cannot be squashed into noticeably less space — there is no empty room between its particles.

In a liquid — water, milk, mustard oil — the particles are still nearly touching, but the grip has loosened: they slide and tumble past one another while remaining in contact, like a jostling crowd at a Chennai bus…

The liquid therefore holds its volume (a litre poured from a bottle stays a litre) but abandons its own shape, taking the shape of its container and flowing under gravity; it can be compressed only negligibly because…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "solid particles move freely from place to place because solids are strong") reveals the misconception of equating a solid's mechanical hardness with particle mobility, when hardness comes precisely from particles being locked in place.
remember: Describe the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid.
Why does a liquid take the shape of its container but not its volume.
Evaluate the claim: "Gases have no particles of their own because you cannot see air, while solids are full of particles because you can see them.".

cards.title: Energy content in the three states of matter refers to the total internal…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy content in the three states of matter refers to the total internal energy stored in a substance due to the kinetic and potential energy of its constituent particles. In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions; their kinetic energy is low and the strong intermolecular forces give a high negative potential energy, resulting in the lowest total internal energy at a given temperature. In a liquid, particles can slide past one another; kinetic energy is higher and intermolecular forces are weaker, so the internal energy is greater than in the solid state. In a gas, particles move freely at high speeds; kinetic energy is highest and intermolecular forces are negligible, giving the greatest internal energy. When a substance changes state, the energy supplied or removed goes into overcoming intermolecular forces (latent heat) rather than raising temperature. Thus, for the same mass and temperature, the energy content increases in the order solid < liquid < gas. This concept links particle motion (covered in the previous node) to the energy required for phase changes (next node).
steps: The energy content of matter rises steadily from solid to liquid to gas because particle motion and freedom increase.
Here is why: first, in a solid the particles are locked in a lattice, vibrating only slightly, so their kinetic energy is minimal and the strong bonds store large negative potential energy.
Second, when the solid melts, the supplied heat breaks some bonds; particles gain freedom to slide, raising both kinetic and potential energy while temperature stays constant.
Third, in the liquid state particles move more vigorously, so the internal energy is higher than in the solid.
Fourth, boiling supplies more heat to overcome the remaining intermolecular forces; particles escape as gas, gaining maximum kinetic energy and almost zero potential energy from attractions.
Fifth, a gas at the same temperature as the liquid therefore contains the most internal energy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “liquid has the lowest energy because it flows”) reveals the misconception that fluidity implies lower energy, confusing macroscopic flow with microscopic particle energy.
remember: Which state of matter has the lowest internal energy for a given substance at the same temperature.
Explain why the temperature of a substance does not rise while it is melting, even though heat is being supplied.
A student claims that steam at 100 °C has the same energy content as water at 100 °C because they are at the same temperature. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Change of state is the reversible transformation of matter between solid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Change of state is the reversible transformation of matter between solid, liquid and gas phases caused by gain or loss of thermal energy. Six distinct transitions exist: melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), boiling (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas) and deposition (gas → solid). During each transition the temperature of the substance remains constant because the supplied or removed energy is used to overcome or form intermolecular forces rather than increase particle kinetic energy. In solids particles vibrate about fixed positions; in liquids they slide past one another; in gases they move freely in random directions. The energy content rises from solid to liquid to gas, so melting and boiling absorb energy (endothermic) while freezing and condensation release energy (exothermic). Sublimation and deposition occur without passing through the liquid phase, as seen with naphthalene balls or camphor. Understanding these changes links the particle model (node) and the energy hierarchy (node) to observable phenomena.
steps: When matter changes state, its particles gain or lose energy, altering their movement and arrangement while the temperature stays constant during the transition.
Here is why: first, heating supplies kinetic energy to particles; in a solid they vibrate more vigorously until the intermolecular forces can no longer hold them in a lattice, and melting begins.
Second, during melting the temperature remains at the melting point because every joule of heat breaks bonds rather than raising kinetic energy.
Third, further heating makes liquid particles move faster until they escape as gas — boiling — again at a fixed boiling point.
Fourth, cooling reverses the process: gas particles lose energy, condense into liquid at the condensation point, then freeze into solid at the freezing point.
Fifth, some solids like naphthalene skip the liquid phase entirely, turning directly into vapour (sublimation) and the reverse (deposition).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “melting”) reveals the misconception that every solid must become liquid before turning into gas, ignoring substances that bypass the liquid phase.
remember: What is the change of state when solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) turns directly into gas at room temperature.
During melting of ice at 0 °C, the temperature of the ice‑water mixture remains constant even though heat is continuously supplied. Explain why.
A student observes water boiling in an open pan at 100 °C. She claims that if she puts a lid on the pan, the boiling point will increase. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Building on children’s previous learning means explicitly linking the particle…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Building on children’s previous learning means explicitly linking the particle model of matter introduced in Classes 5 and 6 to the more detailed description of the three states and their interconversions in Class 7. Students have already encountered the idea that matter consists of tiny particles, that solids have a fixed shape and volume, liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of the container, and gases fill the entire container. They also know that heating makes particles move faster and cooling slows them down. This node consolidates those notions and shows how the arrangement, spacing and motion of particles explain the macroscopic properties of each state. It further connects the concept of energy content: particles in solids possess the least kinetic energy, in liquids more, and in gases the most. By recalling everyday observations — ice melting, water boiling, steam condensing on a lid, water freezing in a freezer — students can map each change of state to a specific change in particle motion and energy. The node also prepares learners for the hands‑on activities that follow (melting naphthalene, boiling water, observing condensation and freezing) by ensuring they can predict what will happen to particle behaviour when heat is added or removed. No quantitative kinetic‑theory equations or latent‑heat calculations are introduced here; those belong to higher classes. The focus remains on qualitative reasoning, using the particle picture as a mental model to explain and predict state changes.
steps: The particle model you learned in earlier classes is the key to understanding why matter exists as solid, liquid or gas and why heating or cooling changes one state into another.
First, in a solid the particles are tightly packed in a regular pattern and only vibrate about fixed positions; this gives the solid a definite shape and volume.
Second, in a liquid the particles are still close but can slide past one another, so the liquid keeps a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
Third, in a gas the particles are far apart and move freely in all directions, filling the whole container with no fixed shape or volume.

Fourth, when heat is supplied, the kinetic energy of the particles increases; in a solid this makes vibrations vigorous enough to break the fixed arrangement, causing melting, and further heating lets particles escape…
Fifth, when heat is removed, particle motion slows; gas particles come together to form a liquid (condensation) and liquid particles lock into a fixed pattern to form a solid (freezing).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “particles in a liquid are stationary”) reveals the misconception that liquids behave like solids because both have fixed volume, confusing volume with particle mobility.
remember: What are the three states of matter and how do their particles move in each state.
Why does a solid have a fixed shape while a gas does not, in terms of particle arrangement.
A student says “When water boils, the particles disappear.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Melting is the change of a solid into a liquid on heating…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Melting is the change of a solid into a liquid on heating, and boiling is the rapid change of a liquid into vapour that occurs throughout the liquid once it reaches its boiling point — with bubbles of vapour forming at the bottom and rising. The classroom activities around these changes are built on the standard melting-and-boiling experiment: heat crushed ice in a beaker over a burner, stir gently, and record the thermometer reading every minute while watching the material. The activity reveals three signature observations. First, during melting the temperature stays constant at the melting point (0°C for pure ice) until every particle of ice has melted — the heat supplied is busy breaking the fixed-particle arrangement, not raising the temperature. Second, after melting, the liquid water's temperature climbs steadily until it reaches the boiling point (about 100°C for pure water at ordinary pressure), when it stops rising even though heating continues; the plateau repeats because the supplied energy is again used for change of state — this time converting liquid into steam. Third, boiling shows vigorous bubbling throughout the liquid, and the vapour escaping is the same substance in its gaseous state. Careful activity technique matters: crushed ice (not a block) melts uniformly, the thermometer bulb must sit in the middle of the material and not touch the beaker, stirring evens out the heating, and readings must be timed regularly. These activities teach the experimental habits of CISCE practical work — tabulating time against temperature, plotting a heating curve, and reading plateaus off it — and they supply the direct evidence that change of state happens at fixed temperatures, the bridge between the energy story of matter and the condensation and freezing changes that follow.
steps: The melting-and-boiling activities earn their place in the chapter because they convert the change-of-state story from a diagram into something the hands have watched.

Run the melting activity as the pattern for all of it. Pile crushed ice — crushed, because small pieces let heat in evenly and the thermometer bulb makes full contact — into a beaker, hang a thermometer so its bulb sits…

The readings tell the story in three acts: first, the temperature rises from below zero up to 0°C; then, at 0°C, it freezes in place on the scale — minute after minute the same reading, while the ice visibly slushes and…

The boiling activity repeats the pattern at the top: heat the water, watch the reading rise steadily to about 100°C, and there it stays — however long the burner roars — while bubbles form at the beaker's bottom, swell…
The plateau is not a stubborn thermometer; it is the signature of change of state, energy going into converting liquid to vapour instead of into motion.
Technique is where marks live in these activities.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the reading rises slowly while the ice melts because heating always warms things") reveals the misconception of treating heating and temperature rise as inseparable, missing the plateau that is the whole point of the activity.
remember: In the ice-melting activity, what happens to the thermometer reading while the ice is melting, and what does this show.
Why is crushed ice preferred over a single large block of ice in the melting activity.
Evaluate a student's thermometer handling: "I pressed the thermometer bulb against the bottom of the beaker so it would read the hottest water.".

cards.title: Condensation is the change of state from gas to liquid when particles lose…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Condensation is the change of state from gas to liquid when particles lose enough kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular forces and form a liquid. Freezing (solidification) is the change from liquid to solid as particles lose further energy and arrange into a fixed, ordered structure. Both processes are exothermic: they release latent heat to the surroundings. The energy released during condensation equals the mass multiplied by the specific latent heat of vaporisation (Lᵥ), while freezing releases energy equal to mass times the specific latent heat of fusion (L_f). In the particle model, gas particles move freely at high speed; on cooling they slow down, come closer and form a liquid (condensation). Further cooling makes liquid particles vibrate about fixed positions, forming a solid (freezing). The temperature remains constant during each change of state because the supplied or removed energy is used to change potential energy of particles, not kinetic energy. These concepts link to the earlier nodes on particle movement, energy content, and melting/boiling, completing the cycle of state changes.
steps: Condensation and freezing are the two exothermic state changes that complete the matter cycle.

Here is why: when a gas cools, its particles lose kinetic energy, move slower and come close enough for intermolecular forces to pull them into a liquid — this is condensation, and the latent heat of vaporisation is…
When a liquid cools further, particles lose more energy, settle into fixed positions and form a solid — this is freezing, releasing the latent heat of fusion.

Consider a cold steel glass on a humid monsoon evening: water vapour from the air condenses on its outer surface, making the glass wet. The same principle works in a refrigerator: the coolant evaporates (absorbing heat)…

For freezing, think of making ice‑candies: the liquid mixture is placed in a freezer; as it loses heat to the cold air, it solidifies, and the released latent heat is carried away by the freezer’s compressor.
In both cases the temperature stays constant during the change because the energy goes into rearranging particles, not raising their speed.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “evaporation”) reveals the misconception that the direction of phase change is always from liquid to gas, confusing the exothermic condensation with the endothermic evaporation.
remember: What is the change of state called when water vapour becomes liquid water on a cold surface.
Explain why the temperature of a substance remains constant during freezing even though heat is being removed.
A student says, “Condensation absorbs heat from the surroundings because the gas becomes a liquid.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Samples of three states of matter are representative substances used to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Samples of three states of matter are representative substances used to illustrate the characteristic properties of solids, liquids and gases. A solid sample (e.g., naphthalene balls or an ice cube) has a fixed shape and volume; its particles vibrate about fixed positions. A liquid sample (e.g., water in a beaker) has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; its particles slide past one another while remaining close. A gaseous sample (e.g., air in the laboratory or steam from a burner) has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume; its particles move freely and fill the available space. The energy content increases from solid to liquid to gas, reflecting greater particle kinetic energy. These samples are linked to the particle model taught earlier and to the equipment (beaker, tripod stand, burner, thermometer, laboratory stand) used in subsequent activities for observing melting, boiling, condensation and freezing.
steps: The key idea is that concrete samples — naphthalene balls, water in a beaker, and the air around us — let us see and feel the three states of matter and connect them to particle behaviour.
Here is why: solids keep their shape because particles are locked in a lattice; liquids flow because particles can slide; gases expand because particles move freely.
Consider the naphthalene balls on the laboratory stand — they hold their shape, feel hard, and do not pour.

When placed on a tripod stand with mesh and heated by a burner, they sublime, showing a solid turning directly into gas. Next, pour water into a beaker; it takes the beaker’s shape, has a flat surface, and can be…
Heating the beaker makes the water boil, producing steam — a gas that fills the room.
Finally, feel the warm air rising from the burner; it has no fixed shape or volume, demonstrating a gas sample.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing water in a beaker) reveals the misconception that any substance in a container is a solid, confusing the container’s shape with the sample’s own properties.
remember: Which of the following is a solid sample commonly used in the laboratory to represent the solid….
Explain why water poured into a beaker is considered a liquid sample rather than a solid.
A student claims that the steam rising from a burner is a liquid because it is visible. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A beaker is a cylindrical, flat‑bottomed laboratory vessel made of borosilicate…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A beaker is a cylindrical, flat‑bottomed laboratory vessel made of borosilicate glass (or sometimes plastic) with a pouring lip and graduated markings on its side. It is used to hold, mix, and heat liquids or solids during experiments on the three states of matter. The graduations indicate approximate volume (e.g., 50 mL, 100 mL, 250 mL, 500 mL) but are not calibrated for high‑precision measurement; their tolerance is typically ±5 % of the marked value. The wide opening allows easy addition of reagents, stirring with a glass rod, and observation of phase changes such as melting, boiling, condensation, and freezing. Because the glass withstands rapid temperature changes, a beaker can be placed directly on a tripod stand with mesh over a burner. It is not airtight, so it cannot be used for reactions requiring a closed system. In the CISCE Class 7 curriculum the beaker is introduced as the primary container for the “Samples of three states of matter” activity and for the heating experiments that follow with a tripod stand, burner, and thermometer.
steps: A beaker is the go‑to container for holding and heating substances when we explore changes of state.

Here is why: its flat bottom gives stability on a tripod stand; the borosilicate glass tolerates sudden heating and cooling; the wide mouth lets us stir and watch ice melt or naphthalene sublime; the printed lines let…
Consider a Class 7 activity where we place a few naphthalene balls in a 250 mL beaker, set it on a tripod stand with mesh, and heat gently with a burner.
The beaker’s graduations let us note the initial solid volume (≈30 mL) and later the vapour volume as it sublimes.
Next, we pour 150 mL of water into the same beaker, insert a thermometer, and heat until boiling — the lip prevents splashes while the graduations show the water level dropping as it turns to steam.
Finally, we cool the beaker to observe condensation on its inner walls, demonstrating the reverse change.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to measure exact volumes for calculations”) reveals the misconception that beaker graduations are precise — they are only rough guides.
remember: What is the primary purpose of a beaker in a Class 7 physics laboratory.
Why are the graduations on a beaker considered approximate rather than exact.
A student uses a 250 mL beaker to measure 200 mL of water for a heating experiment. Evaluate the suitability of this choice.

cards.title: A tripod stand with mesh is a laboratory support apparatus consisting of three…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A tripod stand with mesh is a laboratory support apparatus consisting of three adjustable metal legs joined at a central hub, topped with a rectangular or circular wire gauze (mesh). The legs are usually made of mild steel or cast iron and can be lengthened or shortened by sliding collars, allowing the stand to accommodate beakers of different heights. The mesh, typically woven from stainless‑steel wire of 0.5 mm diameter with 2 mm apertures, serves two purposes: it provides a stable, flat platform for flat‑bottomed glassware and it distributes the flame’s heat uniformly, reducing thermal shock that could fracture the glass. The stand is placed on a laboratory bench; a burner (spirit lamp or Bunsen burner) is positioned beneath the mesh, and a beaker containing the sample rests on the mesh. The tripod’s three‑point contact ensures stability even on slightly uneven surfaces, while the mesh’s open structure permits free convection of hot gases around the beaker. In the CISCE Class 7 curriculum this apparatus is introduced alongside the beaker, burner, thermometer and laboratory stand to enable safe heating experiments such as melting naphthalene, boiling water, and observing condensation.
steps: The tripod stand with mesh is the stable, heat‑spreading platform that lets us heat liquids in a beaker safely.

Here is why: the three legs give a wide base that resists tipping, the adjustable collars let us set the beaker at the right distance from the flame, and the wire mesh spreads the flame’s heat so the glass warms evenly…
Consider a typical Class 7 experiment: we need to melt naphthalene balls in a beaker.

First, spread the three legs on the bench and tighten the collars so the mesh sits about 3 cm above the burner’s tip. Place the spirit lamp (or Bunsen burner) centrally under the mesh, light it, and adjust the flame to…
Now set the beaker containing naphthalene on the mesh; the gauze holds the beaker firmly while hot gases rise through the openings, heating the bottom uniformly.
As the naphthalene melts, the thermometer (clamped to a laboratory stand) records the temperature.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the stand has a single solid metal plate instead of mesh”) reveals the misconception that the platform must be solid, ignoring the purpose of the gauze to allow gas flow and even heating.
remember: What are the three main components of a tripod stand with mesh.
Why is the wire mesh preferred over a solid metal plate for supporting a beaker during heating.
A student sets the tripod legs at unequal lengths, causing the mesh to tilt. Evaluate the effect on the heating experiment.

cards.title: A burner is a laboratory device that provides a controllable heat source by…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A burner is a laboratory device that provides a controllable heat source by mixing a gaseous or liquid fuel with air before combustion. The two common types in ICSE Class 7 laboratories are the Bunsen burner (connected to a gas tap) and the spirit lamp (using denatured ethanol). A Bunsen burner consists of a heavy base, a vertical barrel with an adjustable air hole near the base, a gas inlet, and a needle valve to regulate gas flow. Opening the air hole allows premixing of air and gas, producing a non‑luminous, blue, high‑temperature flame (≈1500 °C) suitable for heating. Closing the air hole yields a luminous, yellow, cooler flame due to incomplete combustion. The burner is placed on a heat‑proof mat, and a tripod stand with wire gauze supports the beaker or crucible above the flame. The thermometer then measures the temperature of the substance being heated. Safety rules include tying back hair, wearing safety goggles, lighting the match before turning on the gas, and never leaving a lit burner unattended. The burner’s role is central to change‑of‑state experiments such as melting naphthalene, boiling water, and observing condensation and freezing, linking the energy content of matter to observable phase transitions.
steps: A burner is a controllable laboratory heat source that mixes fuel with air to produce a hot, adjustable flame for experiments on matter.
Here is why: first, unlike an open fire, the burner lets us regulate the air‑fuel mixture, giving a consistent, soot‑free blue flame that reaches about 1500 °C.
Second, the air hole on the barrel controls whether combustion is complete (blue flame) or incomplete (yellow flame); the blue flame transfers heat more efficiently to a beaker on a wire gauze.
Third, safety features — a stable base, a needle valve, and the practice of lighting the match before opening the gas — prevent accidents.

Consider setting up the apparatus: place the burner on a heat‑proof mat, connect the rubber tubing to the gas tap, put the tripod stand with wire gauze over it, and set a beaker containing naphthalene balls on the gauze.
Light a match, hold it near the top of the barrel, then slowly open the gas tap. Adjust the air hole until the flame roars blue.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “candle and blowtorch”) reveals the misconception that any open flame qualifies as a laboratory burner, ignoring the need for controllable air‑fuel mixing.
remember: Name the two main types of burners used in a school laboratory.
Why is the air hole on a Bunsen burner adjusted to get a blue flame instead of a yellow flame for heating.
A student uses a luminous yellow flame to heat a beaker of water. Evaluate the effectiveness of this choice.

cards.title: A laboratory thermometer measures temperature…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A laboratory thermometer measures temperature — the degree of hotness of a body — for experimental work. Its construction: a glass stem carrying an etched scale in degrees Celsius, joined to a thin-walled glass bulb at the bottom; bulb and capillary bore inside the stem are filled with a thermometric liquid — mercury or a coloured alcohol — and the space above the liquid is evacuated. Its working principle is thermal expansion of liquids: on heating, the liquid in the bulb expands; since the capillary bore is extremely fine, a tiny expansion of the bulb-liquid forces a long, easily readable column of liquid up the stem — a small warming produces a large visible climb. On cooling the liquid contracts and the column falls. The standard laboratory thermometer ranges from −10°C to 110°C, covering melting ice to boiling water and beyond, with a least count of usually 1°C; the scale is calibrated at fixed points (ice point and steam point of water). Reading technique: the bulb must be fully surrounded by the substance measured — in the melting experiment hanging centrally in the ice or water, touching neither beaker bottom nor walls — and the reading is taken with the eye level with the top of the liquid column while the bulb remains in the substance. Unlike the clinical thermometer, the laboratory thermometer has no constriction (kink) in the capillary, so its column falls back on its own as it cools — it reads continuously during an experiment rather than holding a peak reading; its range is also far wider and it is never placed in the mouth. In the chapter's activity it is the thermometer that converts the burner's steady heat into numbers, exposes the melting and boiling plateaus, and names the melting point (0°C) and boiling point (about 100°C) of water.
steps: The thermometer is the chapter's translator: it converts the silent flow of heat into numbers a notebook can hold.
Follow the instrument from bulb to eye. At the bottom sits the bulb — thin-walled so heat crosses it quickly — holding a small store of mercury or coloured alcohol.

Warm the bulb and the liquid expands; the genius of the design is the capillary bore it expands into: a channel so fine that the liquid's small increase in volume is forced to show itself as a long climb up the stem…
Cool it, the liquid contracts, the column falls.

The etched Celsius scale beside the bore turns heights into temperatures, and the standard laboratory range of −10°C to 110°C is no accident: it spans exactly the two change-temperatures this chapter measures — below…
Reading it well is a discipline of three rules.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the liquid rises because heating makes it lighter and it floats up the tube") reveals the misconception of buoyancy inside the bore; the climb is pushed by expansion of the trapped liquid, not by floating.

cards.title: A laboratory stand (also called a retort stand) is a rigid support system used…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A laboratory stand (also called a retort stand) is a rigid support system used to clamp and position apparatus during experiments. It consists of three main components: a heavy, wide base (usually cast iron or steel) that provides a low centre of gravity; a vertical metal rod (typically 60 cm long, 1 cm diameter) that screws into the base; and one or more boss heads (also called clamp holders) that slide along the rod and are locked at any height by a thumbscrew. Each boss head carries a clamp — often a two‑pronged “burette clamp” or a three‑finger clamp — that can be tightened around the neck of a test tube, the stem of a thermometer, or the rim of a beaker. The stand’s adjustability allows the experimenter to place the apparatus at the exact height needed for heating on a tripod stand, for immersion in a water bath, or for observation. Because the base is heavy and the rod is rigid, the assembly resists vibration and accidental knocks, which is essential when using a burner or handling hot substances. The laboratory stand therefore links the thermometer — which must be held at a fixed immersion depth — to the naphthalene sublimation activity where a test tube is clamped above a burner. Proper use includes checking that the base sits flat, the rod is vertical, and all thumbscrews are firm before lighting the burner.
steps: A laboratory stand is the backbone of every heating experiment because it gives a stable, adjustable platform to hold apparatus securely.
First, the heavy base lowers the centre of gravity so the stand does not topple when a burner flame pushes against a clamped test tube.
Second, the vertical rod provides a straight, rigid guide that lets the boss head slide smoothly to any height, allowing precise positioning of a thermometer bulb in a melting‑point tube.
Third, the boss head’s thumbscrew locks the clamp at the chosen height, preventing slippage when the apparatus expands or vibrates.
Fourth, the clamp’s jaws grip the apparatus firmly without crushing glass, so a thermometer stays at a constant immersion depth while naphthalene balls sublime.

cards.title: Sublimation is the change of a substance from its solid state directly into its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Sublimation is the change of a substance from its solid state directly into its gaseous state on heating, without passing through the liquid state; the reverse change — gas turning directly into solid on cooling — is called deposition (or condensation-to-solid). The classroom's standard subliming substance is naphthalene, the white crystalline material of moth balls (locally "kiki") kept in folded woollens: kept in a covered dish or warmed gently, naphthalene balls shrink steadily and fill their container with a characteristic vapour, yet no liquid pool ever forms — the solid's particles escape straight to the gas. Camphor, dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) and iodine crystals show the same behaviour; ammonium chloride, the classic laboratory sublimate, deposits as a white ring when its vapour meets a cool surface. Sublimation happens because particles at the surface of such solids gain enough energy to break free of the solid's grip entirely — these substances have weak inter-particle attractions and noticeable vapour pressures even below their melting points. The demonstration apparatus makes the reverse change visible: naphthalene (or ammonium chloride) warmed gently in a covered china dish or funnel assembly deposits its vapour as fresh solid crystals on the cool inverted funnel or watch-glass above — solid below, gas travelling, solid again above, with never a liquid stage. Everyday India is full of sublimation's fingerprints: the shrinking kiki in a sweater box, camphor tablets (kapoor) vanishing in a puja cupboard between festivals, ice disappearing slowly from frost-lines on a sunny day, and dry-ice fog productions. Sublimation completes the chapter's map of matter — after melting/freezing, boiling/condensation, the sixth change shows that the solid-to-gas journey can also be made in a single leap.
steps: Sublimation is matter's shortcut: the journey from solid to gas that skips the liquid platform entirely.
Watch the standard witness — the naphthalene ball.

Put fresh white balls in a covered dish inside a folded sweater at the start of summer; by the monsoon they are visibly smaller, and after a year a ghost of their former size — yet the sweater box is dry, the dish holds…
Every gram that vanished went straight from crystal to invisible vapour, particle by particle, from the ball's surface.
